titleStmt.title: Summa de exemplis ac similitudinibus rerum, Books IV-V: On Fish and Birds; On Land Animals

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un latiniste) a partir du texte latin du corpus zoomathia sous zoo64/1l (Iohannes de Sancto Geminiano, Summa de exemplis ac similitudinibus rerum, livres IV "De natatilibus et volatilibus" [poissons et oiseaux] et V "De animalibus terre, bestiis, reptilibus, ac iumentis" [animaux terrestres]). Recueil homiletique de similitudines animalieres (bestiaire moralise a l'usage des predicateurs), chaque chapitre associant une ou plusieurs autorites citees (Aristote, Pline, Isidore, peres de l'Eglise, Ecriture) a une exemplification tiree du monde animal, appliquee aux vices et vertus. La structure du texte latin source (oeuvre > section1 livre [2, n=4 et n=5] > section2 prologue/chapitre [224 chapitres au total] > cit avec <bibl> d'attribution et <quote>, 823 citations) est integralement preservee ci-dessous, div par div. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un latiniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte latin deja present dans le corpus sous zoo64/1l.

div.head: PROLOGUS LIBRI QUARTI, IN QUO DE NATATILIBUS, et volatilibus exempla, similitudinesque qumplurimas dicere aggreditur.

cit.quote: 'Ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the air, and they will tell you; speak to the earth, and it will answer you, and the fish of the sea will declare it to you.' The Creator of the heavens, and the ruler of the waters, and the King and Lord of all creation, bearing spiritual care for man, whom he had created in his own image, marked for the enjoyment of himself; in this way he appointed everything he had brought forth to the service of man, so that man might draw comfort not only from the sight of these creatures, but might also gain various benefits from their use or service on every side. Now among these great tokens of his providence, the birds of the air and the fish of the sea (as is gathered from sacred scripture) he ordered for the benefit of human life in three particular ways. For first he appointed them to the service of subjection, and this is more clearly shown by the words of scripture, where God, speaking to men, says: 'have dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air.' For he was saying this so that the other animals should be made subject to him, since man surpassed them all by the summit of natural reason and the rudder of providence. For the other animals have, through a kind of estimation of universal and natural prudence, which is the guiding reason of all that can be done, a certain natural share in it; but in man, universal and natural prudence, which is the guiding reason of all that can be done, thrives of itself. Now everything that exists by participation is subject to what exists by essence; and so it was fitting that all animals should be made subject to man. Hence the Psalm says: 'you have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen,' and so on, down to 'the paths of the sea.'

Second, because the Lord granted the fish of the sea and the birds of the air to men for food and refreshment. For indeed, before the time of the Flood, God granted only plants and the fruits of trees to men and to the other animals for food, saying to them: 'I have given you every plant bearing seed upon the earth, and all the trees that have within themselves the seed of their own kind, that they may be food for you, and for all the living creatures of the earth.' But afterward, once the Flood was over, the eating of animals was permitted, when the Lord said: 'every fish of the sea is given into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you; as I have given you the green plants, I have given you all these, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood.' The Lord granted this indulgence, then, both because of man's frailty, so that he should not be overwhelmed by such devastation of resources, and because of the infertility of the earth caused by the Flood, and also because of the changed variety of the climate: for (as Alcuin attests, who was the teacher of Charlemagne) before the time of the Flood, no rain fell or existed upon the earth, but the earth was watered by the waters of springs and by abundant dew. Hence the plants were sweeter and of greater nourishing power than they were after the time of the Flood, when the air is disturbed and troubled by winds and clouds and rains and other disturbances. But the Lord forbade the eating of flesh mixed with blood for this reason, so that, by man's being kept from taking the blood of beasts, he would shrink all the more from shedding human blood. Hence it is added, in the same chapter: 'whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed.'

Third, the Lord gave the birds of the air and the fish a teaching office of instruction, which is clearly proven from the words of Job quoted above; for it is said: 'ask the beasts, and they will teach you,' and so on. For then we seek out either the beasts, or the birds of the air, or the fish of the sea, when we investigate their natures or their movements closely; and, being questioned, they teach us, speak, or answer, when from considering them we perceive how we ought to order our own actions. And so, speaking of the fish of the sea, blessed Ambrose says that they were made as a sign, so that in them we might see the vices of our own conduct, and beware of them.

For this reason, after the similitudes drawn from plants and trees, it remains to say that, in this fourth book of our work, we shall introduce some examples concerning birds and fish, so that they may be adapted, in our own style, to matters of conduct. It has not, however, been possible for me, in so brief a treatise, to mention every single species of bird or fish, since the kinds of swimming and flying creatures are innumerable; for who — to say nothing of the birds — could number the species of sea creatures, or designate each one by its own name? Hence the Psalm says: 'this great and wide sea,' and so on. And according to Ambrose, there are more kinds of fish in the sea than there are kinds of animal on land. From which it is clear that the species of birds, and even more so of fish, that are known to us are but a small portion compared to those that are unknown. We shall, then, bring forward examples — if not of all, at least of some of the more famous and well-known kinds — treating each subject in turn, to which the examples will be adapted according to the method followed above, in alphabetical order.

div.head: Cap. I. Ex aquile pullis exemplis, a mundo dispectos ad sanctamque penitentiam venientes suscipi, atque a Deo benigne nutriri et trahi declaratur.

cit.quote: Those cast off and despised by the world are received and nourished by God, as the young of the eagle example shows; for, when the eagle raises her young with much difficulty, sometimes, if she has three chicks, she casts one out, whom, however, another bird, called the coot, takes up and nourishes, as Ambrose says. The eagle casts out her chick precisely when the world pursues and afflicts its own lover, whom, however, another bird — namely the grace of Christ — mercifully embraces; and, driven out even against his will by the world, he comes of his own accord to penance. Hence (as Gregory says) the evils that press upon us here compel us to go to God. Ezekiel: 'what was cast off, I will bring back.'

Likewise, though God is exalted, he does not shrink from or despise those cast off and despised by the world, but rather, looking down from on high, draws them to himself. This too is clear from the example of the eagle, which is of such keen sight that, though borne aloft over the sea so high that it can scarcely be seen, it nonetheless watches the little fish in the sea from there, and, swooping down like a stone, seizes, draws up, and eats the little fish. So God, to whose eyes all things are bare and open, though in the height of his own light he is invisible to us, since he dwells in unapproachable light, whom no man can see — he nonetheless does not despise the little fish that exist in the sea, that is, the despised and the humble in spirit, tossed about in the world, but looks down upon them from below, comes to them, illuminating them with his own light, and draws them to himself, kindling them with his love, and, as it were, eats them like food, joining and incorporating them to himself through familiar grace. Psalm: 'who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high, and looks upon the humble things in heaven and on earth?'

div.head: Cap. II Cur bona opera ab homine facta sint celanda, Pavonis, atque Galline exemplis solerter enucleatur.

cit.quote: A man ought to hide his good works, so that the devil does not corrupt them through vain glory and ostentation. For the devil is like the peacock, which searches for the eggs of the hen so as to break and eat them, so that it may more freely indulge its lust; but the hen herself hides her eggs, to keep them safe. So too, since the devil strives to steal our good deeds away, we ought to hide them through humility, according to that saying of Matthew: 'let not your left hand know what your right hand does.' But some are like the domestic hen, which cackles and reveals it the moment she has laid an egg, and so loses it. Isaiah: 'they have seen everything that is in my house; there was nothing I did not show them,' Ezekiel said of the messengers of Babylon, and afterward it was said to him that he would lose everything.

Likewise, that a man ought to hide his good works, for fear of incoming pride or the temptation of vainglory, is also shown by the example of the whale, or 'balena,' which does not lay eggs, as many other fish do, but bears its young alive, as Ambrose says. And once it has borne them, it keeps them with it and leads them about, but as soon as it senses something approaching that might be harmful or terrifying to them, it takes them into its own belly through its open mouth and hides them there, until every danger has passed or withdrawn, and then, as though now safe, it disgorges them alive and unharmed, as the same Ambrose says. In which indeed we are clearly taught that the good deeds we do, we ought sometimes to hide, for fear of vainglory, and sometimes, for the benefit of others, to make known. Hence our Lord, who in one place told his disciples, 'take care not to do your righteousness before men,' himself also said, 'let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works,' and so on, in the same chapter.

div.head: Cap. III. Abstinentiam a cibis moderatam maximopere bonis viris necessariam esse, unice Pavonis exemplo demonstratur.

cit.quote: Discreet abstinence from food frees a man, as with the peacock, from the corruption and burning heat of lust. For an abstinent man is like the peacock, whose flesh is so tough that it scarcely rots, nor can it easily be cooked, as Isidore says. This very toughness, morally speaking, discreet abstinence of the flesh produces and causes, so that it is neither dissolved by the stench of decay, nor burned by the fire of lust: the dissolving of decay ceases once the matter of seed, that is, of nourishment, is withdrawn, and the flame of the flesh grows cold once the kindling-wood of food is removed — just as, when the logs are taken away, the fire's heat is also put out. Proverbs: 'when the wood fails, the fire goes out.' John Cassian says: 'no one will ever be able to check the burning goads of desire, who does not seek to rein in the desires of the belly.' And Ambrose says that hunger is a friend to virginity and an enemy to wantonness, while fullness destroys chastity and nourishes temptation.

div.head: Cap. IIII. Secunda in rebus temporalibus, ac frequens fortuna, peccatorum vulnera haud sentire sinit, quod ceti similitudinibus aperitur.

cit.quote: Abundance of prosperity keeps one from feeling — as with the whale, the fish called 'balena,' which is of such fatness that, when it is struck, it feels no wound, unless its fat has been pierced clean through; but when its inner flesh is injured, it is easily caught, since, unable to bear the bitterness of the water, it makes for the shore and dies quickly. Now just as the fish's fat is an abundance of prosperity, which, when it flows in upon sinners, does not let them feel the wounds or harm to their mind. Hence the Lord said against Jerusalem, in Luke: 'now, on this your day, the things that make for peace — but they are hidden from your eyes.' But the sinner is then touched within, when he is struck by temporal adversity; for the wounds of the mind are, as it were, external to sinners, since they regard spiritual matters, in which they are wounded, as though foreign to them. But when they are hurt in temporal matters, which they love more, they feel wounded as it were in their very depths, and, sometimes unable to bear the bitterness of that wound, either, pricked by their sins, they seek the shore of penance, or, having fallen into the pit of despair, they incur eternal death.

div.head: Cap. V. Pulcherrimis nonnullorum piscium exemplis accidiam, concupiscentieque actum humane, anima valde abesse breviter in hec loco explanatur.

cit.quote: The vice of sloth and the heat of desire do great harm to the soul. An example of this appears in certain fish, which (as Aristotle says) are greatly harmed by immoderate heat. Hence he says that there are fish that die of the heat around the rising of the dog-star; and so fish flee in summer from the warm shores into the depths of the sea.

...crabs [fear] great cold, and especially those that have a stone in the head, like crabs and the like; for such a stone freezes with the cold, and so they easily die. So then, just as the heat of summer is the burning and flame of carnal desire, which, unless extinguished, destroys, one must flee into the depths of the sea — that is, to the abundance of tears arising from bitterness of heart, so that the coolness of tears may quench the heat of desire. And just as the stiffening cold of winter is the sloth of the spirit, which is especially deadly to those who have a stone in the head, that is, hardness of mind. For if the heart is already hard of itself, it is further hardened by the cold of sloth. And so it quite easily brings on the death of a certain despair, and, once hardened, darkens the mind. Zechariah: 'there will be no light, but cold and frost.'

div.head: Cap. VI. Que ad activa et contemplativa vita perfectionem in unoquoque hominum gradu requirantur, per quamplurima, scitaque diversorum avium et piscium exempla edocentur.

cit.quote: ...birds. Some of these love the company of men, like hens, roosters, geese, doves, storks, swallows, and the like. For prelates, that is, those set over others, are likened to hens, whose task it is to gather their subjects together and defend them, just as the hen gathers her chicks under her wings, as Christ said of himself. Powerful worldly men, however, whose task it is to guard justice and the commonwealth's welfare diligently, are likened to geese; for geese, as Ambrose says, are the best watchmen of a place. Cloistered religious, however, are likened to ducks, who, like ducks, ought to dwell in the waters of penance, and frequent the water of tears or of the wisdom of the scriptures. Married people are likened to doves, who, with simplicity, have fecundity, frequently breeding, and who lead a married life purely and simply; pilgrims, however, and especially those who frequently make the pilgrimage overseas, namely to the Holy Land, are likened to storks, which gather at a fixed time to fly across the sea. Preachers, who cry out and chatter against sinners, are likened to noisy, chattering swallows. For all these, and others like them, desire the company of men, and not a solitary life. There are, however, certain birds that flee the company and dwelling of men, and do not want men to know their nests, called wild birds. Anchorites and contemplative men are like these, who flee the company of men and are hidden from the world, dwelling in hiding places and in solitude. Psalm: 'behold, I have fled far away, and remained in the wilderness.'

Likewise, active men are moved with the motion of fish, but contemplatives with the motion of birds. For while a fish swims in water, contracting its body, it gathers itself into a shorter length, and then, extending itself again, presses against the water, and by this pressure, repelling the water, propels itself forward. Hence it uses certain little fins in swimming, just as a bird does in flying, but in a different way; for a swimming fish moves its fins from the rear part forward, and, embracing the water with them as though with arms or oars, extends itself forward. A bird, however, moves its wings upward, and forces the air gathered by the spread of its wings to exit through the rear part; hence, as the air is driven backward, the body moves forward. Now the fish swimming in water is the man who is diligent and industrious in the active life, who then contracts himself into a shorter length when he brings himself down to humility, saying and feeling with the Apostle: 'I am the least of all,' and so on. So too the Lord instructed his disciples, saying: 'when you have done everything well, say: we are useless servants.' But nonetheless he should not stop there, but, even after such a contraction, that is, humility, extend himself again to further good action. For by such a pressure — that is, of humility and labor — divine grace propels him wonderfully forward. Hence these are the two little fins by which the active man makes progress, namely humility and diligent activity — provided that, forgetting what lies behind, he directs and extends himself toward what lies ahead, so that, in the manner of a swimming fish, he advances by moving from behind forward. But the man raised up in contemplation is like a bird flying in the air, who then raises the wings, or feathers, of his intellect and affection upward, when with thought and eagerness he savors the things that are above. And he then releases the air gathered by the beating of his wings backward, when, out of the sweetness he has tasted through contemplation and affection, he turns his mind to despising what lies behind, that is, temporal things; and as the air is driven backward, the body moves forward — because, as the world is fully despised, the soul professes ever more progress in spiritual virtues.

Likewise, concerning birds that dwell in the water. In these (as Aristotle says) nature has implanted the property that they should have broad, webbed feet, not divided between the toes, because of the necessity of swimming — so that, with the breadth of their feet, they strike the water more forcefully, and, the water thus struck backward, propel themselves forward as though rowing. Their tails, however, are short, so that they are not hindered in swimming by the tail becoming waterlogged. In the same way, it is fitting for active men, who serve the needs of their neighbors through works of piety, to have broad feet — that is, affections spread wide toward every poor person, closed to sin or to the desire for worldly favor, and undivided in the toes — that is, without dissension or discord in their works. Or active men ought to have a distinction of toes, yet without division between them — that is, they ought to have distinctness of works, yet without discord and dissension; and the broader the foot, that is, the more generous the affection with which they strive to push away the water of the tribulation and need of their neighbors, the more abundant the fruit with which they advance. They should also have a short tail, that is, swift readiness in action, so that they do not delay giving to one in distress. Hence it is said: 'do not say to your friend' — that is, to Christ, or to his poor — 'go, and come back, and tomorrow I will give to you,' when you could give at once.

Likewise, the active life requires above all purity of intention, as is shown by the example of the blackbird, which, though everywhere black in its feathers, is found white in Achaia. Achaia, which is interpreted 'the sister who labors,' signifies the active life, which requires kinship with contemplation. For there were two sisters, Rachel and Leah, of whom the first signifies the contemplative life, the second the active. And the two other sisters in the Gospel, namely Mary Magdalene and Martha, are said to represent the same thing. The active life also involves the labor of action; hence Martha was busy, laboring over frequent service, for she was anxious about many things, and so on. Now purity of intention in action is, as it were, the white blackbird; and so the white blackbird of Achaia is the pure intention in the works of life, which the Lord taught must be cleansed when he said, 'first cleanse what is inside the cup and the dish' — for since the thirsty drink from the cup, and the hungry are refreshed from the dish, the cup and the dish rightly signify almsgiving and the works of the active life. But what is inside the cup and the dish is the hidden intention of the one giving alms, which indeed he ought to cleanse before giving the alms — for the dish is washed before food is placed in it, and the cup must be cleansed before wine and water are poured into it — according to the saying of the poet Horace: 'whatever you pour into a vessel that is not clean turns sour.' So too the intention must be cleansed before the exercise of good.

Likewise, the good active man is likened to the grayling fish. For the grayling (as Ambrose says) is a fish nourished by the waters of the river Ticino, so named from thyme, because it smells like the scent of the thyme flower. Hence it is said of one who smells sweetly: 'he smells either of a flower or of a fish,' since the scent of that flower and of that fish are alike. Hence in Revelation, bowls full of fragrances are called the prayers of the saints. But the active man smells sweetly to his neighbor in the manner of that fish; for the grayling both smells sweetly and nourishes. And likewise the active man smells sweetly by his example, and nourishes by what he gives.

div.head: Cap. VII. Haretici qui more adulatorum loquuntur, variis marinis belvis, cicadeque comparantur.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: ...can be likened to sea monsters. For the philosopher Jorath says that there is a certain beast in the sea, which breathes out water from its jaws, with a vapor full of fragrance; hence fish, sensing that very scent, follow it, and, for the sake of the scent, enter its jaws, which at once swallows them, and so feeds on them. There is also another fish, called the 'fastes,' in whose mouth the water drawn in becomes sweet, and smaller fish, following it and entering its mouth, are suddenly swallowed by it. Since, then, it is written, 'the words from a man's mouth are like deep waters' — like fragrant or sweet water from a fish's mouth are the smooth, flattering words of heretics, by which the simple, drawn in, are swallowed as though cast into its belly, while, deceiving and seducing them, it draws them toward its intended wickedness.

Likewise, smooth flattery sometimes kills vain minds, whom harsh and truthful speech restores to life. An example of this appears in the cicada, which, if you douse it with oil, dies at once, since its pores being blocked, it can no longer breathe at all; but if you then pour vinegar over it, it revives instantly, since this opens the pores that the power of the oil had blocked — and blessed Ambrose says this same thing, point for point. The cicada, then, is doused with oil precisely when the mind is smeared with vain flattery, and it is killed, its pores blocked, when, its own faults hidden and concealed from itself, it is puffed up with pride; but the sharpness of the biting vinegar restores its life, since harsh reproof brings it back to true knowledge of itself and to life-giving humility. Hence the Psalm rightly says: 'let the righteous man correct me in mercy, and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head.'

div.head: Cap. VIII. Triplex amicitia utilitatis causa contracta defectus, et quamdium perseveret, multis auctoritatibus accipitrisque exemplo aperte monstratur.

cit.quote: A friend who is loved by his master only as long as he is fit for prey, is carried on the hand, stroked on tail and breast, but, when he dies, or becomes useless for prey, is not fed — for he is cast off and, as though he had never existed, is despised and thrown away — is like the hawk. In the same way (as Seneca says), a friend taken up for the sake of usefulness will please only as long as he is useful; for once his usefulness and advantage are removed, he is despised and cast off.

...since it is not true friendship; for he who loves for the sake of usefulness does not love the friend himself, but the friend's possessions. And so it is rather himself alone that he loves, who desires his friend's goods. And so Augustine says: you should not love a friend so that he might provide you with something, like money or some other temporal advantage; for then you do not love him, but what he provides you. A friend should be loved freely, for his own sake, not for the sake of something else. Hence Peter of Blois says that true friendship looks with the same eye upon a friend who is rich and one who is poor, upon the strong and the weak, the healthy and the sick, the humble and the exalted.

The second defect is that such friendship is not faithful. For, as Isidore says, those whom a gift, not affection, joins together are not faithful in friendship; for they quickly desert, unless they keep on receiving; for love that is cemented by a gift dissolves once the gift is withdrawn.

The third defect is that such friendship is not firm, nor destined to last long. Hence Cicero says: if usefulness cemented friendships, then, once that usefulness changed, it would dissolve them too; but since nature cannot be changed, true friendships are therefore everlasting. Proverbs: 'he who is a friend loves at all times.'

div.head: Cap. IX. Avaritie defectus, avarique diritas terminatur, qui etiam avibus preda aptis, et Gryphibus, montes gemmis ornates custodientibus, suibusque marinis, variis comparatur exemplis.

cit.quote: Avarice makes men unsociable and cruel, not only toward strangers but even toward their own household. An example of this appears in birds of prey, in whom the greedy are represented, rapacious in disposition or in deed; for all such birds, as Aristotle says, love solitude, and cannot dwell with any companion. For just as charity seeks fellowship and company, so greed desires solitude and exclusive possession. For the greedy man wants to have alone, and so is suspicious of staying with a companion. Hence the possession of temporal things is the mother of dissensions, for which reason it is said of Abraham and Lot that their substance was great, and they could not dwell together amicably. Hence a quarrel arose between the herdsmen of Abraham and of Lot.

Likewise, such birds of prey, as the same author says, drive their young away from themselves once they can fly, and do not allow them to live with them; for indeed the greedy generally cast off even their own household and children, and consider it a burden if they must provide them their due support.

Likewise, the greedy are likened to griffins, which guard mountains where there are precious gems, and do not allow them to be carried off, as Isidore says; and for this reason, few men venture to approach there, for they swallow living men, and seize an armed knight together with his horse — and yet, of the gems they so fiercely guard, they themselves take no benefit at all. So it is likewise with certain greedy men, who guard their treasures so jealously that, if anyone takes even a little from them, they would, if they could, swallow him alive. Poor men cannot approach such wealthy men, since they repel them shamefully, and so the poor fear to come near them. And yet these men do not even dare to spend, on themselves, what they hold so tightly, but others, after them, enjoy their riches. Psalm: 'he stores up treasure, and does not know for whom he gathers it.' And Ecclesiasticus: 'he who loves riches shall have no fruit from them.'

Likewise, the greedy man, in his appetite for riches, is like the sea-pig. For that sea fish called the pig (as Isidore says) digs in the sand in the manner of a land pig, and seeks its food and fullness there. Since, then, all gold is, as it were, but scant sand, every greedy man, while he seeks his fill in gold or silver, digs, like the pig in the sand, for food with which he might be filled — although it is written: 'the greedy man shall not be filled with money.'

div.head: Cap. X. Blasphemia quando veniale sine mortale sit peccatum, definitur, et Deum ac Sanctos blasphemantes, cornicibus assimilantur.

cit.quote: Those who blaspheme God or the saints are like crows. For the crow harasses the eagle and other birds of prey, which it fears to touch, with its cawing; but sometimes it gains nothing by this, for after a long pretense the eagle chases it down and kills it. So too wicked blasphemers strive to attack with curses God and the saints, whom they cannot harm by deeds; and the eagle, that is, God or Christ, after long enduring their madness with patience, sometimes strikes them in the body with monstrous illnesses, but in the end, if they do not repent, afflicts them with the punishment of eternal death. And note, as a certain Gloss on Isaiah says, that every sin is lighter in comparison to blasphemy. Hence blasphemy, even when it slips out unintentionally and without deliberation, can be a mortal sin, though sometimes it can be venial. For when someone, suddenly, out of some passion, bursts out into imaginative words without considering their meaning, it is then a venial sin; but when he realizes this is blasphemy, considering the meaning of the words, he is then not excused from mortal sin — just as one who, in a sudden fit, kills someone sitting near him.

div.head: Cap. XI. Apum perfectio naturalisque prudentia multisariam necernitur, ac eis per varia exempla, scitasque rationes boni et virtuosi viri comparantur.

cit.quote: Good and virtuous men are likened to bees in three respects. First, in innocence. For bees are so named because they are born without feet. Every good and upright man, then, is like the bees, who are without those feet of which it is written: 'their feet run to evil' — for these are the feet of the sinful soul, by which it runs to evil: the inner workings of wickedness, and malicious affections.

Second, in skill and prudence, since bees (as Isidore says) are very skillful in producing honey and wax, and construct their homes with wondrous art, and gather the honeycomb from various flowers with marvelous craft. So too good men are skillful, and produce honey — that is, they are skillful, judging subtly and quickly how they ought to act or speak; for skill is a ready and prompt conjecture concerning the discovery of a means, as the Philosopher teaches — and so, since what they say they demonstrate through fitting means, and what they do they accomplish through fitting ways, they, like skillful bees, produce honey for others, since they offer honeyed words in speaking to their hearers, and also present honeyed deeds in acting on their word. They also arrange their homes — that is, their own consciences, or their own households — with a wondrous art or skill of prudence; for if they know how to arrange or order the affairs of others, much more so their own. Hence, from fragrant flowers — that is, from the pleasing and gracious deeds or words of others — they gather the honeycomb, that is, the teaching and the manner by which they arrange and order their own cells, or dwellings, that is, their consciences or homes.

A wondrous prudence also appears in bees in three ways. First, with respect to seasons, since the prudent discern the seasons for labor and for rest; for in wintertime they hide, since indeed they lack the strength to withstand winds, snows, and rains — from which it is suggested that, especially in a time of persecution, weaker believers may avoid persecution and hide, according to that saying of the Lord: 'if they persecute you in one city, flee to another.' In springtime, however, bees go out, nor are they idle then, but first build their combs, shape their wax, make their cells, and at last produce their brood and their honey. From which indeed we are taught that, in a time of prosperity and peace, we should not be given over to idleness, but should labor usefully in various exercises.

Then, indeed, combs are to be built — that is, acts of virtue exercised, by which we may attain to the sweetness of our heavenly inheritance. For it is said in Ecclesiasticus: 'my inheritance is above honey and the honeycomb.' Then too the wax is to be shaped — that is, the conscience is to be formed, which, like wax, is suited to take on various shapes, of vices and virtues. Psalm: 'my heart has become like melting wax.' Then too the cells are to be made — that is, the bodily senses, or the inner powers of the soul, are to be ordered; and at last one must strive either for the brood of good works through the active life, or for the sweetness of honey through the contemplative life.

Likewise, bees rest from night until morning, until one rouses them all with a single hum, or, as some say, a threefold one; and then they all fly out together, if the day is to be mild; but if they foresee coming rain or wind, they then stay within their hive, and, as evening falls, enter their homes and buzz, until the one who roused them, with that same signal, calls them to rest. By this example we are taught that rest should indeed be given to the body at night, but, as day begins to dawn, we should rise from the bed of sleep and sloth, according to that saying: 'the night is far spent, the day is at hand; let us therefore cast off the works of darkness.'

For, after the rest of night, one must rise to the works of labor; but after the night of guilt, as the day of grace dawns, one must rise to the works of penance — to which indeed the prelate or preacher ought to rouse others with a threefold hum, that is, in a threefold way: by the word of exhortation, by the example of his conduct, and also by the support of his prayer, according to that saying to Timothy: 'be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity.' But as evening falls, that is, as night draws near, or as some dark temptation arises, one ought to withdraw into one's home — either the bodily home, to rest and remain more honorably, or the home of the mind, lest the tempting enemy catch one wandering outside — and there one ought to make a stir, either by reading, or praying, confessing one's sins, and doing other such things, until, the temptation repelled, the time of rest arrives. And that, once the signal or commotion is heard, they cease — this admonishes cloistered religious that, at the time of quiet, or upon hearing the signal appointed for this, they should keep their silence, so as not to hinder, by their own commotion, those who wish to rest or pray.

Likewise, bees seek a cool place in summer, and a warm one in winter — teaching the good to protect themselves in a time of prosperity with the coolness of humility, and to defend themselves in a time of adversity with the warmth of charity; for charity is patient.

Likewise, bees are found prudent with respect to their work. First, as to the material, since they gather their material from fresh flowers, from which they collect and make honey and wax, and, when the nearby flowers are used up, send out scouts to seek other pastures, and, if night overtakes them, they lie on their backs to protect their wings from dew and rain, so that, when morning comes, they may fly without hindrance. So then, flowers growing on trees are, as it were, the good affections growing in hearts, from which, while they are fresh, honey and wax are gathered by the bees, since, while they are new and fervent, they are sweetly and readily fulfilled in deed by diligent men — for honey is sweet, and wax is easily shaped; but once the nearby flowers are exhausted, they seek out others for pasture, since, once they have carried out their good intentions in deed, they still search with great care for whatever else remains to be done; but, as night falls, they lie on their backs, to protect their wings from rain or dew — since, prostrating themselves, praying before God, they humble themselves, so that, by the merit of humility and the aid of grace, the wings of their affections or works may be protected from the rain of carnal temptations, and from the dew, that is, the more subtle battle of spiritual vices, and, morning come — that is, calm weather returning — they may fly more freely to what they had begun.

Likewise, bees are found prudent with respect to hindrances. First, indeed, because they coat the whole shell of the hive with the dry, gummy, bitter substance of trees, and fortify themselves against enemies as best they can. The dry gum or bitterness of trees is, then, the afflictions, or tears, of the penitent, with which the bees, that is, holy persons, coat the hives of their own minds, and, with the bitterness of weeping, defend themselves against the sweet, malicious temptations suggested by their enemies.

Likewise, laden bees, when they fear the wind, fly close to the ground, so that, laden, they may return quickly, lest they be hindered by any gust, and sometimes they load themselves with tiny stones, so as not to be moved by the wind. In the same way, those persons who carry the burdens or labors of the active life, if they fear the wind of vainglory, or the wind, that is, the effort of some hindering force, ought to fly close to the ground, that is, do what they intend humbly and secretly.

Likewise, to load oneself with stones means to load oneself with the humble examples and warnings of the saints, so that, made firm by these, one may hope to be least moved by the winds of temptation.

Third, bees represent good men because of their social life. For good men always love a common and social life, and flee from isolation — which is indeed found in bees; for bees (according to Ambrose) choose one common dwelling, are enclosed within the threshold of a single gate, share labor in common, common food, common work, common use, common fruit, and common flight. And such community is especially fitting for cloistered and regular religious living in community: that is, not to withdraw from the common observances or works, whether as to place, or food, or labors, or the service of charity and works of humility, or as to the shared use and social living together, or as to flight — that is, the prompt and swift motion of obedience.

div.head: Cap. XII. Divina laudis cantica cordialiter affecta, quibus Angeli mirum in modum latantur, quantum boni nobis gerant, brevi terminatur.

cit.quote: Songs of divine praise and of the Church's office, if poured forth with devotion of heart and attentiveness of mind, delight even the angels, just as the songs and harmonies of men are said to delight dolphins. For Isidore says that dolphins follow the voices of men, and gather together at the sound of music, and take great delight in harmony.

So too the angels do with the songs and harmonies of those who devoutly praise God — not, indeed, by reason of the voice, but by reason of the devotion — for which reason it is said in the Psalm: 'the princes went before, joined with those who sang,' and so on, which blessed Bernard explains of the angels. Hence Basil also says that psalm-singing drives off demons and invites angels to aid our salvation.

Likewise, songs of divine praise are of great value in relieving the tedium of this present life, and also in easing the burden of prolonged temptation, as is shown by the example of the nightingale. For the nightingale (as Ambrose says), while she broods her eggs in sleepless watchfulness, eases the labor of the long night with the sweetness of her song; for he is like the nightingale, brooding with sleepless watchfulness, who strives, with care and diligence, to fulfil in deed the good things conceived in the nest of his mind. And just as the labor is the length and tedium of the long night, so is the rising temptation, or the laborious prolonging of our sojourn in this present life, of which the Psalmist complained, saying: 'woe is me, that my sojourn is prolonged'; but this labor the sweetness of the nightingale's song relieves, since devotion to divine praise refreshes the mind wearied by the tedium either of temptation or of present exile. Hence the same Basil also says of the singing of psalms, that it is a shield against nocturnal terrors, a rest from the labors of the day, a guardian for children, an ornament for the young, a comfort for the old, a most fitting adornment for women; it makes deserted cities inhabited again, teaches sobriety, becomes the first foundation for beginners, nourishment for those making progress, and a firm foundation for the perfect.

div.head: Cap. XIII. Homines carnales vulturibus, lasciveque mulieres hirundini comparantur, quove pacto carnales a spiritualibus discrepent, per Maris, ac fluvii Piscium exemplis elucidatur.

cit.quote: Carnal men are like vultures. For the vulture, being unclean and foul, readily makes for the ground for the sake of a carcass, and, once it has descended, does not readily rise again from there, but scarcely climbs upward, as Jerome says, and adds that, flying aloft, it spies a carcass below, and, for love of the carcass, forsakes the height of the air and lowers itself to the depths; and when it rises again, it beats its wings against the wind, and so, by the wind's help more than by its own strength, lifts itself from the depths into the air. So too carnal men, being unclean in thoughts and foul in affections, readily make for the ground for the sake of a carcass, since, for the sake of the flesh's pleasure, they easily descend to shameful and unclean deeds, and, once they have given themselves to such deeds, do not readily withdraw from them, and scarcely rise again, even in desire. And even if the carnal man is at the summit of dignity, he nonetheless spies the wretched carcass below, since he bends his heart and turns his eyes toward thinking or doing carnal deeds, and, abandoning — that is, disregarding — the height of his own dignity, plunges into base and lowly things. Hence the Psalm says: 'man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts, and became like them.' It happens, nonetheless, sometimes, that even such a man, after he has fallen, is roused by the wind of the Holy Spirit, that is, by an inner breath, and so, beating against that wind, that is, the prompting of the Holy Spirit, with the wing of mind and the wing of deed, through penance, rises again on high and lifts himself up — but more by the help of the wind, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, than by his own merit or effort.

Likewise, the more the care of the flesh grows in a man, the more sluggish it renders his soul toward good works — which indeed appears in vultures, since the vulture, because of its excess of flesh, flies slowly; so too the wretched body, which is subject to corruption, weighs down the human soul, for by the very constant corruptibility of the flesh our soul is compelled to attend to the cares of the flesh, and so, weighed down by corruption and held back by the multiplicity of cares, it becomes very sluggish toward virtuous and spiritual works.

Likewise, carnal men differ from spiritual men as sea fish differ from river fish. For fish born in the sea have hard, coarse scales, because of the dryness of the salt water; river fish, on the contrary, have thin, close, and soft scales. Now scales on a fish's body are, as it were, the considerations that arise in a man's mind. As regards spiritual and divine matters, then, carnal men differ from spiritual men in this: that carnal men all have minds — that is, considerations of mind — that are hard toward perceiving spiritual things, according to that saying of the Apostle: 'the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God.'

Likewise, they have minds that are coarse in understanding. Hence the Lord said to his still-carnal disciples: 'are you even yet without understanding?' But spiritual men have minds that are soft, that is, apt to perceive, subtle to understand, and close, that is, of frequent consideration of divine things.

Likewise, the wantonness of the flesh is likened to the swallow, which is a wandering, noisy, and gaudily-marked bird; so too carnal and wanton women are wandering in their gadding about and in looking around themselves, are noisy in singing, or in quarreling, and are also given to painting and adorning themselves — of whom the wise man rightly spoke, saying: 'and behold, a woman meets him, decked out like a harlot,' and so on.

div.head: Cap. XIIII. Homines per carnales magis, quam per spirituales cogitationes a Diabolo capi, per Avium prope terram volantium similitudines demonstratur.

cit.quote: Earthly thoughts make the soul fall into the devil's snare. For birds that descend for food, flying near the ground, are caught more quickly than those that fly on high. So too men are more quickly caught by the devil through carnal and earthly thoughts than through heavenly ones. Proverbs: 'a net is spread in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.' The Gloss: he easily escapes the devil's snares on earth, who always has his eyes fixed on heaven.

Likewise, unclean thoughts abound in the hearts of sinners, but not in the hearts of the just. For just as a greater swarm of flies usually settles on a scabby sore than on healthy skin, so unclean thoughts settle more on sinners than on the just.

Likewise, devout men are especially plagued by unclean thoughts. For flies invade and foul an anointed place. So too demons strive to defile with wicked thoughts those they see to be in grace. Ecclesiastes: 'dying flies,' that is, unclean thoughts, 'spoil the sweetness of the ointment' — that is, the merit of good works, or the devotion of prayer.

Likewise, bees settle upon flowers and draw honey from them. So too the just think on eternal goods, and yet draw sweetness from them. But flies frequent unclean places, and befoul them; and so unclean thoughts befoul sinful men.

div.head: Cap. XV. Coniux quo pacto sit querenda, coniugiique honestas ac dilectio conservanda, et denique quantum contra naturam vitium sit detestabile, multis pluvium Avium exemplis discrete enucleatur.

cit.quote: The examples of birds teach us to seek and preserve the uprightness of marriage; for among all animals, birds observe decency most closely in the order of generation. For the males seek out the females with diligence, love those they have found, fight for them, expose themselves to danger for their sake, join themselves to them, as it were, only by the bond of marriage, and feed only the offspring they themselves have begotten. From this it is gathered that birds instruct us concerning the married state in five ways.

First, by the example of birds, men who wish to take a wife ought diligently to seek out good women for wives, for it is written: 'blessed is he who finds a good wife' — whom, indeed, when a man wishes to find, he ought to seek, not as the wanton and vain man does, who seeks in a wife nothing but beauty. For beauty in a woman, if it lacks prudence and goodness, is more to be shunned than desired; for, as it is said, 'a beautiful and foolish woman is like a golden ring in a swine's snout.' And so, among men, although each is burdensome — namely, guarding a beautiful wife, or having an ugly one — it is nonetheless more bearable to have an ugly wife than to have to guard a beautiful one. For (as the golden-tongued philosopher said) a beautiful woman is quickly desired, an ugly one easily disdained. It is difficult to guard one whom everyone loves; it is troublesome to possess one whom no one deigns to want; yet it is a lesser misery to have a plain wife than to have to guard a beautiful one.

...he who wishes to find a good wife ought to seek her, not as the greedy man does, who seeks nothing in a wife but riches. Although Theophrastus says that it is hard to support a poor wife, while enduring a rich one is torment; yet Solomon says it is better to take a poor and peaceable wife than a rich and quarrelsome one: 'it is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop than with a quarrelsome woman in a shared house.' Hence Chrysostom too says: 'you, young man, when you wish to take a wife, do not seek a rich one, but a well-mannered one; for good character always acquires riches, but riches have never produced good character. The poverty of the faithful is more glorious than the riches of sinners.'

...they say the philosopher Themistocles was asked to whom he would give his daughter in marriage — to a poor man adorned with learning and good character, or to a rich man of little proven worth; and he answered: 'I prefer a man lacking money to money lacking a man.' He, then, who desires to find a good wife, ought to seek her as a prudent and discerning man would, that is, by attending to the woman's goodness. Ecclesiastes: 'blessed is the husband of a good wife' — he did not say of a beautiful or a rich one, but of a good one.
Likewise, by attending to the woman's prudence and discernment. Proverbs: 'house and riches are given by parents, but a prudent wife comes properly from the Lord.'

Likewise, by attending to the woman's lineage. Chrysostom says that he who wishes to take a wife ought to consider whether both her parents are good, or both bad, or one good and the other bad. If both are good, let him take her without fear; if both are bad, let him give her up entirely; but if one is good and the other bad, let him fear what he is about to do. Nonetheless, if her father is good and her mother bad, there is more reason to fear; but if it is the reverse, less — because children are generally raised more with their mothers than with their fathers, and consequently tend to imitate their mother's character more than their father's.

Second, birds teach spouses to love one another honorably, just as birds themselves love their mates mutually; but one must beware lest love between spouses become excessive or dishonorable. For (as Sextus said in his Sentences) a man is indeed an adulterer with his own wife if he is more ardent a lover with her than with another man's wife would be lawful; all excessive love is shameful, even toward one's own wife; nothing is more shameful than to love one's wife as though she were a mistress.

Likewise, love should not be excessive or jealous. Ecclesiasticus: 'do not be jealous of the wife of your bosom.' And the same book: 'grief of heart and mourning is a jealous wife.' Love, then, ought to be honorable and well-ordered. Ephesians: 'husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the Church.'

Third, birds instruct spouses to protect and defend one another; for birds fight for their mates, and expose themselves to danger. Spouses, too, ought to defend one another mutually, not only from bodily injuries, but also from vices and dishonorable conduct — which happens when one spouse corrects and chastises the other for living wickedly. For if a wife is ill-behaved (as Chrysostom says), she ought to be corrected by her husband in three ways: first, by teaching her according to God's law; and if she does not feel the fear of God, by reproaching her, so that she may at least blush with shame before men; and if she feels no shame even then, frequently confounded, let him do to her what Solomon prescribes: 'strike the hard heart with a rod.' For, as Chrysostom says, teaching righteousness often succeeds. First admonish, then confound, since shame is often the bridle of vice; third, it is right that she be chastised as a servant who does not know how to blush as a free woman does. But if the husband behaves badly, then (as Augustine teaches) his wife ought to restrain him in four ways. First, by admonishing. Second, by rebuking, so that, if loving admonitions do not succeed, she resorts to harsh rebukes. Third, if this does not avail, by appealing to the Church, that is, seeking the aid of prelates or a bishop, especially if the sin itself is notorious. Fourth, by having recourse to God through spiritual men and prayers, since 'the unbelieving husband shall be saved through the believing wife,' as it is said in Corinthians.

Fourth, birds teach how spouses ought to come together for the marital act, namely only within the bond and affection of marriage, that is, with the intention and purpose of begetting offspring; for it is for this reason alone that birds pair with one another, namely for generation, and hence it is that birds appear to be in love, as it were, only during the season of generation. Hence too it is only in the carnal union between the sexes that they distinguish male from female, except in partridges, which do not observe sex, as the Philosopher says; whence among partridges male mounts male and female mounts female. But no chick-producing eggs come from such coupling — indeed, they produce eggs full of wind, and he adds that a foul smell arises from such coupling. In this example, indeed, the vice against nature is shown to be detestable for three reasons. First, on account of its fruitlessness, since it does not lead to generation — hence among partridges no chick-producing eggs are generated from such coupling. Second, on account of its insatiability, since it produces eggs full of wind — for wind, although it fills, does not satisfy by nourishing. So too in such acts, although one fulfills one's evil desire, one is nonetheless not satisfied. Third, on account of the foulness of its stench, since it produces the foul smell of infamy or of bad example.

Likewise, birds observe the fitting season in the work of generation, namely the season of spring, by which it is shown that one should not give oneself over to the marital act at every season; for on holy days, or days of fasting, one should not give oneself over to such embraces. Ecclesiastes: 'a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing.'

Likewise, birds invite each other to mutual love, in the season of generation, with gestures and calls; from which it is shown that the marital debt is to be paid to a wife who asks for it, whether by voice or by gesture.

Likewise, birds breed young and raise the offspring they have produced; for parents are bound to nourish their natural children, and, even if this is not strictly required by civil or positive law, it is nonetheless required by natural law.
Likewise, birds do not come near one another again until the next season of generation returns; for after conception, a husband ought to abstain from his wife until she has given birth.

Fifth, birds teach us by rearing their young; for they feed only the offspring they themselves have begotten, together. In this the danger of adultery is shown, especially on the wife's part; for a woman who conceives through secret adultery imposes on her husband children that are not his, and makes him rear children not begotten by him — for which, as for theft, she is bound to make restitution.

Likewise, the examples of storks teach us to preserve the uprightness of marriage: among these, as long as the female lives, the male never joins with another for the sake of mating, but keeps faith with his own mate as regards the nest and the offspring; but if he senses that his mate has submitted to an adulterous union, he no longer dwells with her — indeed, he even strikes her through and kills her, if he can, as Aristotle says.

Likewise, the male does not tread the female at all except in the nest — an example by which spouses are plainly warned to observe diligently the fidelity of the marriage bed, to shrink from and avoid adulterous unions, and to render the debt of carnal union with a certain decency.

div.head: Cap. XVI. Aspera abstinentia ac vita contemplativa, in quibus designetur, quibusque avibus contemplativis comparentur, contemplationisque perfectio qualis sit, variis definitur exemplis.

cit.quote: The contemplative life, and harsh abstinence, are signified in those fish, or swimming creatures, whose eating was permitted in the Law of Moses. For it is said in Leviticus: 'everything that has fins and scales, in the sea as well as in rivers and pools, you may eat; but whatever among the creatures that move and live in the waters has no fins and scales shall be an abomination and accursed to you.' Literally, such swimming creatures — namely eels and the like — were forbidden to the Jews because of their excess of moisture, and other fish were permitted to them as being drier. But the moral, or figurative, reason was this: that by fins is signified the subtle life, or contemplation, and by scales is signified the harsh life — both of which are necessary for spiritual purity.

Likewise, contemplative men are like songbirds, which love the woods, nest in trees and orchards, sweetly warble and sing, sit diligently upon their eggs, and carefully rear their young — such as the nightingale, the blackbird, and the like. So too perfect and contemplative men love solitary places, and place the nest of their mind and the rest of contemplation in orchards and among the branches of trees — that is, in the examples of the humble and pious, and in the deeds and footsteps of the great saints; they sweetly sing and chant divine praises daily, whether with the voice or at least with the heart; nourishing their holy desires of mind with the warmth of devotion, they carry them through to the completion of the work, sitting as it were upon eggs and, warming them with their own heat, persist until the young are born. But then they send forth their young, as it were, with care, when they do not abandon the good works they have begun, but, nourishing and feeding them fittingly, bring them to their due perfection.

Likewise, the contemplation of a man living in the flesh cannot be lasting, because of the heaviness of the body. For mortal man is like the partridge, a bird of much flesh and little plumage, and so of little flight; for in flying it rises but a little from the ground, and, after a short while, at once returns to earth. In the same way, since man in this life has much of the body's weight and weakness, and little of plumage — that is, of the lightness of spiritual virtues — even if he sometimes strives to rise from earthly things to grasp heavenly things through the flight of contemplation, he is nonetheless weighed down by the burden or weakness of his corruptible flesh, and after a little while returns to the depths. Hence it is said: 'the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things.'

Likewise, the contemplation of divine things puts to flight the onset of temptation, and calms the storms of a raging world, as is shown by the example of the halcyon. For the halcyon (as Ambrose says) is a sea bird which, in the very middle of winter, when the sea is most raging with storms of wind and wave, lays her eggs on the seashore in the sand, and there, facing toward the sea, sits brooding upon them for six days, after which the chicks are born; once they are born, she adds seven more days to nourish them, and through all these thirteen days the sea remains calm and safe. Hence the diligence of sailors observes these thirteen calm days for sailing, and calls them the halcyon days, as Ambrose says. If, then, so small a bird has such power that, by the mere gaze of her contemplation, she calms the raging sea, how much more, if the rational soul, made in the image of God, should direct its inner eyes, in contemplation or in prayer, toward the eternal and unchanging good, will it find the sea — whether of the heart's raging or of the world's fury — calmed and made peaceful at once. Job: 'you too, if you rise at dawn to God, and have besought the Almighty, he too will at once awaken to you, and will make peaceful the dwelling of your righteousness.' This little bird also teaches us that, because of persecutions or temptations that arise, we should neither fear to undertake good things, nor neglect to pursue them to completion; for this bird, though she has seen the stormy sea, neither fears to set herself to brooding her eggs on the shore, nor withdraws before her young have had their due nourishment.

div.head: Cap. XVII. Luxuria deformitas, queve ab ea detrimenta, atque a castimonia continentia oriantur bona, eloquenter explanatur.

cit.quote: The continence of chastity contributes to length of life, which is shown in vultures, which are said to beget their young without mating, and to live a hundred years, as Isidore says. From this it is gathered that those who restrain themselves from the dissipations of carnal acts live longer. For (according to the Philosopher) animals of much mating, like sparrows and the like, are of shorter life. Note, then, that lust shortens bodily life, dishonors civic life, and kills spiritual life. On the first point it is said of the prodigal, wanton young man, who squandered his substance, not only his personal but also his temporal goods, by living wantonly: for in the act of lust there is an evacuation of moisture and an expiration of heat, on which two life is preserved.

And so, from the frequent practice of the sexual act, the vigor and life of the body is drained. Hence Hugh of Saint-Victor says: 'lust,' he says, 'is an immoderate wantonness of the flesh, a sweet poison, an unwelcome plague, a ruinous drink, which weakens the human body and drains the strength of a manly spirit.' And Innocent says, in his treatise on the wretchedness of the human condition: 'O,' he says, 'the extreme baseness of lust, which not only effeminates the mind but drains the body, and not only defiles the soul but defiles the person. For every other sin whatsoever a man commits is outside his body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body. It is always preceded by burning and wantonness, always accompanied by stench and filth, always followed by grief and repentance.'

Likewise, lust dishonors civic life, since it takes glory away from a man, bringing him disgrace and infamy. Hence it is said of the lustful: 'from their carcasses shall rise a stench,' namely of infamy. Hence Valerius, speaking of the vices of the flesh, says: 'what,' he says, 'is more shameful than these vices? What more ruinous? By them virtue is worn away, victories grow faint, sleeping glory turns to infamy, the strength of mind and body is overthrown, so that one cannot tell whether it is more dangerous to be captured by one's enemies or by these vices.'

Likewise, lust destroys spiritual life. Romans: 'if you live according to the flesh, you will die.' Jerome: 'he who lives wantonly is dead even while he lives.' Desire tames even hearts of iron, and hungers all the more in virgins, since they think what they do not know must be sweeter.

Chastity, on the contrary, or continence, multiplies the days of one's life. Job: 'I shall multiply my days like the palm tree.' By the palm understand the victory over the flesh, which is achieved through continence.

Likewise, it adorns and ennobles civic life. Hence Cyprian says: 'modesty,' he says, 'is the ornament of the noble, the exaltation of the humble, the nobility of the ignoble, the beauty of the lowly, the comfort of the sorrowful, the increase of every beauty, the honor of religion, the diminishment of debt, the multiplication of merits, the friend of God the creator of all things.'
Likewise, it strengthens and preserves spiritual life. Romans: 'if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.'

div.head: Cap. XVIII. Conversionis prolixitatem maximopere a Deo plectendam esse, tum exemplis, tum etiam sacre Scripture comprobatur testimoniis.

cit.quote: Conversion should not be put off. For a bird, seeing the bow drawn and the arrow ready, does not delay in flying away; but just as the ready arrow is prepared to strike the bird if it stays still, so God strikes down the one unwilling to be converted. Psalm: 'unless you are converted, he has brandished his sword, he has bent his bow,' and so on. But many act like the foolish bird, which, delaying its flight, is struck. So too many, while they delay their flight and merely intend to convert, die suddenly. Isaiah: 'suddenly, when it is not expected, his ruin will come.' Ecclesiasticus: 'do not delay in converting to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for his wrath will come suddenly,' and so on. Ambrose says: 'you offer gold and do not say to yourself, tomorrow I will come; but you ask it of yourself at once — no one delays, no one makes excuses; the redemption of the soul is promised, and yet no one hastens.' And note that, when a sinner does not convert, the longer he is given time, the more severely he will be judged. Hence Valerius Maximus says that divine wrath proceeds toward vengeance with a slow step, and weighs the delay of punishment by its severity.

div.head: Cap. XIX. Quo pacto sis cor hominis preparandum ut fiat ipsius Dei habitaculum, piscium exemplo fit perspicuum.

cit.quote: The heart of man must first be renewed like fish, and steeped in the fragrance of devout prayers, before it can receive God within its own inner chamber. An example of this appears in fish; for a fish naturally delights in fragrant things. For it is said by Aristotle that certain kinds of fish can smell and hear; and so a fish approaches new vessels more quickly than old ones — indeed, where there is a new vessel, it rarely approaches an old one. So God does not enter the vessel of the human heart unless it is first made new through the renewal of penance. Hence David asked for this newness, saying: 'create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.' Nor does God dwell delightfully in the lodging of a heart from which the sweet fragrance of devout prayer does not rise. But the prayers of the saints are, as it were, bowls full of fragrance.

div.head: Cap. XX. Immanes homines vulturibus, culicibusque comparantur, et qualis corum sit exitus definitur.

cit.quote: Cruel men and plunderers commonly die hungry and begging. For they are like vultures, which follow an army so as to gorge themselves on the carcasses of horses and men; and so it is said that they foresee war by some natural sense, and gather in advance around an army as a sign of coming war. But when a vulture grows old, its beak grows longer above and curves at the tip, and at last it dies of hunger. So too rapacious men, who love wars so as to gain and plunder, as mercenary soldiers and certain powerful tyrants do — though perhaps in their youth, or for some time, they gain and grow rich — yet in old age, or in adversity or sickness, when they can no longer plunder, while the beak, that is, the necessity of sustaining their own mouth, grows, and gain fails, they come to poverty and beggary, and die of hunger. Job: 'the tiger perished,' that is, the plunderer, 'for lack of prey.'

Likewise, cruel men, thirsting for the blood of the weak, often fall into the hands of the greater and more powerful. Hence such men are likened to gnats, which, wishing to suck the blood of others out of thirst, fall into the beaks of swallows, which kill and eat them. Those, then, are like such men, who, while seeking to kill or despoil their lesser fellows, themselves become the prey or the slaughtered victims of the greater. A clearer example of this is found in the book of Esther, namely of Haman, who, wishing out of jealousy of Mordecai to have the Jews crucified, was himself hanged on the gallows by King Ahasuerus.

div.head: Cap. XXI. Dei arcanorum scrutatores curiosi, quam penam accepturi sint, culicum exemplo notabili edocetur.

cit.quote: Curious and presumptuous investigators are likened to gnats. For the gnat, which is the same as the mosquito, loves light, since it gladly looks upon the light of a candle or lamp; but, rushing heedlessly toward that light, it burns itself up. In the same way, those who love the light of divine or human knowledge, sometimes investigating too curiously or presumptuously, when they strike against that very light, kill themselves, as it were, through the burn of some error or pride. Hence it is said in Proverbs that he who searches into majesty shall be overwhelmed by its glory. And so (as Gregory Nazianzen says) the desire for knowledge, and the investigation of questions, unless preceded by the fear of God, leads unbridled minds headlong to ruin. But where the fear of God is, there is the observance of the commandments, there is the purging of the flesh — for the flesh, setting itself before the mind like a dense and darker cloud, does not allow one to behold the light of the divine ray.

div.head: Cap. XXII. Diaboli vis eiusque astutia, ac calliditas quanta sit, bubonis, nicticoracis, pavonisque exemplis aperte monstratur.

cit.quote: The devil is likened to the owl. First, indeed, because the owl feeds on dung; so too the devil delights in the filth of sins. Lamentations: 'those who took delight in scarlet' — namely the demons, before they fell — 'have embraced dung,' that is, the unclean sins in which they now delight.

Second, because the owl goes to temples by night, to fill itself with the oil of the lamps. For any holy man is called a temple of God, whose lamps are the minds of those same saints, which are full of oil; by night, that is, secretly and stealthily, the devil strives to empty the minds of the saints, namely so that, when the bridegroom comes, they may have no oil left in their lamps, and so be shut out from the wedding-feast of the eternal king, as happened to the foolish virgins.

Third, because the owl is hated by other birds, and plucked of its feathers by them; for they fly around it by day and pluck it. So too the devil is hated by the saints, as their adversary, and the birds — that is, holy and prudent men — pluck him by day, when, recognizing his wicked schemes more clearly, they expose and reveal them. Or the feathers clinging to him are his imitators, whom holy men pluck away, when they call such men back to penance.

Fourth, because the owl fights with the jackdaw, a bird of the crow family; for the jackdaw destroys the owl's eggs by day, and the owl eats the jackdaw's eggs by night. The jackdaw, then, is like humble penance, whose eggs can be called the laborious works of the penitent. But the owl's eggs are, as it were, the sins into which the demon has induced these eggs. The jackdaw, then, destroys the owl's eggs by day, since humble penance, as the day of grace dawns, destroys the sins that the penitent committed at the demon's prompting. Conversely, the owl lays waste the jackdaw's eggs by night, since, as the darkness of sin rushes in, the devil himself destroys all the works of penance.

Likewise, the devil is likened to the night-raven, which is a bird that flees the light and loves darkness. It cannot bear the sun, dwells among the tombs of the dead, nests in ruined places, devours the eggs of doves and fights with them; by day it is almost blind, but by night sees keenly, for the splendor of the sun dulls its sight. So too the devil flees the light of grace, loves the darkness of guilt, and cannot bear the Sun of Righteousness, that is, Christ. Hence the demons said to him: 'what have we to do with you, Jesus?' and so on. Or he also cannot bear the Sun, that is, the good man who walks and lives openly in the light; he dwells in the tombs of the dead, that is, in the foul hearts of sinners, full of carnal desires.

Likewise, he nests in ruined places, that is, in those who at once consent to temptations, and are prone and inclined to fall into sin; he fights against doves, that is, the simple; and he gladly devours their eggs, that is, their works, by scattering them; he is blind toward good things, keen-sighted toward evil ones. The splendor of Christ's teaching, however, dulls his sight, since it utterly annihilates the malice of his cunning; and so Peter says, in his first epistle: 'resist him, strong in the faith,' and Ecclesiasticus: 'shining with its own rays, it blinds the eyes.'

Likewise, the devil is likened to the peacock; for the peacock has a serpent's head, but crested, a stealthy gait, a slight neck, an upright, sapphire-colored breast, and an eyed tail. So too the devil has a head — that is, the beginning of his temptation — in the manner of a serpent; for wherever a serpent inserts its head, the whole of it afterward slips in (as Jerome says), since it is there that the beginning of his temptation is received, which is afterward driven out only with difficulty; but he has a crest on his head, insofar as at first he holds out the appearance of some good — for he cannot introduce evil except under the guise of some good, since no one who intends evil acts openly. He also has a stealthy gait, since he secretly draws man to destruction; he also has a curved neck, since, if he seizes a man, he swallows him quickly — for he quickly makes the man who consents to him plunge into the depths of sin. His breast, that is, his appetite, is upright, namely pride, which always aims for the heights. He also has an eyed tail, since he looks chiefly to the end, so that he may deceive man at that very point. Genesis: 'you shall lie in wait for his heel,' that is, his end.

div.head: Cap. XXIII. Deum summopere diligentibus omnia adversa, etiamque peccatorum virus, in bonum converti, per passeris exemplum, brevibus ostenditur verbis.

cit.quote: For those who love God fervently, no adversity harms them, but rather benefits them. Hence they are likened to sparrows, of whom the Lord made mention: 'you are worth more,' he says, 'than many sparrows.' For sparrows are of a very hot nature, and eat the poisonous seeds of henbane without harm. So too, those who love God fervently are, as it were, very hot sparrows, who patiently receive even the poisonous seeds of henbane — that is, the adverse and dangerous evils of the world — without any harm to themselves; indeed, so great is the power of divine love that, for such men, even the poison of sin is turned into good. Romans: 'for those who love God, all things work together for good.' 'All things,' he says, both prosperous and adverse — the prosperous for use, the adverse for exercise — or all things, that is, good and bad, and not only the evils of punishment, but even of guilt, since indeed from these very things they rise more humble, more cautious, and more watchful.

div.head: Cap. XXIIII. Quatuor rationibus verbi Dei concionator gallo comparatur, eiusque officium quale esse debeat variis modis declaratur.

cit.quote: The teaching of holy preachers snatches men away from the deceptions of demons. For it is read that a cock's brain, taken as a drink, is effective against the bites of serpents, since it removes their venom. By the cock is understood the preacher, as upon that saying of Job: 'who gave understanding to the cock?' Now it is chiefly in the parts of the brain that the power of sensitive cognition is rooted. So then, the sense of the holy preacher is, as it were, the cock's brain: when it is taken in, like a drink of teaching, by his hearers, the serpent's bite or venom is put to flight, since the deception of the ancient enemy is uncovered and avoided.

Likewise, the cock represents the teaching of holy preachers, even in his crowing, in three ways. First, because of his discernment of the time: for the cock discerns the first hour of the night, and afterward gives forth a rousing cry. For the holy preacher first considers, in his hearers — that is, in sinners still wrapped in darkness — the quality of their life, and only then shapes a fitting voice for their instruction; for the same exhortation does not suit everyone, since the same disposition does not constrain everyone in the same way. Often, indeed, what helps some harms others. For often certain herbs nourish some animals and kill others; a gentle whistle calms horses, and rouses hunting dogs; and a medicine that lessens this illness strengthens another; and bread, which strengthens the life of the strong, kills infants. According to the disposition of the hearers, then, the sermon of teachers ought to be shaped, as Gregory says.

Second, because of the variation of his voice; for the cock (as Gregory says) usually gives forth stronger, deeper cries in the deeper hours of the night, but toward morning shapes lighter, gentler ones. So too the wise preacher, when he speaks to sinners sunk and darkened in the shadows of sin, speaks more sternly and harshly, either of divine judgments, or the anguish of death, or the torments of hell. But when he speaks to those already illuminated by God, and joined to God's grace, he speaks more gently, more subtly, and more sweetly, namely of divine mercies, or inner rewards, and the like.

Third, because when the cock prepares himself to crow, he first shakes his wings, and, beating his sides, makes himself more watchful. So too holy preachers, when they admonish others with words of holy exhortation, should first exercise themselves in holy actions, lest, sluggish in deeds themselves, they rouse others only with words; rather, they should first shake themselves through lofty deeds, and then make others more diligent toward good action. They first strike themselves with the wings of their own thoughts, since whatever lies uselessly sluggish within them they discover through careful self-examination, and correct and amend through strict self-scrutiny; for before they utter words of holy exhortation, everything they are about to say, they already proclaim through their deeds. And so it is clear that, just as the cock shakes his wings, strikes himself, and gives forth his voice, so the holy preacher shakes himself free of evils, strikes himself, that is, spurs himself on toward good, and only afterward gives forth his voice, that is, preaching to others. From all that has been said, then, you have four reasons why the holy preacher is likened to the cock: for the strength of his remedy, for his discernment of the time, for the variation of his voice, and for the striking of his body.

div.head: Cap. XXV. Eleemosynas pauperibus, precipueque ex ecclesia bonis erogandas esse, Aquila exemplo ac multis auctoritatibus aperitur.

cit.quote: The example of the eagle teaches us to give alms to the poor, at least out of our surplus. For the eagle (as Pliny says) was of such generosity that, unless very hungry, she does not eat her prey alone, but, once she has taken her own portion, shares it, as it were, in common with the birds that follow her — hence other birds always follow her, waiting for a share of her prey to be given them. The vulture, on the contrary, eats what it seizes entirely alone. He becomes a detestable miser, who wishes to eat alone the food he has in abundance — against whom blessed Job says: 'if I have eaten my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat of it.'
