For at the very least, a wretched man, once he is filled with food, ought to feed the hungry poor from what remains; hence it is said in Luke: 'give as alms what remains over.' And clerics are especially bound to this, to whom the goods of the Church have been entrusted — not to be abused for the benefit of their own kin, but rather to be faithfully dispensed, according to that saying: 'a stewardship has been entrusted to me.' And so Caesarius says of them that not only are the tithes not our own, but are appointed to the churches; indeed, whatever we receive from God beyond our own need, we ought to give to the poor. And if we keep for our own greed or vanities what has been appointed for them, however many poor in the places where we live have died of hunger or nakedness, we should know that we will render account for their souls on the day of judgment. But note that one does not always sin mortally by not giving to the poor what one has in surplus, but only when necessity is pressing. And when such necessity exists as would oblige one under pain of mortal sin cannot be determined by reason alone, but is left to the prudence or good faith of the steward. Hence, if he gives in good faith, when it seems fitting to him, he is free from sin; otherwise he sins mortally.

div.head: Cap. XXVI. Cur diabolus interdum hominem (Deo permittente) exaltet, cornicula, aquilaque exemplis aperse exponitur.

cit.quote: The devil sometimes exalts a man, so as to break him in the height of his dignity, whom he could not overcome in humility. For the little crow, when it cannot break a nut, carries it high up, so that it may fall more forcefully and be broken; and the eagle does the same with a tortoise. It was in this way that the poet Aeschylus was killed, as Valerius relates: while he sat, bare-headed, beneath the open sky, an eagle, carrying a tortoise aloft and deceived by the whiteness of his head, which it took for a stone, let the tortoise fall straight down upon him to be broken open; and so, while it meant only to break the tortoise, it shattered his skull instead. Just as the eagle does with the tortoise, then, or the crow with the nut, so the devil raises someone to a dignity he could not overcome before, so as to cast him down into sin — and so he set Christ upon the pinnacle of the temple. Job: 'you have lifted me up, and, setting me as though upon the wind, you have utterly dashed me down.'

div.head: Cap. XXVII. Quomodo fidelis in adversitatibus stabilis persistere queat, vero Christi exemplo. Echinique piscis similitudine demonstratur.

cit.quote: The example of Christ's humility and patience makes the soul strong against every storm of adversity. An example of this appears in a certain little fish called the sea-urchin; of which Ambrose says that, when it senses the storms of the winds, it seizes a strong pebble, and, as though an anchor, draws it to itself so as not to be shaken by the waves; and so it is freed not by its own strength, but is fortified by an outside weight, and, with the help of the stone, made steady against the coming tempest — which sailors, taking note of this, use to protect themselves, so that the storm does not catch them unprepared. So too he who wishes to escape the storms, that is, the adversities of a raging world, should seize the strong pebble of humility, that is, of patience, by the example of Christ, who said: 'if the world hates you, know that it hated me before you'; hence Peter says: 'Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps.' And so, whoever takes up this cornerstone, namely Christ, as his example, no assault of the storm can harm him; for if the Passion of Christ is called to mind, nothing is so harsh that it cannot be borne with an even mind, as Gregory says.

Likewise, the examples of the saints who went before us teach us to despise the riches of the world. For it is read that the bones of cocks and hens are poison to gold; hence, if such bones are mixed into molten gold, the gold is consumed by them. Now the examples of the saints, men and women, who have died, are, as it were, the bones of cocks and hens — for they destroy gold, as it were, when they lead us, while still living, to despise it. Ecclesiasticus: 'blessed is he who has not gone after gold'; and Peter said: 'silver and gold I have none.'

div.head: Cap. XXVIII. Prelates malis exemplis subditorum animos inficere unita Galli senis similitudine explanatur.

cit.quote: ...cock, toad, basilisk. As Pliny says, the cock, in his extreme old age, lays certain small, round, bluish eggs; and if such eggs are brooded, during the dog-days, by some venomous creature, say a toad or the like, a basilisk is generated, which is of such venomousness that it poisons and kills by the mere sight of it. So then, the old cock is, as it were, any aged prelate, or prince held in reverence, whose venomous eggs are his wicked deeds, from which arises the basilisk that poisons by its gaze, that is, a pestilential example, corrupting his subjects — especially if it is brooded by some venomous creature, that is, if his conduct is shaped by some pestilent and malicious tempter. Augustine: 'everyone who lives wickedly in the sight of those over whom he is set kills, as far as it depends on him; and perhaps the one who imitates him dies, and the one who does not imitate him lives — yet, as far as it pertains to the wicked man himself, he has killed both.'

div.head: Cap. XXIX. Quantum devote mentis fervor in tentationibus prosit, hic brevi clarum efficitur.

cit.quote: The heat of the vulture, which (as Pliny says) is so opposed to serpents that, if its feathers are burnt, serpents are driven off by the smell. Indeed, the vulture's feathers are then burnt, when the meditations and affections of the heart are kindled and grow hot, according to that saying of the Psalm: 'in my meditation the fire shall burn.' And it is then, too, that serpents flee, since it is then that the promptings of demons withdraw. Hence Gregory: 'if the power of devotion touches us deep within, all the noise of wicked suggestion is silenced'; for the power of devotion is itself the very heat of affection. Hence Hugh of Saint-Victor says that devotion is the ardor of a good will, which the mind, unable to contain it, manifests through sure signs.

div.head: Cap. XXX. Filios erga parentes foro omni tempore pientissimos, per varia nonnullarum avium exempla, scitu digna terminatur.

cit.quote: ...crow-family birds. Aristotle. Basil. Ambrose. Ecclesiasticus.

Likewise, the examples of the crow lead children who lack filial devotion toward their parents to fulfill their duty. For (as Ambrose says) the crow's compassion toward its own parents is admirable; for when it happens that the parents are stripped bare of feathers and wings in old age, the younger crows warm them with their own feathers, and, having gathered food, nourish them, and support them with the aid of their own wings, and exercise them for flight, so as to restore their disused limbs to their former use. So too the children of men ought to clothe their bare parents with their own feathers, so to speak, if they have no others — feeding the hungry first with food or labor, supporting the sick or the weak with the aid of their own arms, and helping them go where they need to.

But note that disordered love of parents for their children is also, for the parents themselves, a cause of ruin, as with storks. For the stork (as Ambrose says) loves and cares for her young with a wondrous affection, so much so that, through constant brooding over them, she loses her own feathers; so too parents who love their children in a disordered way frequently lose the feathers of virtue, because of excessive care for them, or unlawful gains made for their sake. In this, however, the storks themselves are worthy of imitation: for however much time they spend rearing their young, they are in turn reared by them for just as long a time (as Ambrose says) — namely so that the children of men, whom their parents raised with great care in their infancy, may render the same care back to them in their old age. A similar kind of devotion toward aged parents is also reported of the hoopoe; for when the hoopoe grows old, so that it can no longer see or fly, its young pluck out its weakened feathers, anoint its eyes with the juice of certain herbs, and warm it under their own wings, until its feathers grow back and its sight clears — an example by which it is shown that children ought, as much as they can, to remove harm and trouble from their aged or infirm parents, provide the necessary care for their infirmities, cherish or serve them with their own attentions and their own persons, and not abandon them until they see that their parents no longer need their service or their help.

div.head: Cap. XXXI. Tribulationes, ac afflictiones interdum malos ad vitam spiritualem inducere, apum similitudinibus edocetur.

cit.quote: The scourge of tribulation and affliction sometimes even converts earthly and wanton men into fruitful, spiritual lives, which is shown by the example of bees. For those with experience say that bees are often generated from the carcasses of cattle. For when calves are slaughtered, their flesh is beaten, and so, from the rotting blood, worms are generated, which, once they receive wings, become bees. But what do we understand by oxen or calves, if not earthly and proud men? For oxen plow the earth, and calves, or bulls, are stiff-necked or untamed; but the oxen or calves are killed, and their flesh beaten, since, when such men are troubled by the world, or beaten in the flesh — that is, weakened in the body — their greed is extinguished and their pride slaughtered. The slaughtered calves generate worms, since, the spirit of pride extinguished, they become humble, and, receiving wings, become bees — for, adorned with the feathers of the virtues, they are made perfect both in the contemplative and in the active life. For bees both raise themselves aloft in flying, and make honey fruitfully for others, since holy men both rise on high through contemplation, and pour forth honeyed works, or even words, for the benefit of others. Ecclesiasticus: 'the bee is small among flying things, and the fruit of her labor has the beginning of sweetness.' The small bee is the humble man, who is small through humility, capable of flight through contemplation, and sweet and fruitful through the help he gives out of piety.

div.head: Cap. XXXII. Demonum, Hereticorumque, ac Hypocritarum astu, atque fraus quanta sit, perdices, polypi piscis, et cancri, certis definitur exemplas.

cit.quote: The deceitfulness of demons, or of heretics, is likened to the partridge. For the partridge is a deceitful bird, since, stealing the eggs of others, it broods them; but from this deceit it gains no benefit at all, but rather loss, since it loses its labor: for the young, once born, as soon as they hear the voice of their true mother, entirely abandon the mother who raised them, and go to their true mother, as Ambrose says; hence Jeremiah says: 'the partridge broods what she did not lay.' So too the devil, or the heretic, steals, as it were, the eggs of others, cunningly deceiving the children of holy Church and drawing them to himself. But he more often labors in vain, since those thus deceived, often, once they hear the true, catholic teaching of the Church, their true mother, abandon their treachery or sin, and return to their true mother the Church, or to divine grace through true faith or penance. John: 'my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.'

Likewise, the deceitful man and the hypocrite are likened to the octopus, which is a deceitful fish. For (as Ambrose says) the octopus, on a shallow shore, attaches itself to some rock, and so clings to it that, both in color and in shape, it seems to be itself a piece of the rock, or a part of a sack lying there. And so little fish, deceived, wishing to hide beneath it as though beneath a loose stone, once they have entered the hiding place of its body, are seized by the octopus, enclosed, and, once enclosed, devoured and swallowed. To this fish, then, is likened the deceitful and wicked man, who, clinging to another, takes on his manner and character, and strives to conform himself to him, so that he may be trusted all the more and deceive more easily — of such men Christ said: 'they will come to you in sheep's clothing.' Or such is the hypocrite, who outwardly presents the appearance of the rock, that is, of Christ, while nonetheless being a voracious fish.

Likewise, the deceitful man is likened to the crab, which, wishing to eat oysters, but unable to because of their hard shells that close them up, watches for the moment when the oyster opens itself to the sun's rays, that is, at a time calm and free of winds, and then, so that the oyster cannot close again, secretly takes a little pebble and slips it in unnoticed; after which, its weapon — that is, its claw — inserted without danger, it tears the oyster open and eats it. To this creature, then, is like the deceitful man, who deceives with cunning trickery the one he cannot overcome directly, and feeds on his misfortune, as Ambrose says: 'as with a sharp razor, you have wrought deceit.'

div.head: Cap. XXXIII. Garruli homines, qui semper inanibus abundant verbis, quinque effectibus Graculo comparari explanatur.

cit.quote: The chattering man is likened to the jackdaw, which is shown by its cry: for its song is indeed its chatter. Hence (as Basil says) the jackdaw is named from the chattering of its voice. Now the man who devotes himself to gluttony gladly gossips after eating, gladly slanders, and sometimes quarrels; hence such a man is not undeservedly represented by the jackdaw.

Second, this is shown by its manner of moving, or flying; for the jackdaw, dwelling in the woods, passes chattering from one tree to another — and this is because the chattering man never ceases, at times, to recount even the shameful things he knows about those among whom he lives.

Third, this is shown by its manner of watching; for when the jackdaw sees some bird pass by, it chatters, and, when it finds some hidden ones, it does the same — since the chattering man does not only slander worldly people, but even those whom the seclusion of religious life conceals.

Fourth, this is shown by its disposition; for sometimes a captured jackdaw is shut up, so that it may be taught to speak articulate words. Likewise, sometimes the chattering worldly man, when he comes to conversion and enters religious life, learns the words of religion, so that, like the tongue of a bird, his tongue may speak the words of a man — that is, so that he who was accustomed to speak disorderedly may afterward grow accustomed to speaking in an ordered way.

Fifth, this is shown by the jackdaw's manner of leaving; for it sometimes happens that a jackdaw that was kept shut up, escaping from its confinement, gets free, and, having been chattering before, chatters all the more once it has escaped. In the same way, the chattering man, once he has taken up the religious life, scarcely abandons his tongue; but if, perhaps, casting off the habit, he goes back out into the world, he turns the good of religion into evil by his chattering, that is, by slandering it. Of such a person, then, it is said: 'chattering and restless, impatient of quiet.'

div.head: Cap. XXXIIII. Quando anime gratia reficiantur divina, quos in eis operetur effectus, ac finalis impenitentia, que et peccatum in Spiritum sanctum dicitur, previtas quanta sit, pullorum, corvorum, Galli, Caladriisque exemplis demonstratur.

cit.quote: The soul is not refreshed by heavenly grace except as long as it remains clean from sins, which is shown by the example of ravens. Of these the Gloss says, on that verse of the Psalm, 'giving to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that call upon him': that as long as the young ravens have white feathers, they are left by their parents, and are then fed by the dew of heaven; but when they begin to turn black, then the ravens themselves feed them. Now what are the white-feathered young, if not men clean of heart? These are fed by the dew of heaven, since they are nourished by the richness of heavenly grace; but, once turned black, they are fed by the ravens, since, darkened by sins, they are sustained by demons instead.

Likewise, heavenly grace grants both caution and courage — caution against prosperity, and courage against adversity. For it is read of the cock that whoever is anointed with its fat will be safe from panthers and lions. For Christ can not unfittingly be understood by the cock, who rouses and stirs us in the darkness of our night with the voice of his teaching. The fat of the cock, then, is the grace of Christ himself, whose most sacred anointing — of which it is said, 'you have an anointing from the Holy One' — defends us both against the malice of the panther and against the ferocity of the lion. For the malicious adversary either entices us by tempting us with delights, as the panther does, opening its mouth to draw in, by its scent, the animals it wishes to devour; or he crushes us by pursuing us with adversities, as the raging, roaring lion prowls about, seeking whom he may devour. But the anointing of the cock defends against both, since the grace of Christ makes us cautious in prosperity, and strong and unafraid in adversity; and so the prophet sought this fat of the cock, saying: 'may my soul be filled, as with fat and richness.'

Likewise, the grace of God does not look upon the man whom final impenitence leads to eternal death, a clear example of which appears in the caladrius. For the caladrius (as Aristotle says) is white in color, having no blackness at all, and its nature is such that, when someone is held by a grave illness, if that illness is to be fatal, the caladrius turns its face away from him, and then the man is certain of death; but if the sick man is to be cured, it then fixes its gaze on him, and, as though applauding, attends to him intently. And this caladrius differs from the calandra lark, which is a songbird, as the Gloss on Deuteronomy says. This bird, then, entirely white, is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is pure, and stained by no admixture of blackness, that is, of guilt.

Now just as the sick man who is truly going to die is the man in despair and finally impenitent, destined to arrive at the punishment of eternal death. Hence the grace of the Holy Spirit can never look upon him, since he lacks final penitence and remission. For this very state is called blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come, according to Augustine. Hence John: 'there is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for that.' And just as the sick man who is to be cured is the sinner doing penance, upon whom the regard of divine grace fixes itself joyfully and steadfastly, until, purging him of his sins, it brings him to full health.

div.head: Cap. XXXV. Gulosi, qui ventri semper indulgere intendunt, cygno, locustis, miluisque assimilantur, omnique tempore ad contemplandum inepti redduntur.

cit.quote: The glutton, given over to his belly, is idle and unfit for contemplation. This is shown by the example of the swan. For the swan is of much flesh, and so loves rest, and rarely strives to fly, since its body is heavy. Now those who are of much flesh are those who take great care of their body; these love the rest of idleness, and, moreover, are wholly unfit for the flight of contemplation; for the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul.

Likewise, some are likened to locusts. For the locust is, as it were, all belly, and so is insatiable. It has a squared mouth, and a single intestine, always full of hunger and filth; as long as it lives it is always hungry, and, if it finds anything green, does not stop gnawing it. So too certain gluttons are so entirely given over to their belly that they seem to be nothing but a belly. Hence the Apostle says of such men: 'whose god is their belly.' Such men are so insatiable that, no sooner is one meal finished, than they are already anxious about the next: 'the belly of the wicked is never satisfied.' They also have a squared mouth, since they offend in four ways in eating food: either because they take too much, or because they seek delicate and costly food, or because it is too elaborately prepared, or because they eat in a disorderly way, or too eagerly, or because they eat before the proper time.

Likewise, their bowels, when full, are full of filth; but when they are fasting, that is, empty, they are tormented by want and hunger; and, since they are always intent on food, whatever they find pleasing to themselves, they strive to have and to eat.

Likewise, some are likened to kites. For the kite, out of gluttony, feeds on unclean things, and, for the sake of a little food for its belly, circles about all day long. So too some gluttons are those who, for the sake of gluttony, eagerly eat things that are unusual to others, or generally considered unclean — like the flesh of dogs, serpents, frogs, and the like, which, because of their uncleanness, are generally not in use; and some besides, in the manner of the kite, circle around the kitchen and the cooking-pot all day. Psalm: 'they shall suffer hunger like dogs, and go about the city.'

div.head: Cap. XXXVI.Qua via heretici, atque hypocrite, aspectu, ac eorum affatu multos decipiant, Ceti quadam similitudine clarum efficiunt.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Heretics or hypocrites, just as they deceive others by the appearance of feigned sanctity, likewise overthrow them by the speech, or falsity of language, of false teaching. Hence they are likened to the whale, that is, to the fish called 'balena,' of which Jorath says that, especially when it grows old, because of the size of its body, dust gathers on its back and thickens so much that plants and shrubs grow there, so that it looks like an island; and if sailors, unaware, approach it, they scarcely escape without danger — for it ejects such a quantity of water from its mouth over the ship that it sometimes capsizes it. Just as the whale, then, attracts, or deceives, by its feigned appearance, and the water spewed from its mouth overturns the ship's sail, so too heretics or hypocrites draw many others in mostly by the appearance of a stimulated holiness, but overturn the ships of their minds with the water of their mouth, that is, with the teaching and exhortation of falsehood. Hence the Lord said of them: 'beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.'

div.head: Cap. XXXVII. Humilitatem precipue ex peccati consideratione, ac ex carnis corrupta memoria oriri, summo pereque nos ad Deum contemplandum idoneos reddere, ceti, Echini, Aquileque oculorum exemplis, redditur perspicuum.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: The virtue of humility is born in the spirit from the consideration of weakness — as with the whale, of which Jorath says that it abounds in seed, and that, after mating, what remains over floats on the surface, and, once gathered, dries, and is turned into the substance of the stone called amber. What, then, is signified by the surplus seed, if not the carnal corruption of sin? And its drying is that same sin's repentance. The corruption of the flesh, then, is gathered up and dried, when it is called back to memory together with repentance of mind. And then the softness of the seed is turned into the solidity of stone, since, from the compunction over the corruption of the flesh, humility of mind is born, which, when it touches the mind, presents the solidity of amber. So David, led by the consideration of his own iniquity into the compunction of humility, said: 'for I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you only have I sinned, and done evil before you, that you may be justified,' and so on.

Likewise, humility strengthens a man's spirit against the waves of pride and worldly vanity; hence it is likened to a certain little fish called the sea-urchin, which is indeed a small fish, scarcely half a foot in length, so named from clinging, since, although small of body, it is of admirable power; for the ship to which it clings, though the sea rages with great storms, nonetheless seems to stand as though rooted, and is not moved in any way. In the same way, humility of heart, although it makes a man of small esteem in his own eyes, nonetheless renders the ship of the mind unmoved by the stormy wind of pride and the waves of vanity. Ecclesiasticus: 'it will be made firm in him, and he shall not be bent; it shall sustain him, and he shall not be put to shame,' and so on.

Likewise, humility of mind renders it especially keen-sighted for the contemplation of divine brightness, just as pride, on the contrary, makes it dull. An example of this is (as Avicenna says) that the eagle's eye is small, and yet most keen-sighted for gazing at the light of the sun; while, on the contrary, the eye of the night-raven is large, and yet cannot look upon the light of the sun. The eye of the soul, then, is the mind, which, the smaller it becomes through humility, the keener-sighted it will be for contemplating the brightness of the divine light; but the more it swells through the esteem of pride, on the contrary, the more clouded it will be for contemplation. Hence: 'you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones.'

div.head: Cap. XXXVIII. Homines ad bonum peragendum inconstantes, Avibus in cavea clausis, mutationique Milverum esse similes edocetur.

cit.quote: The inconstant and fickle man is like a caged bird, which cannot rest, but always runs about its cage, now here, now there. Jeremiah: 'thus says the Lord to this people, who loved to move their feet, and did not rest, and did not please the Lord.'

Likewise, the lack of perseverance of certain people who begin fervently is likened to the changing of kites. For the kite, in its youth, does not seem to differ from birds of prey; but the longer it lives, the more it always shows itself increasingly degenerate; hence, according to Aristotle, there is a certain kind of kite that at first catches birds, then eventually scarcely catches flies and little worms, and at last perishes of hunger. Such are those who are good in their youth, and become worse in old age. And those become like the kite who, from the beginning of their conversion, catch birds, that is, begin to imitate the virtues of the saints, but, gradually failing, a little after their initial fervor, from that early ardor, scarcely catch flies, that is, scarcely manage to do the smallest good deeds, and at last, falling from grace, lose the spirit of devotion entirely. To such men the Apostle said: 'having begun in the spirit, are you now made perfect in the flesh?'

div.head: Cap. XXXIX. Ingratitudinis culpa filios quoque exheredari, insigni ipsius pellicani exemplo precise definitur.

cit.quote: ...the pelican, that is, the female bird, which, over her young killed by a serpent, first strikes her own breast to bring them back to life, and pours out her blood, by which discharge of blood she is so weakened that her chicks are forced to come out to feed on it. And those chicks, who, by natural affection, then feed her in turn once she has recovered her strength, she loves most tenderly and nourishes with care. But those who, as though degenerate, showed her no care at all, she casts out as ungrateful, and does not even allow them to live with her. From which it is clear that grateful children ought to be nourished and loved by their parents, while ungrateful ones can, even according to the laws, be driven off and disinherited by their parents. Hence this pelican also represents Christ, who said: 'I have become like the pelican of the wilderness'; for he brought back to life, with his own blood, the men he had created, as children in his own image and likeness, killed by the poison of sin from the ancient serpent. Hence he will at last admit to his own inheritance the grateful children, who nourish him in his poor, saying: 'come, you blessed.' The ungrateful and cruel, however, he will shut out, saying: 'depart, accursed,' and so on.

div.head: Cap. XL. Singularibus apum exemplis gulosi ocioque vacantes, dure esse plectendos, plene demonstratur.

cit.quote: The idle and the gluttonous should be sternly punished, and restrained from their gluttony. For bees (as the Philosopher says) severely punish the idle, and condemn to death those who stop working; and those with a large belly, who eat too much, they drive out or kill, if they can. So too the idle are chastised, and useless men condemned, even by God. Matthew: 'cast the useless servant into the outer darkness.' Likewise, gluttons, who serve not Christ the Lord but their own belly, will not only be driven from the kingdom, but will even be sentenced to the punishment of eternal death. For it will be said to the glutton, given over to the delights of the belly, that saying of Revelation: 'as much as he glorified himself and lived in luxury, give him so much torment and grief.'

Among bees, then, none is idle; but some fight, as though in an open battle, against other bees; some keep watch over provisions; others scout out future flowers; others suck wax from the flowers; others build cells, neither round nor square, with wondrous connection and evenness. And among such diverse tasks, none lies in wait for another's work; none seeks its living by plunder, but each acquires it by its own labor, gathering it among the grasses and flowers. In this they teach us to flee idleness, to labor each in the office or work suited to us, to lay no snares for another's work or advantage, to procure our living not by force of plunder but by our own labor, and likewise to love cleanliness in all our works — for it is among flowers and clean grasses that they gather their own harvest, as has been said.

div.head: Cap. XLI. Delphini exemplo notabili, innocentium persecutores belluisbelvis immaniores existere declaratur.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: The persecutors of the innocent are more savage than sea monsters. For Jorath says that dolphins can tell by smell whether a man who has drowned in the sea ever ate dolphin meat; and if he did, they eat him, but if he did not, they protect him from the bites of other fish, and carry him to the shore. Behold, then, that the monsters of the sea, though they avenge an injury received, do not persecute, but rather protect innocence; yet human cruelty is so great that it sometimes savagely harms those from whom it has never received any injury or harm at all. Hence Aesop says: 'the harmful harm the harmless, and find some cause for harming them.'

div.head: Cap. XLII. Inobedientie varietas, ipsiusque culpa gravitas, et denique quam acriter inobediens puniatur, apum exemplo aperitur.

cit.quote: Bees do not obey their king, seek vengeance for themselves, and kill themselves with the wound of their own sting. Much more, then, ought those who have been disobedient to the commands of the heavenly King to plant the sting of penance in their own hearts, and to extinguish that very fault of disobedience within themselves. And the greater the disobedience, the sharper the grief required to extinguish it. For the fault of disobedience has its own degrees. And an act of disobedience is graver wherever contempt is more dangerous: it is a graver sin not to obey God than not to obey man, unless God's command is included in man's precept; disobedience is also graver where a greater command is despised — for one command outranks another, since love of God is preferred to love of neighbor; disobedience is also graver where the person of the one commanding is despised, than where only his command is rejected. The sin of divination is to rebel, and, like the crime of idolatry, to refuse to submit; for idolatry and disobedience are alike in fault, since both arise from contempt of God — yet they are not equal, but idolatry is the graver.

div.head: Cap. XLIII. Invidie pravitas, invidiosique natura describitur, qui et Pavoni unico exemplo comparatur.

cit.quote: The envious man hides his goods, so that another may not benefit from them, even if he himself has no need of them. Hence he is like the peacock, which hides its own dung — which is highly medicinal — so that it can scarcely be found, as though begrudging man its usefulness. From this it is clear that envy excludes the sharing of good things. Hence Augustine says: 'take away envy, and what I have is yours; take away my envy, and what you have is mine.'

Likewise, this example also shows that envy is properly a fault of lesser men — for the peacock is inferior to man. Hence Job: 'envy kills the little one' — although envy can exist both between equals and between unequals. Hence Augustine says: 'envy is hatred of another's happiness — of those beneath us, lest they become our equals; of those above us, since we are not their equals; of our equals, since they are equal to us.' Hence Cain envied Abel's prosperity, Rachel envied Leah's fertility, Saul envied David's good fortune; through envy the fall of the world was brought about, and the death of Christ.

div.head: Cap. XLIIII. Hypocrita sthrutioni, cygno, aliisque nonnullis animantibus camparatur, taliumque exemplis ipsius malignitas hypocrisis rectissime demonstratur.

cit.quote: The hypocrite is likened to the ostrich, which (as Isidore says) has the body of a beast, but the feathers and beak of a bird, though, because of its weight, it cannot be lifted into the air. Hence (as Gregory says) the ostrich's feather is like the falcon's feather in color, but not in power; for it has the likeness of a feather, but lacks flight — it raises its wings as though to fly, yet does not rise from the ground; for it is clothed in sparse feathers, and weighed down by a great body. So the hypocrite is a beast, that is, secretly carnal in himself, yet displays the feathers and beak of a bird, since he displays the manners and words of a spiritual man. Hence his feather, that is, his outward appearance, resembles the feather of the falcon, that is, the manner of life of some perfect man; but he lacks its flight, that is, of contemplation, or love, by which the mind flies to God. Hence, although he raises his wings, that is, stretches his arm toward heaven, he nonetheless does not separate his heart from earth, that is, from earthly affection. For he has sparse feathers, that is, few virtuous affections, and has heavy flesh, that is, carnal appetites weighing down the soul, which do not allow him to rise on high to God.

Likewise, the hypocrite is likened to the swan. For the swan has, on the outside, a most white feather, entirely unmixed with blackness, but has black flesh within, tough to digest. So too the hypocrite, although outwardly he appears white, that is, innocent and clean, is nonetheless within black and dark with the blackness of baser things. Hence: 'woe to you, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, but within are full of hypocrisy and iniquity,' says the Lord. The hypocrite is also, toward his neighbor, not generous or kind, but hard of heart.

Likewise, hypocrites and double-minded men, who now seem to pursue spiritual things, now become entangled in earthly actions and affairs, are like certain fish, or animals, that dwell now in the water, now on land — hence they are called by Isidore 'doubtful' creatures, since they are by nature not only swimming but also walking creatures; and such are seals, crocodiles, beavers, and river-horses, and the like, which are generally fierce or malicious animals. So too such men seem doubtful — whether they belong to God or to the world — yet they are generally found, in the end, to be deceivers and wicked. Isaiah: 'every hypocrite is wicked and worthless.' Hence the Apostle: 'no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proven himself.'

div.head: Cap. XLV. Proximi odium, in anima mortis aculeum infigere, Apum exemplo edocetur.

cit.quote: Anger or hatred toward one's neighbor takes away the sweetness of the bee's gentleness, and even the life of the mind. An example of this is that bees, when they fight, become useless for making honey afterward, or die soon after, as Aristotle says, especially if they have driven their sting in fully, since it is impossible to drive the sting in fully without the intestine coming out with it. Likewise, he who hates his neighbor, and, angered, strives to harm or wound him — at least in intention — drives a sting into his own soul; and from that very anger or hatred of mind, like the bee from its own sting, he loses the honey, that is, the sweetness of gentleness, and, casting out the intestine of charity, loses the life of his soul. Hence it is written: 'he who hates his brother is a murderer' — namely, the killer of his own soul.

div.head: Cap. XLVI. Hominem exterius nequaquam fore iudicandum, unica ipsius accipitris similitudine palam sit.

cit.quote: A man's spirit ought not to be judged by outward, fleshly appearance, since he who is sometimes despised in body is great in virtue. An example of this indeed appears in the hawk. For the hawk is a royal bird, armed more with spirit than with claws; and so, whatever nature denies it in bodily size, it makes up for in strength of spirit and boldness, as Isidore says. So too, sometimes in many men, whatever appears despicable in the body — whether from a defect of nature or from some accidental infirmity — is made up for and compensated in the mind, whether by natural cunning or by the special gift of divine grace; for which reason the Lord also said: 'do not judge according to appearance' — for such a judgment is especially rash before God, since men see what is visible, but God looks upon the heart.

div.head: Cap. XLVII. Tentationis pugna, que ex compunctionis lachrymis crebro oriri comportum est, orationis fervore sedatur : quod Merguli animaliumque aquatilium exemplo indicitur.

cit.quote: Tears of compunction are followed by the battle of temptation, against which the cry of prayer must be set. An example of this appears in the diving-bird, of which Isidore says that, often diving with its head into the water, it recognizes the signs of coming winds beneath the waves, and, foreseeing a coming storm, flees to the shore with a cry. Hence it is a most certain sign of an approaching storm when diving-birds flee to the shore crying out. He, then, dives his head into the water, who, stung with compunction in his mind, turns to weep over his own sins. But the wicked spirit, fearing to lose him, soon raises against him the gust of temptation, so that he grows cold from the fervor of compunction; but the cautious and provident mind, when it senses the rising storm of temptation, at once flees back to the shore of humility with the cry of prayer, mindful of what the Lord said: 'pray, that you do not enter into temptation.'

Likewise, the water of tears nourishes the soul of the penitent, and in it extinguishes the burning heat of temptations and vices. An example of this is found in water creatures, which, according to Avicenna, draw water to themselves for two different reasons. For some of them take water into their belly only as a kind of nourishment, not by way of breathing, like sea shellfish. Penitents are like these, who are fed by the water of tears, as though by a kind of food, according to that saying: 'my tears have been my bread day and night.' On which verse Cassiodorus says that weeping is the food of souls, the strengthening of the senses, the absolution of sins, the refreshment of minds, the washing away of faults. But there are some water creatures that take in water by way of breathing, that is, by drawing it in and expelling it, so as to release inner heat, to expel excess warmth; and those who weep are like these, so that the water of their tears may extinguish the burning heat of temptation. Psalm: 'we have passed through fire' — that is, the burning heat of temptation — 'and through water' — that is, of compunction and devotion — 'and you have brought us out into a place of refreshment.'

div.head: Cap. XLVIII. Quando laus divina clarior at laudabilior existat, cicade exemplo delcaratur.

cit.quote: Divine praise is the more resplendent and praiseworthy, the more it proceeds from a fervent and beautiful mind — which is shown by the example of the cicada, which, in the very midst of the summer heat, when other creatures are, as it were, on fire, gives forth a song the clearer the purer the air it then draws in. So too the voice of divine praise is rendered the clearer and more acceptable, the more fervently and purely the spirit that sings or shapes it. Hence the praise and hymn of the three young men, with which they praised God in the furnace, is commended with great acclaim, since in the young men it shows the purity of heart, and in the furnace, the affection and fervor of devotion. Daniel: 'they walked in the midst of the flame, praising and blessing the Lord.'

div.head: Cap. XLIX. Variis sacre Scripture exemplis, Delphinique similitudine choreas fore fugiendas lucide demonstratur.

cit.quote: The disordered play and dancing leaps of men are commonly a forewarning, or a cause, of an evil outcome — an example of which is shown in dolphins, of which Isidore says that nothing in the sea is swifter than they; for they often leap right over passing ships; yet their leaping and playing signals an approaching storm, and something similar happens with human games too. For the people of Israel played in the wilderness, but, once the game was over, suffered a great slaughter of their own. After the game of the young men of David and Ishbosheth, too, a grave war followed. So too, after Samson's playing, the destruction of the Philistines followed. And again, after the girl's dancing, John's head was cut off. Chrysostom also says that where there is dancing, there is the devil; nor did God give us feet for this, that we should leap about like camels, but that we should form a chorus with the angels. In dances demons rejoice, and the ministers of demons exult.

div.head: Cap. L. Luxuriosi, prolis conceptionem in muliere impedimentum inferentes, Pavoni comparantur.

cit.quote: The lustful man, who strives to hinder conception in a woman, so that he can indulge his lust more safely or for longer, is like the peacock; for the peacock is a bird that does not care for its offspring. Hence the male pursues the female, so as to find where she lays her eggs and break them, so that he can devote himself all the more to lust. Onan, the second son of Judah, is said to have done this: going in to his brother's wife, he spilled his seed on the ground, so that children would not be born in his brother's name, and so the Lord struck him down for doing a detestable thing. It is not believed, however, that he did this out of lust, but rather out of the bitterness of envy, since he could not have children by his own wife.

div.head: Cap. LI. Malorum hominum insidia ex columbarum variis similitudinibus, pluvium auctoritate Doctorum approbatis, patefiunt.

cit.quote: Wicked men are sometimes likened to doves, according to that saying: 'Ephraim has become like a deceived dove.'

First, indeed, by reason of deceit; for a dove is found that is trained to deceive other birds. For she joins herself to others, and leads them to the net, and, as it were, enters the fowler's net first, and lets herself be entangled with them; and so, under the guise of friendship, while luring them to feed, she draws them to destruction. In this literal way, indeed, certain deceitful gamblers act, who, playing a game with certain unwary men, place themselves in a partnership, sharing in the gain to be made, and, under the guise of partnership, lead them into the hands of their own true confederates, and sometimes let themselves be beaten and stripped along with them, until, through them, those unwary men who were not true partners lose all their money. Likewise, the confederates of certain highway robbers act the same way, joining travelers and, under the guise of company, leading them into the hands of those who will rob them, and sometimes even letting themselves be robbed by others along with them, so that no one notices the trick; and many other deceivers do things similar to these.

Second, by reason of curiosity. For the dove is curious, since, sitting on a tree, she looks all around at which branch she might climb or fly to, and, as though deliberating, turns her neck this way and that; but often, while she is still deliberating, before she takes flight, an arrow pierces her, and so she never completes her flight — since what she could have done sooner, she did not do at the time she could, as Gregory says. So it happens to those sinners who, although they resolved to leave the branch of the tree, that is, the act or the awareness of some crime, and decided to move themselves through penance to a better branch, that is, a better state, nonetheless deliberate so long, procrastinating, and, looking about at the difficulties, delay in fulfilling their resolve, that the arrow of death, or of divine vengeance, suddenly pierces them, often not only in body but even in soul. And so it is advised: 'do not delay in converting to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you.'

Third, by reason of human humility. For in Syria (as Ambrose says) a dove is taught to be a bearer of letters, a messenger from one province to another. For a letter is tied under her wing, and, once released this way, she lifts herself into the air, and so returns to her own home, just as she was taught; but sometimes, discovered by enemies, she is struck by an arrow, and killed for the sake of the letter. So then, an unlearned or simple man is like the dove, to whom the letter is entrusted to carry, when he undertakes to expound the sacred scriptures in preaching to others; and the letter is tied under his arm, when preaching is imposed on him as a duty — who, carrying the letters, lifts himself into the air, and sometimes attempts to expound to others what he himself does not understand; and unless humility brings him back to his own home more quickly, the cunning enemy kills him with the arrow of error.

div.head: Cap. LII. Vitam solitariam Monachis necessariam esse, unita piscium similitudine confirmatur.

cit.quote: Monks and solitaries are likened to fish. For Ambrose says that there is a great closeness and kinship between fish and water; for they cannot live long outside the water. But what water is to fish, the cell is to monks and solitaries. Hence blessed Anthony says, as it is found in the Lives of the Fathers, that just as fish, if delayed too long on dry land, quickly die, so too monks who linger outside their cell, or dwell too long among worldly lives, are undone in their resolve for quiet. Hence it is also said, in Isaiah: 'the fish rot without water,' that is, monks without their cell.

div.head: Cap. LIII. Quantopere mortis, iudiciique memoria extremi nobis profit, hic galli, Pavonis, nonnullorumque animantium exemplis clarissimum fit.

cit.quote: The fearful memory, or consideration, of death and judgment, ought to be always before our eyes, as shown by the cock. For the cock, fearing the eagle and the hawk, plunderers of the land, which have keen sight, lowers one eye toward its food, and directs the other toward the air, so that it may know the approach of the eagle or the vulture, as Pliny says. The eagle signifies Christ, and the hawk signifies death. The holy man, signified by the cock, ought then to fear the coming of both — that is, of Christ to judgment, and of death to destruction. Hence, even while nourishing his body, he ought to fear the destruction of the body, and turn the eye of death toward that very destruction of the body, and also look toward the coming of the strict judge with fearful consideration. Hence Jerome says, speaking of the day of judgment: 'as often as I consider that day, my heart trembles; for whether I eat, or drink, or do anything else, that terrible trumpet always seems to sound in my ears: rise, you dead, come to judgment.'

Likewise, the memory of death brings to nothing all the glory of the peacock's beauty — which is shown by the example of the peacock. For the peacock, when it beholds the beauty of its own feathers, raises its tail, and spreads it in a circle around its head like a net or a bow; but, while doing this, if it looks down and sees the ugliness of its feet, it blushes deeply, and, forgetting its own beauty, lowers and puts down its tail. The foot, then, by which the body touches the ground, signifies man's death, through which the body returns to the earth. Whoever, then, glories in some bodily beauty, let him look at the foot of the body, that is, its end; for if he considers well what the body will be like after death, sorrow, rather than glory, will befall him. Hence it is said: 'why are you proud, earth and ashes?'

Likewise, the memory of death directs the soul, and defends it from temptations; for birds and fish steer themselves with their tail, and draught animals and oxen defend themselves from flies with their tail. So too men direct their lives, and drive off temptations, by the memory of death. 'Ask the beasts, and the birds of the air too, and they will tell you; and the fish of the sea will declare it to you.'

div.head: Cap. LIIII. Mentis munditiem iugiter ab homine custodiendam fere exemplo suo apes ostendere docetur.

cit.quote: ...bees show. For there is a marvelous cleanliness among bees, since they leave no filth in their work; for they carry outside whatever waste they produce within, gathering it together in one place and then casting it out, since they cannot bear any stench at all. So too a man ought to keep his works clean, that is, free from the filth of sin, and, when it happens that his conscience is polluted within by the uncleanness of some sin, he ought to cast out that filth diligently through penance, so that his soul harbors the stench of no sin within. James: 'casting off all uncleanness.'

div.head: Cap. LV. Christum nonnunquam percussionis flagello, interdum etiam rerum temporalium subtractione nostram expellere ignaviam, Aquila, accipitrisque exemplis demonstratur.

cit.quote: Negligence and sloth of soul are sometimes driven out by the scourge of divine punishment, and sometimes by the withdrawal of temporal substance, as is shown by the example of the eagle. For the eagle (as Ambrose says) prompts her grown young to fly, flying over them; and if they are slow to leave, she strikes them with her beak, withdraws their food, and so compels them to leave. So too the eagle, king of birds — that is, Christ, who is King of kings and Lord of lords — prompts her young, that is, the men created by her, or her faithful, reborn by baptism, to fly, that is, to love God fervently, both by words and by examples. For love of God and of neighbor are the two wings of the soul, by which it flies to eternal life; or she prompts them to fly, that is, to live and act diligently and well; for it is not by places, but by good actions, that we tend toward God, according to Augustine. She herself flies above them, so as to teach them to fly by her example, since she instructs them by her own example toward good action. Hence: 'like the eagle prompting her young to fly, and hovering over them.' But when she finds them sluggish to leave, whether the nest of sin or the nest of idleness, she strikes them with the beak of the scourge, since, by her just sentence, she strikes them with the dart of adversity; from whom she also withdraws food, since, their riches taken away, she sometimes brings them to the very depths of temporal want; and these, stung on one side by the goad of adversity, and, on the other, humiliated by the nakedness of poverty, are at least drawn from the nest of their sloth by the compulsion, or the confusion, of their circumstance. This the prodigal son himself well showed, once reduced to the utmost poverty, saying: 'how many hired servants in my father's house have bread in abundance, while I here perish with hunger.'

Likewise, prelates ought to correct their negligent and lazy subjects with discipline and fasting, so as to spur them to labor. An example of this correction appears in hawks, of which Basil says that, when their young are fit to fly, they withdraw their food, strike them with their beak, and drive them from the nest. This (as Ambrose and Bede say) they do not do out of cruelty, but so as to train them for hunting, lest they perhaps grow sluggish through idleness and neglect to seek their own food. Subjects, then, ought to be driven by their prelate, as young hawks are by the parent hawk, from the nest of idleness or negligence — not only by the striking of words, but even by the withdrawal of food, so that they eat their bread not in idleness, but through the labor of work. The Apostle: 'if anyone will not work, let him not eat.' She does not eat the bread of idleness.

div.head: Cap. LVI. Quid religiosus, ut Deo sit gratus, creatori suo offerre debeat, paris turturum, columbarumque significatione, et activa contemplativaque vite perfectione recte explanatur.

cit.quote: A man of religion ought to offer his whole self to God — his body through chastity, and his soul through charity. Hence, in the Law of Moses, concerning birds, the turtledove and the dove were commanded to be offered; for chastity is signified in the turtledove, but charity in the dove. But the turtledove, when prescribed for offering in the Law, was sometimes plucked, as is clear in the purification of a woman after childbirth, in Leviticus, where it was commanded that the poor offer a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons — where note, as to the letter, that it does not say two young turtledoves, as it says two young pigeons, since young pigeons are always to be found, but young turtledoves are not always to be found; nor did it say a pair of doves, as it says a pair of turtledoves, since the dove is a lustful bird, and so God did not wish it offered in his sacrifice; the turtledove, however, is a chaste bird. A pair of turtledoves, however, is commanded to be offered to God, so as to signify a twofold chastity in man, namely of mind and of body. Or because chastity requires two things, namely continence of the flesh, and humility of heart. Hence it was not only the abstinence of the flesh that pleased Christ in the Blessed Virgin, but also the humility of her heart, according to her own words: 'because he has regarded,' and so on.

For, as Gregory says, there is no chastity of the flesh that humility of mind does not commend. And hence it is, as the same Gregory says, that when the mind is touched by pride even over that very continence, Almighty God, destroying that pride, often allows it to fall into the uncleanness of deed; indeed Augustine even says: 'I dare to say that it is expedient for the continent to fall, so that they may be humbled in that very thing in which they exalt themselves. For what does it profit a man, if he has continence, yet pride governs him?' The two young doves, however, signify a twofold affection of those who love out of charity, namely love of God and of neighbor. Some, however, say that those who pursue the contemplative life offer the turtledove, which is a solitary bird, while those who pursue the active life offer the dove, which is a bird that flies in flocks. And both are offered in pairs, and both are said to have moaning in place of song: they are offered in pairs, indeed, because the contemplative life ought to have a double eye, and the active life a double action — for the contemplative ought to have one eye, with which he contemplates heavenly things to desire them, and another with which he looks upon temporal things to despise them.

Likewise, the active man ought to exercise himself toward himself, for his own correction, and toward his neighbor, for his edification and support. Both lives, moreover, are comforted in this valley of misery by a twofold groaning. For the contemplative groans out of love, from desire for the heavenly homeland, and out of devotion, through consideration of the Lord's passion. The active man groans out of compunction for his own sins. Psalm: 'every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears.'

Likewise, out of compassion for sin, or for the miseries of others. Jeremiah: 'who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people?'

div.head: Cap. LVII. Otium precipue ab hominibus ad male agendum accensis, nunquam non fugiendum fore, struthionis exemplo aperitur.

cit.quote: Some lawful or non-dangerous occupation should be given to men who are tempted, or inflamed to do evil, so that, kept busy with it, they may avoid worse things. And indeed the nature of the ostrich shows an example of this: nature gave it, according to Avicenna, the property of laying very large eggs with a very tough shell, so that the heat, occupied in their generation, may be tempered within them, lest, inflamed, the bird die more quickly. So too, for the man who is much inflamed — that is, violently kindled to sin, or strongly tempted — great and hard eggs, that is, strong and difficult exercises or duties, ought to be imposed, so that, through this difficult occupation, the fire of those vices and the heat of temptations may cool. Hence: 'send him to your work, that he not be idle; for idleness has taught much wickedness.'

div.head: Cap. LVIII. Pulcherrimo Aquile exemplo fidem at charitatem in operibus meritoriis omnimode necessarias existere breviter edocetur.

cit.quote: Meritorious works cannot come forth from the soul without faith and love, which is shown by the example of the eagle, which is said to place two precious stones called 'aetites' in her nest, without which she cannot give birth. These two precious stones, then, placed in the eagle's nest so that she can bring forth her young, are two virtues, namely faith and charity; unless these are in the nest of the mind — that is, faith in the intellect, and charity in the affection — no work acceptable to God can be brought forth. For without faith it is impossible to please God, as is said in Hebrews, and faith works through love.

div.head: Cap. LIX. Quo pacto nonnullorum opera infructuosa remaneant, milui similitudine exprimitur.

cit.quote: Works that are remiss and soft, even though laborious, are nonetheless of little fruit — which appears through the example of kites. The kite, though it is a bird patient of labor, nonetheless has a soft flight; hence it is called 'milvus' as it were flying softly, since it is borne through the air on a soft and almost motionless wing, and seems to stir the air with a light touch, seeking food here and there, and, looking down at the ground, circles softly through the air, and loses, with a plaintive cry, the hunger it endures. A man is like the kite, then, who is soft and lukewarm in his work, who, although he suffers much labor over a small amount of food — that is, over a small work — his lukewarmness and softness nonetheless hinder the reward of the work; and so it happens that, while he circles about a great deal and produces little fruit, he goes about, like a kite suffering hunger, always as a beggar and always complaining. Hence Solomon says: 'he who is soft and slack in his work is brother to him who wastes his own works.'

div.head: Cap. LX. Quam pauperis ac divitis sit exitus dispar, accipitris, gallineque unico exemplo monstratur.

cit.quote: Just as the poor are despised in this world, so they are glorified in the other, but the rich, the opposite. For a young hen, in the house of a rich man, is held cheap, so that if she enters the house, she is shamefully thrown out; but the hawk, or falcon, is set honorably in the house upon a perch, and carefully fed with choice morsels; yet if the hen dies, she is carried before the Lord with great reverence and light, while the hawk, after death, is thrown onto the dungheap. So too the poor and simple are held cheap and pressed down in the world, but after death are carried with honor by angels to the table of the King; while, conversely, the rich are honored here, but after death are cast onto the dungheap of hell. Luke: 'the beggar died, and was carried into Abraham's bosom; and the rich man also died, and was buried in hell.'

div.head: Cap. LXI. Iurgia inter domesticos serentes a societate penitus seiungendos esse, Apum exemplo comprobatur.

cit.quote: Those who sow quarrels among members of a household must be altogether cut off from fellowship, or removed entirely from the company of the community — which bees show by their own example; for (as the Philosopher says) bees mortally attack, or entirely drive from themselves, other bees that disturb the peace and seek to steal their honey. For those are like such bees who, by their own restlessness or divisiveness, sever or destroy the peace of their neighbors.

Likewise, those who strive by some malicious art to snatch away the sweet company or services of friends, which are signified by honey. Such men, then, rightly deserve to be struck either with the sharp stings of words, or with the sharp goads of correction, and, besides, to be driven away by all as pestilent. The Apostle: 'would that they who trouble you were even cut off.'

div.head: Cap. LXII. Peccati, quod profecto natura vitium existit, perversitas quanta sit, ex Ephimera piscis, cuiusdamque Delphini ac Turturis marini natura, haud dubie percipitur.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Sin is likened to the ephemeral fish, which is born without coupling, of which Iorach says that it dies three hours after the day on which it is born. For the day that illuminates the soul is penance, through which we look toward grace, and the three hours of such a day, after which the ephemeral fish dies, are the three parts of penance, through which sin is extinguished, namely contrition, confession, and satisfaction. But that the ephemeral fish is generated without coupling, that is, from putrefaction, signifies that sin, contrary to the order of nature, is contracted from the corruption of appetite. Hence Augustine says that sin is not a nature, but the vice of a nature desiring what does not belong to its own order.

Likewise, sin, though it delights beforehand, afterward tears and kills the mind. And so it is likened to a certain kind of dolphin that is found in the Nile: for there are dolphins there with an iron-plated back, which kill crocodiles by cutting open their bellies from within. The dolphin, then, tearing the crocodile's belly not with its front breast but with its iron-plated back, represents mortal sin, which does not infect at first, that is, at the beginning, but afterward tears and destroys the sinner's mind. Proverbs: 'it enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent.'

Likewise, sin, existing only in the affection, as with the sea turtledove, can be mortal — an example of which appears in the sea turtledove, of which Ambrose says that if anyone tramples it even when dead, it drives a poisonous and deadly sting into him. For what is a dead turtledove, but a mortal fault? If anyone clings to it with the foot of affection, without doubt the guilt drives a deadly sting into him.

div.head: Cap. LXIII. Peccantium peccatorum omnium capitalium varietas, gravitas, et malignitas, ex equi fluvialis, murenula, et serpentis, canis quoque maris aquilarum, corui, cygni, ac cynomea, vespertilionis, proprietatibus quamplurimis clare demonstratur.

cit.quote: ...it is said of fish, which are so naturally gluttonous and eager for food that they do not notice the snare or the hook. But what nature does in fish, depraved desire does in men, namely that they attend so avidly to the delight of sin that they do not notice the devil's hook, or snare, which drags them toward the pain of punishment. Hence it is said that just as fish are caught by the hook, so men are caught in an evil time.

Likewise, sinners are like river-horses, which the Nile river produces, and which are so named because they resemble land-horses in back and mane. These remain in the waters by day, but at night, going across the land, they graze on the crops. Those, then, are like these horses who, placed in the day of prosperity, living beneath the waters of delights, become given over to pleasure, but, led out at the night of adversity and poverty, become robbers and harmful. Hence they live well at no time, for whom either the abundance of pleasure or the want brought on by rapacity becomes an occasion for evil.

Likewise, the sinner cannot beget, that is, cannot do a meritorious work, unless he puts off sin — an example of which is found in the eel and the serpent. For the eel (as Isidore says) is found only of female sex; it couples with the serpent, and from it begets another eel; but (as the same author says) the serpent puts off its venom before coupling with the eel, but takes it up again after coupling; on account of which the eel is neither harmed by the serpent, nor does it beget anything venomous or serpent-like, but something like itself by nature. The venomous serpent, then, is like the man infected with sin, who, if he did not put off the venom of sin, would not beget a good eel, that is, a good and meritorious action, since otherwise he could not join himself with its mother, that is, with grace or charity, which is the mother of every good work. This, however, is not to be imitated, but rather detested — that after coupling with the eel the serpent takes up its venom again, that is, that after receiving grace someone returns to sin. Peter: 'the dog returned to its own vomit,' and 'the sow that was washed, to her wallowing in the mire.'

Likewise, certain sinners are like sea-dogs. For just as the dog is an animal that bites and is harmful on land, so too the dogfish is a fearsome fish in the sea. Hence (as Ambrose says) dogs are to be guarded against both at sea and on land. Such are sinners, who are harmful and dangerous to others not only on land, that is, in the tranquility of peace, but also at sea, that is, in the turmoil of war and strife. The Apostle speaks of these: 'beware of dogs, beware of evil workers.' Or land-dogs are like robbers, who do harm on land; but sea-dogs are like pirates, who do harm at sea. Hence the Apostle: 'in dangers on land, in dangers at sea.'

Likewise, sinners are likened to the eagle. For there is a certain kind of eagle that snatches its prey in the air, and all birds generally fear this kind. Such an eagle represents pride; for the proud snatch on high, since they strive to seize and usurp for themselves the height of glory and honor, which is owed to God alone. Hence they themselves snatch from God what God has reserved for himself, namely glory, according to that saying: 'I will not give my glory to another.' All birds — that is, all spiritual men — ought to fear and flee this eagle, that is, pride, since Augustine says: whatever other wickedness is practiced in evil works, so that they may be done, pride alone lies in wait even for good works, so that they may perish. But there are certain eagles that snatch on land. To these the avaricious are likened, who attend only to earthly gain, and sometimes even violently seize it from others. But some eagles snatch in the water. To these the lustful are likened, who immerse themselves in the waters of pleasure. And Aristotle says that such an eagle fears the vulture, and when it sees it coming, flees to the water, from which, if it came out, the vulture would seize it. Such an eagle has one foot broad, like a goose's, with which it steers itself in the water, and the other divided, with very sharp talons, with which it seizes its prey. But just as this eagle fears the vulture, so the lustful man fears the one who rebukes and detracts him, or the vulture — that is, death seizing him, or the scourge of divine punishment — which, if he wishes to escape it, he must flee back to the water of penance. The broad foot for swimming in the water is the disposition toward the delight of lust. But the foot with talons for seizing the food of prey is the appetite for the delights of gluttony, and both feet are found in the given over to pleasure.

Likewise, sinners are likened to crows. First, because crows are noisy, and vary their voices in different ways. This fits the proud, who command with shouting, blaspheme, chatter, quarrel, and revile, and so form various discordant voices in many ways. Second, because crows are deceitful, thievishly seizing and hiding things. This fits the avaricious, who snatch away others' goods by deceit and fraud. 'Like a sharpened razor, you have worked deceit.' Third, because crows are unclean, that is, settling on corpses and seeking food from foul things. This fits the lustful, who delight in the foul and unclean works of the flesh. Isaiah: 'from their corpses a stench shall rise.'

Likewise, one may be likened to the swan. For the swan, at the approach of death, with a feather fixed into its brain, sings, and, contrary to the custom of all animals, gives forth song instead of groaning — as Ambrose says: for the feather is then fixed into the brain when consent of the heart is given to the wicked suggestion of sin, and then the soul dies more completely, when the sin itself is carried out in deed. Those, then, sing after the manner of the swan at the moment of death, who rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst of things.

Likewise, sinners are likened to the 'cynomya,' that is, to dog-flies, of which the Psalm speaks, saying: 'he spoke, and the dog-fly came, and gnats, in all their coasts.' For such a fly is large in body, and broad in belly, and of weaker flight than other flies.

Likewise, it is greatly pricking, ulcerating, and corrosive to the flesh, and moreover it is a great bloodsucker. Those, then, may be called large in body who wish to be magnified in carnal things; hence proud men are compared to giants: 'from the beginning, when the proud giants perished,' and so on. Those broad in belly are the gluttonous, who, filling their belly, widen and stretch it out. Those of weak flight are the slothful and listless, who do little and rare good works. The foul are the lustful, who feed on and take great delight in the stenches of carnal vices; the stinging are the wrathful; but the corrosive and ulcerating are the detractors and envious. Isidore: 'the fly passes over sound flesh, and settles on the sore; so do demons and detractors.' The bloodsuckers, however, are the avaricious and usurers, who, sweetly despoiling the poor, suck their blood. Proverbs: 'the leech has two daughters, saying, give, give.'

Likewise, sinners are like bats. For bats, as the Gloss says on that verse of Isaiah, 'in that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his images of gold, which he made for himself to worship, to the moles and the bats,' and the rest, flee the light. And in this respect they signify the lustful, who seek hiding places and dark corners. Job: 'the eye of the adulterer watches for darkness.'
Likewise, they lick dust, and in this respect they signify the avaricious, who love earthly things. Psalm: 'his enemies shall lick the earth.'

Likewise, they suck oil from lamps, and in this they signify the envious, who strive to strip away the favor of good men by detracting them with their mouths; for by the oil, grace is signified, and by the lamps, illustrious men. Envious men, then, suck oil from lamps as it were, when, by detracting an illustrious man with their mouth, they strive to strip away his favor. Hence the envious man rejoices at another's misfortune, and grieves at another's good, according to that saying, 'the envious man wastes away at another's rich fortunes'; so, then, he tries to strip good men of their favor by secretly detracting them.
Likewise, they hide by day in the cracks of walls, and so signify the proud and the tyrants, who search out malicious and hidden ways by which they can harm others.
Likewise, by day they are as blind as moles, and signify the wrathful, in whom the eye of reason is blinded by excessive fury.

Likewise, they are of a very cold nature. Hence blood of the bat smeared on the eyelids does not let hair grow there (as Constantine says), which is believed to happen from the coldness closing the pores; in which it signifies the slothful, who become cold in spirit, so that the hair of the eyes — that is, the good desires of the mind — do not grow forth in them.

div.head: Cap. LXIIII. Vera penitentia quam plurima bona recensentur, qua ex Phenicis, Merguli, et denique Trocte piscis natura lucidissimis exemplis eliciuntur.

cit.quote: The fervor and humility of penance revive the dead sinner, which is shown by the example of the phoenix. For the phoenix is a bird which (according to the Philosopher) after it has lived three hundred, or five hundred, years, when it senses its own decline, builds a nest of aromatic woods, so dry that they can be kindled by a warm wind; and once these are kindled, it enters the nest of its own accord, and is burned to ashes among the burning wood. And from this ash, within three days, a little worm is born, which, gradually receiving feathers, is transformed into a bird. It is a most beautiful bird, very like a peacock in its feathers, loving solitude, and seeking its food from clean fruits. So the sinner, after he has lived long in his sins, and comes to recognize the decline of his life or state, whether through fear of death or through some adversity, ought, out of consideration of the offense, out of contemplation of divine justice, and moreover out of fear of hell and the uncertainty of death, to build, as it were from aromatic woods, a nest of the mind; and these considerations ought to be so dry, that is, so strong, that the breath of the Holy Spirit can easily kindle the mind's nest; then, willing and swift, the penitent should enter into his own heart, and, placed in the aforesaid fears, burning himself with fervent compunction, be reduced to the ash of humility; for from this humility, within the three days of penance — namely contrition, confession, satisfaction — a new worm will be born, unclean, and a humble spirit, which will gradually receive the feathers of the virtues, and be transformed into a complete bird, that is, into a perfect and contemplative man, having the beauty of the sight of holy contemplation, likewise having the variety of colors in its feathers, that is, the variety of virtues and manifold grace, loving the solitude of holy prayer, and seeking the clean food of sacred reading, or clean action.

Likewise, penance frees, and defends against the temptations or deceptions of demons, which is clear through the example of the diving-bird. For when birds of prey pursue diving-birds, the latter, fleeing to the water, are freed by the benefit of diving under. The birds of prey attack the diving-bird just when demons, by tempting, strive to entrap a man's soul; but if the soul flees to the waters of penance, and, humbling itself, submerges itself in them, it is freed from the deceit of demons. Psalm: 'you have crushed the heads of dragons' — that is, the temptations of demons — 'in the waters' — namely, of penance.

Likewise, penance makes man's works to be like the trout, alive and meritorious. An example of this appears in the various larger fish called trout, which lay their eggs in the water, and entrust them to the water's care; and the water, like a gentle mother receiving them, gives them life, and forms fish from them. So the good works of men are like the eggs of trout, which come forth in the water only when they are done in true penance, and from that very water, that is, from the tearful and compunctious tears of penance, become living — that is, freely given and fruitful, that is, meritorious.

div.head: Cap. LXV. Penitentes in eorum vera penitentia quales esse debeant, multorum animantium in terris ac in aquis variabilis nature, pracipueque coturnicis, ciconie, at turdi similitudinibus non paucis artificiose palam fit.

cit.quote: Penitents who live lukewarm and idle easily return to the putrefaction of sin — an example of which appears in fish. For when the water in which fish live is not stirred or renewed, it quickly turns to putrefaction, and the fish in it are corrupted. Likewise, those who are in the water of penance, if they are not renewed, and not stirred by the diligence of good works, are easily corrupted by temptations, and infected again by the putrefaction of their sins. The Apostle: 'be renewed in the spirit of your mind.'

Likewise, penitents change their character by the virtue of penance. Hence they are likened to certain animals of which Ambrose says that they have a contrary nature on land and in water, as is clear with the lion. For the lion, though terrible on land, is nonetheless gentle in the sea, that is, the sea-lion fish. In which it is signified that the water of the sea, that is, bitter penance, transforms and converts an unyielding and fierce man into a gentle one.

Likewise the frog, which is a hideous thing in the marshes, is nonetheless lovely in the water, and provides food for almost everything. In which it is signified that the water of penance makes hideous and impious men most pleasing, and accepted above others.
Likewise, the weasel's smell, heavy on land, is sweet in the water; in which it is understood that those who stink from a bad reputation become, in the waters of penance, fragrant through grace.
Likewise, the hare is a timid animal on land, but a formidable one at sea, since the washing of penance makes fainthearted and fearful men magnanimous and most brave.

The wolf is a ravening animal on land, but a powerless animal in the water; hence the lamb has no need to fear these wolves. So too, through penance, men who were fierce and rapacious become kind and merciful.

Likewise, the pig is an unclean animal on land, but a clean animal in the sea. Hence sea-pigs (as Ambrose says) are pleasing even to the Jews, who nonetheless do not eat land-pigs. In which it is signified that the water of penance cleanses every uncleanness of guilt, and so those who were unclean through the sin of lust likewise become clean, in the waters of penance, through continence.

Likewise, the land scorpion strikes and injects venom; the sea-scorpion, however, does not strike, but restores. In which it is signified that detractors and the envious, who strike others from behind, are transformed in the water of penance, and become benefactors.
Likewise, the land-crow has hard flesh, but the sea-crow has tender flesh. In which it is signified that the sea of penance makes a dry and hard heart soft, devout, and pious.
Hence penance makes a heart of stone and rigidity into a heart of flesh and flexibility; for it makes a proud man humble, a cruel and savage man gentle, and so on.
