Likewise, examples of quail show what penitents ought to be like. The quail, crossing the sea, when it grows weary, descends onto the water, and, raising one wing, makes a sail of it. Quail also fear the hawk, and do not rise from the ground as long as they see it. So too the sinner, crossing through the sea of this world, when he feels himself weary from the weight of sin, ought, if he wishes to escape, to humble himself and descend to the water of penance, and to hold himself in that water, that is, in penance, with one wing, namely fear, but to raise the other, namely hope, upward toward God, since just as he ought to fear on account of justice, so he ought to hope on account of mercy; and this wing of hope will be the sail leading him to pious works. But the penitent sinner ought especially and fearfully to beware the hawk, that is, the severity of the devil, since the devil rages most fiercely against a man precisely when he perceives that the man has rebelled against him. And so, when the tempted penitent notices his presence, he ought to remain on the ground, that is, to hold himself in humility. For humility alone (as blessed Anthony said) is what escapes the devil's snares. Or: he ought not rise from the ground, that is, from humble prayer.

Likewise, quail run very swiftly over land, love their own kind, and call to one another by crying out — as Ambrose says. Those, then, run very swiftly over the land who, although placed on earth, love heavenly things vehemently; for he who loves more fervently runs more swiftly, and arrives sooner, as Bernard says. And he loves his own kind who loves any man whatsoever. For, by the sharing of a common nature, many men are one man, as Porphyry says. Where, then, there is unity of nature, there ought also to be unity of charity and concord together. Every man, too, ought diligently to seek out his neighbor, whom he perceives to have perished by straying, whether by crying out to him with the voice of preaching or exhortation, or by crying out on his behalf to God with the fervor of earnest prayer.

Likewise, quail have, for their most pleasing food, poisonous seeds: for they eat hellebore, which is deadly to others; and quail also suffer, like man, from the falling sickness. Now the poisonous seeds of hellebore are, as it were, the opportunities and occasions for sinning, on which if the penitent feeds, that is, if he takes delight in them, he will suffer the falling sickness, that is, the relapse of sin.

Likewise, penitents ought to be like the stork: first, indeed, because the stork is skillful at purging itself. For when it senses itself weighed down by food, it gathers seawater into its beak, which it sends down to its inner parts, and so softens hardened food, and, cleansing its intestines, casts out what is excessive. Now just as excessive or bad food weighs down the stomach, so too sin weighs down or straitens the soul. Whoever, then, desires to purge himself ought to have seawater, that is, ought to be so purged within that he pours out bitter tears; which it is necessary that he also gather with his beak, just as he sends it to his intestines to cleanse the belly — that is, that, stricken with compunction, he should so confess his sins with his mouth and say them, that his humble confession, in order to purge the dregs of sin, may send the water of compunction, that is, the power of tears, down to the depths of the mind.

Second, because the stork is skillful at nourishing itself. For it feeds on the eggs of serpents, and from them prepares most pleasing food for its young; and although it eats venomous things, their venom nonetheless does not overpower or affect its own nature, but becomes nourishment for it — though the same thing is venom to many other animals. For, by the force of the heat that rules within it, the power of the venom is extinguished. Now the eggs of serpents are, as it were, the temptations of wicked spirits; which, although they are venom to animals — that is, to men living carnally — nonetheless provide beneficial nourishment to spiritual men. For, by the force of the love kindled in them, the wickedness of the tempter is entirely overcome.

Third, because the stork is vigorous against serpents; for it strikes them with its beak, kills, and eats them. The stork strikes serpents with its beak, indeed, because by praying often and confessing humbly, the penitent confounds wicked spirits. It kills them, however, when, with the fervor of penance, by a flood of tears, it utterly extinguishes their temptations. Hence the Psalm: 'you have crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters' — since of course the temptations of demons are extinguished in the waters of tears. But still the stork eats those serpents, since indeed the humility of penitents is nourished and grows strong from the very temptations of demons.

Fourth, because the stork is fond of human company, and so builds its nest in the houses of men. So too every penitent ought to love the company of men, that is, of those living rationally and gently; for man is by nature a rational and gentle animal: nothing, then, is more beastly than a man possessing reason and not using reason. Likewise, whoever lives cruelly ought not to be called a man, but is like wild beasts and monsters. And so, whoever lives or associates dwelling with such people places his nest not in the houses of men, but among beasts; according to that saying, 'I am become a brother to dragons, and a companion to ostriches,' and as Ezekiel says, 'you dwell among scorpions.'

Fifth, because the stork is diligent in preserving its nest or place. For it does not easily give up the nest or place it first took; but when, around winter, it withdraws, it binds earth, twigs, and thorns together with mud, so that it cannot be scattered by the wind. On its return, it occupies the same place again, and, fighting, defends it against those who would seize it. Likewise, the penitent diligently guards the nest of the mind. For he persists in the same — that is, the same low regard of humility — that he first accepted, or because he never loses, by carrying it carelessly, the grace he first accepted. But if the winter of adversity threatens, so that, contending with outward things, he must for a time go out, he covers the mind's nest with the earth of humility, joining twigs and thorns — that is, harsh abstinences — with mud; or because the harshnesses of the flesh must be joined with the mud of humility, lest they be scattered by the wind of pride, or by the temptation of desire. But when he returns from outward cares to the secret places of the heart, he occupies the same place again, that is, the nest of humility, which he also manfully defends against the proud demons striving to tear it away.

Likewise, penitents ought always to look to the example of their betters, and always hide themselves in the humility of penance, as the ostrich shows. For the ostrich, when the time comes for it to lay eggs, lifts its eyes to the Pleiades: for it lays no eggs except when that constellation rises. But when it sees this star rising, it digs in the sand of the sea, lays its eggs there, and covers them with sand, and immediately forgets where it laid them, and never seeks them further; but the sand, warmed, is cooked by the heat of the sun, and produces chicks within it; and when these are brought forth, breaking the shell, the mother then gathers them together, and recognizes them as her own.

Likewise, the ostrich naturally hates the horse, so much so that the horse cannot see it without terror; but if a horse meets it, the ostrich raises its wings as against an enemy, and, by the beating of its wings, forces the horse to flee. Just as the ostrich, then, laying its eggs, looks to the rising Pleiades, so the penitent, in his work, ought to look to his betters, that is, to those further advanced, according to that saying, 'be zealous for the better gifts,' of the Apostle. Likewise, when the ostrich has seen the example of these men shining like the Pleiades, it ought then to lay its eggs in the sand of the sea — that is, to carry out its works in heavy and bitter penance — and it ought to cover them with sand, that is, to guard them in humility, and not look at them further, that is, not to look at them so as to grow proud or to display them; and then, the sand being warmed, that is, penance growing fervent, the heat of the sun, that is, the love of God, kindles it, and brings forth from it the offspring of many good works, which, once brought forth with the shell broken — that is, the flesh dead — before the sight of the strict judgment, are then more clearly recognized by their mother, that is, the penitent soul, and gathered up as its own glorious fruits. Yet this ostrich, that is, the penitent, ought to flee the horse, that is, sin, by which the soul is carried to death, as its own deadly enemy, and to raise the wings of the virtues against it, and by their beating, that is, by effort and action, turn it to flight, that is, drive it from himself.

Likewise, it is especially against penitents returning to God that demons stretch the snares of temptation, which is shown by the example of the thrush. For thrushes (as Ambrose says), at the end of autumn, on the border of winter, when summer is, as it were, over, return to us again — for whom we contrive snares, and strive to deceive them, now with a treacherous hedge, now to trick them with birdlime, now to catch them with snares. Likewise, when penitents return to God and to justice, demons contrive snares for them just as men do for thrushes of every different kind, and now strive to deceive them with a treacherous hedge, that is, the temptation of rank and pride, now to trick them with the birdlime of lust, now to catch them with the snares of avarice; on account of which, whoever approaches God is warned by Ecclesiasticus: 'my son, coming to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.' For our life on earth is a warfare: for we have three enemies, namely the flesh, the world, and the demon.

div.head: Cap. LXVI. Irrationalia animantia, qua charitatis precepta penitus ignorans, legem tamen charitatis interdum adimplere nos erudiunt.

cit.quote: That travelers and wayfarers ought to be helped on their journey by pious charity, kites show. For the kite (as Isidore says) takes cuckoos onto its shoulders, and, lest they fail over the great distance of the journey, carries them with it from the regions of Spain. If, then, kites do this for those birds that are not of their own kind, how much more ought man to do this for man, and the Christian for Christ — sharing not only the same nature, but the same faith? Behold, irrational birds, knowing neither the laws of reason nor of virtue, nonetheless fulfill the law of charity, of which the Apostle says: 'bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.' Do not, then, despise or abandon your fellow traveler, even one lesser or weaker than yourself, but rather, having compassion on his weakness, take care of him, so that you may be at least like that Samaritan, whom the Gospel narrative also commends, who, finding a man wounded on the road, set him on his own beast, led him to the inn, took care to heal his wounds, and finally commended him to the innkeeper with payment. Behold, then, how many services of charity, duties of piety, and examples of heavenly compassion you have, that you too should strive to do likewise.

div.head: Cap. LXVII. Viri perfecti qui sint, quidque agant, ac agere debeant, dum vitam ducunt, optimorum piscium, aviumque preda atque Ardee natura multis aperitur exemplis.

cit.quote: ...of fish. For (according to Avicenna) the best fish are those that dwell in deep waters; hence, of the sea fish, the more praiseworthy are those that live nowhere but in the deepest ocean.

Likewise, those that live in open waters, where the winds blow freely, are better than others that behave the opposite way, and better are those that live in waters most strongly stirred, than in waters unmoved. From which gather that the best fish are those that dwell in waters much uncovered, and most strongly stirred. Likewise, the most perfect and best men are those who are high through the sublimity of contemplation. Isaiah: 'behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.'

Likewise, those who are uncovered through simplicity of conduct; for among men who are false and covered over by hypocrisy, the wind of the Holy Spirit does not blow. Wisdom: 'the spirit, namely of discipline, will flee the deceitful.'
Likewise, those who are stirred through the mobility of action, namely those who do not give themselves to idleness, but labor assiduously at good works. 'Whatever your hand can do, do it promptly.'

Likewise, perfect and spiritual men are like birds of prey, which (as the Philosopher says) fly the highest and swiftest, and have the keenest sight, and the greatest boldness, as is clear in the eagle, the falcon, and the like. Likewise, perfect men too are the highest in their conduct. The Apostle: 'our conversation is in heaven.'
Likewise, they are swiftest through love; for he who loves works more swiftly, and arrives sooner, as blessed Bernard says.
Likewise, they are keenest of sight through contemplation. Job: 'they see everything that is lofty.'
Likewise, they are boldest through the rigor of spirit. For 'the just, like a lion, shall be without fear,' as is said in Proverbs.

Likewise, the perfect man is likened to the heron. First, on account of its flight; for the heron ('ardea') is named as it were from being 'ardua' (lofty), because of its high flight. For it dreads rainstorms, and flies above the clouds, so that it cannot feel the storms of rain; and when it flies this way, it signifies a storm to come; and some call this bird the Tantalus. Likewise, perfect men, fearing lest, at the devil's instigation, they be caught up in the storms of persecution, set their intention above all temporal things, and lift their minds toward the serenity of the heavenly homeland, where the face of God is beheld. Of such men was Gregory, who tells of himself that his mind, while he was in the monastery, was such that all fleeting things were beneath him, and he rose above everything that is subject to change, and was accustomed to think of nothing but heavenly things. 'Mind the things that are above, not the things that are on the earth.'

Second, on account of its nest; for although the heron seeks its food in the waters, it nonetheless places its nest in the woods, in tall trees. For the perfect man, although as to the body he feeds on fleeting and transitory things, nonetheless places his own likeness among things above and spiritual. Hence the Psalmist said: 'it is good for me to cling to God, to put my hope in the Lord God.'

Third, on account of its zeal; for the heron is zealous for its young, and labors to defend them, lest they be snatched from the nest by other birds. So perfect men labor for their subjects, lest they be perverted by the wicked, and drawn away from the nest of the catholic faith, or from the uprightness of justice. John: 'the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.' Every perfect man, too, ought to fight with all his strength, lest the conceptions or the affections of the virtues he possesses in the nest of his soul be snatched away by the demon or by another. Ecclesiasticus: 'strive for justice for your soul.'

Fourth, because some herons have a white color, and some an ash-grey color. In the first, purity is signified; in the second, penance. For spiritual men are adorned both within, in the mind, with cleanliness, and outwardly, in the flesh, with penance. So Job, who had already spoken of his purity — 'until I fail, I will not depart from my innocence' — added of his own accord, concerning penance: 'I do penance in ashes and dust.'

div.head: Cap. LXVIII. In bonis actionibus perseverantia, Apum exemplo, multisque auctoritatibus, ipsis Dei electis magnopere prodesse comprobatur.

cit.quote: Perseverance in a good work is to be maintained, and multiplicity, or variety, of work is generally to be avoided — which is shown by the example of the bee. For the bee (as Aristotle says), when it goes out, or flies, does not attend to different flowers, nor does it leave one flower and go to another, until it finds in that flower what it seeks. And so, in like manner, man ought not to occupy himself with various acts; according to Ecclesiasticus: 'my son, let not your acts be in many things.' For the mind of man (as Gregory says), when divided in confusion among many and various things, becomes lesser toward each single one. Therefore, in that work — namely the good work — which he has begun, a man ought to persist for as long as he finds it profitable and wholesome. Seneca: 'it is the mark of a queasy stomach to taste many things,' and so it is the mark of a queasy spirit to begin many works. The Apostle: 'he who has begun a good work in you will himself bring it to completion.' And Matthew: 'he who perseveres to the end shall be saved.'

div.head: Cap. LXIX. Quo Pacto spiritualiter ipse intellectiva anima pinguescat, unica Merguli similitudine demonstratur.

cit.quote: ...the diving-bird, in winter, when the season is lean and harsh, grows very fat, which happens because of the scarcity of its movements; but in summer, when the season is refreshed with an abundance of fruits, it is stripped of flesh and fat, which happens because of the frequency of its flight. So a soul given to God, while it is freed from outward things through poverty, is set at rest from the inner movements of anxiety, and the more it rests within itself, the more it grows fat with abundant divine grace. But when the flighty mind abounds in outward things, it is caught up, through that very care for things and frequent inner anxiety and outward occupation, and gradually becomes so — that from this very restlessness of mind, the fatness of devotion diminished, the soul withers away. Hence Genesis: 'after the years of plenty, years of famine followed immediately' — since, without doubt, after abundance of the body follows the thinning of the mind. Job: 'let his strength be weakened by hunger.'

div.head: Cap. LXX. Predicatorum munus, ac partes qua sint ut Deo grati esse queant, per Avium preda, nec non aquatilium, at Scari piscis naturam, variis aperitur exemplis.

cit.quote: What preachers ought to be like, in life and in prudence, is shown in birds of prey, to which (as Aristotle says) nature gave a curved and sharp beak, so that they might hold their prey more firmly, and tear its flesh more easily. They are also of little flesh and much feather, so that their flight may be swifter. They have a thin, long, and slender tail, with which they steer themselves in flying, just as a rudder steers a ship. Preachers, then, have a beak, that is, a curved mouth, when they turn back upon themselves what they say to others — that is, when they themselves carry out in deed what they urge on others in their preaching. For what is curved is bent back toward itself, and this is necessary so that the prey they have taken — that is, the grace or reward they have earned by preaching — is not lost, but preserved.

Likewise, they ought to have a beak, that is, a sharp mouth — that is, piercing and cutting — to strike the hearts of carnal men, and to tear away or cut off their vices. 'The Lord has made my mouth like a sharp sword.'
Likewise, they ought to be of little flesh, that is, to care little for the flesh, and of much feather, that is, to abound in the feathers of the virtues.
Likewise, they ought to be swift of flight, that is, prompt in obedience. Or: he flies more swiftly who loves more fervently.

Likewise, they ought to have a tail, that is, the prudence of discretion, which is likened to a tail, because prudence looks ahead to the outcome of a thing. Hence Boethius: 'prudence weighs the outcomes of things.' By this tail the whole of life is steered and governed; but this tail, that is, man's prudence, ought to be long as regards the memory of past things, sharp as regards the understanding of present things, but can only be thin as regards the foreknowledge of future things, since the thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our foresight uncertain.

Likewise, note that the preacher who is clean in his work, and carries Christ in his heart, is feared even by the demon: for the cock carries within its gizzard a certain precious stone called the 'alectorius,' on account of which the lion fears it, especially if the cock itself is white in its feathers, as Pliny says. The cock, then, that carries the stone in its belly, is the holy preacher who carries Christ in his heart; and if he is white in his feathers, that is, clean in his works, even the lion — that is, the wicked spirit — fears him; of whom it is said in the first epistle of Peter: 'our adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about,' and so on.

Likewise, preachers ought to be like water birds, which have broad beaks, so as to gather grasses and roots more readily. For the breadth of the beak is, as it were, the amplification of the word. To this end preachers, in explaining and impressing words on their hearers, amplify them, so as to root out the grasses of vice and the roots of sin from their hearts.

Likewise, they have long necks, so as to draw their food from the depths of the water more easily; for indeed, from a long neck, the vocal breath is not released at once, since, passing through the length of the windpipe, it is somewhat delayed. Hence the sound of the voice comes forth, as it were, from a long neck, when the preacher's word is uttered with careful meditation. Hence the Psalm: 'the just man will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment.' By the very length of the neck, moreover, food is drawn easily from the depth of the water; since through unhurried reflection, as it were from the depth of the water — that is, the innermost sense of Scripture — the teaching that feeds the minds of the faithful is drawn out by the preacher.

Likewise, the preacher ought to be like the parrotfish, of which Ambrose says that alone among fish, it chews the cud. This properly suits the preacher, namely to chew over the words of sacred Scripture by continual meditation. Hence the Psalm: 'he will meditate on his law day and night.'

div.head: Cap. LXXI. Quid pradonibus nonnunquam eveniat, nonnullorum piscium exemplo describitur.

cit.quote: Those who prey upon others often themselves become the prey of others; hence they are like fish. For (as Ambrose says) certain fish devour one another, and the smaller often becomes food for the larger. Again, while the larger devours another, it is afterward devoured by yet another. Hence Aristotle says that the crayfish overcomes large fish and eats them, but the octopus overcomes the crayfish and eats it. Hence Isaiah said: 'woe to you who despoil; shall not you too be despoiled?'

div.head: Cap. LXXII. Prelati partes in subdites quales esse debeant, ceti natura, illius quam variis similitudinibus ostenditur.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: ...of the whale, or the sea-fish called cetus, which is reported to cherish its young with wondrous care. For it loves them with marvelous affection, and carries them about with it in the deep for a long time; and if it happens that they are hindered by heaps of sand, it gathers a great quantity of water in its mouth, pours it over them, and so, freeing them from danger, leads them back to the deep; it exposes itself to every danger for their sake, and always keeps them between itself and the sea in the safer place, and when a storm grows strong, it takes its still-tender young into its belly, and, once calm returns, releases them without any harm, as Iorach says.

Likewise, the prelate too ought to love his subjects like children, with great love, and lead them through the stormy sea of this life with anxious care: if he sees them hindered by heaps of sand, that is, by cares for riches or temporal things, he ought diligently to help them with the water of his mouth, that is, the teaching of exhortation, and even expose himself to whatever dangers for their salvation; for the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. He also ought to place and set them, when in doubt, in the safer position, and if the storm of persecution should rise up, he ought to gather into his belly — that is, into the affection of his mind, or the care of his inmost solicitude — those he sees to be more tender, that is, weaker, and hold them, strengthening and securing them with his counsel and help, until calm returns. So too Paul did, who said: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you,' and, to the Philippians: 'because I have you in my heart.'

div.head: Cap. LXXIII. Quantum superbi, qui falconibus, ab humilibus, qui muscardis comparantur, inter se differant, aperitur.

cit.quote: ...of falcons and sparrowhawks, or merlins. For the falcon is a very bold bird. For it attacks birds far larger than itself, striking them with breast and talon; the presumptuous and bold man is like it, who reaches for things beyond himself, against that saying of Ecclesiasticus: 'seek not the things that are too high for you, and search not into things too mighty for you.' But the sparrowhawk, which some call the merlin, though it is a small bird, takes only small birds; and so it signifies the sobriety of the humble, of whose number was the Psalmist: 'neither have I walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me.'

Likewise, the presumptuous, who take on excessive and laborious tasks, soon fail. For, as Aristotle says, hens that lay too many eggs soon die. What, then, are hens that lay too many eggs, but certain presumptuous men who take on excessive labors, and begin very many great works? These without doubt soon fail, because, even if they have the strength to begin, they do not have enough to carry through or complete; and so it is advised: 'my son, let not your acts be in many things.'

div.head: Cap. LXXIIII. Hominum peccatorum prosperitas, quoddam futura calamitatis iudicium esse, exemplo unico Bubonis demonstratur.

cit.quote: The prosperity of rich and sinful men is likened to a certain bird called the owl. For the owl is a bird laden with feathers, but held back by sloth, and weak in flight; it dwells day and night in the tombs of the dead, and is said to foretell evil to come, and to announce the desolation of the place where it lives, as Isidore says. The owl laden with feathers, then, is like the sinner abounding in riches; and this, because he is very slothful in the exercise of good works, and also weak for the flight of contemplation, and, remaining in the tombs of the dead, that is, in the stench of works, or of carnal sins, his very prosperity is to him a portent of future desolation, and a sign of eternal damnation. Hence Luke: 'woe to you rich, who have your consolation in this world' — as if to say more openly: this very consolation which you now receive in the present signifies woe to come upon you, that is, eternal damnation. Boethius: 'fortune is a certain sign of calamity to come.'

div.head: Cap. LXXV. Prudens homo quid agere debeat, ut sapienter tempora dispenset ac mensuret.

cit.quote: The prudent man divides his time: for he distributes and grants a part of the quiet of his mind to contemplation and prayer, and a part to the necessities of the body through the labor of action. For he is like the vulture, of which Aristotle says that it hunts from noon until night, and rests in silence from sunrise until noon, so that man, instructed by its example, might spend part of his time at rest in prayers, and part attending to the hunt, that is, to the procuring of necessities. Hence Haimo reports of the Apostle Paul that (as the holy doctors relate) from morning until the fifth hour he devoted himself to the labor of his hands, and from then until evening he devoted himself to public disputation.

div.head: Cap. LXXVI. Quemadmodum contra diabolum sit pugnandum, Ceti contra Cocodrillum pugna nos instruit.

cit.quote: One must fight against the devil as fish fight against the crocodile. For when the crocodile fights against the whale, the fish flee to the whale's tail, and it fights for itself and for them; and the crocodile, seeing that it cannot win, releases a most foul smoke into the water; but the whale, on the contrary, driving out a fragrant smoke from its mouth, repels that foul odor of the beast. If, then, the crocodile, that is, the devil, attacks any with persecutions, let them flee to the tail of the whale, that is, to the end of Christ's life, namely to the example of the cross and the passion of Christ; for if the passion of Christ is recalled to memory, nothing is so hard that it cannot be borne with an even mind; for he himself fought against the devil for us, and conquered. But if the stench of the flesh and of carnal enticements assails him, let it be driven off by the fragrance of the mouth, that is, the power of devout prayer. And note that some say the cetus and the whale (balena) are the same, but Isidore distinguishes between them, on the ground that the whale (balena) is a fish of wondrous size, which spouts water up high — which the cetus does not do.

div.head: Cap. LXXVII. Religionem ingredi, in eaque laudabiliter permanere quarentes, quove pacto eorum prelati seipsos atque alios regere debeant, plurium avium exemplis, multisque Anseris, et Gruis similitudinibus sapienter edocetur.

cit.quote: ...whatever better suits their disposition and condition — namely by the example of birds, which, according to their various temperaments, seek various dwellings for themselves. Hence those that are more cold and moist inhabit marshes and rivers, for the sake of food and breeding, such as diving-birds, ducks, and swans, by which are understood men who are weaker in body or spirit, who ought to take up more humble callings, whether for the sake of nourishment, if they are weak or infirm in body, or for the sake of the nest, that is, the place of their dwelling. For sometimes it is even dangerous for certain men to remain spiritually in certain places, whether as regards breeding, that is, the labor of regular works. But birds of a warmer nature inhabit mountainous places and the hollows of cliffs, by which are signified those who are stronger in body and more fervent in spirit, who can more safely take up higher and more difficult states of life.

Likewise, those who live religiously in community ought to be like cranes, or geese, especially wild ones; for these go together, eat together, love their own kind, and set up a king for themselves. These cranes or wild geese also fly in order, and if they sometimes fight among themselves, they are soon reconciled and fly together again, and do not depart from their former fellowship. They also know a coming storm; for when a storm threatens, they cry out, organize watches, and, in keeping watch, alternate their voices, as Basil and Ambrose say. Aristotle, however, adds that the one who keeps watch holds a small stone in its foot, so that, if it should perhaps fall asleep, it might be roused by the stone's fall. The same Aristotle also says that their king always sets himself down first, and always rises first from the ground, and looks around; if he sees anyone approaching, he begins to cry out, and rouses them to keep guard. In this, then, that they go and eat together, religious living in community are taught to love their common life, and to flee singularity, whether in food or in other things.

For religious ought to live without private property, but all things ought to be held in common, just as it is read that all things were common to the Apostles. But in this, that they love their own kind, religious are taught to love their own community and order especially. In this, that they set up a king for themselves, they are taught to live under obedience. In this, that the birds fly in order, they are taught to walk modestly and in order. And in this, that they are quickly reconciled and again joined together, they are taught, if anger or quarrels should ever arise, to end them quickly, and, through the remission or forgetting of injuries, to restore their former peace and charity the more swiftly. And in this too, that they sense coming storms, they are taught to guard carefully against dangers or temptations to come, and, when these press upon them, to cry out to God. And in this too, that they keep watch, and, in watching, alternate their voices, they are taught that they ought to guard themselves watchfully, and labor in turn for their mutual preservation. But the prelate, who ought to be solicitous for all, ought always to hold the little stone, that is, the humble example of Christ (who was the cornerstone), in his foot, that is, in the affection of his mind or in his gaze. For Christ said: 'I am the good shepherd, and the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.' Hence, by the sound of that little stone, that is, by consideration or imitation of that example, all sleep and negligence of the prelate is driven away.
Likewise, the prelate himself, although he is greater than all the rest by reason of dignity, nonetheless ought to set himself down first, that is, to be first of all in works of humility.

Likewise, to rise from the ground, namely through the pursuit of holy prayer and contemplation; or to be first in contempt of earthly desire, and especially, when his subjects are in the pastures, that is, in bodily comfort, the prelate ought to raise and keep a watchful mind concerning their guardianship; and if he perceives that something adverse or harmful is happening to them, he ought to cry out, warning and rebuking.

div.head: Cap. LXXVIII. Multis aquila similitudinibus, Accepitrique cruditissimis exemplis, quo modo anima humana spiritualiter instauretur, enucleatur.

cit.quote: The soul is renewed spiritually, like the eagle. Hence the Psalm: 'your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's.' For Augustine says that the eagle, in old age, suffers dimness in its eyes and heaviness in its wings, on account of which it seeks a spring of water, over which, flying as high as it can, it ascends; and so, from the effort and heat of the air, its crop grows hotter, and thus, with its pores opened and its feathers loosened, it suddenly lets itself fall into the spring; where, its feathers changed and the dimness purged from its eyes, it takes up renewed strength, as it were made new again. And (as is said on the Psalm) when it grows old, its beak curves so that it can scarcely take food. It therefore seeks a rock, against which it strikes and dashes its beak, and so lays down the weight of its beak, takes food, and, its strength renewed, grows young again. So the soul, aged, blinded, and weighed down by sin, if it ever rises up from earthly deeds, and is lifted higher into itself, considering the state of its own mind, weighing its own misery, a stronger heat of compunction is kindled in it, and then, if it casts itself into the spring of tears, the old age of sins will be renewed and purged; and if its beak, that is, the mouth of the heart, is weighed down, and so bent toward earthly things that it cannot take spiritual food, let it strike that beak against the rock, considering the example of Christ, by which he taught us to despise all things; and then the curve of the beak will be broken, that is, earthly affection will be corrected and directed toward God.

Likewise, the soul is renewed from its vices, as the hawk in its feathers. Job: 'is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows its feathers?' For there are three things that bring about its renewal, namely wind, sun, and food. For the hawk has the property that, when it grows old and feels itself weighed down, it spreads its wings against the rays of the sun, while the south wind blows, so that, with the sudden breeze and the melting heat, its pores are opened; and, once opened, it shakes itself, and so the old feathers fall out, and new ones grow back; and so, with the renewal of its feathers, it becomes fitter for movement. So too, to the tame hawk, which is kept in the mews so that it may be renewed, food of poisonous flesh is given in a small amount, so that it may be changed more easily; and so it is clear that the breath of the south wind, the heat of the sky, that is, the sun's rays, and the force of the poison, bring about its renewal. By the breath of that south wind, understand the inspiration of grace; by the heat, understand the fervor of penance; but by the poisonous flesh, understand the blow of some adversity or bodily infirmity, which frequently drives the sinner to be renewed through penance. For Bede says that the hawk is marvelously harmed by smoke; hence their mews are kept entirely away from smoky places. Now harmful smokes are, as it were, the temptations to sin, which rise up most strongly where there are occasions, and also opportunities, for sin. And so penitents, like hawks, ought to be kept entirely away from such smoky places.

Likewise, note that the hawk's diet ought not to be too generous, but moderate; for from too much it grows fat, and once fattened, it does not return when called; but if it is too lean, it fails, so that it cannot fly. So too the penitent's diet ought to be discreet, so that neither, through its excess, does the fattened body fail to obey the soul, according to that saying of Deuteronomy: 'the beloved grew fat, and kicked'; nor is the body so weakened by excessive abstinence that it becomes useless. The Apostle: 'I beseech you, that you present your bodies to God, a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God' — he says living, not slain.

div.head: Cap. LXXIX. Sanctorum virorum perfectiones quamplurima, ex columba, falconis, vulturisque variis similitudinibus naturalibus deprompta, connumerantur.

cit.quote: Holy and perfect men are likened to doves, according to that saying of Isaiah: 'who are these, that fly as clouds, and as doves to their windows?' For the dove is a messenger of peace; hence, as a sign of peace and reconciliation, she brought an olive branch to the ark. So too holy men announce peace by preaching it. Isaiah: 'how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, and that preacheth peace.' Holy preachers also announce the peace of the sinner, that is, of conscience, to penitents; the peace of time, to those who love it; and the peace of eternity, to those who persist, that is, persevere.

Second, the dove is a figure of simplicity, for she lacks the gall of malice. So too holy men are simple, that is, without the fold of malice or duplicity, according to that saying: 'be wise as serpents, and simple as doves.'

Third, she is clean by nature; for she does not eat unclean things, but chooses clean grains. So too holy men strive to be clean in all things, according to that saying of Tobit: 'I have kept my soul clean.' Hence they take the cleaner grains, that is, works or examples, but flee the unclean, according to that saying of Corinthians: 'touch not the unclean thing.'

Fourth, doves breed the whole year round in a warm region, once a month. Hence Aristotle says that they generally lay ten times a year, and sometimes eleven or twelve, and so are very fruitful. So too holy men strive to be fruitful, whether in the breeding of spiritual sons, whom they beget for God from the teaching of gospel knowledge, according to that saying of Corinthians: 'for in Christ Jesus, through the gospel, I have begotten you' — or at least they are fruitful in the fruitfulness of good works: for we are lords of our own works, just as of our own children, as the Philosopher says.

Fifth, the dove is a rival of piety. For she shows great affection of piety and solicitude toward her own young; moreover, she nourishes the young of others, and gathers and joins to herself other doves that have gone astray. All these things holy men do out of an affection of piety. For they bear anxious care for their own subjects or household, and moreover even extend the benefits of charity to strangers, and gather in and guide those who have gone astray or wander, according to that saying: 'bring the needy and the wandering into your house.'

Sixth, the dove is a friend of company. For doves love their own kind, and love the company of men; for holy men love those like themselves, and seek the company of those living reasonably and in order.

Seventh, the dove is forgetful. Hence, once her young have been taken, unmindful of the loss, she nests again in the same place, as Jerome says. So too holy men are unmindful of injuries, and do not, on account of harm done to them, withdraw from the nest of charity, but repay their very persecutors with the fruit of good works.

Likewise, holy and perfect men are most like the falcon: first, because the falcon is a bird of little flesh; for holy men have little care for their flesh, since they do not fulfill its desires, but rather torment it. Hence the Apostle: 'walking in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh.'
Second, because the falcon is of great boldness. For holy men are bold, that is, magnanimous and secure, according to that saying of Proverbs: 'the just, like a lion, shall be without fear.'
Third, it also has much plumage, since the saints have the feathers of many virtues. Ecclesiasticus: 'men rich in virtue.'

Fourth, because it has great agility, and so flies high in the air; for (as Gregory says) it has little of what weighs it down, and much of what lifts it up. So too holy men have little of the heaviness, that is, of the love of greed and pleasure, and much of lightness, that is, of the love of charity, and so fly on high, whether in contemplation or in conduct. Isaiah: 'behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and lifted up.'

Fifth, holy and perfect men are likened to the falcon, because it is of great nobility: for if it does not seize its prey on the first or second attempt, it seeks, as it were, vengeance on itself, and does not easily return to the hand afterward for shame, but wanders about through the air. For it considers itself defeated and as it were degenerate, when it does not triumph over the bird it has attacked, as Gregory says. He, then, who does not seize the prey on the first or second attempt is one who, whether beginning well or proceeding well, does not press on to the end of a good work, and such a one without doubt shows himself degenerate from Christ, who said: 'not he who begins, but he who perseveres to the end, shall be saved.' Such a man ought to return to Christ with the shame of penance, and humbly seek the help of his hand. Sixth, it is of great piety, namely not only toward its own young, but even toward those of others: for with the same diligent care with which it feeds its own children, it nourishes a young bird abandoned by the eagle, and takes it in with its own, as some say.

Likewise too, holy men bear care not only for their own household, but also for strangers, and for wretched orphans, especially those abandoned by others. James: 'religion clean and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans.' Hence Job: 'if I have eaten my morsel alone, and the orphan has not eaten of it.'

Seventh, holy and perfect men are likened to the falcon by reason of purity, because it is of great purity or cleanliness in taking food: for it flees carrion, and, even in the extremity of hunger, does not touch rotten flesh, but patiently waits until it finds prey fitting for itself, as Gregory says. In this are rebuked not only those who eat harmful foods to satisfy their gluttony, but also all those who take delight in foul carrion, that is, in the foul works of the flesh.

Likewise, holy men, even in this world, perceive a certain scent of the things that are in heaven. Hence they are likened to vultures: for in the vulture (as Pliny says) the sense of smell is especially strong. Hence, being beyond the sea, it perceives the smell of carrion on the other side, and conversely. Now the saints who are in heaven have already crossed the sea of this world, but we, in this mortal life, are still on this side of the sea. Nonetheless, the things that are beyond, that is, that are in the other life, if we are good and clean, we delightfully perceive by contemplating and loving them. Likewise, the vultures that are beyond the sea, that is, the saints who dwell in heaven, perceive the scent of our prayers with a certain eagerness. Hence the prayers of the saints are called bowls full of perfumes.

div.head: Cap. LXXX. Unito apum exemplo, Dei sapientia tantum a iustis perfecte adipisci, declaratur.

cit.quote: No one can perceive heavenly wisdom unless clean from the filth of guilt — which appears through the example of bees. Bees drink only clear water, nor do they drink until they have first cast out their waste, as Avicenna says. Clear water, then, is drunk by whoever is watchful for the attainment of heavenly wisdom, of which Ecclesiasticus says: 'the water of saving wisdom shall give him to drink,' and again: 'wisdom is clear, that never fades away'; but nonetheless no one drinks this clear water of heavenly wisdom unless he has first cast the dregs of sin out of himself; as it is written, 'wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXI. Simplicis columbe naturales proprietates et qua de causa Spiritus sanctus sub hac forma apparverit, aperitur.

cit.quote: The Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove at Christ's baptism, which, although it was truly an animal (as Augustine says), nonetheless, by its own properties, signified the spiritual effects that the Holy Spirit produces in the baptized: for first, the dove (as the Gloss on the Song of Songs says) has groaning instead of song, since the Holy Spirit makes us groan for our sins. Isaiah: 'we groan like doves, in meditation.' Romans: 'the Spirit himself asks for us with unspeakable groanings' — that is, he makes us ask, and groan.

Likewise, the dove lacks gall; for the Holy Spirit takes away the bitterness of anger, and fills us with the sweetness of kindness. Wisdom: 'O how good and sweet is your spirit, Lord, in us.' And in the same book the Holy Spirit is called sweet, kind, and humane, because he makes us sweet, kind, and humane: sweet in speech, kind in heart, humane in conduct.

Likewise, the dove dwells in the clefts of the rock, since the Holy Spirit makes us dwell often in mind upon the wounds of Christ and his sufferings. Hence the Song of Songs says, as the Holy Spirit speaks: 'my dove, in the clefts of the rock' — the Gloss says, that is, in the wounds of Christ.

Likewise, the dove settles by the streams of water, since the Holy Spirit makes his faithful dwell on the streams of Scripture. Genesis: 'the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters,' namely of the Scriptures.

Likewise, the dove fears the shadow of the hawk, and hides herself in concealment, since the Holy Spirit makes the saints weigh the devil's temptations, and escape them through flight from the world and the concealment of humility: for the shadow of the hawk is, as it were, the devil's own temptation. Hence Jesus was led into the desert, that is, into the hidden places of the desert, so that, hidden there from the world, he might more easily overcome temptations.

div.head: Cap. LXXXII. Per piscium comparationem diversis in locis commorantium, varietas pariter utrorum spiritualium per eorum diversa bona opera, multis similitudinibus demonstratur.

cit.quote: Spiritual men are like fish, of which some live only in the sea, others dwell in ponds and rivers, and others yet, sometimes in the sea, sometimes in fresh waters. Now fish going out from the sea into sweeter waters delight and fatten in their sweetness, and likewise, conversely; hence such fish, dwelling now in fresh water, now in the sea, delight the more in the one, the more they have experienced the other. But there are certain river fish so enticed by fresh waters that, unable to bear the bitterness of the sea, they die at once on tasting salt water. Likewise, although all good and spiritual men ought to live in the waters of penance, some nonetheless dwell in the sea, that is, in the exercise and restlessness of the active life, in which, like the sea, they are frequently troubled, just as the Lord said to Martha, 'you are anxious, and troubled about many things'; nonetheless they are good and praiseworthy sea-fish, that is, good and commendable active men. But there are others who always wish to be in fresh water, that is, never to be separated from the sweetness of the contemplative life, and of this kind was Magdalene, who, sitting at the Lord's feet, heard his word; and so the Lord said that she had chosen the best part. For Avicenna says that fish that dwell in rocky places and in running fresh waters, in which there is no filth, are sweeter and better than others. Now those dwell in rocky places who contemplate the works and words of Christ, since Christ was the rock, as the Apostle says.

But those are in fresh, running waters, who contemplate heavenly and divine goods, which, although they always remain in themselves, the sweetness of their contemplation nonetheless passes and runs swiftly through us, while we are in this life. Those, however, remain in places clean of filth, who contemplate the examples of the saints, who were full of cleanliness. Such contemplative men, then, have more of sweetness and purity of life than the first, and so are better. But there are others who dwell successively in both, now in the sea, now in fresh water, now in the exercise of action, now in the sweetness of contemplation. And these are the fish that grow fattest, that is, are the more enlarged in merit, because they benefit not only themselves through contemplation, but also many others through manifold action. Hence the Apostle: 'not seeking what is profitable to myself, but to many, that they may be saved.' There are, however, certain saints so wholly given over to the delights of contemplation, that if anyone were to place them in the exercise of action, they would perish in spirit or in body. Hence the Lord chooses such men (as Gregory says) to serve him in a solitary life.

div.head: Cap. LXXXIII. Superiorum electio quo pacto sit agenda, qualisque subditorum obedientia ac dilectio esse debeat, clarissimis definitur apum exemplis.

cit.quote: How subjects ought to conduct themselves toward their prelate is shown by the example of bees. For bees make a king for themselves, and he arranges his people; and although they are under a king, they are nonetheless free, and love, with a natural affection, the king they have made, and defend him with the utmost protection, and believe it a fine thing to die for him; and they show such great reverence to the king himself that they dare by no means leave their houses, or go out to feed, unless the king has gone out and claimed the flight as his own to lead. They choose as king the one they see distinguished by size of body, and, what matters most in a king, more renowned for gentleness. Hence he has no sting, or, if he has one, does not use it for vengeance. Their obedience toward the king is a marvel. For when he goes forth, the whole swarm gathers into a ball and surrounds the king, so that he cannot then be seen. Each one then offers to attend the king, and strives to be nearest him, and lifts him, weary, on their shoulders, and sometimes carries him entirely; and wherever the king settles, there the whole army pitches its camp; when the king is seen, the whole army is heartened, and when he is lost, the swarm disperses, for they cannot exist without a king. So, while part of the bees are at labor, the king alone is exempt from labor, and sits within alone, around whom certain bees with strong stings are always present, like lictors guarding the king, and punishing those who offend; and the king rarely goes out. Hence if anyone were to clip the king's wing at such a time, the army would not go out. But when the king dies, they gather around him, and, in the manner of mourners, grow numb with grief, and the whole people mourns; they do not eat, do not go forth, all groan with a sorrowful murmur, and their grief is not lessened — indeed, they let themselves die of hunger, unless the king's body is removed from their midst.

From all these things, then, it is gathered that a ruler and prelate must be chosen who is virtuous and gentle, and must be loved with affection by the people or subjects, not compelled but freely, that is, willingly obedient; he must be defended to the utmost, awaited with reverence, and obeyed by all, and served willingly; he must be helped in his labors, borne with in his failings, commonly imitated, kept before the eyes, exempted from servile labors, guarded carefully and honorably, rarely occupied with outward matters, and, at his death, committed to burial with due sorrow and reverence — and, comprising all these things in one, Peter said: 'honor the king.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXIIII. Superborum actiones, locustarum similitudinibus quibusdam, brevi patefiunt.

cit.quote: The proud are likened to locusts. For locusts raise themselves up in leaping, but soon fall in their rising; they are produced and borne by the south wind, but die in the north wind.

Likewise, they eat one another, and the larger do not spare the smaller; and they appear in summer, and hide in winter. So too the proud raise themselves up in mind by their temporal leaping, and, by that very fact, think themselves the more worthy the more they see themselves honored; but raising themselves up, they fall, since by the very fact that they are great in their own eyes, they are nothing before God. Very often, too, an unforeseen ruinous fall follows the exalted ascent of pride. They arise from the south wind, which is warm, since the proud are made so by the heat of temporal prosperity; but they themselves die in the cold of the north wind, since they are cast down by the harshness of adversity. The proud likewise consume one another, and the more powerful do not spare the weaker; in summer, that is, in prosperity, they appear splendid, but in winter, that is, adversity, they lie hidden and despised.

div.head: Cap. LXXXV. Mugilis exemplo, tentationum laqueos vitare edocemur.

cit.quote: When a man notices the snares of temptation, he ought shrewdly to flee, and remove himself swiftly from their occasions — an example of which appears in the mullet, a fish that is remarkably agile; when it senses the fisherman's trap, it at once darts backward, and leaps away so swiftly that it seems to those standing by to have flown. That fish, then, senses the trap, who takes note of rising temptations; and he draws back, as it were, when he withdraws himself from the occasions of temptation; and he leaps away most swiftly, when, at the very outset of the temptation, he at once turns his mind from it. Hence Isidore says: 'when a thought titillates you, when it suggests to you something unlawful, do not hold your mind there — crush the serpent's head; crush the beginning of the wicked thought.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXVI. Tyrannorum perversitas ac immunitas quanta sit. Aquile, Miluique exemplis, ac sacre scripture monitis, lucide describitur.

cit.quote: Tyrants are likened to eagles. For the eagle, because it is excessive in heat and dryness, is exceedingly wrathful — for wrath has no lot except in bodies very dry, as Aristotle says. The eagle is also hostile and dangerous to innocent birds, which it seizes with its talon and strikes and kills with its beak.

Likewise, the eagle keeps no company, but flees it, as Aristotle says. It is also cruel to its young, casting them out, striking them with its beak, and forcing them to leave the nest. All these things fit tyrants: first, because they are commonly wrathful and furious. Hence it is said of a certain such man, in the second book of Maccabees: 'bearing the spirit of a cruel tyrant, and the wrath of a wild beast.'

Likewise, because they favor wicked men, and are hostile and enemies to the good and innocent and to God, persecuting them, either by plundering their goods, or by injuring their persons, or sometimes depriving them of life — as Ahab did to Naboth the Israelite, whose person he killed, and whose vineyard he seized.

Likewise, tyrants love no companions, nor do they wish to have partners or equals in dominion, honor, or riches. Hence they even strive to impoverish everyone, lest others rise up against them or become their equals. Sometimes, indeed, tyrants are of such cruelty that they do not even spare their own; for they sometimes cast off their own children, sometimes strike them, and sometimes force them into exile not only from the house but even from the homeland — indeed (what is more execrable) sometimes even kill them, as is read of Herod, who first expelled his sons, then killed them; on account of which the Roman emperor is said to have remarked of him that he would rather have been Herod's pig than his son — since Herod, being bound by the law of the Jews, spared pigs, but killed his sons.

Likewise, certain tyrants are like kites. For the kite is a bird of prey, bold with the smallest, but timid with the great. For it does not dare to attack wild birds, but does not fear to snatch small domestic chicks. Likewise, certain tyrants, though rapacious out of avarice, and bold against the weak and powerless, are nonetheless fainthearted and fearful against the more powerful, or their equals, and those who resist them — indeed, they are sometimes overcome even by lesser men. For the kite is attacked by the sparrowhawk, and, on account of its own faintheartedness, is overcome by the smaller bird.

div.head: Cap. LXXXVII. Tribulationes Dei electis, maximopere expedire, per piscium in Aquilonari pelage commorantium similitudinem efficitur manifestum.

cit.quote: The onslaught of tribulations and temptations preserves the just better than the applause of consolations — an example of which appears in fish, which are better, and better preserved, in the northern and eastern sea than in the southern; because, from the forceful blowing of those winds, the waters are more greatly stirred, and better purified, on account of which the fish that dwell in them are more cleansed of what is superfluous. By the north wind, then, which is harsh, understand the harshness of one who opposes and afflicts; but by the east wind, which is warm in its origin, take the fervor of an assailing temptation. From the force of these, the soul, like water, is stirred or driven toward the good, and purged from evil, if it resists strongly; and so the just man, like the fish, prospers and is saved. Job: 'your visit has preserved my spirit.' But by the south wind, which is gentler and sweeter, understand the sweetness of temporal consolations, by which fish, that is, men living in the water of penance or justice, are frequently dissolved through negligence. And so they are less preserved, and grow more corrupt.

div.head: Cap. LXXXVIII. Anima cibum verbum Dei esse, auctoritate Sanctorum scripturarum, atque pulli gallinarum similitudine definitur.

cit.quote: The soul is fed by the word of God, according to that saying of Deuteronomy: 'not by bread alone,' and so on. The reason for this is that we are nourished by the same things from which we come into being, as the Philosopher says. For the chick that is born from the egg is nourished by the egg. For Aristotle says that the chick is born from the white of the egg, and nourished by the yolk. Since, then, we are spiritually begotten in faith by the word of God, according to that saying of James, 'of his own will he begot us by the word of truth,' we are also nourished by it. Hence Gregory says that the food of the mind is the word of God.

div.head: Cap. LXXXIX. Nonnullarum mulierum vetularum malignitas, que vulgo striges nuncupantur, manifestatur, que et cornicibus comparantur.

cit.quote: ...like crows. For crows (as Isidore says) are birds long-lived, garrulous, wicked, and harmful to those among whom they dwell; although their feathers whiten with age, nonetheless, within, in their flesh, the longer they live the blacker they become. Crows are also said, by their chattering or their flight, to be the foretellers or messengers of a change in the weather.

Likewise, as Ambrose says, crows are the guides and companions of storks, since when storks fly across the sea, crows precede and guide them, and wage war against hostile birds on their behalf. All these things, then, fit certain malicious and old women, who, if they live to a great age, chatter constantly, are wicked and cruel toward girls, and even harm those among whom they dwell, since they infect children by bewitching them — as the Gloss says on that saying of the Apostle: 'O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?'
Likewise, the more they whiten with old age outwardly, the more they blacken inwardly with the darkness of sin.

Likewise, they are the procuresses of demons, who sometimes cunningly seduce and lead even honest women, like storks, into adulteries and dishonorable deeds. These same women are also the ones who falsely claim to be witches, and presume, like the devil's prophetesses, to divine future things.

div.head: Cap. XC. Ex pluribus Turturis proprietatibus, quale sit Viduarum munus, laude dignum ac Deo gratum, elicitur.

cit.quote: How the continence of widowhood ought to be kept, turtledoves show. For the turtledove is the most chaste of birds, in that, when she loses her mate, she seeks no further union with another, but always goes about solitary, and, mindful of her lost companion, always mourns; she loves solitude and greatly avoids the company of men; she descends to gardens and fields, where she seeks food, but, food obtained, seeks again the accustomed places suited to mourning. In these things, then, widows are admonished to remain widows, to be solitary; likewise, to flee harmful company and vain spectacles, and, once the necessities of life are taken, to gather themselves to places of prayer and compunction. Likewise, the turtledove loses her feathers in winter, and then hides in the hollows of trees, but at springtime, her feathers regrown, comes out from the places where she had hidden, and seeks fitting places for breeding, as Aristotle says. In this it is figured that widows, in the time of winter, that is, of temptation or adversity, or with the feathers of their ornaments laid aside, ought to lie in the hollows of trees, that is, to remain humbly in their homes; or, having lost the feathers of delights or riches, ought to dwell, through the mind's meditation, in the hollows of trees, that is, in the examples of the humility and poverty of the saints; but in the time of spring, that is, of prosperity, when they have the feathers of riches, they ought to go forth to breed and bear fruit in the works of the active life, in alms or other good works — as Saint Elizabeth, daughter of the king of Hungary, did after the death of her husband, giving herself to alms and to the service of the poor.
Likewise, the turtledove does not descend upon a foul thing, nor upon a corpse; which happens when a widow does not consent to base temptation, and does not commit the baseness of a carnal deed.

Likewise, the turtledove chooses few and clean grains for herself and her young, and gathers, in clean places, that on which she lives; since a widow too ought to be content, both for herself and for her children, with few and lawful expenses.

div.head: Cap. XCI. Peccatorum via, Avium viis in volando assimilantur, quod quidem earum naturalibus similitudinibus confirmatur.

cit.quote: The ways of sinners are like the ways of birds in flying. For birds in flying have no fixed paths. Hence, according to Isidore, birds ('aves') are so named as it were 'devia' (off the path) in flying, since it is agreed they go without a path, in that their paths are not fixed in the air. So too sinners in their acts do not follow reason, which sets the bounds of virtue upon human acts, on account of which the Philosopher says that virtue is an elective habit, consisting in a mean determined by reason, exactly as the wise man would determine it. Hence they are said to be undetermined, and, in erring, to wander — now rising through pride, now sinking through avarice; now turning aside to the right, that is, to the delights of gluttony and lust, for delights are said to belong to the right, according to that saying of the Psalm, 'delights are at your right hand'; now turning aside to the left through impatience and anger, namely in adversity; now going forward through presumption, now going backward through faintheartedness or despair.

Likewise, birds divide the air with the beat of their wings, but, as the air soon closes again, leave no trace of their passage. So too the life and prosperity of sinners, once they are dead and shut in the tomb, wholly fails. Hence it is said, in their own person: 'all those things have passed away like a shadow, and like a bird that flies through the air.'

div.head: Cap. XCII. Virginitatis statum, omnem alium mulierum precellere, multis apum exemplis terminatur.

cit.quote: ...of bees. For the wholeness of the flesh, or of virginal body, is common to all bees, since they mingle in no coupling, are dissolved by no lust, nor are shaken by the pains of birth, and yet they produce the greatest swarm of offspring; for while other birds bring forth a single brood once a year, bees create twins, and outweigh the rest by a twofold fruitfulness. So too holy women, who guard the wholeness of their bodies, are free from the stenches of lustful dissolution, exempt from the pains of childbirth, and nonetheless bear much fruit to God in the spiritual offspring of their works. For sacred virgins surpass married women by a twofold fruitfulness; for the latter bear fruit only in the flesh, but the former in flesh and spirit: the latter bear fruit by begetting corruptible offspring for the world, the former bear fruit in the body by earning incorruptible glory in heaven. 'They shall be,' says the Lord, 'like the angels in heaven, where they neither marry.' Sacred virgins also sometimes beget for the Lord, if not fleshly children, nonetheless spiritual ones. For all those whom they draw to God, whether by the examples of their works, or by prayers, or even by their words, can be called their spiritual children.

Likewise, although the married sometimes also bear fruit for God through the works of the active life, virgins nonetheless can bear him fruit more freely, both of the works of the contemplative life and of the active. From which it is clear what is said in Isaiah: 'many are the children of the desolate, more than of her that has a husband' — that is, of the virgin, more than of the married woman.

Likewise, young and virgin bees make better honey, as Avicenna says. So too in holy virgins and young people, honey — that is, the sweetness of heavenly contemplation — is produced the more sweetly, the more strongly the flesh in them is made subject to the spirit. Hence it is said in the book of Judges: 'out of the strong came forth sweetness.'

div.head: Cap. XCIII. Quatuor Cardinales virtutes hominibus valde necessarias esse, per multas hirundinis similitudines aperitur.

cit.quote: The examples of the swallow teach us to have the cardinal virtues: for first, the swallow teaches us to have temperance, especially in food. For the swallow (as Isidore says) is named from 'going,' because it does not acquire its food by sitting, but by flying. So too man ought to take the food necessary for his body in passing, for necessity, and not lingering over it for pleasure. Exodus: 'you shall eat in haste.' For he who eats in haste is not accustomed to take great delight in eating, nor even much food.

Second, it teaches us to have prudence: first, from the fact that it builds its nest so skillfully that human industry could scarcely make one like it from any material. Hence some believed that swallows have intellect (as the Philosopher says). Though this is not true, they nonetheless teach us to be prudent, so that we may build the nest of the mind with the virtues according to prudence. Swallows also teach us to purge the nest of our conscience, from the fact that they instruct their young to cast their droppings out of the nest, so that we too may learn to purge our consciences of the dregs of sin.

Likewise, the swallow has prudence in discerning times and places. For in the time of cold, it seeks warm regions, and so crosses the sea; but in summer it returns, and keeps watch over the other seasons, and foretells the coming of summer, as Ambrose says. Likewise, prudent men discern the times, and manage their affairs as suits the season. It is also the mark of the prudent man to change or seek out places, as he sees fits the time. The prudent man is also accustomed to be a foreteller of the future, from the fact that prudence weighs the outcomes of things, as Boethius says.

Third, it teaches us to keep justice, especially punitive or judicial justice, which, in shedding the blood of the wrongdoer, opens the eyes of others, and instructs them to be cautious. Hence Augustine says that the blood that comes out of the right wing of a swallow heals the sick eyes of a dove: for the swallow's right wing is the just sentence of a prince, from which, when living blood is shed, the eyes of others are enlightened to guard themselves; for the eyes that guilt closes, punishment opens, as Gregory says, and it enlightens and helps frequently not only one's own punishment, but that of others too.

Fourth, the swallow also teaches us to have fortitude; for there is said to be a certain kind of swallow that all birds fear, so that even the eagle flees it as an enemy, and, once it is seen, dares not swoop upon its prey, since its bite is thought to be poisonous, as Pliny says. Such swallows are the saints, whose fortitude and virtue all birds fear, that is, all demons, and the eagle, which is king of birds, that is, Satan himself, who is king over all the children of pride. For the bite of such a swallow, that is, the prayer of a holy, patient, and humble man, is, as it were, poisonous to them, namely to the demons, and greatly to be feared. The fullness and abundance of the virtues, moreover, does not weigh down the soul, but rather lightens it, and fits it for ascending to heaven. Hence it is that birds, the more abundantly they have feathers, the more easily they are lifted up, and the more swiftly they go, as is clear in birds of prey, which fly the highest. For the air enclosed beneath the hollow of the feathers lightens the bird, and fits it to be borne upward. So too, by the feathers of the virtues, the saints are lightened, and lifted up sublimely to contemplate or desire heavenly things. Hence the prophet, desiring these feathers and this flight, said: 'who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and be at rest?' On the other hand, from the lack of virtues, the soul is left heavy, like a bird without feathers. Hence Augustine says, of God from whom the virtues come: 'when I am not full of you, I am a burden to myself.'

div.head: Cap. XCIIII. Hominum vita spiritualis qua via perficiatur, per volatilium, eorumque pullorum vitam naturalem, pluribus similitudinibus naturalibus demonstratur.

cit.quote: The spiritual life of men advances and is perfected like that of birds. For the Philosopher says that after ten days of gestation the chick is completed in all its parts, and then has a head larger than its whole body, and has its head bent down over its right leg, and its wings spread over its head; after this, on the eighteenth or twentieth day, the shell breaks, and the chicks, now brought to life, come out, sometimes as twins, but of twins one is larger, the other smaller. The first completion of the chicks, then, happens in ten days, because the first formation of man in the spiritual life happens through the observance of the ten commandments. Hence the Lord said: 'if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments' — and then the head exceeds the body, since then reason rules the body, namely so that man is not animal, but rather spiritual. The head, too, that is, the mind, is bent down, not only through obedience, but also through humility — not feigned, but true — and this bending is over the right leg.

...he who humbles himself wickedly (as is said in Ecclesiasticus) bends toward the left side; the wings too of the intellect, namely and of the affections, are stretched, through faith and love, above the head, that is, above the grasp of natural reason, so that now the earthly man may begin to lift his mind toward heavenly things. But to the second completion of the chick eight or ten more days are added, so that it is twenty or eighteen days in all. For if anyone wishes to be truly perfect, he must, besides observing the ten commandments, keep also the observance of the new law, that is, of Christ's counsels, such as that saying of Matthew: 'if you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor,' and the like, which are contained in the Gospels; for to the perfection of the new law, that is, of the Gospel, the number eight belongs, on account of the eighth day of Christ's resurrection, that is, the Lord's Day, which we celebrate, just as the Jews celebrate the seventh day, or on account of the eighth day of our own resurrection, which we await, in which, the shell of the egg broken — that is, this mortal life ended — like chicks newly brought to life we shall come forth as twins, that is, glorified in soul and body; yet one twin will be greater, since the glory of the soul will be greater than that of the body. Likewise, to the perfection of the Gospel belongs the addition of the number ten; for besides the observance of the decalogue, the sacraments of the new law are necessary, along with faith in the Trinity, or the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, together with the three theological virtues: for seven and three make up the number ten. After the shell of fear, or of love of this corruptible life, is broken, the twins come forth, that is, made perfect in the spiritual life both in flesh and in spirit — although, in the governing of life and the sweetness of heavenly conduct, the spirit goes before the flesh; for the spirit desires more than the body can bear, or because the spirit perceives more of sweetness than the body can sustain of labor.

Likewise, mortal life is like the natural life of birds. For there are certain birds that feed on flesh, such as hawks and birds of prey, and to these are likened men who live carnally, on account of which the Apostle says: 'we are debtors, not to the flesh, that we should live according to the flesh.' But certain others feed on grasses, such as geese and the like; and to these are likened penitents who are just beginning, who still require softer things, unable as yet to take solid food. Ezekiel: 'they shall rest in green pastures.'

But certain others feed on grain and seeds, like doves and the like, to which perfect and spiritual men are likened; for the food of the perfect is solid (as the Apostle says). For contemplatives feed on the seeds of divine words: for the seed is the word of God; but the active feed on the seeds of good works, especially of alms. Galatians: 'whatsoever a man shall sow,' and so on. They also feed on the seeds of tears through compunction. Psalm: 'going they went and wept, casting their seeds' — namely the seeds that feed and restore souls, according to that saying of the Psalm: 'you have fed us with the bread of tears.'

div.head: Cap. XCV. Plurimorum volatilium species enumerantur, varia figurantes peccata, qua prefecta in veteri lege a Deo prohibebuntur, eiuscemodique rei diversa rationes assignantur.

cit.quote: Various vices were forbidden to the Jews in the law of Moses under the figures of various birds. For the eagle was forbidden them, in which, since it flies high, pride is forbidden and figured.
Likewise the griffin, in which, since it is hostile to horses and men, the cruelty of the powerful is forbidden.
Likewise the osprey, in which, since it feeds on birds, are signified those who are oppressive to the poor.
Likewise the kite, in which, since it makes the most use of snares, the deceitful are signified.
Likewise the vulture, which, because it follows armies, hoping to eat of the corpses of the dead, signifies those who desire the death and slaughter of men, so as to profit from it.
Likewise the crow-kind was forbidden, in which are signified some who, once without good affection, do not return; for the raven sent out from the ark never returned.
Likewise the ostrich, which, though a bird, cannot fly, but always stays near the ground, and so signifies soldiers, and those who entangle themselves in worldly business.
Likewise the night-raven, which by night has sharp sight, but by day cannot see; and so signifies those who are shrewd in temporal matters, and sluggish in spiritual ones.

Likewise the gull, which swims in the water and flies in the air; and so signifies those who honor both circumcision and baptism, or signifies those who wish to fly through contemplation, and yet live in the waters of pleasure.
Likewise the hawk, which serves men for hunting prey, and so signifies those who serve the powerful in preying upon the poor.
...the owl, which by night seeks its food, but by day hides; and so signifies the lustful, who seek to conceal the deeds they do under cover of night.
Likewise the diving-bird, whose nature is to remain long beneath the waves, and so signifies the gluttonous, who submerge themselves in the waters of delight.

Likewise the ibis, a bird of Africa, having a long beak, and born from serpents — perhaps the same as the stork — and it signifies the envious, who are refreshed, as it were, by the evils of others as by serpents.
The swan, which is of white color and has a long neck, by which it draws food from the depths of the earth or water, can signify men who, through an outward whiteness of justice, seek earthly gain.

Likewise the pelican, which is found in the regions of the East, with a long beak, having certain pouches in its throat, in which it first stores food, and after a while sends it down to its belly; and it signifies the avaricious, who gather the necessities of life with immoderate anxiety.

Likewise the porphyrio, which, unlike other birds, has one foot broad for swimming and the other cloven for walking, since it swims in water like ducks, and walks on land like partridges, and drinks only by biting, dipping all its food in water; and it signifies those who wish to do nothing at another's judgment, but only what has been steeped in the water of their own will.
Likewise the eating of the heron, commonly called the falcon, was forbidden, and it signifies those whose feet are swift to shed blood.
Likewise the law forbade the 'caradon,' a garrulous bird signifying the talkative.
The hoopoe, which nests in dung, and, as a chick, feeds on filth, and feigns groaning in its song, signifies the sorrow of the world, which brings death to unclean men.
