Likewise the bat, which flies low over the ground, signifying those who, gifted in worldly knowledge, savor only earthly things.

Likewise, one who unduly flees one vice sometimes falls into another: for the partridge, fearing the sparrowhawk and wishing to flee it, while it senses the hawk in the air, does not rise from the ground, but often, while it flees along the ground as though safe, throws itself into a net or a snare. So too, sometimes, someone wishing to flee the assault of pride or tyranny, while lowering himself too much to the ground in humbling himself, or softening indiscreetly, either falls into the snare of faintheartedness, or entangles himself in the nets of excessive laxity.

Likewise, three more general vices are represented in the hoopoe, namely avarice, lust, and pride. For the hoopoe eats human dung — it is an altogether unclean bird — but wears a crest raised upon its head, like a helmet. He indeed eats human dung who gapes after temporal gain, of whom the Apostle says, in Philippians: 'I have counted all things as loss, and I think them as dung, that I may gain Christ.' He is unclean, however, who lies subject to the pollutions of a lustful life. Of whom the Apostle says: 'every fornicator, or unclean person,' and so on. But it bears a crest on its head, when pride rules in the mind, against that saying of Tobit: 'never let pride rule in your mind.'

div.head: Cap. XCVI. Vita voluptates qua in tertium Aquila ovum designantur, tanquam noxias esse abiiciendas, edocemur.

cit.quote: We are taught to cast off pleasures by the example of the eagle. For the eagle lays at most three eggs, but casts out the third, because it is greatly burdened by brooding over it — so much so that it is then weakened to the point of being scarcely able to hunt. The eagle's three eggs, then, are the three appetites of the soul. For the soul sometimes desires something that pertains to its own salvation, and that is the first egg. It also desires something that pertains to the necessity of the body, and this is the second. But it desires something that pertains to the pleasure of life, and this is the third, which, as superfluous and harmful, must be cast away. For the superfluity of pleasure frequently weighs down the mind, and weakens it so much that it cannot hunt for spiritual things. Hence the Lord warned his disciples, saying: 'take heed, lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness.'

div.head: Cap. XCVII. Usura, que et plumis Aquila assimilatur, quantum sit hominibus damnosa declaratur.

cit.quote: Usury is likened to a feather, or the feathers of the eagle, which (as Pliny says) has a certain corrosive power; hence, placed among the feathers of other birds, it corrodes them. So too usurious gain, mixed in with good gain, reduces it to nothing; hence riches gained by usury, even when mixed with others, commonly last but a short time. For usury has a corrosive power, since it quickly consumes the resources of the one who borrows. For a usurious loan is, to the debtor, like those worms of which Job spoke: 'they that eat me do not sleep, and by their abundance my garment is consumed' — since through the multiplication of usury, sometimes even the garment given in pledge is consumed, and passes to the creditor.

div.head: Cap. XCVIII. Leprosi quando in veteri lege mundati dicebantur. Ac Christus passeribus a leprosis ablatis, Gallinaque multis pulcherrimis similitudinibus comparari, explanatur.

cit.quote: Christ was prefigured in the sparrows that were offered at the purification of a leper in the law of Moses. For lepers were said to be purified when, by the priest's judgment, they were restored to the company of men and given back to divine worship; yet it sometimes happened, by divine miracle, that leprosy was cleansed through the rite of the carnal law; and sometimes, too, the priest was mistaken in his judgment. He was first judged clean, and afterward restored, as clean, to the company of men and to divine worship — namely after seven days; but at the first purification, the cleansed leper offered for himself two live sparrows, cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop, in this manner: the sparrows and the hyssop were bound together with scarlet thread along with the cedar wood, so that the cedar wood served as the handle of the sprinkler, while the hyssop and the sparrow formed the part that was dipped in the blood of the other sparrow, which was sacrificed over living water. These four things were offered against the four defects of leprosy. For against putrefaction, cedar was offered, which does not rot; against the stench, hyssop, which is a fragrant herb; against numbness, live sparrows; against ugliness of color, the scarlet thread, which has a living color. The live sparrow was then let fly away into the field, because the leper was restored to his former freedom. On the eighth day he was admitted to divine worship, and restored to the company of men, but only after the hair of his whole body was shaved, and his garments washed, since leprosy corrodes the hair and defiles and makes foul the garments; and afterward a sacrifice was offered for his fault; and with the blood of the sacrifice the tip of the ear of the cleansed man was anointed, and afterward the thumbs of his right hand and his feet, since leprosy is first recognized and felt in these parts. Three liquids were used in this rite, namely blood against the corruption of blood, oil to signify the healing of the disease, and living water to cleanse filth. By the two sparrows, then, were figuratively signified the divinity and the humanity of Christ, of whom the one, namely the humanity, is sacrificed in an earthen vessel over living waters, since, through the passion of Christ, the waters of baptism are consecrated. But the other, namely the impassible divinity, remained alive, since divinity cannot die; hence it also flew away, since it cannot be bound by suffering. This live sparrow, then, together with the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop — that is, faith, hope, and charity — is put into the water for sprinkling, since we are baptized in faith in God and in man. Man washes his garments, that is, his works, in the water of baptism or of tears, and shaves off all his hair, that is, his thoughts; the tip of his right ear is also anointed, when he is cleansed, with blood and oil, so that his hearing may be fortified against corrupting words; and the thumbs of his right hand and foot are anointed, so that his action and his affection may be holy.

Likewise, Christ likened himself to a hen. Matthew: 'how often,' he said, 'have I wished to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings.' For the hen (as the Gloss says there) is most devoted to her chicks. For she gathers them under her wings, defends them against the kite, grows sick with labor and love for her young, cares more for her chicks than for herself, feeds and fills them more than herself, calls them when food is found, attacks a man in their defense, grows hoarse and changes her voice out of love for them, sheds her feathers, becomes altogether unkempt, and walks with her wings drooping. All these things suit Christ: for he bears a great affection of piety toward his chicks, that is, the faithful; he has gathered them under the wings of his protection, into one faith and church; he has defended them against the kite, that is, the raging world; for our labor and love he appeared entirely faint on the cross; he cared more for us than for himself; he fed us not only with material bread, but also with the sacramental and spiritual bread of his teaching; he calls us when food is found, saying: 'come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you'; for our defense he fought against the devil; languishing with love and failing of voice on the cross, he grew hoarse, according to that saying of the Psalm, 'my jaws have grown hoarse.' There too he laid down his feathers and garments, that is, scourged in body, he became altogether unkempt, and, hiding the power of his divinity, he walked with his wings, that is, his powers, let fall. All these things, then, Christ did for the love of us, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, world without end. Amen.

div.head: PROLOGVS LIBRI QVINTI, IN QVO PLVRIMA DE ANIMALIBUS terre, videlicet bestiis, reptilibus, ac iumentis, exempla introducere, eaque moribus adaptare proponit.

cit.quote: 'God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth in its kind.' Genesis 1. God, at the first origin of things, created man in this dignity, that all the animals of the earth should be subject to him, for as long as he remained, without transgression of the command God had given him, in innocence. Hence sacred Scripture testifies that God, as three and one, said of man, in creating him: 'let us make man to our image and likeness, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and all living creatures that move upon the earth.' And so that those very animals too might obey man at his nod, as soon as our first parents were created, he granted them dominion over those animals of the earth, saying: 'increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and all living creatures that move upon the earth.' And so that man might use their service at his pleasure, God gathered them all before his sight, that he might designate each of them by various names, according to the property of its own nature, as is clear in the same place. But afterward, when sin intervened through the transgression of the command by our first parents, although that aforesaid dominion of men over the brute animals was diminished — so that their disobedience should become, as the avenger of man's disobedience, a cause even in the beasts — it was nonetheless not wholly taken away, the author of mercy having pity; for mercy so tempered the severity of justice that some of the aforesaid animals of the earth were turned to the punishment of man, while others were left for man's service, and some were granted for the relief of man's sickness.

...he named the beasts of the earth in three ways. For he named beasts, creeping things, and cattle. 'God made,' it says, 'the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth in its kind.' For those that exist for man's punishment he named beasts, since 'bestia' (beast) is said, according to Isidore, as it were 'vastia,' from laying waste — such as lions, and bears, and wild animals, which sometimes savagely tear and lay waste to men. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: 'all these things are created for vengeance, the teeth of beasts, and scorpions,' and so on. But those that furnish remedies, he called creeping things. For from vipers, and serpents, and other things that creep upon the earth, although they are venomous, healthful antidotes are nonetheless taught by physicians to be made, which beneficially resist poisons and various diseases.

Moreover, those animals that serve man in various services and uses, Moses, in the passage cited, named cattle. These are rightly called cattle ('iumenta,' as Basil says) as it were man's 'helpers' ('iuvamenta'), such as horses, or oxen, and other similar animals, which offer help to men in their needs. But these cattle offer not only bodily help to all, but also, beyond that, extend to them spiritual lessons, on account of which we are bidden to seek their teaching. 'Ask the cattle,' it says, 'and they will teach you' — not indeed by the teaching of word, but rather of example; in the same way that the Wise Man says, in Proverbs: 'go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom.' Further, since divine Scripture brings in examples for our instruction not only from cattle of this kind, but also from other animals, such as beasts and creeping things — as Solomon likened the strength of the just man to the lion, saying, 'the just, like a lion, shall be without fear,' and the Lord commanded us to imitate the prudence of the serpent, saying, 'be wise as serpents' — my purpose in this fifth book is, generally, to bring in very many examples concerning the animals of the earth, both beasts, and creeping things, and cattle, and to adapt them (though briefly) to morals, following the order of the preceding books in their subject matter and chapters, to the praise and glory, namely, of him who teaches us above the cattle of the earth, who is God, blessed forever and ever.

div.head: Cap. I. Abstinentiam, ieiuniumque valde hominibus prodesse, variis canis, ac serpentis exemplis, sacrorumque Doctorum auctoritatibus confirmatur.

cit.quote: Abstinence, in many men, generates anger, or impatience. For just as a starving dog, if it is too greatly tormented by hunger, is turned to rabid madness, so too a gluttonous man, if he abstains and fasts even a little, becomes impatient and furious, since, accustomed to delicacies, he cannot bear hunger. And such were the fasting Jews, to whom the Lord said: 'behold, you fast for quarrels and contentions, and you strike with a wicked fist' — against which Maximus said, in his sermon on the Nativity: 'fasting ought to nourish peace, not quarrels.' For what is this, that you do not eat meat, yet from your mouth comes forth every kind of filthy curse?

Likewise, devout abstinence puts the devil to flight. For just as strong hunger drives the wolf from the forest, so devout abstinence drives the devil from man. Matthew: 'this kind of demon is not cast out, except by prayer and fasting.' Ambrose says that a fasting man kills a bodily serpent with his spittle; how much more, then, does devout fasting kill the spiritual serpent? Judith, after fasting, cut off the head of Holofernes. Jerome: 'we ought to quench the burning arrows of the devil with the coldness of fasts and vigils.' Psalm: 'but I, when they troubled me, put on sackcloth, and humbled my soul with fasting.'

Likewise, abstinence is of great use for putting off the old age of a wicked habit. For the serpent, when it feels itself weighed down by old age, and desires to put off its old skin, so as to be renewed, first abstains from food for many days, so that its skin may be more easily loosened. Now what is the serpent's old skin, but a wicked and old habit of carnal corruption? which, if anyone desires to put off, he must first abstain from food and delicacies. Hence Pope Leo says that through the voluntary afflictions of abstinence, the flesh dies to its desires, and the spirit is renewed in virtues.

Likewise, the excessive delights of gluttony are to be avenged through the afflictions of abstinence: for the lion, when it feels it has gorged itself too much, abstains from food for many days without eating. So too the excess and pleasure of food must be atoned for in the withdrawal of food, and the affliction of fasting. Gregory: 'the flesh, made joyful, drew us to fault; afflicted, let it lead us back to pardon.' Hence Bernard says: 'through this, that we abstain from lawful things, the unlawful things we formerly committed are forgiven us.'

div.head: Cap. II. Illis qui Canis rabidi morsum passi sunt, accidiosi comparantur, quod pluribus similitudinibus demonstratur.

cit.quote: The temptation of sloth is like the bite of a rabid dog. For those bitten by a rabid dog dream terrible things, and are afraid in sleep, and are troubled; without cause they become stupefied, they look at everyone, and wish to be looked at by no one; and, if the disease has taken hold, they refuse every drink, fear water, and bark like dogs; and they become so fearful that they collapse from sheer fright, and such people quickly die, unless help is brought to them swiftly. He, then, is bitten by a rabid dog who is tempted by the vice of sloth, and such people dream terrible things, and are afraid without cause: for they dream terrible things, as it were, since they judge things that are easy to be difficult, and so are afraid, without cause, to undertake or pursue them. For one who dreams something terrible fears where no danger threatens, since what he perceives in sleep is not a true thing, but the image of a thing; for a dream (as the Philosopher says) is a certain phantasm appearing from outside in sleep, and a phantasm is the likeness of an imagined thing, and not the thing itself. Such is the slothful man: when something laborious comes up to be done, failing in spirit, he becomes, as it were, stupefied.

Likewise, he looks at all dogs laboring, and, being himself lazy, nonetheless does not allow himself to seem or be thought lazy. And if the affliction of sloth grows strong in him, he refuses every drink, that is, the reception of saving teaching; he fears and shuns the water of penance, and, out of weariness with life, barks like a dog, since in all things, impatient, he always complains and murmurs. Toward spiritual and virtuous things, the slothful are so fearful and sometimes so fainthearted that, abandoning all things, they rush into despair; on account of which such men, having lost divine grace, quickly die in soul, unless some spiritual remedy is applied to them, by which they might be roused with the medicine they need. And so the Apostle says: 'the sorrow of the world,' that is, sloth, 'works death' — namely, of the soul. Hence, just as every animal motion is impossible for a dead body, so too every laborious work seems impossible to the slothful soul. Hence Seneca says: 'the slothful do not think anything can be done, that they themselves cannot do from their own weakness; they pass judgment on virtue from their own infirmity. For the things to which we are weak, we believe to be hard and intolerable torments' — thinking it torture to be put to death, or to be roused at first light: 'these things are not difficult, but we ourselves are soft and feeble.'

div.head: Cap. III. Ex similitudinibus naturalibus carnium animalium, adversitates hominibus elatis prodesse, rerumque temporalium prosperitates nonnullis obesse, nec non aliquibus prodesse explanatur.

cit.quote: Adversity benefits proud and hardened men more than prosperity: for the flesh of animals in which heat and dryness dominate, such as camel meat, is bad in summer, but excellent in winter. Now the heat of summer is, as it were, the favor of prosperity, which makes many men wicked, while it exalts them into pride; but the harshness of winter is, as it were, the affliction of tribulation, which leads the mind back to humble recognition of itself, and brings it to the best disposition. Gregory says that the prosperity of the present life is no witness to innocence; many return to eternal life through scourges, and very many, destined for endless punishment, die without any scourge at all. So it commonly happens to men, that the winter of adversity makes good those whom the summer of prosperity had made bad.

Likewise, temporal prosperity benefits some and harms others, according to the lack or abundance of their charity: for the flesh of animals that are warm and moist, such as mutton, is good in winter, and can also suit in autumn; but that which is cold and dry, such as goat meat, and that which is cold and moist, such as pork, is excellent from mid-summer to its end, and worst in winter. Likewise too, men who are warm with the love of charity, and moist with the devotion of tears, are good in the time of winter, that is, of adversity, since charity is patient, and is not provoked. But even in autumn, in the abundance of prosperity, since autumn abounds in fruits, such men also conduct themselves fittingly, since they know how to abound, and how to suffer want. But those who are cold in heat, namely lacking charity, and dry, having no moisture of grace, or cold toward spiritual things and moist, that is, prone to flow toward carnal ones — these are worst, both in winter, that is, in adversity, since they cannot bear the harshness of adversity; yet they can be good from mid-summer, that is, prosperity, since if they used prosperity with moderation and restraint, it would not harm them, but rather help them; for in prosperity, as such, temperance is necessary for it to be beneficial; otherwise it is harmful. Hence Seneca says that happiness itself, unless it is tempered, crushes or destroys the luxurious empires of many cities that fell in their very flower. And whatever had been won by virtue, intemperance ruined.

div.head: Cap. IIII. Corporis nimiam debilitatem exemplo Taxi etiam anime vires frangere erudimur.

cit.quote: Indiscreet affliction of the flesh does more harm than good, as appears in the example of the badger. For (as Aristotle says) there is a certain species of badger that, together with its mate, gathers food against the winter; but afterward, fearing that the food will run short, it does not allow its mate to eat her fill. But she feigns patience, and, yielding to the male, leaves the den, and, entering the hiding place by another way while the male is unaware, devours and consumes the food. The badger and its mate are like the spirit and the human flesh; and while the spirit withdraws from the flesh more than is necessary, although the body endures it for a time, nonetheless, through another part — namely some infirmity or weakness of virtue that it incurs — it withdraws more from the spirit improvidently, and takes for itself more than the spirit had first withdrawn from it; and so, abstaining or laboring indiscreetly, it loses what it thought to gain. And so Gregory says: 'often, while the flesh is restrained more than is just, it is enervated for good work, so that it is not equal to prayer or preaching, while it hastens to smother the incitements of vice utterly within itself.'

div.head: Cap. V. Ambitionem non mediocriter hominem in periculo detinere, quidque ambitiosis eveniat, canium similitudinibus aperitur.

cit.quote: Ambition so holds a man in a dangerous state that, because of the danger itself, he does not wish to let it go. For just as a dog will by no means let go a fleshy bone, and even hot meat by a fire, however much it may harm him, or however much he is driven off by threats — so too the ambitious man does not wish to let go of positions of dignity, however much anguish and danger he suffers on their account. Proverbs: 'how long, you simple ones, will you love childishness, and fools covet those things which are hurtful to themselves?' For a boy climbs onto a horse with difficulty, but once he has ridden a little, he cannot be gotten down, until he suddenly falls; so too the ambitious man scarcely gives up positions of dignity, until he suddenly dies. Psalm: 'I have seen the wicked highly exalted, and lifted up,' and so on.

Likewise, it happens to the ambitious as it does to dogs: for once the meat is eaten, the bone is thrown to the dogs. Big dogs, the bone left over, quarrel among themselves over it; meanwhile another, small dog comes, finds the bone, and eats it in peace, while the big dogs fight over it and get nothing from it. So too, when a great benefice falls vacant, while one man rises up on one side, and another on the other, to obtain that same benefice, they appeal to the Pope, and, the benefice left aside, quarrel and dispute over it. And meanwhile God bestows it on some simple and good man, who neither expected it nor sought it. Luke: 'he has put down the mighty from their seat, and has exalted the humble.'

div.head: Cap. VI. Improborum amicorum usus qualis existat, mirificis vulpium filiorum, taniumque ac Murium exemplis declaratur.

cit.quote: A treacherous friend, who attends only to his own advantage, sometimes becomes an enemy when the advantage fails: for the cubs of foxes, when they find no milk in their mother's teats, bite her with their teeth, and tear at her, and treat her as a stranger. So too treacherous friends, unless something is put into their mouth as before, stir up war against those who fail them, as is said in Micah.

Likewise, it is clear that a friend who is a friend only for the sake of advantage lasts only as long as the advantage lasts, as shown by the example of the dog, which loves a fleshy bone, embraces it, and guards it, as long as it finds something on it to gnaw, but abandons it once it is stripped bare of flesh; hence Seneca: 'he who has been taken up for the sake of advantage will please only as long as he is useful.'

Likewise, friends who are friends for advantage are likened to mice, which grow fat at the full moon, as certain sea creatures also do, but shrink as the moon wanes. So too friends who are friends for advantage grow as their fortune grows, that is, waxes, but diminish as it wanes — as the Poet says: 'while you are fortunate, you will count many friends; if the times grow cloudy, you will be alone.'

div.head: Cap. VII. Spiritualis, carnalisque amoris discrimen, et effectus, ex forma bruti, ac hominis exemplo agnoscitur: amoremque spiritualem, anime vitam esse, et sanctis viris summopere prodesse, pluribus animalium similitudinibus ostenditur.

cit.quote: Spiritual love draws us toward things above, but animal and carnal love draws us toward earthly things — which appears through the example of the formation of animals: for the formation of the complete brute animal has a face bent down toward the earth; nature has preserved an upright face for man alone. Hence the Poet: 'while the other animals look prone upon the earth, he gave to man a sublime countenance, and bade him look upon the sky.' Hence Basil says: 'all cattle belong to the earth, and so they are bent down toward the earth. But there is another planting: the heavenly man, who is distinguished from the brutes only in the dignity of his posture and form. Theirs is a downward face; but your head is raised on high. But if you defile yourself with bodily pleasure, you have become comparable to senseless cattle, and have become like them.' So then, since a certain spiritual formation comes about through love — because the soul is transformed into the likeness of the thing it loves — he who has spiritual and rational love has his head, that is, his mind, raised toward things above; but he who has animal love, that is, voluptuous or carnal love, has it, like a brute animal, bent only toward the lowest things. The Apostle: 'mind the things that are above, not the things that are on the earth.'

Likewise, spiritual love, in which the life of the soul consists, is preserved the longer, the less a man has of the burning heat of earthly desire. For the stag, which (as Pliny says) never feels fever, lives the longest — more than a hundred years, indeed, as was discovered in the stags of Alexander, caught a hundred years after his death, which had golden collars in their nostrils, sent to them by him. For what is a burning fever, but the heat of desire? He, then, who lacks this fever remains longer in life, since he who lacks desire is preserved for long in charity: for the love of charity is the vital warmth of the soul. Hence Hugh of Saint Victor: 'I know, my soul,' he says, 'that love is your life.' Hence John: 'we know that we have passed from death to life, because we love.' Now the poison of desire extinguishes this life of love. Hence Augustine says that the poison of charity is desire.

Likewise, spiritual quickness of mind makes holy men not feel the ruin, or the adversity, of temporal things. For the cat, when it falls from a height, recovers itself onto its front feet, and scarcely feels or suffers any harm from the fall. So too holy men, when, through the onset of adversity, they fall from the height of temporal prosperity, gather themselves onto their front feet, that is, steady themselves in spiritual affections; for the front feet of the soul are, as it were, the spiritual affections, while the back feet are, as it were, the temporal ones. The Apostle: 'forgetting the things that are behind, stretching forward to those that are before.' And so holy men feel the fall of temporal things the less, the more vehemently they burn in the love of spiritual ones.

Likewise, the love of charity is a spiritual fire, which does not lay waste the soul, but renews it. Hence the minds of those who love God are like certain belts made of salamander skin: for there is a certain kind of salamander whose hairy hide, like the skin of a seal, is used to make belts for the use of kings; and these belts, after long age, thrown into the fire, are not burned up, but are renewed. The Apostle: 'be renewed in the spirit of your mind.'

div.head: Cap. VIII. Anima rationalis quo magis humiliatur, et a terrenis seiungitur, eo magis exercitiis spiritualibus aptior efficitur, quod per araneam, ipsiusque tele artificium singularibus similitudinibus elucidatur.

cit.quote: The more the soul is humbled, like the spider, and set free from earthly love, the more ingenious and industrious it becomes in spiritual exercises. For the spider is small in body, and yet is marvelously industrious in making its web. And it is a great wonder how it draws so much material from its own belly. For Avicenna, and also Dioscorides, say that spiders' webs are generated, by an artifice of nature, from their own inner substance, although (as some say) their belly is always found empty of such material. In the spider, then, there is smallness of body, emptiness of belly, and nonetheless a marvelous art or diligence of work. For (as Pliny says) with a measured claw it draws out a round thread, and with wondrous artifice joins the threads together, which it carries from bottom to top, and crosswise from point to point, with a certain regular spacing, and joins all the radiating strands at a central point, equally distant from the center; and the intervals, or spaces, between the threads of its web are, by a wondrous artifice, now square, now oblong, now round, and the closer to the middle, the narrower, and the closer to the edges, the wider; but how it joins thread to thread so indissolubly, sight does not reveal, and the judgment of reason can scarcely affirm. In a marvelous way, too, by the finest thread, scarcely visible, it lightly lifts and lowers itself, so that it seems to fly. The smallness of the body, then, signifies humility of mind; the emptiness of the belly, freedom from earthly love; the ingenuity of the craft, the prudence of a work by which holy men perform spiritual works in a wondrous way, ordered, connected, distinct, well-formed, and firm, sometimes humbly lowering themselves through condescension, sometimes lifting themselves sublimely through contemplation — like those angels whom Jacob saw ascending and descending on the ladder.

Likewise, the lower powers of the soul are governed through the higher. For in the soul the lower powers correspond to the higher, just as, in an animal, the hooves correspond to the horns. For there is such a kinship between hooves and horns that Aristotle bids that a cow suffering in her hooves be anointed with oil between the horns. Now by the horns understand the higher powers, namely the will and reason; but by the hooves, the lower powers of sensitive appetite, namely the irascible and the concupiscible, which are then tempered and healed of the diseases of disordered passions, when those higher powers themselves are anointed with the oil of divine grace; and such a soul is like that vineyard of which it is said: 'my beloved had a vineyard on a hill, a horn, the son of oil.'

div.head: Cap. IX. Quibus armis spiritualibus contra inimicos Dei electi seipsos tueri debeant, per naturales animalium terrestrium armaturas instruuntur.

cit.quote: The spiritual armor of men is likened to the natural armor of earthly animals. For it is inborn in animals by nature that they should always have some defense against injury: stags have horns for their defense, bees have stings, lions have claws, wolves have teeth, and small animals, which cannot defend themselves, have received agility for fleeing, such as hares and the like. Likewise, against the body, that is, against the temptations of the flesh, stags — that is, spiritual men — help themselves with two horns, namely prayer, by which inward thoughts are put to flight, and fasting, by which outward movements of the flesh are put to flight. Hence this kind of demon, namely of carnal temptations, is not cast out except by prayer and fasting. But the devil often draws men toward the sin from which man must rise again and escape the devil's hand, aiding himself with the tooth by which food is ground, in which contrition for sins is signified. Hence the sinner who has contrition in his mind is, as it were, a wolf that grinds.

Likewise, he ought to help himself with the claw, with which he cuts and opens, and, by opening, brings forth what is within, and this signifies confession, by which the sin hidden in conscience is opened for salvation.

Likewise he ought to help himself, like the bee, with a sting, that is, with the diligence of satisfaction: for the memory of the offense is, as it were, a piercing sting, driving one to make satisfaction. Or: bees — that is, penitents bearing fruit through good works — ought to have the sting of pricking, that is, fear of divine judgment, or the memory of death. But if anyone is not strong enough to resist the world, he ought to help himself by flight, as the ancient holy Fathers did, avoiding persecution by fleeing to the deserts. Psalm: 'behold, I have gone far off flying, and I remained in the wilderness.' Or at least they ought to flee in mind, that is, by removing the heart from worldly things. Psalm: 'if riches abound, set not your heart upon them.'

div.head: Cap. X. Auaritie damna auarique praui effectus, per sanguisuge, Apum, Aranee, Simea, variisque tandem formica exemplis demonstrantur.

cit.quote: Avarice is likened to the leech, which has a triangular mouth, and a tube in its mouth with which it drinks blood, and, applied to flesh, sucks the blood, and, when it has become too full, vomits it out, so that it can suck again, as Isidore says. Likewise, avarice has a triangular mouth, since it has three chief ways of acquiring wrongfully: through robbery, through theft, and through usury; and its insatiable tube is unquenchable greed. This sucks the blood of the poor, as clearly appears in usurers, who sometimes strip their debtors of everything necessary for life, and, once the usurer has filled his purse with usurious gain, he still vomits it out, that is, still lends out that gain received as interest, so as to profit again. 'The leech has two daughters, saying: give, give.'

Likewise, the avaricious man is like a dog lying on a heap of hay, guarding the hay, eating none of it himself, yet barking, and allowing nothing of it to be taken away. And certain serpents are said to do the same, which guard balsam, and allow nothing to be carried off, although they themselves make no use of it. The avaricious are also like bees, which gather honey through flowers, and yet die in the dregs of their own honey.

Likewise, the avaricious man is like the spider, which, in a short time, draws out long threads, and, its web always stretched taut, never ceases from laboring, sustaining perpetual loss in its own work, since, at the slightest wind or rain, the web on which it labored so long is torn. So too the avaricious man acquires great riches in a short time, and, always intent on weaving, that is, increasing or managing them, never ceases from labor; but often, after he has gathered a great web, that is, a great substance, at the slightest wind, that is, the onslaught of some rising war, or a tyrant's plundering, or even at the slightest rain of some misfortune that occurs, what was gathered with such long and great labor is suddenly swept away. 'They have woven the webs of spiders.'

Likewise, the avaricious man is likened to the ape, which, when it has two young, carries the one it loves more in its arms, but carries the other on its shoulders; but when the necessity of fleeing presses upon it, it is forced to cast away the beloved young one, while, weighed down by the other, which it carries on its shoulders, it is more easily caught. The ape, then, is the avaricious man: the young one he loves is the world, which he clasps and carries in his arms, that is, his affections. The young one he loves less is his own spirit, which he carries, as it were, on his back, since he cares little for it. But when, after death, he is compelled to flee, or go out, from here, then he is forced to let go of the beloved young one, that is, the world; and his spirit, of which he took no care, weighed down by sin, is seized by demons, and led to eternal ruin. Luke: 'the rich man died, and was buried in hell.'

Likewise, the avaricious are like the great ants that the historians themselves call Indian ants, which guard gold with marvelous greed, and wage war against men to defend it, and yet reap no benefit from it. For Solinus says that these ants are large and horned, and have a marvelous ferocity out of love for gold. But men go there in the summer season, when, because of the heat, the ants are lying hidden in their burrows, and so steal the gold and gems; but the ants perceive them by scent, come out, attack them, and defend the gold as best they can, and yet neither eat nor drink that gold, nor make anything from it. The same thing happens to many avaricious men, who labor day and night for gold, yet get no good from it. Ecclesiastes: 'a man to whom God has given riches, and substance, and honor, and nothing is wanting to his soul of all that he desires; yet God does not give him the power to eat of it, but a stranger will devour it: this is vanity, and a great misery.'

div.head: Cap. XI. Unico elephantis exemplo, mentes feras sedare, uniceque Deum amare edocemur.

cit.quote: The ferocity of the mind is softened by acts of kindness — which appears in elephants, which are caught in this way (as Solinus says): a pit is dug underground in the path by which they are accustomed to go, into which the elephant unknowingly falls; one hunter, coming to it, strikes and pricks it; but another hunter, coming, strikes the one who struck it, and drives him away, and gives the elephant barley to eat. And when he has done this three or four times, the beast comes to love the one who freed it, and, obeying him, grows tame; from which it is clear that, as the Poet says, 'a friendly hand appeases every fierce animal.' But if a brute animal so loves one who defends it, or soothes it, or draws it out of the pit, even deceitfully, how much more ought the soul to love Christ, who truly defends it from the devil, refreshes it with heavenly food, and leads it out of the pit of sin? Hence every Christian ought to say: 'what shall I render to the Lord for all that he has given me?'

div.head: Cap. XII. Scorpionum natura describitur, qui hominibus blandis assimilantur, peccatoresque blanditiis linire prohibetur.

cit.quote: For the scorpion, as Gregory says, approaches with flattery, but strikes with its tail; it does not bite in the face, but harms from behind. Hence the scorpion is named from 'scortari,' which means to charm, and 'poiein,' which means to feign, since it feigns flattery in front, and stings from behind. All flattering and malicious men, then, are scorpions, who do not oppose the good to their face, but carry behind their back the venom they pour out.

Likewise, it is a great evil for sinners to soften a young man with flattery. Hence the Lord commanded: 'you shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' — for by the kid the sinner is signified, and by the milk, flattery, of which Proverbs says: 'my son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them.' To boil the kid in milk is indeed to soften a sinful man with flattery. Otherwise, however, the kid signifies Christ: on account of the likeness of the flesh of sin, who was to be boiled — that is, killed — by the Jews, in his mother's milk, in the time of his infancy.

div.head: Cap. XIII. Bonitatem atque hominum malitiam ex tribus augeri, precipueque ex voluntate manare, variis exemplis naturalibusque brutorum affectibus aperitur.

cit.quote: The goodness and wickedness of men depend greatly on the place where they dwell, on the company they keep, and on the occupation in which they are engaged. For (according to Hippocrates), for knowledge of the goodness of animals as they are used for man's food, it helps to know the pastures where they are fed; for those that graze in the mountains, that is, in dry places, are better and tastier for eating than those that graze in moist and watery valleys. In this it is also signified that, even for penitents, poor places are better than luxurious ones. Ezekiel: 'this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: abundance, and fullness of bread.' Likewise, it also helps to know the moist or dry air in which they live: for the air by which a man is surrounded is, as it were, the company in which he lives, and it matters greatly whether it is moist or dry, that is, whether it is devout or undevout and arid.

Likewise, it helps to know the degree of their rest and movement. Now domestic animals move less, and so have more moisture, than wild ones, on account of which the flesh of domestic animals is softer and easier to digest: for from much rest the pores are closed, and heat is enclosed within, on account of which the coarse humors are dissolved, and so the flesh softens and grows tender. But because they eat and drink too much, the excess of their humors increases, and multiplies into fat, and so the flesh of such animals is proven to nourish very greatly. So too spiritual and contemplative men, being more at rest and less active than carnal or active men, remain, on that account, moist through the compunction of tears — that is, in them too, from much rest of mind, the pores, that is, the senses of the body, are closed, and the coarse humors dissolved, that is, earthly thoughts and affections are dispersed in them; they grow soft through piety, and tender through sparing food and drink; but because they enjoy an abundance of inward spiritual nourishment, they are filled with the fatness of consolation and grace, of which it is said: 'let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness.'

Likewise, in men, goodness and wickedness of character follow from the goodness and wickedness of the will, just as in brute animals it arises from the goodness and wickedness of their temperament. For what natural temperament does in brutes, the disposition of the will does in men, on account of which Augustine says that it is the will by which one sins and lives rightly. That the characters of brutes vary according to their various temperaments is clear from many examples: hence, although all animals have both the power of movement and of sensation, it is nonetheless present in them by greater or lesser degree. For some are of livelier sense, stronger judgment, and subtler cunning. Hence the ox is full of sluggishness and slow to move, the ass stupid, the horse prone to lust, the wolf untamed, the dog a grateful and faithful friend. And this likewise happens (as Aristotle says) because some animals are of great gentleness, like the cow and the sheep; some of untamed ferocity, like the unicorn; some of great boldness, like the lion; some of cunning deceit and great malice, like the wolf and the fox. Hence too (as the same says) some animals love company, and go in herds, like stags, wild asses, and camels, and the like; and some flee company, such as those that live by plunder. Avicenna, however, says that, of all animals, man cannot live alone, and cranes, ants, and bees agree with man in this. All these various characters, then, which are present variously in brute animals from the diversity of their temperament, fit men too, in their own way, from the diverse disposition of the will: for it is said that, first, all men in common have a sense of discretion, and an impulse toward good work; prelates and superiors ought to have a sense — that is, of the lamb — livelier with respect to God, a stronger and truer judgment with respect to themselves, and a greater cunning with respect to their neighbor; or there ought to be in them a sense excelling in the contemplation of divine things, a judgment vigorous in the provision for the future, and a prudent cunning in the governing of their subjects; or a sense as to the exposition of the Scriptures, a judgment as to the distribution of alms, and a cunning as to the correction of faults.

Men, too, are found like oxen in the slowness of sluggishness, like asses in the stupidity of imprudence, like horses in proneness to lust, like dogs in the faithfulness of friendship. Some are found gentle, like cows, through mildness; and some fierce, like unicorns, through tyranny; some bold, like lions, through presumption; some deceitful, like foxes, through trickery. Some, too, love the solitary life and the secrecy of contemplation, while others strive to serve the Lord in the gatherings of monasteries or convents; but commonly a man does not live safely alone, neither as regards bodily life, nor as regards spiritual life. Hence it is said: 'woe to him that is alone, for when he falls,' and so on. Those who live together in cloisters are said to agree with cranes in guarding themselves well: for cranes are said to be the best guardians of themselves, since cranes (as Ambrose says) seek the ground with the herald-cry of their voice, where they rest from labor, and set watchful guards for the camp, so that the others may rest securely. For the watchers stand upright on one leg, and hold a small stone in the other foot, raised from the ground, so that, if sleep should creep in, they would be roused by the falling of the stone.

Likewise, they ought to agree with ants, namely in providing shrewdly for the future. Proverbs: 'go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom; which, having no guide, nor master, nor captain, provides her food in the summer, and gathers in the harvest what she may eat.'
Likewise, one ought to agree with bees, doing good works sweetly. Ecclesiasticus: 'the bee is small among flying things, but her fruit has the chiefest sweetness.'

div.head: Cap. XIIII. Fraterne dilectionis lex quemadmodum sit a nobis adimplenda, castorum, cervorumque exemplis perfecte instruimur.

cit.quote: Beavers teach us to fulfill the law of brotherly love. For these animals live in a herd, love their own kind, cut down wood with their teeth, carry it to their dens, and bring it there in a marvelous way: for they lay one of their own kind on its back, as a cart, with its feet raised, and lay the cut wood between its legs; and so, when they have loaded it, they drag it to their dens, where they unload it, and, with great skill, prepare their dwellings for themselves. Beavers, then, teach us to live sociably and in friendship among men, to eagerly seize the examples of virtue from others — which is to cut wood from the trees with our mouths — and to bring it home to dwell in our minds; and that one carries burdens for the others teaches us to fulfill that law of charity of which the Apostle says: 'bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ' — and we ought especially to help one another in building the house of the mind, as a dwelling for God.

Likewise, the order of stags requires that the stronger, in their labors, go before the weaker, so that, both by their example and their help, the weaker may bear the labor more easily. For example, when stags cross vast rivers and seas, the stronger go before in swimming, and the weaker lay their heads upon them as they swim, and so, taking turns to succeed one another, they bear the labor more lightly; for (as Isidore says) the Apostle says: 'we, that are stronger, ought to bear the infirmities of the weak.'

div.head: Cap. XV. Hominis carnalis, qui Herydi serpenti comparatur, miseria quanta sit, breviter demonstratur.

cit.quote: ...to the water-serpent, which dwells in the water, by whose bite those who are struck become swollen with dropsy, which many call 'ox-dropsy,' since it makes use of ox dung, as Isidore says. Such are carnal men, living in the waters of pleasure, who become, as it were, dropsical, insatiable for the very delights of the flesh, just as the man with dropsy is insatiable for drink. And there, while they glory in carnal things, they make use, as it were, of good dung: for the glory of a sinful man is dung and worms. As it were dung to the good, is the very uncleanness of the flesh, in which the lustful man delights. Lamentations: 'they that were fed delicately on saffron have embraced the dung' — that is, spurning the delights of the spirit, they embrace carnal vices. And there is also the swimming serpent, which poisons the waters with its venom, as Lucan says, and such is the delight of lust, which also poisons the waters of marriage with the venom of sin.

div.head: Cap. XVI. Caro humana que vacce, et ipsiusmet concupiscentia, que Sirene, Scorpioni, et rubete assimilatur, quomodo sit edomanda pariter, et a peccato purganda edocetur.

cit.quote: Our flesh is likened to a cow. For the cow, once fattened, throws off the yoke, to which she readily submitted when less well fed. But lying in her own dung and growing sluggish, she fattens, especially if withdrawn from labor. Just as the cow, then, fattened by food, by lying in dung, and by idleness, refuses the yoke, so too our flesh, fattened by the pleasure of gluttony, the dung of lust, and idleness, kicks back, and refuses to bear the yoke of the spirit. 'The beloved grew fat, and kicked.' Deuteronomy. But, on the contrary, flesh tamed by labors and abstinence submits meekly to the yoke of the spirit; on account of which the Apostle said: 'I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection.' Hence the wantonness of the flesh must be tamed like that of a heifer: for a heifer is a young cow, when she is already fit for the yoke (as Isidore says); and because she is a wanton animal, she is pressed with a stronger yoke and pricked with the goad, so that she follows the ox rightly. If ever the flesh is wanton, it ought to be pressed with the strong yoke of penance, and troubled with the goad of penal works. Ecclesiasticus: 'torture and fetters for a malicious servant.'

...the siren, by her song, makes a man sleep, and when she sees him overcome by sleep, carries him to a dry place, and forces him to couple with her; and if he is unwilling or unable, she kills and eats him. The pestilent siren, then, is, as it were, the concupiscence of the flesh, whose sweet song is the suggestion of delight; to which a man sleeps, when reason fails to resist it through negligence; but he is then led to the dry place, when, through inward consent, he is emptied of the water of grace; but he couples with the siren, when he arrives at the deed of sin; and if a man, perhaps already touched within by some compunction, should flee, or, by some hindrance, be unable to complete it, then he is attacked by a fiercer battle of temptation, by which he is sometimes thrown down, and devoured by the habit of sin. Isaiah: 'sirens in the temples of pleasure.'

Likewise, the concupiscence of the flesh is likened to the scorpion, whose venom (as Pliny says) does great harm for three days, and finally kills by a slow death, unless help is quickly given. Likewise, the venom of concupiscence does great harm for, as it were, three days: first, in delightful thought; second, in giving consent; and third, in carrying out the deed. For the deed of lust kills by a slow death, since it does not lead at once, but only after the end of life, to eternal punishment.

Likewise, our flesh, mortified by the humility of penance, becomes a medicine for the soul — an example of which appears in the toad, or rather in the 'boracia,' which is a kind of venomous frog; which, although it is very venomous, nonetheless, through being burned to ash, loses the power of its venom, and receives a great medicinal virtue. Hence it is effective for the recovery of lost skin and flesh, the strengthening of sinews, and the drying of wounds, if one uses that ash rightly. So too, although the flesh is infected with the venom of concupiscence, nonetheless, through being reduced to ash, that is, humbled through the mortification of penance, it becomes the soul's medicine: for, through its affliction and mortification, the poison of lust is extinguished; merit, first lost through sin, is restored; the sinews, that is, the powers of the soul, are strengthened and made firm; and the wounds of temptation cease, and dry up.

Likewise, the vices of the flesh are removed by constant labor — an example of which appears in the roe deer, since (as Constantine says) through the swiftness of its movement and the constancy of its running, the roe's flesh is purged of excess, and the heaviness of taste and smell is removed from its flesh, and it becomes more tender and digestible. So too, from diligence in good work, and constant movement of labor, our flesh is purged of the passions of carnal vices, whose nourishment is idleness. Ecclesiasticus: 'send the servant,' that is, the flesh, 'to work, lest he be idle: for idleness has taught much wickedness.'

Likewise, the vice of the flesh, like the roe or a temptation, is better escaped by fleeing than by resisting; just as the roe defends itself from dogs not with claw nor tooth, but by swiftness of flight alone. Hence the Apostle: 'flee fornication.'

div.head: Cap. XVII. Castitatem seruantes multa suscipiunt bona, et a multis liberantur curis: quod quidem per bonis castrationem, et caloris similitudinem aperitur.

cit.quote: The chastity of man is likened to the castration of an ox. For the ox, after castration, advances in strength and vigor, and becomes more tame, more mature, more quiet, more fit for labor, and of weightier gait; in which it signifies that, through chastity voluntarily and wholly kept — which castration signifies (of which the Lord said that there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven) — a man is disposed toward growth in grace, toward taking up the tame yoke of discipline, toward maturity in penance, toward quiet of conscience, toward labor in obedience, and toward the weight of modesty.

Likewise, those who live in continence are freed from the many cares and dangers that the married suffer and are entangled in. And so those who vow continence, and live continently, are like the beaver, which, sensing that it is being hunted by hunters for its testicles, which are useful for medicine, when it perceives the hunters, bites off its own testicles and leaves them behind, and so redeems itself from them; and so beavers ('castores') are named from 'castrating.' And this is attested of the beaver by Isidore, Cicero, Juvenal, the Physiologus, and Pliny; certain authors, however, deny this, though perhaps some particular species of beaver does this. Like this beaver, then, are those who vow continence, namely who castrate themselves, not carnally but spiritually, for the kingdom of heaven, lest, through the desires and pleasures of the flesh, they be captured by the hunters of hell, that is, by demons.

div.head: Cap. XVIII. Sanctorum virorum prudentia quanta sit, panthere unico demonstratur exemplo.

cit.quote: Many holy men abound in caution and circumspection, especially in outward things. Hence they are like the panther, which, on its outer hide, is painted over with small circles, so that, from the variety of its markings, it appears entirely covered with eyes on the outside. As the Apocalypse says of the holy animals, that they were 'full of eyes, before and behind.' And these eyes are their most prudent cautions and provident circumspections, by which they see how they must walk cautiously in all things, as it is said there, that these eyes of the holy animals were before and behind. For in front is the manifold caution and circumspection of the virtues; but behind, the caution and circumspection concerning vices; or they have eyes in front, that is, cautions, in providing for the future, and behind, from the memory of the past; or they have eyes in front, in the contemplation of spiritual things, but behind they have eyes, that is, many cautions, in the management of temporal things. Hence they subtly contemplate eternal things, which are before them, and prudently manage temporal things, which are behind.

div.head: Cap. XIX. Mentis cetitatem, lacerte pulcherrimo exemplo, a nobis expellere, ac per penitentie partes lumen gratie recipere erudimur.

cit.quote: The lizard teaches us to put blindness of mind to flight. For there is a certain lizard called the 'saura' (as Isidore says), whose eyes, when they grow dim with approaching old age, enter a hole in a wall, and, opening its eyes toward the sun, receive light. The lizard grown dim with old age is, as it were, the sinner blinded by a long habit of sinning. If he wishes to receive the light of divine grace, he must enter the hole in the wall, that is, the bitterness of penance, or of regular obedience, and there open the eyes of his mind, that is, his understanding through prayer, and his affection through devotion, to the Sun, that is, to Christ. Or: the eyes of the soul are opened to the light of heavenly grace through contrition and confession in the hole of the wall, that is, in the narrowness of satisfaction, and then the light of heavenly grace is received. Isaiah: 'the eyes of the blind shall be opened.'

div.head: Cap. XX. Cameli singulari exemplo, verbum, quod profecto cibus anime est, digne suscipere instruimur.

cit.quote: ...of the camel. For the camel has several stomachs. It first receives food in the first stomach, which begins to be digested in the second, and better in the third, and its digestion is completed in the fourth. So too the food of spiritual teaching requires four receptacles. For first it must be received in the ear, namely so that it is heard attentively. John: 'he that is of God hears the words of God.'

Second, in the heart, so that it is understood, so that it is held in memory. James: 'not becoming a forgetful hearer' — and there it begins to be digested through affection, namely in the heart, in which digestion, however, the word is not itself transformed, but transforms.

Third, in the hand, that is, in deed, so that it is carried out. James: 'be doers of the word, and not hearers only' — and in this way it is better digested, since it is applied more to the man, and is more assimilated to him. James: 'the doer of the work shall be blessed in his deed.' But fourth, it is received in the mouth, so that it may be wisely taught; and this is the complete digestion of the word, that is, its common usefulness, when it perfects the one learning it. Hence Matthew: 'he who shall do and teach, shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.'

div.head: Cap. XXI. Vita claustralis commendatur, que et testudini non immerito assimilatur.

cit.quote: ...the tortoise. For the tortoise is enclosed in its shell; and that which lives in rivers is venomous and deadly, but the land tortoise, which dwells in houses or woods, is good. Its flesh is good for the consumptive and wasted, since its properties are restorative. So too the religious life is enclosed in a shell, that is, the enclosure of the cloister, of obedience, and of continence. But if it is of the river kind, that is, lax or fluid, and restrained by no rein of discipline, as certain monasteries are, then it is venomous and deadly — deadly, namely, to those in it, and venomous to others who imitate them. But the land kind, that is, that which is kept firm within the bounds of due discipline, whether of cenobites dwelling in cities or of hermits living in the woods, is good and praiseworthy. This is useful and profitable to take up for the consumptive, that is, the wasted — that is, for those in the world who lack the strength to escape the battles of the world or the devil — since it restores and confers on them spiritual virtues. Psalm: 'behold, I have gone far off flying' — namely, from the world — 'and I remained in the wilderness.'

div.head: Cap. XXII. Peccata illico confiteri canis exemplo, ac ne per verecundiam confiteri in grauioribus a diabolo illaqueamur peccatis, leonis similitudine admonemur.

cit.quote: Dogs teach us to confess and to purge our sins, since, when they grow sick, they eat the root of a certain herb, so as to vomit, and so are cured; and Pliny says that dogs were the first to show evacuation and purgation, since, filled with harmful food, they eat grass, and purge themselves by vomiting. If anyone has the sickness of sin, if he eats the root of the herb, that is, if he has contrition, which is the root of penance, it will lead him to the vomiting of confession, through which the soul is purged by expelling the sin: through the grass of penance, then, the sin is vomited out in confession, which had been a poisonous nourishment to the soul; and so the purging of conscience comes about. Ecclesiasticus: 'vomit it up, and it will refresh you.'

Likewise, confession of sin must be made while the sin is still recent, since then it effectively frees the penitent, being before the sin has become habitual — just as a nursing pup, its wound still open, exposed to the bites of serpents, draws out the poison, relieves the pain, and restores the whole limb to health, along with other remedies applied, as Pliny says. For the sin's newness, delighting and enticing, is, as it were, the nursing pup; and it is opened, and exposed to the serpent's bite, when it is set forth with compunction in confession. For the serpent's bite is, as it were, the fall into temptation itself, which brings both the poison of guilt through consent, and the pain of conscience through remorse. But while, through confession, the sin, still recent, is uncovered like the nursing pup with its wound still open, and exposed to the wound, both the poison of guilt is drawn out, and the pain of conscience is taken away; and, with the remedies applied, the health of the mind is fully restored through satisfaction.

But it should be noted that shame at confessing keeps a man in sin, and causes him to be held and entangled by the devil, just as the lion is held and caught by man. For to catch a lion, a double pit is dug: one right next to the other, and a sheep is placed in the first, but a certain cage, which closes easily, is placed in the second. The lion, coming for the sheep, leaps into the first pit, and, seeing that it cannot get out of it, driven by shame, to hide itself, enters the second, and so falls into the trap. Afterward it is led by the hunter from the second pit back into the first, and is kept there until it is tamed, as Jerome relates. Likewise, there is a double pit for catching and entangling the sinner: the first is when the sin is committed; the second is when the sin is retained, or continued. In the first is placed the sheep, that is, bestial delight, on account of which the sinner throws himself headlong. In the second is the little cage that closes itself, that is, the habit of sin, which holds the sinner as if enclosed, so that he can scarcely get out; and the sinner enters the second from the first, out of shame, namely so as to hide himself; since, after a man has fallen into sin, he is so ashamed to confess, and so afraid of it being known, that he rather remains in that very sin. But because, while one sin is retained, it draws in another, he passes from the first pit to the second, since, from the single act of sin, he passes to the habit of sinning; on account of which a man is held strongly and for a long time by the devil, so that he is never released by him, once he has been enclosed by him through a wicked habit.

...the dog: for there is a certain frog which, put into a dog's mouth, makes it mute. The dog, then, is the unclean sinner, whom the frog, that is, human shame, makes mute in the confession of sin. And likewise the frog, that is, worldly fear, makes the dog, that is, the preacher, mute in rebuking vice. 'Dumb dogs, not able to bark.'

div.head: Cap. XXIII. Sanctorum confidentia Leonis exemplo spiritualiter in capite Christo, et in pectore, id est, corde persistere edocetur.

cit.quote: The confidence of holy men is not in outward show, but in inward spirit, and in Christ's help and power. For they are like lions, whose whole strength is in the chest, and firmness in the head; so too the strength of the saints is in the chest, that is, inwardly in the heart, since the heart is enclosed in the chest. The Apostle: 'that you may be strengthened by his Spirit in the inner man.'

Likewise, their firmness is in the head, that is, in Christ. Psalm: 'by the word of the Lord the heavens' — namely the saints — 'were made firm.' For Christ himself, who is the Word of God, is the head of the saints, that is, of the Church, according to that saying of the Apostle: 'he gave him to be head over all the Church, which is his body.' Proverbs: 'the just, like a lion, shall be without fear.'

div.head: Cap. XXIIII. Quemadmodum contriti peccatores, aliquoue infortunio afflicti, subleuentur, miro elephantis exemplo demonstratur.

cit.quote: Men are said to show compassion and help to one who has fallen into sin, or into any misfortune, in the same way as with the elephant. For the Philosopher says that when an elephant, for the sake of rest, leans against a tree, especially a palm, it sometimes breaks the tree, and falls to the ground; seeing its own fall past remedy, it trumpets in a marvelous way, and at its trumpeting, a multitude of young elephants suddenly come, who lift the old one up with all their strength, and, to raise it, bend down with a wondrous affection. Now a man leans on a tree, wishing to rest, when he clings to the world, or to the delight of sin, so as to satisfy his desire; but when the tree breaks, he falls, since, either the world failing him, or the delight passing, he plunges into adversity or sin. And then, recognizing his own wretched fall, he ought to trumpet, that is, tearfully beg the help of others, crying out to the saints, or to pious and humble men; and then the stronger or more powerful others ought to have compassion on him, and help him as they can, so that he may be raised up. Ecclesiastes: 'if one falls, he shall be supported by the other.'

div.head: Cap. XXV. Tentationum sagittas, quedam capreoli singulari similitudine, expellere erudimur.

cit.quote: The humility of compunction drives back the arrows of temptations. For Aristotle says of the roe deer that, when it is wounded, it seeks and eats cumin, by which it drives the arrow from its body. Now the darts of arrows are, as it were, the burning attacks of temptations, and when anyone finds himself struck by them, he ought to eat cumin; and one eats cumin, when he anxiously brings himself back to the humility of compunction: for this is what represses the swelling of pride, just as cumin seed checks the swelling of the belly. This humility of compunction, then, while it fortifies the heart with a strong guard, drives back the arrows of temptations from a greater distance. Gregory: 'if the power of compunction affects us inwardly, all the noise of wicked thought falls silent.'

div.head: Cap. XXVI. Hominis domus interior que sit, quamque solerter a nobis sit edificanda, paranda, ac custodienda, Bombicis exemplo aperitur.

cit.quote: Every man ought to have the house of his own conscience, like the silkworm, that is, that worm from whose weaving silk is made. For it first builds itself a house, in which it dwells, and in which it defends itself against the cold, and afterward weaves webs, in the manner of spiders. The inner house of man is conscience, which wisdom builds, which penance purges, which charity adorns; and to these, above all, man ought to attend. Ecclesiasticus: 'run to your house,' and so on. This house, when it is well prepared, becomes God's dwelling place, the home of peace, the refectory of heavenly delights, and, against the cold, that is, against the harshness of any adversity, the strongest bulwark. With this house first built, then, a man can safely weave webs on the outside, that is, attend to outward things, ordered for the benefit of others.

Likewise, the house of conscience is built with labor, but easily laid waste. Hence it is likened to a spider's web, which is put together with much labor, and yet is easily destroyed. So too the conscience, by a single act of mortal sin. James: 'whoever offends in one point, is become guilty of all.'

div.head: Cap. XXVII. Precipuus contemplationis, seu orationis locus ubi sit, eiusdemque effectus, et utilitates, animalium nonnullorum exemplis, naturalibusque rationibus declaratur.

cit.quote: Contemplation and prayer correspond, by likeness, to the dwelling of earthly animals, of which some (as Avicenna says) dwell in the mountains, like stags and the like. Psalm: 'the high mountains are a refuge for the stags.' But some dwell in caves, like foxes and moles and the like. Matthew: 'the foxes have holes.' But some dwell in fields and open places, like sheep and the like. Psalm: 'all sheep and oxen, moreover, and the beasts also of the field.' So too the contemplative life, or that of those who pray, requires a mountain, that is, the height of one's conduct. Isaiah: 'come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.' As a sign of this, the Lord, wishing to pray, went up a mountain.
Likewise, it requires a cave, that is, a hiding place of safety and solitude. Matthew: 'but you, when you pray, enter into your room, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father.'

Likewise, it requires the openness and breadth of love, or the openness, that is, the lowness of humility, or the openness, that is, the moderation of sobriety, namely so that the contemplative does not know more than he ought to know; and so they ought not to rise up through presumption, but keep themselves in humility: 'seek not the things that are too high for you.'

Likewise, the stillness of contemplation fattens souls, just as sleep fattens dormice. For dormice are long-bodied mice, which sleep makes fat: for they sleep and rest, as if dead, the whole winter through. They signify, then, those who persist for a long time in contemplation, who, withdrawn inwardly into themselves from outward tumults, persisting long in contemplation, as though resting in a long sleep, grow fat with inward consolation, and, while they die to outward cares and deeds, are inwardly filled with a marvelous fatness of grace.

Likewise, contemplation, or prayer, makes us know the state of our own mind, and its defect. For the wild ass, when it does not know where its mate is, climbs a high mountain, and by scent alone perceives where she is. So too a man, who does not know where, that is, in what state, his own mind or conscience stands, ought, through contemplation and prayer, to climb on high, and there, enlightened, even if not by sight, that is, by certain knowledge, at least by a certain scent, that is, by a probable conjecture, weigh and come to know the state, or the defect, of his own soul. Isaiah: 'behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and lifted up' — then the servant of God will understand what he is, when he rises up into the height of contemplation.

div.head: Cap. XXVIII. Vere contritionis vis, que culpe venenum est, immundis muscis pulcherrimo exemplo comparatur.

cit.quote: Humble contrition draws the poison of guilt from the sinner's heart, and soothes the bite and sorrow of conscience, just as crushed flies, applied to the bite of a venomous spider, draw out the venom, and ease or relieve the pain. For the crushing of the unclean flies is the contrition and penance for shameful actions; but the bite of the venomous spider is the consent to, or commission of, an evil action or temptation. Hence, concerning this example, note that the living fly is food for the spider, but the fly, dead and crushed, becomes the medicine for the spider's bite. In which it is signified that sin, living in a man, feeds the devil; but when it is mortified through penance and contrition, the devil's power is emptied out. Or: the fly, dead and crushed, is the manly flesh mortified and worn down by the afflictions of penance, which resists the bites of spiders, since it repels the temptations of demons.

div.head: Cap. XXIX. Diabolum, qui sui assimilatur, prauam cordis hominis intentionem magnifacere, pluribus rationibus demonstratur: Araneaque exemplo qua via reparetur anima peccatrix edocetur.

cit.quote: The devil loves the vice of the heart above all things — indeed, so as to nourish it, he sometimes extinguishes all outward vices. And so the devil is like itself. For the sow (as Pliny says) sometimes bears twenty piglets, and sometimes devours them all, except the first, which she loves above the rest, and to which she first gives the first teat. Likewise, although the devil brings forth many vices in a man, as it were many children, nonetheless, because the first root of all of them is in the heart, he therefore cherishes and loves the corruption of the heart above all else, and, in order to preserve and nourish it, does not care even to extinguish other vices — which appears most of all in hypocrites, in whom almost all vices arise from a crooked intention of the heart. To nourish and preserve this in them, the devil does not care — indeed, he rejoices — that all outward vices be restrained: namely that the vice of gluttony be restrained through abstinence, or of lust through continence, or of the tongue through holy teaching, or of avarice through almsgiving; and so of all the rest the devil does not care, provided that the heart's intention, which is, as it were, his firstborn, remains and is preserved corrupt: for the devil knows well that, if the intention that precedes is wicked, every work that follows is perverse, however right it may seem, as Gregory says.

Likewise, the spider, its web broken, does not go out to hunt until it has first repaired it, which it always begins to mend from the middle, counting the outer edges as nothing, so long as the middle is broken. So too, when the soul or life is broken by sin, a man must first repair it through penance, beginning from the middle, that is, from the heart, before he goes out to do outward works, since, while the fracture of sin remains within, outward works would not be meritorious. Matthew: 'cleanse first that which is within.' Gregory: 'if once the heart is corrupted in its intention, the middle and the end of the action that follows are securely held by the cunning enemy; since he sees the whole tree bearing fruit for himself, which he has poisoned with the tooth of venom at the root.'

div.head: Cap. XXX. Quantum sit immanis hominis peruersa natura, canis similitudine sit manifestum.

cit.quote: ...dogs, which all tear and pursue a dog that has been struck and is howling. So too, cruel men do not help a man struck by adversity, but rather tear him further by detraction, saying that he deserved it well. 'They have added to the grief of my wounds.' Psalm. Boethius: 'this weight is added to our misfortunes, that when something grievous is inflicted on the wretched, they are believed to have deserved what they suffer.' Sometimes, too, such cruel men pursue not only with curses, but even with deeds and injuries, according to that saying: 'he persecuted the poor and needy man.' Psalm.

div.head: Cap. XXXI. Quod Christus sua cruce, rubeis humanitatis indutus vestimentis, demonem deceperit atque vicerit, ipsius bouis sylvestris mirabili explanatur exemplo.

cit.quote: The cross of Christ bound the devil, as with a wild bull, and overthrew his power. An example of this is found in the wild bull, which hates and pursues everything red; and so the hunter clothes himself in red, and so draws it toward himself. But when he sees it approaching, he hides behind a large tree, and the bull strikes the tree so forcefully with its horns that it drives them into the wood, so that it cannot pull them out; and so, while seeking to kill another, it kills itself. This wild bull, then, bears the likeness of the devil, who hates everything red, since he thirsts to shed the blood of the saints; but Christ, the heavenly hunter, came, and clothed himself in red, when he put on and took up passible flesh, which was formed from the most pure blood of the Blessed Virgin, as Damascene says. Or: he was clothed in red when his most holy body grew red with blood, as in the prayer, and the scourging, and the crucifixion. Isaiah: 'why is your apparel red?' Christ, then, seeing the devil, in the time of his passion, pursuing him ever closer, hid himself behind the great tree, namely, concealing the power of his divinity, when he allowed himself to be fixed to the cross; and while the devil faithfully worked to have him crucified, he drove himself forcefully against that very cross, and so, while he believed he was crushing and casting down Christ, he himself was seized and cast down. For this (as the Church says) the order of our salvation demanded: that the cunning of the many-shaped betrayer should be deceived by its own art, and that the enemy should be struck at the very root by which he had done harm.

div.head: Cap. XXXII. Leopardi exemplo singularis auaritie cupiditatem maiorem in modum fore vitandam manifestatur.

cit.quote: The greed of avarice leads to the ruin of the soul. For the avaricious man is like the leopard, which, when it has eaten something poisonous, seeks human dung, so as to extinguish the poison with it; hence hunters hang that dung in a vessel high on a tree, and, as the leopard leaps up to it, to get the dung, the hunters kill it meanwhile. The leopard, then, is infected by the poison, just when the avaricious man is inflamed by greed, since the poison of charity is greed, as Augustine says. But he seeks human dung to expel the poison, just when, pursuing greed to the full, he pursues temporal gains, of which the Apostle says: 'I have counted all things as loss, and I think them as dung, that I may gain Christ.' But the hunters hang this dung high on a tree, just when demons show the greedy mind the splendor of temporal riches, so as to inflame it. So the devil did to Christ, when he led him onto a high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and then said: 'all these I will give you,' and so on. What, then, he did to Christ by open vision, he does more often to the greedy man by hidden suggestion; hence, when the greedy man strives to seize the dung of temporal riches through unlawful gains, he is deprived, by the hunters, that is, the demons, of the soul's life. Hence the Apostle: 'they that will become rich fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil, and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires, which drown men into destruction and perdition.'

div.head: Cap. XXXIII. Inordinatam rerum temporalium occupationem Bombicis exemplo hominem ab interiori virtute penitus priuare monstratur.

cit.quote: Excessive care and preoccupation with temporal things empties a man of inward virtue — an example of which appears in the silkworm, that is, in that little worm from whose weaving silk is made, which weaves webs in the manner of spiders.
