But, as Isidore says, while it heaps up thread, it empties itself, and nothing remains in it but air: for he heaps up thread for weaving webs who turns the pursuits of his life to the management and occupation of temporal things; since, while he is wholly entangled in the affairs of the world, he is inwardly emptied entirely of the virtues. Hence the Apostle says that no man, serving as a soldier for God, entangles himself with secular business, that he may please him to whom he has proved himself.

div.head: Cap. XXXIIII. Hominis curiositate diabolum animas sepenumero inficere, Cerui sylvestris exemplo confirmatur.

cit.quote: Curiosity for novelties is the devil's instrument for killing souls: for curious men are like wild stags, who are of such simplicity that they marvel and are stunned at every novelty, and, when a horse or a buffalo approaches them, look at it so intently that they do not notice a man coming up beside them and shooting arrows at them. So too curious minds, when they are occupied with certain useless novelties that seem wonderful to them, are struck by the devil with the dart of error, or of pride, or of some other sin. The Apostle says: 'avoid profane novelties of words.' So too were the Athenians curious, of whom it is said in Acts 12 that they spent their time on nothing else but telling or hearing something new.

div.head: Cap. XXXV. Peccati delectationem mortem inferre menti, unico muris atque ursi naturalis exemplo manifestatur.

cit.quote: The delight of sin kills the mind, just as a drink kills the mouse. For Aristotle says that the mouse does not drink, and if it drinks, it dies. Then, indeed, is the delight of sin drunk, when consent is given to it: 'it entered like water into his inward parts,' and then the soul is killed, since sin, when it is consummated, generates death.

Likewise, delight is the cause of the soul's death, just as the sweetness of honey is the cause of the bear's death. For the bear sometimes climbs the very tallest trees, and seeks fruit and honey there, and, often, when hungry, returns to the same place; hence the hunter surrounds the foot of the tree on all sides with ropes and very sharp stakes, and, before the opening from which the honey comes out, hangs a heavy hammer on a rope; the hungry bear, coming, and eager to draw the honey from the tree, is blocked by the hammer; it then pushes the hammer away from itself, but the harder it pushes it, the more forcefully it swings back and strikes its head, and so it continues, until, from the repeated blows, its head grows weak and fails, and, falling, it plunges onto the stakes, and so kills itself by its own foolishness. Likewise, while a man seeks the sweetness, or the delights, of sin, the hammer of the divine word — of which Jeremiah says, 'my words are like a hammer that breaks the rock' — resists him, forbidding that very sin; and when the sinner pushes it away and casts it from himself, according to that saying of the Psalm, 'you have cast my words behind you,' he strikes against it all the more forcefully, and, finally failing, plunges into sin, which drags him to eternal ruin.

div.head: Cap. XXXVI. Quod charitas cum bona cordis desiderio semper debeat copulari ut meritum suscipiat singulari bouis similitudine demonstratur.

cit.quote: The good desires of the heart then have efficacy, and lead to good works, when they are informed by charity: for those oxen are excellent for work that have broad horns, while those with small, black horns are reckoned useless for work. Now the horns of the head are, as it were, the desires of the mind, which are then broadened, so long as the oxen are informed by charity; and then such men work excellently, since the love of God is never idle, for it works great things, if it is present. 'This shall please God more than a young calf, that brings forth horns.' But black oxen, that is, men darkened in sin, since they lack the extension of charity, have small horns, that is, small good desires. And so they are entirely useless for working well. Hence, in such an ox, the warmth of charity failing and the cold of iniquity abounding, the sluggishness of the plow abounds, that is, of fruitful work, according to that saying: 'the sluggard would not plow because of the cold.'

div.head: Cap. XXXVII. Detractoris natura breuiter aperitur, qui tribus rationibus serpenti comparatur.

cit.quote: The detractor is likened to the serpent. First, because the serpent silently inflicts its bite, as is said of the 'dipsas,' which kills before it is felt, and brings no sorrow to the dying man. Such is the secret detractor. Ecclesiastes: 'if a serpent bite in silence, he is nothing better that backbites secretly.'

Second, because the serpent moves not straight, but in a winding way. Hence, according to Isidore, it is called 'anguis,' as it were 'angulosus' (full of angles), since it never goes straight; and such is the deceitful detractor, who begins with praise, so that he is not readily believed to speak out of hatred, but after the commendation, turns back to reproach.

Third, because the serpent eats earth: for there are certain serpents that hide in caves, and lick dust, and suck up the moisture of the earth, as Pliny says. Such is the treacherous and malicious detractor, who secretly lies in wait for the deeds of others, and eats only what he sees as earthly, that is, useful, or contemptible — that is, he speaks of it by biting and detracting; but any good things he knows, he suppresses by concealing them. Isaiah: 'dust shall be the serpent's food.'

div.head: Cap. XXXVIII. Hominis devotio quo pacto perficiatur, naturali animalium exemplo docetur.

cit.quote: Devout men, the more they remove themselves from the flesh, the more they advance in goodness and savor of mind. For animals that are naturally moist are better and tastier the further they are removed from milk, as is clear in the flesh of pigs. So too those moist with many tears, that is, devout men, the further they withdraw from the milk of that carnal sweetness, the more they increase in the savor of inward consolation. Psalm: 'my soul refused to be comforted' — namely, in carnal things — and so it follows: 'I remembered God, and was delighted.' Isaiah: 'whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand the hearing? them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts,' and so on.

div.head: Cap. XXXIX. Per multas naturales Draconis, serpentis colubri, lupi, Vulpis, taxi, tandemque cati proprietates, Diaboli malignitas, ac qua via hominem decipiat, quoue pacto homo ei resistere debeat, non obscuris similitudinibus, varie explanatur.

cit.quote: ...to the dragon, of which the Psalm says: 'this dragon which you have formed' — that is, to mock it: for the dragon has an evil hiss, since, by hissing, it emits a contagious breath, and poisons the air, and so generates a pestilential disease. So too the devil has an evil hiss, that is, an evil suggestion, which, by insinuating itself, poisons the heart, and induces the pestilential disease of sin through delight.

Likewise, the dragon has an evil bite. For Aristotle says that, since the dragon's bite is venomous and evil, the fish that are bitten by it die at once. This bite of the dragon, that is, of the demon, is in the consent to sin, in which the soul dies at once;

Likewise, the devil is like the serpent, which fears the naked man, and leaps upon the clothed one; so the devil fears the poor man, the despiser of temporal things, and entangles the rich man, the possessor of temporal things. The Apostle: 'they that will become rich fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil.'

Likewise, the devil is likened to the 'coluber' snake. First, because it dwells in the shade, hence it is called 'coluber,' as it were 'colens umbram' (dwelling in shadow) — that is, hearts shadowed and darkened by sins; or shadows, that is, minds lulled asleep in sins, since shadow induces sleep. Job: 'he sleeps in the shade.'

Likewise, the 'coluber' flees the deer, and the devil flees the soul that is diligent in good works; for he loves an idle mind, and hates a diligent one, which is signified in the deer, which is swift for running.
Likewise, because the 'coluber' kills the lion, so the devil destroys the proud man, since pride is his own particular dart.
Likewise, because it hates rue, that is, bitter penance.
Likewise, because it sheds its skin, that is, its apparent wickedness; and this happens when it transforms itself into an angel of light.

...because it loves wild beasts: for woods are hearts destitute of rational pursuits, and full of the desires of beasts. For woods are dwellings not of men, but of beasts. But the hollows of trees are the very minds of men, empty of the virtues, which the devil greatly loves.
Likewise, it very willingly drinks milk, that is, it eagerly leads men to take up the sweetness of the flesh, or of sin.

Likewise, because it wounds with its tail, that is, it overthrows in the end; for at the beginning it enters smoothly and cunningly. Proverbs: 'it enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent.'
Likewise, because it pours out venom, namely of sin.
Likewise, because it flees dogs, that is, preachers, who uncover its wickedness; hence it draws many away from hearing preachers.
Likewise, because it eats flies, since the devil feeds on unclean thoughts.
Likewise, it licks dust, since it flatters the avaricious man, and grants him prosperity in evil gains.

Likewise, the devil lies in wait most of all for man's end, since, if he deceives a man at the end, he destroys both soul and body. Hence he is likened to the horned serpent, which lies in wait deceitfully in paths, watching to bite the hoof of a passing horse. For (as the Gloss on Genesis says) the horned serpent is a serpent of the basilisk kind, of such destructive power that, if its poison touches only the hoof of a horse, it kills the horse and its rider at once. This, then, is the devil, who lies in wait for man by hidden means: for man is like a rider, whose horse is the body, while the one who sits upon it is the spirit, and the hoof, which is the extremity of the body, signifies the day of death; into which, if the devil can inject the poison of his wickedness, he drives both the horse, that is, the body, and the rider, that is, the soul, to eternal ruin. Genesis: 'a horned serpent in the path, biting the horse's heels, that the rider thereof may fall backward.'

Likewise, the devil's most wicked will, unless it were restrained by divine power and providence, men could not escape. For the devil is like a certain little beast said to be found among the Ethiopians, sluggish in all its limbs, and with a very heavy head, which it always carries bent down, lowered toward the ground, by God's provision for men; since, if it carried its head raised, it would kill everyone, all of whom expire as soon as they see its eyes. This little beast is the devil, whose limbs are all wicked men, all of whom the devil renders useless for good works: his head, that is, his mind, is weighed down with manifold wickedness. Hence he always carries that head bent down toward the earth, since his whole study and contemplation tends toward drawing the souls of the elect from things above, and plunging them into the depths. Or: divine providence keeps his head bent down, since it does not allow him to raise his head against men as much as he wishes; hence, although he always desires the affliction of the just, nonetheless, if he does not receive power from God, he never grows strong to the point of temptation: for his poisonous eyes, that is, his malicious conceptions and cunning against men, are so keen that no one would escape him, if he had the power to lead them about, that is, to act freely, as he wished.

Likewise, the devil is likened to the wolf. First, by reason of his name: for the wolf is called, as it were, 'leopes' (as Isidore says), because it has, as it were, the power of a lion's feet, so that whatever it seizes does not survive. The devil's feet, then, are the delights of sin, through which he enters into man, in which there is such power that, if he wins the mind's consent to them, he finally kills it. 'Their feet run to evil.'

Second, by reason of deceit. For it is read that the wolf sometimes utters sounds like a man's voice, sometimes imitates the barking of dogs, so as thereby to deceive shepherds and sheep. So too the devil sometimes sends in some suggestion that has a certain appearance of good, so as thereby to deceive men. Corinthians: 'Satan transforms himself into an angel of light.' For he transforms himself into an angel of light precisely when he seems to suggest the things that good angels are accustomed to persuade. For Aristotle says that envy is a kind of wolf that has a man's face and a scorpion's tail: for the devil, who at first suggests, as it were, reasonable things by deceit, afterward pours in the poison.

Likewise, so that the wolf may catch goats, it hides itself under leaves, and conquers them more by cunning than by force. So the devil deceives by hiding himself under leaves, that is, under the appearance of good things: for he is a shape-shifter, full of malice, just as, in Ethiopia, wolves are said to be so varied that they seem to lack no color — so too the devil lacks no way of deceit.

Third, by reason of tyranny, since the devil tempts a man more strongly when he sees him more wearied by adversities. For it is read that the wolf, when it goes toward the sheepfold, moves against the wind, so that the dogs will not catch its scent. Now by the wind is understood adversity: hence the devil goes against the wind, when he assails a man, already in adversity, by tempting him again. For often, by God's permitting justice, to a man afflicted by the loss of his substance, he adds affliction of the body, and then temptation of the mind, so as thereby to lead him to impatience and despair — as is clear in Job, from whom he first took away his goods, then destroyed his children, then struck him with a grievous ulcer, and finally, through his wife and friends, sent grave temptations into his heart; but Job overcame him in all things. And note that the devil tempts and pursues the just more than sinners. For the Physiologus says that the wolf does not hunt near the place where it nurses its cubs, but hunts far away. Now the places where the wolves' cubs are nursed are, as it were, the hearts of wicked men, in which the delights and afflictions of sins are nursed; there, then, the devil does not hunt, since he does not try to tempt such men. Gregory: 'the devil neglects to assail those whom he senses he already possesses undisturbed by right'; but the places far from him are, as it were, the hearts of the just, which resist him: and so the devil pursues and troubles such men especially. Gregory: 'the more our enemy sees us, placed in this life, rebel against him, the more fiercely he strives to overcome us.'

Fourth, by reason of delight in play, since the wolf greatly loves play, as Pliny says, and so, if it can seize a child, it plays with him, and afterward eats him. How the devil plays with the sinner, Gregory shows, saying: the devil says now that others' deeds are more grave, now that what was done is nothing, now that God is merciful, now that there will still be time afterward for penance — so that, while the deceived mind is led on by this, it is kept from turning to penance. Proverbs: 'sin mocks fools' — that is, the devil, who is the cause of sin. But after he has played with the sinner, he eats him. Ambrose: 'the devil does not love his own children, but hates them; for he so loves them as to destroy them, just as a glutton loves a morsel, so as to eat it.'

For the wolf has great strength in its head and neck, but weak intestines — namely because the whole force of the devil is at the beginning of temptation, since, if he is resisted at the start, he afterward becomes weak. Ambrose says that a man loses his voice, if the wolf sees him first; but if the man catches sight of the wolf first, the wolf loses its boldness, and drops its tail. The wolf, that is, the devil, then, forestalls a man by seeing him first, when he finds him not resisting at the outset. But, on the contrary, a man sees the wolf first, when he arms and prepares himself to repel the beginning of temptation: for afterward the devil loses his boldness and drops his tail, when he gives up tempting, and does not carry that temptation through to its intended end. Chrysostom: 'at first the devil's assault is heavy and unbearable; but if one bears it bravely, he will find it weaker the second time; for the more it is repelled, the more it cools.'

Sixth, by reason of the shortness of time. For it is read, in the book on animals, that when the wolf grows old, since it cannot hunt, it goes by night near cities, and lies in wait for men: so the devil, knowing his time is short, no longer cares for bestial men, but hastens to devour the good. Isidore: 'the devil then rages more fiercely against the one he possesses, when he knows he is about to be driven out of him by divine power.' Apocalypse: 'woe to the earth, and to the sea, for the devil has come down to you, having great wrath.'
Seventh, by reason of fear: for the wolf greatly fears fire, as Homer says.

Likewise, it greatly fears stones. So too the devil greatly fears fiery prayer, that is, fervent prayer, and stones, that is, alms. Hence it is said that if anyone strikes two stones together, the wolf loses its boldness. The two stones are the twofold almsgiving, namely bodily and spiritual: and if both are done, it is greatly dreadful to the devil.

Likewise, the devil deceives man just as the fox deceives the badger: for the badger hates the fox, but the fox, seeing that it cannot overcome it, because of the toughness of its hide, takes flight; and while the badger seeks its prey, the fox, entering its burrow, defiles the badger's bed with the filth of urine and other unclean things, and the badger, unable to bear the stench, leaves and seeks another den for itself. The fox, then, since it is a deceitful animal, signifies the cunning adversary. The badger, however, signifies the good but incautious man, whom the devil, when he sees himself unable to overcome by tempting him, because of his constancy, flees — that is, he withdraws temptations from him for a time; and while that man's mind, with incautious security, having laid aside inward care, occupies itself with outward things, the deceitful adversary defiles the inner bed of his conscience with the uncleanness of some sin, which the man scarcely notices. When he does perceive its stench, or its displeasing effect, he is sometimes overcome, from impat...

Likewise, of the wild bull: for Aristotle says that there is a certain kind of wild ox, of the size of a bull, which, when it sees that it cannot escape the hunter's hand or the dogs, casts its own dung four paces behind it; and while the dogs smell the dung and are held up by that scent, the beast escapes them by fleeing, and gets away. The devil's hunters, as it were, have their dogs, which are deceitful temptations, or biting persecutions, from which the soul would not escape, unless it cast away its own dung, that is, the uncleanness of sin, over four paces: the first is in contrition, the second in confession, the third in satisfaction, and the fourth in the continuation of perseverance. Or: the dung is glory, or the prosperity of temporal things, of which the Apostle said: 'I count all things as dung.' Maccabees: 'do not fear the glory of a sinful man, for his glory is dung and worms.' Man must cast this away over four paces: the first is if he gives up what he has; the second, if he does not seek what he does not have; the third, if he refuses what is offered; the fourth, if he despises it in his heart; and such a man escapes the devil's hand, free and safe.

Likewise, the devil lies in wait for men just as a cat does for mice. For it lies in wait for them cautiously, and attacks in hiding. And once the cat has caught the mouse, it first plays with it, and afterward kills and eats it. So the devil shrewdly watches a man, namely to see in what disposition he can more easily deceive and catch him unawares. He attacks him, namely by hiding from him, in the temptation, everything that might draw him back from sin, and showing or suggesting only what delights and pleases; or he attacks him unawares, when he tempts him under the appearance of good. And once he has caught the man through his consent, he plays with him, that is, he mocks him, by showing him that the sin is light, and that God is merciful, and that it is impossible not to sin, and that he will easily be able to get out of it and repent, and the like. And after he has thus mocked him, drawing him to the deed, he kills him spiritually, and, through wicked habit, eats him, so incorporating him into himself.

div.head: Cap. XL. Hominem cunctis animantibus esse prelatum, ipsiusque dignitas ac miseria non absque ratione demonstratur.

cit.quote: The dignity and the weakness of man are known from the brute animals: for the kinds of all animals were created for the use of man (as the Philosopher and Damascene say). For some are given to man for food, like sheep and the like; some for service, like horses and the like; some for comfort, like apes and the like; some for exercise, so that man may know his own weakness, like fleas and the like; and some for the remedy of sickness, like vipers and asps, from which theriac is made, and so for many other medicines. For those that sometimes seem more harmful are more useful, as Asclepius says: a patient suffering from hemorrhoids is cured if he sits on a lion's skin, and he also says that whoever anoints his body with the fat of a lion's kidneys, the wolf flees from him, and likewise those who are anointed with its dung, and similar powers are read of concerning the various limbs and parts of many animals. Man's dignity, then, appears from the fact that he is set over all the animals, and all of them serve the uses of his life. But his weakness is clear alongside his dignity, from the fact that man sees himself in need of lesser creatures, and unable to lead his life well without their nourishment, or without their service, or without their comfort, or without their remedy.

div.head: Cap. XLI. Panthere unico exemplo, quid homo odisse, diligereue debeat, breuiter declaratur.

cit.quote: Man ought to love all men, and hate sin, like the panther; which is called 'panthera,' from the Greek 'pan,' meaning 'all' in Latin, since it is a friend to all animals, and an enemy to the dragon alone. So too man ought to be a friend to all men, but an enemy to sin alone. Seneca: 'you shall have peace with men, war with vices.' Hence Augustine says that men are to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved. For it is one thing to love what they are, another to hate what they do.

div.head: Cap. XLII. Publici doctoris partes que existant, quantaque diligentia Sanctorum doctrina sit sequenda, onagri, ac cerui non absurda similitudine definitur.

cit.quote: We ought diligently to seek out the teachings of the saints, and delight and linger in them: for the wild ass seeks green herbs on high mountains, and, when it finds them, at once brays for joy, and, as long as it finds green grasses, does not leave that place unless driven off. Now what are high mountains, but holy teachers, whose green herbs are gracious teachings? For they are mountains through the eminence of their life, high through the contemplation of wisdom, bearing herbs through the nourishment of their teaching, since they feed the souls of their neighbors on the pasture of their teachings, as on the hay of herbs. Wild asses, that is, simple and devout men, seek these herbs, and, when they find them, rejoicing and exulting, proclaim them to others by braying, since they rouse and draw others too to the pursuit of holy teachings; and as long as they find pasture, refreshing and restoring their minds, they do not depart from it. Or: the virtue of the herbs of the mountains is the virtues and examples of perfect men, which wild asses, that is, imperfect men, seek, and find by investigating, proclaim by imitating, spread by preaching, and linger over by continuing. The Apostle: 'be zealous for the better gifts.'

Likewise, the office of public teacher, or prelate, ought not to be assumed or sought by one who lacks the virtues, or is not yet grounded in them. For stags, as long as they lack horns, or do not yet have them hardened, do not go out in public; hence they go to pasture not by day, but by night; but by day they expose their horns to the sun, so that they may harden, and when they know them to be hardened, they go out into the open to pasture. Those, then, who feel themselves to lack the horns of the virtues — how dare they go out to dispense the pasture of public teaching? Those who are still imperfect and weak must be strengthened and hardened by the heat of the sun, that is, the fervor of divine love, and, once they have been made firm by the strength of the spiritual virtues, they can then go forth to the pasture of spiritual teaching. Habakkuk: 'his brightness shall be as the light; horns are in his hands.' For in the holy teacher there ought to appear together the brightness of teaching, the light of knowledge, and the example of life: for horns are the virtues, which are then carried in the hands, when they are shown forth in deeds.

div.head: Cap. XLIII. Hominis dolosi ve proditoris malignitas, hypocritarumque infecta simulatio recensetur, qui tum Mygali tum vulpi comparantur.

cit.quote: ...the 'mygale,' a small animal like a weasel, and a deceitful animal. Hence it sometimes feigns tameness, when it sees someone approaching, but soon leaps upon him, and injects its venom. So many deceitful men and traitors do, feigning themselves friends, or peaceable, when they are not, and watching for the time when they can do harm. Ecclesiasticus: 'many are the snares of the deceitful.'

Likewise, the deceitful man is likened to the fox, since the fox is a treacherous animal, accustomed to deception, and never goes by straight paths, but by winding, twisting ones. And so it is called 'vulpes,' as it were 'volubilis pedibus' (turning about on its feet).
Likewise, when it does not catch prey, it feigns itself dead, and so, when birds come down to the carcass, it seizes and eats them, as Isidore says.

...the dog has a hairy hide, and a large tail, which, when the dog thinks to seize it, fills its mouth with hair. And Pliny says that when it is too closely pressed by dogs, it gathers its tail between its legs, and lets out urine among the hairs of its tail, which it sprinkles over itself; and the dog, unable to bear the stench, gives way somewhat — all of which is found in deceitful men: for there are certain deceivers who, accustomed to fraud and deception, never go straight and simply, but always seek by malicious ways to entangle and deceive others.

Likewise, certain hypocrites feign themselves dead, so that others may cling to them and trust them the more, and so obtain from them some temporal advantage; and they also have a hairy hide, that is, a great appearance of penance, but drag behind them a tail, that is, a final intention, or some action, full of hairs, that is, of snares or deceptions. But if anyone tries to catch them, they splash him with urine, that is, with the stench of infamy, defaming and pursuing him out of envy — just as certain deceitful hypocrites or heretics, when they see that religious men or inquisitors wish to know or expose them, sometimes tell secular men that this is done out of envy, on account of which the dogs, that is, the preachers, sometimes give way to them, fearing the reproach. Matthew: 'the foxes have holes' — that is, hypocrites, or heretics, have deep cunning, by which they hide their wickedness.

div.head: Cap. XLIIII. Quo pacto mentis domus, quibusque virtutibus sit edificanda pariter et muniende, castorum exemplo edocetur: et quot modis Dei domus capiatur, describitur.

cit.quote: Every man ought diligently to build the house of his mind, and often consider the end of his life — an example of which is found in the beaver, which prepares its dwellings with great skill: for from the wood it cuts with its teeth, on the steep banks of waters, it builds its houses with two or three chambers, divided by partitions, and, as the water rises, it inhabits the upper chambers; but as it falls, it settles into the lower part, and, through a certain opening made on purpose, on each floor, it puts its tail, which is of a fish-like nature, into the water, since, outside the water, it would not long survive without decaying. So too every man ought diligently to build the dwelling of his soul out of wood, that is, the solid works of the virtues; but the house of wisdom is built on the banks of the waters, that is, in the study of the Scriptures; and this house has two chambers, since it ought to be both practical and speculative, that is, active and contemplative; or the house of penance is built on the banks of the waters, that is, in the compunction of tears, and this house has three chambers, since penance has three parts, namely contrition, confession, and satisfaction. Now as the water of wisdom rises, the soul is lifted to the contemplation of higher things; or the more the water of compunction or of tribulation rises, the more the soul rises to the perfection of purity and virtue; and the more it falls, the further the soul falls below.

Likewise, as the water of tribulation rises, the soul ought to climb to higher things by praying; but as the flood of tribulation falls, it ought to draw itself down to lower things, keeping itself in humility, always or often putting its tail through the opening of the mind into the water, that is, wisely considering the end of its life: for by the water we understand wisdom, and by the tail, the end of life. Hence, he puts his tail into the water, who wisely attends to the end of his life; for thus he is preserved from the corruption of sin, according to that saying: 'remember your last end, and you shall never sin.' Note that the house of God is understood in many ways.
First, the whole fabric of the world, according to that saying of Baruch: 'O Israel, how great is the house of God.'
Second, the hall of the heavenly homeland. Psalm: 'I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: we shall go into the house of the Lord.'
Third, a house dedicated to God. Isaiah: 'my house shall be called a house of prayer.'
Fourth, the soul of any just man, as here in Hebrews: 'whose house we are.'
Fifth, the Church militant. Timothy: 'in a great house there are not only vessels of gold,' and so on.
Sixth, the Blessed Virgin. Psalm: 'holiness becomes your house, Lord.'
Seventh, the flesh taken up by the Word. Proverbs: 'wisdom has built herself a house.'

div.head: Cap. XLV. Quale sit cor obstinatum, menique dura, que Cocodrillo comparatur, Pharaonis estenditur exemplo.

cit.quote: Hard minds are not amended by scourges; hence they are likened to the crocodile. For such is the crocodile's hardness that, although it receives the blows of powerful stones on its back, it takes no notice at all. Such was Pharaoh, whose heart was so hardened that, through many plagues, he would not let the people go. So too the hardened sinner, scourged with many afflictions, does not let go of sin; and of such a hard heart Bernard says: it is a hard heart, that is neither rent by compunction, nor softened by pity, nor moved by prayers; it does not yield to threats, but hardens under scourges; it is ungrateful for benefits, unfaithful to counsel, cruel in judgment, shameless in disgraceful things, fearless of dangers, inhuman toward human things, reckless toward divine things, forgetful of the past, negligent of the present, and does not provide for the future: it is one for whom, of the past, nothing at all passes except the wrongs done to it, of the present, nothing at all is lost, and of the future, there is no foresight at all, except perhaps to take revenge.

div.head: Cap. XLVI. Electorum Dei perfectio, eorumque vera innocentia quanta sit, ex pluribus ovium naturalibus proprietatibus quam restissime colligi potest.

cit.quote: The elect are likened to sheep. First, on account of innocence: for the sheep is an innocent animal, that is, one that harms no one. And so nature gave it no armor at all, neither horns for striking, nor claws for tearing, nor teeth for biting; although they are called 'bidentes' (two-toothed), since they are said to be born with two teeth, their teeth are not for biting, but for grazing. This innocence fits God's elect, who do nothing by which they intend to harm others; hence it is said, in Kings: 'these sheep, what have they done?' — as if to say: these that are innocent in themselves, what have they done, that is, what evil, to others? So that a twofold innocence is noted in them, namely with respect to themselves and with respect to their neighbor. Augustine: 'true innocence is that which harms neither itself nor others.'

Second, on account of the sheep. Psalm: 'for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.' Here the patience of the saints is first commended for its cause; for it is for your sake, namely God's, not for theft, or murder. Psalm: 'for your sake I have borne reproach.' Second, for its punishment, since we are killed — namely by ourselves, through penance — all the day long, that is, through our whole life. Apostle: 'daily I die' — namely, to vices.

Likewise, by others, as sheep for the slaughter, that is, worthy of slaughter. And truly the holy Martyrs were like sheep, when they were slain, following him of whom it was said: 'he shall be led as a sheep to the slaughter,' who goes meekly, and, without resistance, allows himself to be killed.

Third, on account of abundance, according to that saying of the Psalm: 'their sheep are fruitful, abounding in their goings forth.' For the elect, as sheep, abound in their offspring, and in their goings forth, that is, in the milk that comes forth from their udders.

Likewise, those that abound in good fleece, of which Job says: 'the poor man was warmed by the fleece of my sheep.' So too God's elect abound in offspring, that is, in merits, and in udders, that is, in teachings, and in fleeces, that is, in examples or in alms. And note that there are four things that make sheep abound in offspring, namely wind, drink, pasture, and movement. As to wind: for, as Aristotle says, if sheep conceive facing the north wind, they bring forth males; but facing the south wind, females. By the north wind understand the inspiration of the sevenfold grace, which is noted by the north, where too the seven stars are around the pole, designating the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; and this is the wind that makes God's elect bring forth male offspring, that is, virtuous works. But by the warm south wind, understand the kindling of the wicked spirit, which causes the bringing forth of females, that is, vicious and defective works.

The second is the sheep's drink, since the same Aristotle says that sheep are fattened by drinking water; hence they are given salt to eat, so that they thirst more, and drink more. This is the water of saving wisdom, which, when God's elect and the saints drink it, makes them abound in the offspring of good works. The Apostle: 'bearing fruit, and increasing in the knowledge of God.'

For pasture, especially at the end, helps them toward generating, and so too does movement, which is the fourth help; and so the food and pasture of tears, of which the Psalm speaks: 'you will feed us with the bread of tears,' and the movement of obedience, or of charity, are also for the saints a cause of fruitfulness in merits.

Likewise, the saints abound in the milk of teaching, in which milk (according to Constantine) there is a threefold substance, namely the watery, the buttery, and the cheesy: the first, namely the watery or serous, is cleansing and refining; the second, the buttery or oily, is softening, expanding, and cleansing; the third, the cheesy, is thick and clogging. So too the teaching of Christ's sheep is refining, when they speak to the wise; it is softening, that is, compunction-inducing, and expanding toward good and cleansing away from evil, when they speak to those advancing; but it is thick and clogging, that is, closing off, or restraining, from evil ways, when they speak to the unwise. The Apostle: 'as to little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: Likewise, from Christ's sheep are had fleeces of various colors, that is, examples of various virtues, with which the soul is clothed and adorned, and grows warm in divine love. The sheep (as blessed Martin said) teaches us to keep the Lord's commandment: since, having two coats, namely hide and wool, it keeps one for itself, and gives the other to him who has none — namely, its wool, to man.

...sheep, on account of obedience: for sheep hear and follow the whistle and voice of the shepherd. And holy men hear and follow the teaching and voice of Christ. 'My sheep hear my voice' — namely, listening with the ear, believing with the heart, and fulfilling, or obeying, in deed. 'At the hearing of the ear he has obeyed me.'

Likewise, God's elect and holy men, who are of his household, are not harmed by the temptations of demons, but the reprobate, who are like adulterine offspring, are at once conquered and poisoned by them — just as Pliny says that there is a certain people, or family, whom the asp does not harm; hence they expose to the asp children born to them whom they suspect; the asp does not harm them if they look at it, but if they are of adulterine birth, it soon kills them. Psalm: 'you shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk.'

div.head: Cap. XLVII. Evangelistarum dignitas et officium per equorum, qui et sonipedes vorantur, plures similitudines naturales, ac etiam caballi etymologiam clare ostentatur.

cit.quote: The Evangelists were horses: for horses ('equi') are so called because they are matched ('equantur') in teams, and yoked together equally. This team, in which the holy Evangelists are matched by holy Church, and received together, is the teaching, or writing, of the four Gospels, in which, instructed by Christ, they brought us the helps of our salvation. Hence Jerome: 'Matthew,' he says, 'Mark, Luke, and John are the Lord's team, and the true cherub' — which is interpreted 'fullness of knowledge' — 'and they are full of eyes over their whole body.'

Likewise, they were Christ's steeds ('caballi'), since 'caballus' is named from 'cavus pes' (hollow foot), because, its hoof pressed down, it hollows out the earth, as Isidore says. This hollowness of the foot, or hollowing of the earth, is the emptying out of earthly love, since they despised all things for Christ's sake, and followed him in poverty. Matthew: 'behold, we have left all things, and followed you.'

Likewise, they were Christ's sounding steeds ('sonipedes'); for they are called 'sonipedes' because they sound with their feet: for they resounded in preaching, not only with the sound of words, but also with the tread of their deeds; or they sounded with their feet, when, running from place to place, they preached. Psalm: 'their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world.'

div.head: Cap. XLVIII. Omnes cum excommunicatis in casibus non concessis versantes, effici excommunicatos, rabidi canis exemplo, et auctoritate probatur.

cit.quote: Excommunication is likened to the bite of a rabid dog: since all animals bitten by a rabid dog become rabid and furious themselves. So too all who associate with an excommunicate in cases not permitted become themselves excommunicate, at least by the lesser excommunication. Hence excommunicates are to be driven out of the church like dogs. 'Outside are the dogs.' And they are to be avoided by all, like a rabid dog. Thessalonians: 'do not associate with him' — namely, with the excommunicate.

div.head: Cap. XLIX. Sanctorum exempla, qui interdum a Dei gratia ceciderunt, et postea surrexerunt, eos in bonis actionibus imitantibus maiorem in modum prodesse, malique prelati exempla subditis valde obesse, musco, capreolisque ac candele extincte exemplis declaratur.

cit.quote: The examples of saints who fell from grace, and afterward rose again, are of great benefit to others. Hence they are likened to musk; for it is said that in the mountains of India there are certain roe deer, that is, that feed on aromatic herbs, in whose claws are hollows in which humors gather toward an abscess, but, through movement and running, these are broken open; and that gathered humor, drawn out with its hairy follicles, has a substance that is exceedingly fragrant, and among spices most precious, and of great virtue in medicines (as Dioscorides says), and this we commonly call musk. Now such roe deer are, as it were, every humble and diligent man, who, feeding as it were on aromatic herbs, is frequently filled with many gifts and graces of God. But it sometimes happens that, in their claws, that is, in their senses or affections, certain hollows remain, that is, certain defects or leanings toward certain vices, in which sometimes humors, that is, affections, from carelessness or negligence, gradually multiply so much that an abscess of some grave sin is generated in them, into which they are allowed to fall; but afterward, through the movement of compunction and the exercise of good work, or through the process of inward reflection and repentance of mind, this affection of sin is broken, and drawn from the heart into hairy follicles, that is, harsh and afflictive exercises.

Now the example of penance, humility, and patience, which they show in such afflictions, and of the imitation of life that they produce, makes them, by their example, a fragrant musk to others — the use of which, whether through consideration or imitation, becomes a medicine, or a preservative, for other just men, namely to fear and guard themselves, according to that saying of Corinthians: 'let him who thinks he stands, take heed lest he fall'; and for sinners, to repent and correct themselves, as blessed Ambrose said to the Emperor Theodosius, who cited to him the example of David's sin: 'if,' he said, 'you have followed him erring, follow him correcting himself.'

Likewise, the example of a bad prelate extinguishes the good resolve in a subject: for an extinguished candle, smelled by a pregnant mare, causes her to miscarry. For the candle is then extinguished, when some prelate, or teacher, falls into manifest sin; and the pregnant mare is, as it were, the soul bearing a good resolve, which, when, by imitating him, it smells the sin of its prelate or master, extinguishing the good it had conceived, miscarries.

div.head: Cap. L. Cur fatuus non sit sapienti sociandus, ratione et auctoritate patefit.

cit.quote: The foolish man is not to be paired with the wise, hence it was commanded in Deuteronomy: 'you shall not plow with an ox and an ass together'; for by the ox is understood the wise man, by the ass, the foolish, and by plowing, preaching is signified. The ox of a good man, then, is not to be joined in plowing with the ass, since the fool in preaching ought not to be paired with the wise man, lest, through the discord of his foolishness, the grace of the wise man be hindered.

div.head: Cap. LI. Carnis lasciuiam per spiritus feruorem consumi, Cameli exemplo monstratur.

cit.quote: The fervor of the spirit consumes the wantonness of the flesh, just as the fervor of natural heat consumes the fat of the body — which appears in the camel, of which Constantine says that it is by nature a very hot animal, and so lean, since heat consumes the oiliness of the blood. Likewise, the heat of charity, and the fervor of devotion, consume the sliminess, or slipperiness, of lust and carnal desire. Ecclesiasticus: 'the vapor of fire burns the flesh' — that is, the fervor of spiritual love consumes the desires of the flesh. James: 'the sun rose with a burning heat, and dried up the grass' — that is, the flesh. Isaiah: 'all flesh is grass.'

div.head: Cap. LII. Ficte penitentis, qui vitam in bonum interdum mutare videtur, simulatio, nec non hypocritarum in fallendo malignitas, Rubeta exemplo.

cit.quote: The feigned penitent is like the 'boracia,' called the toad, a kind of venomous frog which is said to shed its old skin by feeding on certain herbs, yet does not shed its venom, but keeps it. So too the feigned penitent, by the show of a certain outward, pretended penance, seems to change his life, so as to be believed to have shed the old age of sin, yet inwardly retains the venom of his evil will, and keeps it hidden only for a time. And it is said that, however many spots the toad has spread beneath its belly, in so many ways is its venom said to be harmful — since, indeed, however many vicious malices the feigned man and hypocrite has in himself, in so many ways he also has means of harming or deceiving. And so the Holy Spirit rightly flees such a man, according to that saying of Wisdom: 'the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful.'

div.head: Cap. LIII. Quid nobis prestet fides, fideliumque spes in quo consistat, unico ceruorum exemplo edocetur.

cit.quote: Faith draws us on, like stags, though the mind of the wayfarer cannot grasp it: for the faithful are like stags, which, crossing the seas, seek land not by sight, but by scent. Likewise we seek the land of the living, that is, the solidity of eternal goods, by a certain scent of faith, since, placed as we are in the crossing of this sea, we cannot see them as they are in themselves; hence the Apostle: 'what eye has not seen, nor ear heard,' and so on. But although this scent may seem faint, it is nonetheless very sweet, and drawing; hence the Song of Songs: 'draw me after you; we will run to the odor of your ointments,' and so on. And it is by this scent that blessed John the Evangelist, drawn on, is read to have said to God in a certain prayer of his: 'your fragrance has stirred up eternal desires in me.'

div.head: Cap. LIIII. Filios erga parentes fore pientissimos, Glirium instruuntur exemplo singulari.

cit.quote: That children owe their parents the dutiful services of piety, especially in need, dormice teach, which, with a remarkable piety, help nourish their parents in old age, and provide them food. Let wretched men, then, blush, who are cruel to their own parents; for, by failing them in their need, they show themselves crueler than dormice and mice. Ecclesiasticus: 'take care of your father's old age.'

div.head: Cap. LV. Dei gratie effectus ipsi cordi variis similitudinibus comparetur, quod membrum radicale esse iure optimo affirmatur.

cit.quote: The grace of the Holy Spirit is likened to a root-organ; for, as Aristotle says, in every animal there is a root-organ, which is the principle of all natural and spiritual powers: and this is the heart, or something in its place, from whose root (as Avicenna says) the creation, formation, and shaping of animals begins. This root principle, then, is the gift of God's grace, from which all virtues and freely-given gifts proceed, by which the soul is made perfect. From this principle begins the creation, formation, and shaping of the virtues: for the creation of virtues is through the acquiring of habits, since virtue (as the Philosopher says) is an elective habit; but their formation is through the love of charity, since charity is the forming of the virtues, as Ambrose says. But the shaping of the virtues is through the production of acts, since acts are shaped by the habits from which they proceed, and are manifested in acts, as a shaped thing in its shape. But the root principle of all these is divine grace itself. Hence the Apostle attributes his whole spiritual being to the grace of God, saying: 'by the grace of God, I am what I am.'

Likewise, man does not receive divine grace for his consolation as long as he carries sin in his conscience. For the foal of a mare, which is born with a certain black membrane on its forehead, is not admitted to its mother's udders as long as that membrane has not been cut off. The foal, then, bearing blackness on its forehead, is the man who has sin in his mind, which, as long as he has not removed it through penance, the mother of the virtues and of grace does not admit him to the udders of her consolation. Wisdom: 'nothing defiled comes into her.'

div.head: Cap. LVI. Panthere pulcherrimo exemplo, grates semper benefactoribus esse reddendas admonemur.

cit.quote: ...the panther teaches us, which, although it is a very fierce beast, is nonetheless not ungrateful to its benefactors. Hence it is told of a certain man who freed her cubs from a pit, that the panther accompanied him, and, fawning on him with her tail and her face, led him all the way out of the wilderness. If, then, the nature of cruel wild beasts is so grateful to its benefactors, how much more does it befit men, in whom gentleness and rational judgment are naturally present? Hence the Apostle: 'be grateful.'

div.head: Cap. LVII. Gule damna enarrantur, Voracisque natura per ursi ac Cocodrilli naturalem usum in edendo: quoue pacto gule vitium curetur, exprimitur.

cit.quote: The gluttonous man is likened to the bear: for the bear (according to Aristotle) eats indiscriminately everything; hence it climbs trees for fruit, and breaks open hives for honey, and eats crabs and ants as medicine. So too the gluttonous man, sometimes under the appearance of necessity, sometimes from the sweetness of pleasure, sometimes under the pretext of sickness, seeks out and takes voluptuous delights. 'The belly' — namely of the glutton — 'will eat every kind of food.'

Likewise, the gluttonous man is likened to the crocodile, which willingly eats grasses, among which the little 'endros' serpent, its enemy, coils itself, so that, while the crocodile crops the grasses, it swallows the serpent, which, while it is in its belly, kills the crocodile, and comes out unharmed. So too the gluttonous man willingly eats good and tasty morsels, with which he frequently swallows, through delight, the venom of pleasure and sin, which kills his mind.

Likewise, gluttony leads a man to lust and incontinence: for stags, when they feel themselves grown too fat, seek hiding places, since they can neither flee well nor keep up a sustained run; but now they flee, now they stop, and look back — so too the fatness of gluttony seeks the hiding places of lust. And a man given over to gluttony, made incontinent, can neither flee the temptations of the flesh, nor sustain the course of penance; but now, pricked in conscience, he flees, that is, resolves to flee; now he stops, that is, waits for and takes up temptations; now he looks back, since he returns, in desire or in deed, to baseness. The strength of gluttony, then, must be treated with the affliction of abstinence, but the dryness of the soul must be watered with the compunction of tears. For (according to Isaac) the fat flesh of animals should be roasted, since roasting dries out their unwholesome moisture, but dry flesh should rather be boiled, since water tempers and moistens it; the flesh of pig and sheep is best roasted, but that of goat and ox is better boiled. For boiling moistens dry flesh, and roasting dries moist flesh. Fat flesh, then, is flesh accustomed to delights, which must be roasted by fire, that is, by the affliction of abstinence, subdued by the heat of hunger, so that the affliction of abstinence may check the delights of gluttony; but dry flesh is, as it were, arid, that is, unwatered minds, which are then boiled in bubbling water, when they are watered by fervent and tearful compunction.

div.head: Cap. LVIII. Temporalium rerum exuberantia, quantum hominibus divitiis abutentibus obsit, pinguia animantia ad esum pessima, valde hominis stomachum dissoluentia, naturali quadam similitudine estentunt.

cit.quote: Those who have an abundance of temporal things are likened to fat animals. Animals too fat are worst for eating, since they harm digestion, because they float on the food and burden it, and soften the villi of the stomach, and induce slipperiness in the stomach, hence excessive fat dissolves the stomach, weakening its power to retain, to shape, and to expel. From fat, too, the stomach is inflamed like fire, when fat is thrown onto it. Now the fat of the flesh is, as it were, temporal abundance, of which the Psalm says: 'their iniquity came forth as it were from fatness,' that is, from the abundance and fullness of temporal things. This, then, harms the soul just as fat harms the stomach: for it induces inflammation, or the swelling of pride, the softness and slipperiness of lust. For it dissolves the virtue of continence, excludes the consolation or strengthening of grace, does not care for the expulsion of vileness through the confession of penance; nor does it extinguish, but rather kindles, the fire of avarice, just as an abundance of wood does not extinguish, but rather increases, the fire. Ecclesiasticus: 'as the wood of the forest increases, so the fire burns more fiercely.'

Likewise, too great an abundance of temporal consolation generates vices of the mind: for wood that is cut or planted at the full moon, since at that time moisture abounds in bodies, cannot, because of that very excess, be governed by nature, and so decays, and generates worms by which it is gnawed, and reduced to dust. Now consolation, or the fullness of the flesh, is, as it were, the moisture of the tree; and if it is abundant, it generates corruption not only of the body, but also of the soul, and produces worms of vices, by which the virtues of the soul are utterly dissipated. Hence it is (as Gregory says) that the chief of the cooks, namely Nebuzaradan, destroyed the walls of Jerusalem, since the belly, which cooks serve, destroys the virtues of the soul by its own creeping.

div.head: Cap. LIX. Diversorum animalium diversa natura, eorumque naturales proprietates egregie describuntur: quibus non paucis nec obscuris exemplis, homines tam boni quam mali iure comparantur.

cit.quote: Men, both good and bad, are likened to earthly animals. For, as was said above, at the beginning of this fifth book, Moses set out three kinds of animals, namely cattle, creeping things, and beasts. And according to Basil, cattle are those named as suited to man's use; and some of them are for labor, like horses, oxen, and asses; some for wool-working, like sheep and the like; some for eating, like pigs and the like. By cattle, then, are understood active men, who are diligent in helping their neighbors, hence they are called 'iumenta,' as it were 'iuvamenta' (helps); of these, some labor in works of obedience, like the cloistered, and these are like horses: for the horse is subjected to man, bridled by him, and moved and led about according to his will, and so is subject with respect to a prelate. James: 'we put bits into horses' mouths, that they may obey us, and we turn about their whole body.' These bits are the precepts and institutions of the rule, or the corrections of prelates.

But some labor in the work of teaching, and these are like oxen with which the earth is plowed, namely preachers, by whom the earth of the soul is plowed with the plowshare of the tongue, and sown with the seed of teaching. Others, however, labor in the work of patience, namely in the care of governance, like prelates, who are likened to the humbler animals bearing others' burdens, namely camels, asses, and the like, since the greater they are, the more humble they ought to be, and bear burdens for their subjects. Psalm: 'I have become as a beast of burden before you.' For such cattle, namely asses and camels, though large in body, are nonetheless held cheap in esteem, and burdened by the great weight of their knowledge. Likewise, the prelate, though great in dignity, ought nonetheless to be, in his own eyes, held cheap and humble in esteem. He is also burdened by a load of great weight, since he must render account to God for his subjects. Hence Gregory says: 'great honor, but a heavy burden.' Those, however, who devote themselves to clothing the poor, are likened to sheep, who, fulfilling the Lord's command as it were (as blessed Martin did), since they have two coats, namely wool and hide, give one, namely the wool, to him who has none. But those who feed the poor with their food and alms are like animals useful for food, such as rams, kids, and pigs, and the like, to which they are likened not by reason of vileness, but of usefulness.

Creeping things are worms, snakes, and serpents, which move and creep by the action and extension of their bodies. Now by creeping things can be understood perfect and contemplative men, whose nature it is to draw themselves in, that is, to withdraw from outward things to inward ones, to contemplate God, and nonetheless to stretch themselves out to love their neighbor. Hence they ought to be like worms, through the reckoning of humility; like snakes, through the mortification of the flesh, since the snake ('coluber') is named as it were 'colens umbram' (dwelling in shade). Likewise they ought to be like serpents, through the prudence of discretion. Matthew: 'be wise as serpents.' Or they ought to be like worms, since it is theirs to praise God constantly. For worms, like caterpillars and the like, draw themselves along with their mouths. Psalm: 'his praise shall be always in my mouth.' Or like serpents, since it is theirs to make the flesh lean through abstinence: for serpents draw themselves along by the strength of their ribs. Job: 'let hunger invade his ribs' — for leanness appears most of all in the ribs of one who fasts. They ought also to be like lizards, since they ought to burn with good affections. For lizards creep on their feet, and the feet of the soul are its affections, by which it runs the more swiftly, the more fervent it is.

Beasts, however, are so called as it were 'vastia' (wasting), since they lay waste all things through their ferocity. For they are fierce, and attack now with claw, now with horn, now with tooth, like boars, lions, and wolves; and so sinners are likened to such beasts, since they lay waste all their goods: for they diminish their natural goods, reject the freely-given ones, despise the heavenly ones, and lose the temporal ones. They are cruel to themselves, and much more so to others, whom they harm and hinder, either with the tooth of envious detraction, or the horn of proud condemnation, or the claw of violent plunder. And some are like boars, through carnal pleasure; some like lions, through the power of pride; some like wolves, through the rapacity of avarice, and so of others like them. Ecclesiastes: 'I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God would prove them, and show them to be like beasts.'

div.head: Cap. LX. Elephantis in coitu admiranda natura, homines coniugalem pudicitiam conseruare erudit.

cit.quote: Elephants teach us to keep honesty and modesty in the conjugal act, in which there is a certain admirable modesty, especially compared to other animals. For they do not know one another except in secret, and this not until they are two years old — namely when the male is five years old and the female ten — and, in those two years, only for five days, a sixth being rarely added. In this example men are taught to conduct themselves honestly in the conjugal act, as to place, as to time, and as to charity. Hence young Tobias said to his wife: 'let us rise, and pray to the Lord today, and tomorrow, and the day after; for these three nights we are joined to God, but the third night being over, we shall be in our own union: for we are the children of saints, and we cannot be joined together like the heathen, who know not God.'

div.head: Cap. LXI. Humilis hominis natura que siluestri capre aliquibus exemplis assimilatur, atque humilitatis virtus quantum fidelibus prosit, Deoque grata existat, plurimis rationibus naturalibus aperitur.

cit.quote: The humble man is likened to the roe deer, that is, to the wild goat, which is a timid and weak animal, and knows how to defend itself only by the benefit of flight; for it has, as its arms, the agility of its limbs, and flight. Hence (according to Isidore) it is called 'damula,' since it escapes from the hand ('de manu effugiat'); it loves mountainous and wooded places, eats aromatic herbs, and crops the tips of small branches; when wounded, it chews dragonwort, and so drives the dart from its body. Serpents hate the roe deer, and cannot bear its breath. So too the humble man always fears to offend God, and, counting himself weak, defends himself, by his own virtue, through the flight of vice; he arms himself with the agility of obedience, and the flight of pride, and so escapes the hand of the devil's temptation; he loves the mountain of contemplation, the wood of solitude, and feeds, as it were, on aromatic herbs — namely, on their examples. He crops the tips of small branches, that is, humble works. Wounded by sin, he chews dragonwort, a medicinal herb, that is, penance, and so draws the dart of temptation, or of sin, from his heart. The infernal serpent, too, that is, the demon, hates him especially, and cannot bear his breath, that is, his willing disdain. Ecclesiasticus: 'humility is an abomination to the proud.'

Likewise, humble self-recognition frees a man from sin: for the leopard, when it falls sick, eats human dung, and is cured; for what is human dung, but the abominable act of sin? — dung, indeed, because of its usefulness, human because of its property, since it is proper to man alone, among the animals, to sin. He, then, eats this dung, who humbly recognizes the baseness of his own sin, and such a one escapes deadly sickness, since, before the merciful Judge, the very acknowledgment of guilt obtains pardon, as Gregory says, commenting on that Psalm verse: 'for I acknowledge my iniquity.'

Likewise, deep humility of mind, and diligent attention to the word of God, help men against the devil's temptations — an example of this being that (as Aristotle and Avicenna say) the crow greatly hates the ass, and tries to peck out its eyes with its beak; but the ass is helped by the depth of its eyes, and the thickness of the hide of its brows, with which it covers its sight, and it is also helped by the length and mobility of its ears, with which it defends itself. The crow is the devil, the ass the simple man devoted to God's service, whom the devil lies in wait for, to tear out his eyes, namely his good faith and good will; but if he has them deep, that is, grounded in humility and hidden beneath a thick, hard hide, that is, beneath a lowly and coarse habit, or outward appearance, and if he has ears large and mobile, that is, attentive at length to hearing the divine word, and quick to move toward fulfilling it and obeying it, he escapes the devil's malice. Likewise, the humble and the poor are readier for doing good than the great and the rich, just as Aristotle says that small spiders are of sharp and swift movement, but the large and black ones slower; and the small ones are accustomed to weave near the ground, and always lie hidden in holes, until some little creature falls into their net, which they seize and devour, and sometimes store away until they are hungry. So too those who are small, in their own esteem, like the humble, or in others' esteem, like the poor, are sharp and swift for doing good, that is, keen and diligent and ready. For humility makes them sharp-sighted in foreseeing and considering; but poverty makes them swift and unencumbered. But the great and rich, who are reckoned great in the world, are slow to do good, and weave near the ground, when they attend only to arranging or gathering earthly things; the little creatures, that is, the simple, they deceive by fraud and treachery, and, plundering their goods, take them for their own use, or store them away for a future time.

Likewise, ants, though small and narrow around the belly, as they grow, become winged, and fly. So too he who is small in his own eyes, through humility, and narrow around the belly, through abstinence, grows in spirit, and, feathered with the wings of the virtues, is made ready, and so follows the flight of contemplation.

Likewise, humility bears more fruit than pride: for small-bodied animals have more offspring than the very large; for the works pleasing to God are humble works, which the great, that is, the proud, disdain to do, and so remain barren.

div.head: Cap. LXII. Inferni ignem, miro Salamandre exemplo, perpetuo humana corpora post iudicii diem fore cruciaturum, eaque nunquam consumpturum, adaptatur.

cit.quote: The fire of hell will torment human bodies after the day of judgment, and yet will not kill them, nor consume them, nor reduce them to ash — an example of which appears in the salamander, which lives in the midst of fire. And from the hide of a certain kind of salamander, wicks are made for lamps and lanterns, which are not consumed by any burning, but are proven to burn perpetually; and if this is achieved by the power of nature, how much more will it be possible, by divine power, in the bodies of the damned? Isaiah: 'their fire shall not be quenched.'

div.head: Cap. LXIII. Equi Camelique exempla hic apposita, incesti graue peccatum quantopere sit fugiendum nos erudiunt.

cit.quote: ...the horse teaches, which utterly shuns coupling with its mother. Hence Aristotle relates that the king of the North had a most beautiful mare, which bore him a most beautiful horse; wishing to breed another horse from these two, he covered the horse's face, so that it would not recognize its mother. When at last it was uncovered, and, seeing that it had known its mother, it fled, and threw itself down from a height, and died. How much, then, ought a rational man to abhor an incestuous mingling of his own blood, when a brute animal so abhors it? Likewise, the camel abhors coupling with its mother so much that Aristotle says that, when in a certain covered enclosure a mother was mounted from behind, the camel, not recognizing her, mounted her; but when it at last sensed it was its mother, it dismounted at once without completing the coupling, and attacked the one who had contrived it, and killed it, biting it with its teeth. Let the wretched man blush, who is supported by the judgment of reason, not only to have done such a thing, but even to have thought of doing it. Deuteronomy: 'cursed is he who sleeps with his father's wife.'

div.head: Cap. LXIIII. Hiene in sexu naturalis variatis, cui non incongrut inconstans homo comparatur, breui declaratur.

cit.quote: The inconstant man is like the hyena, whose nature is said to be such that it changes its sex, one and the same animal; hence it is found now male, now female. Likewise, the inconstant man is found sometimes male, that is, robust in resolve, but afterward found female in deed. Or male, that is, manly at the beginning, but female, that is, weak, in the course of things. Luke: 'he began to build, and was not able to finish.' But note that some say this change of sex happens only in appearance, since (as they say) the hyena always has both sexes, like a hermaphrodite, but sometimes one is hidden and the other apparent. And this perhaps varies according to the seasons, on account of which it sometimes appears male, sometimes female. Hence some say that the hyena conceives without a male, but Aristotle denies this.

div.head: Cap. LXV. Quantum sit coniugalis incontinentia evitanda, ceruorum exemplo, doctorumque auctoritate admonemur.

cit.quote: Stags teach us to avoid conjugal incontinence, of which Pliny says that, from the time of conception, the females withdraw from the males until they are purified after giving birth. And yet the lust of certain men is so great that they cannot restrain themselves even when their wife is pregnant. And note here — though the matter is not pleasant to hear, it is nonetheless useful to know — that, although the womb is closed after conception, it is nonetheless moved and opened by delight (as Avicenna says), and from this the danger of miscarriage threatens. And so Jerome condemns a husband's approach to his pregnant wife — not, however, that it is always a mortal sin, unless there is a probable fear of the danger of miscarriage.

div.head: Cap. LXVI. Infirmitatem corporalem multum interdum homini ad vitia cohibenda prodesse, Leonis exemplo, quoue pacto sit rite curanda, Elephantis similitudine naturali erudimur.

cit.quote: Bodily infirmity is sometimes a medicine for the heart, since it restrains vices. For the lion (as Solinus says) suffers from a quartan fever at all times, and this disease is brought on, by God's providence, so that its wrathfulness may be tempered. Likewise, in men, various infirmities correct various vices, on account of which Seneca said: 'I give thanks to my infirmity, which compels me not to be able to do what I ought not wish to do.'

Likewise, the sick man ought to seek the remedy for his sickness chiefly from God, and also to take medicines with prayer, and the invocation of divine power. For elephants, when they fall sick, gather certain healing herbs, and, before eating them, lift their heads to the sky, and raise the herbs to the sky too, and, as it were with a certain reverence, beg help from God. Much more, then, ought man, when he suffers, to seek help from God, and, in using medicine, begin with prayer. James: 'the prayer of faith shall save the sick man.'

div.head: Cap. LXVII. Ingenium nonnunquam plus valere quam vires, unico Leopardi leonem insidiantis exemplo: ac quemadmodum Diabolus sit ab homine superandus, edocetur.

cit.quote: ...the leopard, which the lion marvelously hates; hence the leopard, fearing the lion, since it is smaller than it, digs a pit with two openings, one through which it enters, and another through which it exits, and the pit is very wide at both openings, but narrow in the middle: when the lion comes, then, the leopard flees through the pit, and the lion, pursuing it, enters the pit too; but, coming to the middle, and finding the pit narrow, it can neither pass through nor turn itself back. Hence the leopard, coming out by the other opening, and entering behind the lion, bites it from behind, and so often triumphs over it by cunning, over which it could not triumph by strength. The leopard, then, is likened to man, whose pit is this present life, which has its entrance through birth and its exit through death, and at both openings there is ample room for humility, whether you consider man's beginning or his end. But in the middle it ought to be narrow, with the narrowness of penance; and when the lion, that is, the devil, finds this in a man, he can neither go forward, to deceive the man further, nor go back, to hold him by his past sins, which have already been blotted out through penance. Hence the leopard, coming out and biting the lion from behind, kills it, since his later life, or his penance, extinguishes the devil's wickedness within itself.

div.head: Cap. LXVIII. Impatiens ac iracundus quemadmodum sit edomandus, ursi exemplo monstratur.

cit.quote: ...the bear, for the bear is an impatient and wrathful animal, wishing to avenge itself on each and every thing. Hence, when it has attacked someone, if another touches it, it at once lets go of the first and rushes at the other; but when it is caught, it is blinded by the sight of a burning basin, chained, and tamed with blows. So too the impatient and wrathful man desires to avenge himself for each and every injury, and does not, for that reason, let go of one enemy without taking up war against another; but his raging anger is like the burning basin, by which he is blinded, since anger disturbs the eye of reason, which fury and infamy utterly blind; but the furious man must be chained, or tamed with blows.

div.head: Cap. LXIX. In bonum peragendum non perseverantes variis similitudinibus Satyris, et Fauniis: nec non Leopardo assimilari demonstratur.

cit.quote: [The source text at this point is fragmentary in the manuscript, preserving only isolated words rather than continuous prose: it names monstrous animals, satyrs, Isidore, horns like a goat's, a monster, blessed Anthony, and the Apostle — evidently the opening of an exemplum, now lost, likening those who do not persevere in good to satyrs or fauns, the goat-horned monsters of the desert that blessed Anthony is said to have encountered.]

Likewise, those who lack perseverance, and the impatient, are like the leopard, which catches its prey by leaping, not by pursuing it; if it does not catch it in three or four leaps, it gives up out of indignation, and, as though defeated, turns back. Such are those who wish to obtain what they seek not by laboring long, but by getting it as quickly as possible. Hence, if they do not obtain it at once, and do not find what they want, as though overcome by weariness, they turn back from the good work they had begun, not considering that stubborn labor conquers all things, as Virgil says. Hence, too, the perseverance of one who prays obtains from God what he desires. Luke: 'if he continues knocking, he will give him as much as he needs.'

div.head: Cap. LXX. Chamaleontis natura describitur, cui quidem rationabiliter inconstans homo assimilatur.

cit.quote: The unstable and inconstant man is likened to the chameleon, a small beast sprinkled with varied colors, whose little body easily changes to the various colors it sees; for no animal is found that so readily takes on the changing colors of the things opposite it, as Isidore says. So too a small mind, small through faintheartedness or small in virtue, easily takes the impression of love, or fear, or joy, or pain, or sadness, from everything it encounters, and so has no stability, since it is changed and led about by various affections. James: 'a man of two minds is inconstant in all his ways.'

div.head: Cap. LXXI. Invidie malum virus, invidio sorumque natura per quam plurimas Indie serpentium, Cerui, ursi, Syrene, Salamandre, Lyncis, Draconis, ac tandem Papilionis similitudines dilucide aperitur.

cit.quote: The envious are like certain serpents of India, which flee at once when they see aromatic trees flowering, which they are also said to gnaw so that they will not flower, since they cannot bear their scent. So too the envious cannot bear the prosperity of their neighbors, and rejoice at their misfortune. Ecclesiasticus: 'they that rejoice at the fall of the just shall perish in the snare.'

Likewise, the envious grieve if anyone derives benefit from their goods, even from things they themselves do not need: for they are like stags, which, when they shed their antlers, hide them out of envy, and seem to grieve if anyone takes medicine from them.

Likewise, the envious man is likened to the bear. For the bear has a poisonous brain, and so its head and shoulder-blades are burned, lest those who taste of its brain be turned into rabid madness like the bear's own; for no animal has such cunning for doing evil as the bear, as Pliny says. So too the envious man has a poisonous head, that is, a mind infected with the poison of hatred and malice. Hence it would be necessary for him to make use of the fire of charity, which does not envy, and so he would harm no one. And so no vice makes a man so cunning at doing evil and harming others as envy. Hence, through the devil's envy, death entered into all men. 'By the envy of the devil, death entered into the world.'
Likewise, the envious man is like the siren, which rejoices in storms, and grieves in calm weather. So too the envious man rejoices at another's adversity, and grieves at his prosperity.

Likewise, the envious man is like the salamander. First, by reason of timing: for the salamander, which has a shape like a lizard's, appears only in heavy rains, and, in fair weather, is entirely absent. By heavy rains understand great tribulations, or adversities befalling someone. Then the envious and malicious man reveals himself, to mock and harm him, as Saul once did to David. But in fair weather, that is, while he sees the man in prosperity, he lies low in silence, and is consumed by sadness.
Second, by reason of coldness. For it is so cold that it extinguishes fire, like ice. So too envy extinguishes the fire of charity.

Third, by reason of its mouth. For it vomits venom from its mouth, namely a certain milky discharge which, if it touches a man's body, causes the hair to fall out continuously from that spot; likewise, the envious man vomits venom from his mouth by detracting and defaming. Psalm: 'the venom of asps is under their lips.'

Likewise, the envious man, where he thinks to harm another, sometimes does good instead, and so is likened to the lynx, whose urine turns into a precious gem; and the lynx, knowing this, and, as it were, envying and grudging man this gem, if it should find it, hides its urine underground as it releases it; and yet it is deceived, since there (as Pliny says) it turns into stone all the more quickly.

Likewise, the envious man is likened to the dragon. For the dragon has its venom in its tongue and in its gall; for Pliny says that, from the force of its venom, its tongue is always raised, and, from the heat of its state, the air is so inflamed that it sometimes seems to be on fire. It has force in its tail, and does more harm with a lash than a bite; whatever its tail binds, it kills; it rarely sleeps, and has the keenest sight, so that it sees its prey from far off. Likewise, the envious man has the venom of hatred in his gall, that is, inwardly in his mind, and in his tongue, that is, in detraction, and his tongue is raised to curse, and to speak proudly, and to kindle and stir up hatred. He too has force in his tail, since he strikes from behind through hidden detraction, and kills through defamation; he rarely sleeps, that is, rarely rests from harming and scheming; and he has the keenest sight for his neighbor's faults, so that he sees from far off what he can seize upon against him.

Likewise, the envious man frequently harms himself where he thinks to harm another. Hence he is like the moth, which, striving to extinguish the light, rushes into the flame and is itself burned up. Psalm: 'his sorrow shall be turned on his own head, and his iniquity shall come down upon his own crown.'

div.head: Cap. LXXII. Hypocritarum defectus et fallacia, per varias cocodrilli, panthere, eruce, ac etiam Papilionis similitudines, recte et apposite patefiunt.

cit.quote: ...the crocodile, of which the Physiologus says that, if it finds a man by the shore, it kills him, but afterward weeps for him, and yet devours him. Such was Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, of whom it is related in Jeremiah that, walking with the friends of Gedaliah, whom he himself had killed, he went along weeping, and yet also killed those with whom he was walking that way, as is said there.
