Likewise, all animals are drawn to look at the panther, because of the beauty of its outer coat, or the variety of its colors, and the fragrance it sends forth from its mouth, but they are deterred by the ugliness of its head; hence it hides its head, and, when an animal draws near to it, it seizes and eats it. So too, because of the appearance of outward sanctity, and the various spiritual works that a hypocrite or heretic outwardly pretends, and sometimes because of a reputation for learning, which is like the fragrance of the mouth, many devout and simple people desire to see him, or cling to him, from whom he hides the head of his malice — that is, his malicious intention, or corrupted faith — at first. But once someone, trusting him, clings to him familiarly, then he deceives and seizes and eats him, that is, incorporates him into himself, that is, corrupts and makes him like himself.

Likewise, the hypocrite is likened to the caterpillar; for the caterpillar is a harmful worm, since, growing on the leaves of vegetables, it gnaws the tendrils, fruits, foliage, and flowers. Hence it is called 'eruca,' from 'eroding' ('eradendo'), as Isidore says. So too the vice of hypocrisy destroys every spiritual and good fruit of a man, namely of the flowers, that is, of his affections, and of the foliage, that is, of his words, and of the fruits, that is, of his deeds, since the hypocrite, in everything, aims only at human favor.

Second, because it is a cunning worm, namely at preserving itself against the harshness of the season: for, as Pliny says, once the caterpillar has consumed the leaves and fruit at the tips of the trees, it weaves webs from its own inner substance, in the manner of spiders, in which it wraps itself for the whole winter, guarding its pestilent seed. For it lays certain eggs, from which, in spring, when the buds burst forth, a great brood is born. So too the hypocrite, when the winter comes on, that is, the harshness of some adversity or tribulation, weaves webs from his own inner substance, that is, from his own hidden malices, that is, he arranges marvelous and cunning ways in which he can wrap himself, that is, cover and defend himself. And, wrapping himself in such ways, that is, covering himself, he guards his pestilent seed, that is, his malicious disposition. And he lays certain eggs, that is, he performs certain secret works, from which many evils sometimes arise.

Third, because it is a spotted worm: for the caterpillar is soft, and covered with matter of various colors, shining like a star by night, but appearing misshapen by day. So too the hypocrite is soft, that is, given to pleasures, or soft, that is, yielding to temptations: for what is soft does not resist the one who touches it, but gives way.

Likewise, it is covered with matter, that is, full of the putrefaction of sins, or the moisture of lust, and spotted with various colors, that is, with vices or malices, or tinged with various colors, that is, various displays of sanctity, since he strives in many ways to seem good. But although by night, that is, in the obscurity of the present life, he shines like a star, namely through the brightness of his reputation, or his outward appearance, nonetheless, when the day of death comes, or the day of the brightness of divine judgment, in which the hidden things of darkness are illuminated, and the counsels of hearts are made manifest, then his ugliness will be revealed.

Fourth, because the caterpillar is a worm almost monstrous in transforming itself. For, in the manner of the silkworm that makes silk, it changes its form, and transforms itself from a creeping thing into a flying one: for it takes on thin, broad wings, with which, flying, it lifts itself into the air, and shows on its wings as many colors as it had on its body. And such a flying creature is called a butterfly ('papilio'), as Isidore says. And so, as he says, butterflies are made from caterpillars, and from the butterflies' droppings caterpillars are generated again; and when they fly they are less harmful than when they crawl. For then the caterpillar takes on a flying form, or that of a butterfly, when the hypocrite rises to a rank of prelacy. For then, in the manner of the silkworm making silk, he takes on another form, since, like a holy man, he pretends he will do many good things. He takes on thin, broad wings, with which he lifts himself into the air, since he begins and takes up certain works that appear wonderful, but are in reality very weak, by which he boastfully exalts himself, and makes himself great in his rule. And just as butterflies are made from caterpillars, since proud and vainglorious men come forth in the same way from hypocrites, from whose droppings, that is, temporal glory (for the glory of a sinful man is a worm, as it were dung, as it is said in Maccabees) caterpillars are generated again, since other ambitious men, seeing the temporal glory of hypocrites, strive to follow, and even imitate, their pretended life; but in this the flying hypocrites are less harmful than the crawling ones, since their hypocrisy is less hidden in a state of high rank. For high office reveals the man, and the less hidden hypocrisy is, the less harmful it is.
Likewise, in a state of high rank, the hypocrite guards himself all the more, lest he lose his reputation, or honor, for sanctity.

div.head: Cap. LXXIII. Ire damna, iratorumque praua natura apertit monstratur: quibus Apri, Canes rabidi, cyrogryllique per plures eorum similitudines naturales iure comparantur.

cit.quote: Anger frequently drives a man into deadly dangers, out of the desire for vengeance. Hence the wrathful man is like the boar, that is, the wild pig, which (according to Avicenna and Pliny) is a fierce animal, and of such ferocity that it thinks little of death, and, undaunted, sets itself against the hunter's iron blade; indeed, run through with the blade, it takes up new strength against those who wounded it, and attacks them with its own tusks. So too men frequently, in order to avenge themselves on their enemies, out of that very anger, thinking little of the danger of death, throw themselves undaunted even onto iron weapons, and, wounded, do not flee, but rise up with greater fury against those who wounded them. John: 'anger kills the foolish man.' Maccabees: 'bearing the wrath of a wild beast.'

Likewise, the wrathful man is like the rabid dog, which always goes about alone — for other dogs flee it as a plague — and moves as though staggering, like a drunkard, and runs with its mouth open, tongue hanging, and drool flowing; it has bloodshot eyes, and, though it keeps them open, still crashes into everything in its path, as though it were blind; it fights against everything, and barks at its own shadow. And Constantine says that the dog is warm and dry by nature, ruled by black bile, which, when it corrupts, turns the dog to rabies. Likewise too the wrathful man goes about alone, since he can bear neither friend nor companion, on account of which it is said: 'be not a friend to a wrathful man.' He deserves to be shunned by all as a plague, since he spares no one. Likewise he runs with his mouth open, since he does not stop uttering cursed words. Hence his tongue hangs outside his mouth, since he cannot restrain it, for the fool utters his whole spirit, whose drool of wisdom or discretion flows away, since, if the angry man has any sense, he loses it entirely in his fury. Now, literally, he has bloodshot eyes because of the heat of the blood, which rises in vapor to the face and eyes of the wrathful man: for anger is naturally a boiling of the blood around the heart (as Damascene says), on account of the inflaming of the visible spirits.

But, as though blind, he crashes into everything that opposes him, whether by hearing or seeing: for he is offended by every word, or laugh, or other gesture, and so fights against everything he hears or sees; and even by himself, alone, he mutters, and so, in the manner of a rabid dog, barks at his own shadow; and he is most easily kindled into rabid fury when his black bile, that is, melancholy, is corrupted; for when the wrathful man is in some sloth or melancholy, then, from a trivial cause, he is kindled to fury, since he is then most prone to anger, from the conception or imagination of some saddening thing. Rightly, then, ought a man to strive not to be overcome by anger, from which such great madness arises. Job: 'let not anger overcome you.'

Likewise, the wrathful or impatient man, when something happens to him, destroys even what he had done well, like the hedgehog. Hence he is like the 'cyrogryllus,' which is the same as the hedgehog, except larger. This creature knocks grapes or apples down from a vine or tree, and, rolling over them, spikes them onto its quills, and always takes one in its mouth as well; but while carrying them to its den, if any should fall off, in anger it shakes off all the rest, and returns again to the tree, to load itself once more.

Likewise, whatever the wrathful do while in the grip of anger, they commonly, and for the most part, do defectively. A natural example of this is that wrathful animals bear more imperfect offspring, just as the dog bears blind puppies, and the bear bears formless lumps of flesh, without distinct features, which it warms under its armpit, as the hen does her eggs, giving them their proper shape by licking. Likewise, the wrathful man, in the very heat of his passion, does blind works, not preceded by the counsel of reason, and again, confused and disordered works, unless they are afterward repaired and shaped through the gentleness of wisdom. And so Seneca rightly says: 'let nothing be permitted to you while you are angry.'

Likewise, wrathful men are like certain animals of which Aristotle says that they move their horns as they do their ears, and are found in the region of Africa, which (as Avicenna says) was Aristotle's own region; for in them the joining of the horns is more with the skin than with the bone. Likewise, wrathful men, at any contrary word they hear, are at once moved to do harm. And these are the ones who move their horns like their ears: for their ears, for hearing, and their horns, for striking, are equally ready in them, and the fury of such men, breaking out so suddenly, has no mercy, according to that saying: 'anger has no mercy, nor does fury, once it breaks out.'

div.head: Cap. LXXIIII. Hominem secundum exteriora non esse, nec in bonum, nec in malum omnino iudicandum, minimumque peccatum fore fugiendum, Hedi, Tyrique serpentis exemplo confirmatur.

cit.quote: A man is not to be judged, whether good or bad, solely by outward, external appearance. For the kid, to the touch, has a hide or hair rougher than the lamb's, and yet has better flesh — especially the male, whose flesh is best and sweetest, because of its balanced temperament. So too, among men, sometimes the one who appears shaggy and contemptible outwardly is best within; hence Job: 'do not judge according to appearance.' But such judgment fails not only in good things, but also in bad ones; for often the one who seems smaller in appearance is greater in malice. For the 'tyrus' is a serpent small in appearance, and yet exceeds large serpents in venom. Hence the small 'tyrus' is found (as Aristotle says) to be feared and fled even by large serpents, and this 'tyrus' has hair. There is also found a 'tyrus' against whose bite there is no remedy. So too a man ought to fear evil or sin, however small it may seem. The Apostle: 'a little leaven corrupts the whole lump.'

div.head: Cap. LXXV. Peccata, vitiorumque pruritus, per penitentie lachrymas facillime ablui, Elephantium naturali proprietate probatur.

cit.quote: Elephants teach us to wash away sins with the tears of penance, which (according to Pliny) gather together in herds at the new moon, and wash themselves in a river, and so return to their own place. Now, as it were, a new moon appears to men, when some change, or new adversity, comes upon them, and then, in the manner of elephants, they ought to hasten together, in herds, to the waters of teaching or preaching, and wash their sins in the river of penance and tearful compunction, so that the scourges of sin's onslaught may be removed. They likewise run together in herds to the waters, when they go in procession, with litanies and prayers, to entreat God's mercy — which ought also to be done when a new moon comes, that is, a change bringing new adversity. And when the elephants go this way, they make their young go before them too, both coming and going, whom they guard and instruct to do likewise. And so, in the aforesaid matters, men ought to do the same with their boys and young people. Joel: 'gather together the little ones, and them that suck the breasts' — hence too Christ, when he was twelve years old, was taken with the others to the feasts at Jerusalem.

Likewise, the mourning of tears extinguishes the itch of vices, just as sea water, or salt water, kills lice. So the water of tears, with the salt of discretion and the vinegar of compunction, extinguishes the itch of vices, and especially of the flesh. Psalm: 'you have crushed the heads of the dragons' — that is, the itching, or the beginnings, of temptations — 'in the waters,' namely of tears.

div.head: Cap. LXXVI. Humanas leges magni viri facile transgrediuntur: quod similitudine Aranearum tela iure optimo fulcitur.

cit.quote: Human laws (as Anacharsis says) are like spiders' webs: for in them small and feeble creatures are caught and entangled, like flies and the like, but the great and powerful, like birds and the like, pass through them easily, and tear them apart. So too the great, when they transgress the law, are not punished, but only the feeble and small.

div.head: Cap. LXXVII. Onagri in eorum siti tolerantia, patienter debitas penas sufferre nos erudiunt.

cit.quote: The wild ass teaches us long-suffering and patience, since it is an animal that greatly endures thirst: it waits a long time until it finds drink fit for itself. But the greedy, like thirsty men, impatient of their thirst, seek to fill themselves with turbid and unclean waters, that is, temporal riches, which both trouble the soul's peace and stain its knowledge, and yet do not take away their thirst. But holy men, like wild asses, patiently wait until they come to that fountain of life, where there will be full satisfaction. Psalm: 'the wild asses shall wait in their thirst.'

div.head: Cap. LXXVIII. Luxurie damna quam plurima, luxuriantiumque natura atque defectus, per naturales Hirci, Porci, Boracis, Elephantis, et denique Tinee proprietates, et similitudines clare cognoscuntur.

cit.quote: The lustful are likened to he-goats. First, by reason of wantonness: since the he-goat (according to Isidore) is a wanton animal, and burning for coupling. So too the lustful are wanton, and burn for slippery deeds. Jeremiah: 'I see a boiling pot, and the face thereof from the north.' The face from the north, which the prophet saw, is the suggestion of the wicked spirit, kindling the pot, that is, the flesh, in which the water of carnal desire boils.

Second, by reason of lewdness: since the he-goat (as Isidore says) is a lecherous animal; hence its eyes look sideways toward lust. So too the lustful have a sideways and shameless glance, which shows a shameless mind, since (as Augustine says) a shameless eye is the messenger of a shameless heart.

Third, by reason of infamy: since he-goats are foul-smelling, and so the lustful stink through infamy. Hence the Lord rained sulphur and fire upon Sodom: for in the sin of the flesh the fire of desire burns, and the sulphur of infamy stinks.

Fourth, by reason of persistence: since this vice clings more incorrigibly (as Democritus says, and Pliny relates) because the he-goat is never without a fever: for the he-goat is of such heat that its warm blood softens the diamond, which neither iron nor fire can tame, as Isidore says. Hence it suffers a continuous fever, and so some men are so slippery that they are always in the heat of evil desire. But note that the burnt horn of the he-goat is said to drive away serpents. The he-goat's horn, then, is the vigor of the lustful body, which, if burned by the fire of affliction, drives away serpents, that is, the poisonous temptations of the flesh.
Likewise, its gall is said to clarify sight, since the bitterness and tribulation of the flesh sometimes opens the soul's sight, and restores clarity.

Likewise, the lustful man is likened to the pig. First, since the pig ('porcus') is named, as it were, from 'foul' ('spurcus'), since it always lies at rest in filth and stench. So too the lustful man rests in the filth and stench of carnal sins. Hence Jeremiah: 'Moab has rested in her own filth.'

Second, since the pig is born with teeth already (as Pliny says); the teeth of the piglets, with which they hold fast the mind, are the delights that are present in the sin of lust from its very origin, or root, namely in the very thought itself. It is not so, however, with the sin of anger, which has its pain rather at the end, namely when the wrathful man takes his revenge.

Third, since the pig quickly dies if it loses an eye. So too, since the shameless and wandering eye is the incitement and kindling of lust, once that fault is removed, lust easily ceases. Job: 'I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not so much as think upon a virgin.'

Fourth, since pigs, when wallowing in the mud, lie more on their right side than their left, since man too lies more in the mud of lust when he is on the right side of prosperity than on the left of adversity, since the wickedness of one hour brings forgetfulness of lust, as it is said in Ecclesiastes.

Likewise, the lustful man is likened to the toad, which is a kind of venomous frog: for it has eyes, as it were, of fire, and is the more harmful, the more burning its gaze. It hates the sight of the sun, and seeks darkness. It loves sweet herbs, and eats their roots, but, in eating them, poisons them. And so rue is customarily planted in gardens as its enemy. It loves foul and dungy places, and hates fragrant ones, hence it flees when the vineyard begins to flower. Likewise, the lustful man too has eyes of fire, as it were, inflamed with the fire of inward desire, and the more burning the eye, the worse the mind in its lusting. Second Peter: 'having eyes full of adultery.' Here, literally, he hates the light, and seeks the darkness, since 'the eye of the adulterer watches for darkness.' Job. Or he hates the sight of the sun, that is, the revealing of his sin, and seeks darkness, that is, concealment. He loves sweet herbs, that is, the delights of pleasure, which are sweet to the flesh, and eats their roots, that is, he feeds on their inward thoughts, since, if he cannot carry them out in deed, he at least turns them over in his heart, and so breeds foul and unclean thoughts within himself. But if rue, that is, some bitter tribulation, could be planted there, such infections would cease. The lustful man also loves foul and dungy places, that is, dishonorable and infamous ones, like brothels and the like; but he hates and flees honest places and company.

...and so, where he sees the vineyard of penance beginning to flower, he does not draw near, but flees, and keeps his distance. Hence it should be noted that the fervor of lust, or desire, is extinguished by the affliction of harsh penance — an example of which still appears in the 'boraco' or toad. For authors relate (as Pliny says) that, on the right side of the toad, there is a hidden bone which, cast into boiling water, at once makes it stop boiling, nor, as long as that bone remains in it, can it boil further; and they say it drives away a quartan fever. Now, as it were, the toad is human life, whose left side is the state of guilt, but whose right side is the state of penance. On this side is the bone, that is, the hard affliction of the flesh, which ought to be undertaken as a burden, that is, not done for show, as hypocrites do. This extinguishes the boiling of the water, that is, the burning of desire, and drives away the quartan fever, that is, lust, which burns in four ways, namely in thought, in affection, in gaze, and in touch.

Likewise, the vice of gluttony, or of lust, rules over great and powerful men, since it is chiefly through carnal pleasure that the devil conquers them. Just as the unicorn, often warring against the elephant, strikes the elephant in the belly and throws it down: for the elephant has a soft belly. By the unicorn is understood the devil, whose horn signifies the power permitted to him by God to tempt, or to persecute, men. This devil strikes elephants, that is, great men, established in positions of dignity, especially in the belly, since it is through the vices that belong to the belly, namely through gluttony and through lust, that he conquers them, to which they are especially soft, that is, prone, because of the delights they continually enjoy, and because of the freedom they have. Hence the Philosopher says that many of those established in positions of power seem to suffer things like Sardanapalus, namely the king of the Assyrians, who was entirely dissolute, lustful, and given to pleasure.

Likewise, the lustful man is likened to the moth. For the moth is the worm of the garment, so called because it clings to the garment, and does not stop at it until it has eaten it through. Now what is the worm of a garment, but the vice of the flesh, which, because of the insatiability of its delight, clings to man's appetite so long that it strips him of every good? Hence lust, as is said in Job, is a fire devouring even to destruction, and rooting out all increase.

div.head: Cap. LXXIX. Quemadmodum Domini matrem, diligere ac venerari debeant peccatores, ut recreentur: insigni catulorum canum exemplo explanatur.

cit.quote: ...the puppies of dogs love their mother, and, still blind, recognize her by voice and by scent; they seek her teats, and, pressing them with the sharpness of their teeth, force the milk to flow from her udders; and when they are hungry, they seek her breasts with a whimpering voice. Now sinful men are like the puppies of dogs, that is, of demons — men who are the devil's children not by nature, but by imitation and malice.

Likewise, to draw in her fragrance: of which she herself says, 'I, like the vine, have brought forth the fragrance of sweetness,' and again, 'like cinnamon, and balsam,' and so on. Or they are said to recognize her voice in her words, as when she says, 'my soul does magnify the Lord.' Likewise in her other words, which are read in the Gospel — all of which teach us beneficially.

Likewise, they ought to recognize her fragrance, through the examples of all the virtues that she has left us. They ought to seek her breasts: for she has one breast to give the milk of grace, namely to the just, and another to give the milk of mercy, namely to sinners. And so she is called the mother of grace. And they ought to press them too, with sharp teeth, that is, with insistent prayers, so that she may help them from her breasts; and if they hunger, that is, if they truly desire the remedy of their salvation, with a whimpering voice, that is, with sorrowful confession and prayer, they ought often to beg for those breasts. 'May her breasts inebriate you at all times.'

div.head: Cap. LXXX. Hyene seva natura, variabilis, et monstruosa, cui mors comparatur, quoue pacto eamet, quo ad culpam, et quo ad penam in hominem intrauerit, mortisque meditatio quantum prosit aperitur.

cit.quote: Death is likened to a certain animal called the hyena, which has the neck of a viper, the back of an elephant, imitates the voices of men, resembles the wolf in size and voracity, has the hair of a horse on its neck, and, it is said, changes sex, since it is found now male, now female, in the same animal. So too death is likened to the viper, on account of swiftness, since men frequently die unexpectedly, and before their time, especially by violent deaths — just as happens with the viper, whose young, when the time comes for her to give birth, do not wait for the operation of nature, but gnaw through her sides, and come out at the cost of their mother's death. So too many are torn apart by death before their time, that is, before old age and natural death. It is likened to the elephant, on account of its warlike nature, since the elephant is an animal fit for war, but the war or battle of death is the greatest of all: for there is the battle of nature, which is dissolved by sickness. There is also the battle of the soul, which is forced to leave its own home, and enter a region unknown to it. There is also the battle of conscience, which has above it an angry judge, if the man is a sinner, and within it the remorse of sins, and beneath it hell prepared, and beside it a savage adversary; and it is a fearful thing to come to such a judgment, or such a battle. It imitates man's voice, on account of deceptiveness, for it deceives man through uncertainty, since man does not know his own end. It is likened to the wolf, on account of voracity: for it devours men, and is never satisfied. It has the neck of a horse, on account of its being restrainable, since it places a bridle and a limit on human wickedness. It changes sex, since it carries off now women, now men. Kings: 'we all die,' and so on.

Likewise, death, both of nature and of guilt, entered into man through the procurement and temptation of the ancient serpent, that is, the devil. A sign of this is that, as Hippocrates says, a serpent is born from the spinal marrow of a dead man, which indeed (as Isidore says) rightly happens, so that, just as man's death came about through the serpent, so through man's death the serpent should come forth from him, though it too is destined to die. Wisdom: 'by the envy of the devil, death entered into the world.'

Likewise, the memory of death makes a man leave the world, or sin, more quickly and easily, and so it is likened to that herb called 'dracontea,' which deer, since they give birth with difficulty, eat so that the offspring may come out more easily: for man, placed in sin, or entangled in worldly things, is, as it were, offspring still in the womb, which is brought forth with difficulty, unless driven by the fear of death. Hence the meditation and fear of death make one easily come forth from the womb of the world, or of sin: for he easily despises all things who always thinks himself about to die, as Jerome says. And this coming-forth is like a birth, which comes about through the pain of penance. John: 'a woman,' that is, grace, 'when she gives birth,' namely to a new man in righteousness, 'has sorrow,' namely of penance, and this sorrow makes him come forth from sin, which the memory of death drives him to abandon. Ecclesiasticus: 'remember your last end, and you shall never sin.'

Likewise, the memory of death, with compunction of heart, resists the venom of carnal temptation. Just as the ash of a scorpion, drunk in wine, is a remedy for a man struck by it. The scorpion's sting is, as it were, the temptation of the flesh itself: for the scorpion approaches by feeling its way, and strikes backward with its tail; and so the flesh first delights, and afterward torments. For a man struck by the scorpion, that is, tempted by the flesh, the remedy is the ash of the scorpion mixed with wine. For what is the ash of the scorpion, but the dissolution of the flesh, which, drunk with the wine of compunction, that is, considered with an attentive mind, frees one from the venomous sting of the scorpion, that is, from the venomous temptation of the flesh? Augustine: 'nothing so calls one back from sin as the frequent meditation on death.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXI. Animantia in veteri lege ad esum concessa, ac etiam prohibita, que mentis munditiam, seu immunditiam signare videntur, manifestantur: ac cur a Deo id factum sit, rationes assignantur.

cit.quote: Cleanness of mind is signified by the cleanness of those animals that were permitted for food in the law of Moses. It is said in Leviticus: 'whatsoever has the hoof divided, and chews the cud, among cattle, you shall eat. But that which chews the cud, and has a hoof, but does not divide it, like the camel, you shall not eat. The hedgehog, which chews the cud, but does not divide the hoof, is unclean, and so is the hare: for it too chews the cud, but does not divide the hoof; and the swine, which, though it divides the hoof, does not chew the cud, you shall not eat its flesh.' Likewise it is said in the same place: 'whatsoever of fowls that walks upon four feet shall be abominable to you.'

But whatsoever walks on four feet, and yet has longer hind legs, by which it leaps upon the ground, you shall eat, such as the locust in its kind, and the 'attractus,' and the 'ophiomachus,' and the grasshopper, each according to its kind. Note here that the animal that chews the cud and divides its feet, that is, its hooves, is granted as clean, as Augustine says, for a certain reason: since the cloven hoof signifies the distinction of the two Testaments, or of the Father and the Son, or the discernment of good and evil. Chewing the cud, however, signifies meditation on the Scriptures, and a sound understanding of them. Whatever lacks either of these is spiritually unclean, and so is forbidden as an unclean animal, if it lacks either of the two. But flying and four-footed creatures that have longer hind legs, so that they can leap, are eaten. But those that cling more to the earth are forbidden, since those who misuse the teaching of the four Evangelists, so as not to be lifted on high by it, are counted unclean.

div.head: Cap. LXXXII. Muneribus sepe iudices, seu Principes placari ac corrumpi, Catuli exemplo probatur.

cit.quote: Gifts appease, as does a barking puppy — and gifts also frequently corrupt prelates and judges: for sometimes a barking puppy runs at someone, as though it would bite him, but if one threw it a piece of bread, it would take it and be silent. So too sometimes a prelate comes to some subject with such barking that he seems about to devour him, but the subject throws him a mark of silver, and this takes away his speech. Ecclesiasticus: 'gifts and presents blind the eyes of judges, and, as it were, make him mute in the mouth, and turn away his rebukes.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXIII. Per Cameli nominis interpretationem, eiusque naturam, libenter obedientiam, seu penitentiam fore a fidelibus subeundam, paucis demonstrat verbis.

cit.quote: Camels teach us to take up the work of obedience, or of penance, humbly, and to bear it patiently. For camels (as Isidore says) took their name from the Greek, since, when they are loaded, they bow and humble themselves before men, and bend down on their knees. For 'came' in Greek means 'humble,' or, in Latin, 'short.' They are animals fit for burdens, and gentle for carrying them. So too a man ought to take up humbly the burden of obedience laid on him by superiors, or of penance imposed on him, and bear it gently and patiently. Hence, even of bad prelates, it is said to their subjects: 'whatsoever they shall tell you, observe and do.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXIIII. Tria sacrificiorum genera veteris legis, nec non animalia in his sacrificiis oblata, rerumque modus ac significatio declaratur: quibus omnibus modis vero Deo se dedendi aperitur.

cit.quote: A man ought to offer himself to God's service in the way that animals were offered as sacrifice in the law of Moses. For there were three kinds of sacrifice. One was that which was burned up entirely, hence called 'holocaust,' as it were wholly burnt. This kind of sacrifice was offered to God in reverence for his majesty, and in love for his goodness, and suited the state of the perfect in the fulfillment of the counsels; and so it was burned entirely, so that, just as the whole animal rose up in vapor, so too it might be signified that the whole man, and everything that is his, is subject to God the Lord, and is to be offered to him.

...to God, through the ministry of the priests, except when it was offered for the sin of the whole people, or specially for the sin of the priest: then it was burned entirely. For those things offered for their sins were not to come into the use of the priests, so that nothing of the sin should remain in them, and because this would not have been satisfaction for the sin. For if they had passed into the use of those for whose sin they were offered, it would have seemed the same as if they had not been offered at all.

The third sacrifice was called the peace-offering ('hostia'), which was offered to God either in thanksgiving, or for the health and prosperity of the offerers, out of duty for a benefit received or to be received. And it suited the state of those advancing in the fulfillment of the commandments. And this was divided into three parts: for one part was burned in honor of the one God; another part went to the use of the priests; and the third part to the use of the offerers — to signify that man's salvation proceeds from God, the ministers directing it, and the men who are saved themselves cooperating in it. Now this was generally observed, that the blood and the fat did not come into the use of the priests, nor into the use of the offerers. Rather, the blood was offered at the base of the altar in honor of God, while the fat was burned in fire. Now the eating of blood was forbidden them, so that they would abhor the shedding of human blood. Hence it is said in Genesis: 'you shall not eat flesh with the blood, for I will require the blood of your souls.' The use of fat, however, was forbidden them, to keep them from wantonness; hence it is said in Ezekiel that the fat part was to be burned. Or by this was signified the shedding of Christ's blood, and the richness of charity, by which he offered himself for us. Of the peace-offerings, the breast and the right shoulder went to the use of the priests, to exclude a certain kind of divination called 'shoulder-blade divination,' since the pagans divined by the shoulder-blades of sacrificed animals, and by the breastbone, and so these were withheld from the offerers. By this it was also figured that the breast, which is the covering of the heart, and also strength for sustaining service to God, which is signified by the right shoulder, belong to God. And note that whoever could not afford a four-footed animal was at least to offer flour, or an ear of grain. Its figurative meaning was that bread signifies Christ, who is the living bread. He was, as it were, in the ear of grain, in the state of the law of nature; but in the faith of the patriarchs he was, as it were, in the fine flour. In the teaching of the law and the prophets, he was, as it were, in the dough; but he was, as it were, bread already formed, after human nature was assumed. Baked in fire, that is, formed by the Holy Spirit in the oven of the Virgin's womb. He was also cooked in a pan, through the labors he bore in the world; but on the cross, roasted as on a grill. Likewise, too, every other offering that was made figured Christ in some way, whether of the produce of the earth used for food, like bread, or for drink, like wine, or as seasoning, like oil and salt, or as medicine, like incense, which is aromatic and healing. For by bread was figured the flesh of Christ, by wine his blood, by which we are redeemed, by oil the grace of Christ, by salt his knowledge, but by incense, prayer. Among the offerers, unleavened bread signified sincerity and truth of life. In salt was designated the discretion of wisdom, or the mortification of carnal desire. Incense, however, was offered to signify devotion of mind, which is necessary for offerers, and also to signify the fragrance of a good reputation; for incense is both rich and fragrant. In the sacrifice of jealousy, however, incense was not offered, since jealousy proceeds not from devotion, but from suspicion.

div.head: Cap. LXXXV. Occasiones peccatorum esse a nobis remouendas: Elephantium exemplo, Christique precepto admonemur.

cit.quote: The occasions of sin, and elephants, teach us about their tusks. For the elephant, having two ivory tusks, when pressed hard by hunters, strikes and breaks them both at once, so that, once the ivory is lost, the hunters no longer pursue it: for it senses that this is the cause of its danger. Likewise the Lord taught us to cut off even those things dearest to us, so that we may not be put in danger of our soul on their account. Matthew: 'if your eye scandalize you, pluck it out, and cast it from you.' The Poet: 'I would rather bear lesser losses, that I not bear graver ones.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXVI. Cur bona opera sint a fidelibus secreto facienda, Elephantis similitudine declaratur.

cit.quote: ...the elephant teaches, which, giving birth in water or in a forest, leaves its offspring there where it gives birth, because of the dragons that lie in wait for them. So too, whoever does a good work, whether in the waters of penance, or of wisdom, or in the forest, that is, in the solitude of the contemplative life, if he does not wish it to be snatched away by dragons, that is, by demons lying in wait, should, just as he does it in secret, keep it secret when no necessity requires otherwise, and not bring it into the open through display. Matthew: 'do not appear to men to be fasting, but to your Father, who is in secret.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXVII. Quemadmodum divina officia sint a Religiosis dicenda, omniaque bona opera perficienda: ac equinoctium unde ortum habuerit, et denique cornuum animalium variatio ac significatio scite enucleatur.

cit.quote: The example of the wild ass reminds us, of which the Physiologus says that it always brays exactly as many times a day as the day has hours, and does likewise at night. From this the philosophers discovered the equinox, since at that time it brays twelve times in the day, and as many times at night. If, then, the wild ass does not miss the hours, so much the less ought a churchman to fail to do so. For the elephant, which, throughout its whole life — said to be prolonged to four hundred years — bears young only once, and only a single offspring, carries its young for two years before giving birth. So too a man ought to hold that good which can be done only once, long in the womb of his mind through deliberation, before bringing it forth by doing it. Hence Seneca: 'that which is to be done only once must be long deliberated.'

Likewise, mighty works too are void of the merit of eternal reward, unless they are done with purity of mind and unity of charity: for every horned animal has its horn hollow, except the stag and the unicorn. For what is signified by the animal producing a horn from its head, but the man who does some notable and manly work? For a virtuous work comes out of reason, just as the horn comes out of the head. Now this horn is full in the stag, that is, in the pure man: for the stag, which is a simple animal (according to Aristotle and Avicenna), has no gall-bladder in its belly, and loves clean pasture; it signifies the simple man, free of the gall of wickedness, who keeps himself pure from sin.

Likewise, it is full in the unicorn: for whoever keeps the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace is, as it were, a unicorn. For while he does not divide himself, in what he does, from the unity of brotherly love, he produces only one horn. Only the horns of such men, then, that is, their virtuous and mighty works, are full of bone, that is, of the solidity of grace, and of the fruit of eternal reward; but, on the contrary, of the sinner's works it is said: 'I do not find his works full.'

div.head: Cap. LXXXVIII. Scytali atque ophitis discoloris, nec non Cate naturales proprietates, et similitudines apponuntur, quibus compta mulieres comparantur.

cit.quote: The ornamentation of women is like the 'scytale' serpent, which (as Isidore says) so shines with the variety of its back that it draws the admiration of those who look upon it. And since it is slow, it seizes by the admiration it inspires those it cannot catch by running, and the more varied its colors, the worse its venom. So too the adorned woman draws the eyes and hearts of onlookers to herself, and renders them stupefied and senseless, and seizes them through desire, and destroys them with the venom of evil consent. And so, the more adorned and beautiful, the more dangerous. Likewise, the 'ophites' is a serpent covered with spots, which has as many ways of doing harm as it has varied colors. And so is the woman painted with various colors, or clothed in various ornaments. Hence Jerome says: if a man or a woman adorns himself, and thereby provokes the gaze of others, even if no actual harm follows from it, he will still suffer eternal judgment, since he brought poison, even if there was no one to drink it. Proverbs: 'there met him a woman dressed as a harlot.'

Likewise, adorned and beautiful women are like cats. For the cat, when it has a beautiful coat, glories in it, and, on that account, sometimes becomes a wanderer; but if that coat is singed off, it stays indoors. Yet often, while it glories in its coat, it is caught and killed precisely because of its beauty. So too a woman, sensing her own beautiful complexion, or a beautiful garment on her back, willingly glories in it, and goes about to show it to others. But if her complexion is spoiled or disfigured by fever or other sickness, or her clothes are worn out, then she stays more firmly at home.

Likewise, while she glories in her fragile clothing, or complexion, she is caught by the devil through vainglory and wantonness, and sometimes is led into the baseness of sin, and at last is killed by a sudden or evil death, and is further tormented by eternal punishment. Hence Cyprian says that those clothed in silk and purple cannot sincerely clothe themselves with Christ; adorned with gold, and silver, and pearls, they have lost the ornaments of soul and body. Hence too that rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, was buried in hell.

div.head: Cap. LXXXIX. Paschalis Agni, Christi passionem prefigurantis, immolatio, quibus in veteri lege perficiebatur ceremoniis, eorumque perfecta significatio artificiose explanatur.

cit.quote: The passion of Christ was prefigured in the sacrifice of the paschal lamb, of which it is written in Exodus 12. For the sacrifice of the lamb itself signifies the sacrifice of Christ, according to that saying: 'Christ our Passover is sacrificed.' The blood of the lamb, freeing from the destroyer, smeared on the lintels of the houses, signifies the passion of Christ in the heart and mouth of the faithful, through which we are freed from sins and eternal death, according to that saying of Peter: 'we are redeemed by the precious blood of the spotless lamb.' That flesh, moreover, was eaten, to signify the eating of Christ's body in the sacrament. It was roasted with fire, to signify the passion and charity of Christ. It was eaten with unleavened bread, to signify the pure conduct of the faithful who receive the body of Christ, according to that saying: 'let us feast in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.' Wild lettuces were added, as a sign of penance for sins, which is necessary for those who receive the body of Christ. The loins were to be girded with the belt of chastity, and the shoes on the feet are the examples of the dead Fathers. Staves in hand signify pastoral guardianship. It is also commanded that the paschal lamb be eaten in one house, that is, in the Church of catholic men, not in the conventicles of heretics.

div.head: Cap. XC. Deum leuem, benignumque existere in sustinendo: ac denique durum esse in peccatorem puniendo, teredinis exemplo probabili demonstratur.

cit.quote: God's patience is gentle in enduring, but severe and harsh in punishing; hence it is likened to the shipworm, that is, the worm of wood, which gnaws through wood, as Isidore says. Though soft in substance, it grinds down the hardest woods, and reduces them to finer dust than a file itself could make. So too divine patience, though it bears long with a sinner, gently and mildly, nonetheless finally crushes him, and afflicts him with the severest punishment. Romans: 'according to your hardness, and impenitent heart, you store up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath.' Kings: he is like the tenderest little worm of wood — which indeed is very gentle when touched, but, when it touches, or gnaws, is most hard. So too God is gentle in enduring, hard in punishing. Psalm: 'I am a worm, and no man.'

div.head: Cap. XCI. Pulcherrimo Onagri exemplo patientie ac perseverantie homines coronari confirmatur.

cit.quote: Patience and perseverance make a man victorious. For the wild ass, though a feeble animal, escaping only by the benefit of flight, nonetheless overcomes the lion in the wilderness, and likewise the wolf. For it holds out so long in fleeing that they give out in pursuing; so too the saints overcome the world, or sin, by fleeing, and by persevering in the endurance of labors. Psalm: 'behold, I have gone far off flying, and I remained in the wilderness.' Cassiodorus: 'patience is that which overcomes all adversities, not by struggling, but by enduring.' Likewise Bernard: 'without perseverance, neither does the one who fights obtain victory, nor the victor the palm.'

div.head: Cap. XCII. Peccatores Satyris ac Faunis monstris, etiamque canibus, Capris, Asinis, Cocodrillis, Ranis, et Talpis comparantur: quorum naturalibus similitudinibus diversis, delictorum omnium grauitas, delinquentiumque preceps status plane declaratur.

cit.quote: ...monstrous animals, called satyrs or fauns; for there are certain monstrous beasts, having the form of a man, but not sharing in reason, nor teachable by art or nature to speak: for they have a wild and beastly mind, and the appetite of a beast. Hence they are so prone to lust that they kill women in coupling, if they seize any in the woods; hence they are called satyrs, since they cannot be satisfied with lust, as Isidore says. So too the sinner is monstrous, having a man's face, and a beast's mind, or a brutish life. What, indeed, is more beastly than a man possessing reason, and not using reason? as Bernard says. Such especially are the proud, who have a cruel and savage mind, and the foolish, who can be led by no skill to speak sweetly and reasonably, as was Rehoboam. So too are the given-to-pleasure, since they have a beastly appetite for gluttony, and an insatiable one for lust. All such are compared to senseless cattle, and are made like them.

Likewise, sinners are likened to dogs. First, on account of gluttony: for the dog is gluttonous. Hence, when it has eaten too much, it throws it up, and eats it again — in which it also represents those who, through relapse, return to the uncleanness of whatever sin. Peter: 'the dog is returned to his own vomit,' and so on.

Likewise, on account of lust: for the dog is lustful, and distinguishes neither mother nor sister. Hence, among the ancients, an offering made of a dog was like that of a harlot, who exposes herself to every kind of lust. Ecclesiasticus: 'the woman will receive every male.'

Likewise, on account of wrathfulness: for the dog is wrathful and malicious. Hence it often bites, with its teeth, the very stone with which it is struck, so as to avenge itself on it, and yet it harms not the stone, but its own tooth. So too the wrathful man frequently harms himself, where he thinks to harm another. Psalm: 'his sorrow shall be turned upon his own head.'

Likewise, on account of pride: for the dog is bold among those it knows, but timid among strangers. So too the proud man, among his own household and in his own house, is like a lion, but is more fearful of others.

The dog also hates sticks, and fears stones, since the proud man hates correction, and fears harsh rebukes: for the proud man does not acknowledge his own fault, or sin. Seneca: 'he who does not know he has sinned does not wish to be corrected.'

Likewise, on account of the dog too being envious. Hence Avicenna says that it secretly gathers herbs with which it purges itself, grieving if another gets medicine from them. It also grieves if another comes to its house, fearing lest that one find favor, and something be taken from it; and so too the envious man grieves at the advantage or favor of others. The Philosopher: 'envy is sorrow at another's good.'

Likewise, on account of the dog being like a miser, which cannot eat something, yet studiously hoards it, and does not wish to give it to others, but guards it. So too the avaricious man does, by hoarding and guarding. Luke: 'my soul, you have many good things laid up for many years.'

Likewise, on account of sloth, since the dog, when it is old, and lazy, and idle, sleeps all day, even among flies, and although flies bore into its ears, it is nonetheless so lazy that it only rarely shakes itself, to drive them further off. So too the slothful man is lazy in beginning, idle in working, drowsy in praying, or in resisting, that is, temptations, which are understood by the troublesome flies. Or by the boring flies, understand rebukes and the pricks of words, by which he is neither roused nor amended. There are also, like stinging flies, the needs or wants that the lazy man has, which nonetheless do not amend the lazy man, but consume him, since he is consumed by desires or needs rather than willing to labor. Proverbs: 'desires kill the sluggard.'

The dog, in the end, after much service, is bound with a rope, and led away by it to be killed, and drowned in water, or thrown from a bank; nor is its hide taken, nor its flesh eaten, but it is left exposed to be gnawed by worms. So too the sinner, after much service to the world, or to sin, is bound by the devil with a rope, that is, the habit of sinning, and by it is dragged along, that is, held fast until the death of the body, and killed in the water, that is, fails through the natural decay of a life ebbing away. Kings: 'we all die, and, like water, slip away.' Or he is thrown from the bank, that is, by the fall of a violent death, into the pit of hell, namely as regards his soul. His dead body, however, remains entirely useless. For of other animals, after they are killed, either the flesh remains, useful for eating, or at least the hide, useful for clothing or footwear; but human flesh, dead or killed, is worth nothing further, except that it is left as food for worms.

...goats, first, on account of pride. For the goat always strains upward, to crop and eat the topmost leaves, as Isidore says. So too are the proud, who always gape after higher positions, so that they may snatch and possess the tops of the leaves, that is, the dignities and honors of the great, which they themselves reckon highest. Psalm: 'the pride of them that hate you rises up continually.'

Likewise, on account of lust: for, as Pliny says, goats, because of their heat, do not abound in fat, and are rarely without fever, and so their coupling is burning, and they are said to see no less by night than by day. These things fit the lustful, in whom, because of the use of Venus, both the fat of the body and of the mind are laid waste, and, even with a burning fever, they are rarely found free of desire, and are themselves defiled by the very burning delight of the act of the flesh. Likewise, the lustful watch for their foul deeds by night no less than by day. Job: 'the eye of the adulterer watches for darkness.'

Likewise, on account of avarice. For goats (as the same author says) gnaw the tips of the plants on which sheep feed, right down to the roots; hence the goat ('capra') is named from cropping ('carpendo') the shoots. So too are the avaricious, who always intend to crop, and the tips on which sheep feed, that is, the temporal goods that the good, that is, spiritual men, use for their food and their sustenance, they pull up right down to the roots, since they frequently strip the poor so thoroughly that they leave them nothing.

Likewise, the sinner is likened to the ass, which is naturally a heavy, slow, lazy, timid, stupid animal, fit for burdens, and very patient of labor. So too the sinner is heavy in falling, slow to repent, lazy in working, timid at temporal loss, stupid in providing for himself, fit for bearing the burden of sin, or of eternal punishment, and patient in enduring the fruitless labor of the world.

Likewise, the sinner is deceived by sin, just as the crocodile is deceived by that little bird called the king of birds. For while the crocodile lies by the shore, that little bird comes and flies around its mouth, and the crocodile opens its jaws, and lets it enter; but the bird first lightly scratches it with its claws, so that the beast, from the pleasure of it, at once falls asleep, and, when the bird senses it asleep, it at once descends into its belly, and pierces it through the belly, and kills it: for the crocodile is very soft in the belly. The crocodile lying on the shore, then, is, as it were, the man grown sluggish in idleness. The little bird coming to its mouth is the temptation of sin entering the imagination, to which the mouth is opened, when it is received in thought and delight. And then it lightly scratches, since it generates an itch of delight; and if the man then sleeps, so as not to resist the temptation through negligence, it enters into his mind, and, through his consent, pierces and kills him.

Likewise, the sinner is likened to the frog, which is muddy, and noisy, and puffed up, and hateful, spotted beneath the belly, talkative, and lives not only in water but also on land. So too the sinner is muddy through lust, that is, unclean; noisy through wrath; puffed up through pride; hateful to men through avarice — for (as Boethius says) avarice makes one hateful, but generosity makes one renowned; spotted beneath the belly through gluttony; talkative through envy. For the frog (as Aristotle says) has a tongue, and a croaking voice. So too the envious and talkative man detracts.
Likewise, it lives on land, which is heavy and cold through sloth, which renders the soul heavy and cold.

Likewise, the sinner is likened to the mole. First, since the mole, like the pig, has a snout, and such is the sinner, through the uncleanness of lust, or gluttony; and with such a snout the mole pulls roots from the earth, since, through the sins of the flesh, the affections of the mind are emptied out and torn away. Hence, in Job 31, it is said of lust that it is a fire rooting out all increase.

Second, since the mole digs the earth, and does not live long once drawn out from the earth. And so Pliny says that moles hear better when covered by earth than when drawn out — and such is the sinner through the vice of avarice, whose whole study is to turn over earthly things, and who does not believe he can live without earthly entanglements, and wishes to discuss and hear only of earthly things. John: 'he that is of the earth, speaks of the earth.'

Third, since the mole hates the sun, and this the sinner has from the vice of pride, namely that he hates God, who is the true Sun, according to that saying of the Psalm already cited: 'the pride of them that hate you,' and so on. For pride sets itself most of all against God, on account of which God resists the proud most of all; and in this respect they hate him, or the proud hate the sun, that is, the one who reveals or rebukes their vices. Hence the proud man does not come to the light, lest his works be exposed.

Fourth, as Aristotle says, the mole does not have open eyes, but eyes hidden beneath its hide, which it opens only in death — eyes it kept closed its whole life through. So too the sinner, who walks through his whole life as though blind, that is, erring and falling into sin, is compelled, willing or not, to open his eyes at death, and to recognize his sins before the tribunal of God, and even to experience the punishments that, while living, he neglected to consider. Gregory: 'for the eyes that guilt closes, punishment opens.'

div.head: Cap. XCIII. Peccati grauitas ac malitia, omniumque delictorum variatio, per cuiusdam monstri Indie naturam, mulique ac Salamandre, Burestis, Formice, Basilisci, Aspidis, Cocodrilli, Musre bouine, nonnullorumque serpentium naturales effectus, venenique proprietates, multis perspicuis exemplis manifestatur.

cit.quote: Sin is likened to a certain monstrous animal said to be found in India, like a bear in body, a lion in its mane, and a man in its face, having a red head, and a large, round mouth, with three rows of teeth in each jaw, whose extremities are like a lion's, whose tail is like a scorpion's, and it strikes with its bristles like a wild boar, and its voice is like a trumpet, and it is swift of running, and eats men, and no beast is more cruel than it. The likeness to the bear, then, pertains to the sin of wrath, since the bear is an impatient animal. The likeness to the lion pertains to the sin of pride. The likeness to man pertains to the sin of avarice, since man alone, of all creatures, gathers wealth out of greed — which also makes the head red, that is, the mind fiery and burning to possess, or because it is the cause of murder and the shedding of blood. The largeness of the mouth is referred to gluttony, which the various rows of teeth serve, that is, the various ranks of those who provide for it — farmers, butchers, cooks, and the like. The scorpion's tail is referred to the envious, who detract most sharply from behind, that is, slander in absence. The likeness to the pig is referred to the lustful, because of their uncleanness. The trumpet-like voice is sin made manifest and public; but its swift running is the delight of sin, which passes quickly; it devours men, meanwhile, when it catches them through delight, swallows them through consent, and turns them into itself through action or habit; no beast is found crueler, since nothing is found more harmful to man.

Likewise, sin is likened to the mule. First, by reason of its unnaturalness, since the mule is generated against the order of nature, namely from the mixing of two species, from a mare and an ass, or, conversely, from an ass and a horse, producing a hinny. And Isidore says that Anah, grandson of Esau, was the first to put mares to asses, so that mules would be born against nature. So too sin — and Augustine says that it is not from nature, but a vice of nature desiring what does not belong to its own order. And just as the mule is generated by putting a mare to an ass, so too sin is born, and the order of nature is perverted, when reason is subjected to sensuality, so that sensuality is subjected not to reason, but rather sensuality rules over reason. Ecclesiastes: 'I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the ground.'

Second, by reason of the mule's barrenness, since the mule is sterile, nature withholding its own benefit from it, since it is produced, as it were, in an offense against nature. But Aristotle says that the mule is sterile because of an excess of coldness dominating in it. So too sin is barren, that is, without the fruit and fruitfulness of merit, or of glorious reward. Now the excess of coldness in the soul is because of the lack of charity, which is, as it were, the vital heat of the soul, without which a meritorious work for eternal life is not produced. Matthew: 'because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold.'

Third, by reason of its being turned about. For the mule ('mulus') is named from grinding ('molendo'), since, subdued under the yoke of millers, it turns the millstones in a circle, as Isidore says. So too the sinner, dragged from one sin to another, is turned about, as it were, around a millstone. Psalm: 'they walk round about.'

Likewise, sin is likened to the salamander, which is a venomous animal. Hence Pliny says that it poisons the fruits of trees, corrupts waters, and, if its saliva touches only a man's foot, it corrupts his whole body. So too sin is the worst poison, which poisons the fruits of trees, that is, good works, or their substance.

Likewise, it corrupts the waters, that is, graces, and if its saliva, that is, delight, touches the foot, that is, the affection of the soul, through consent, it ruins the whole man. Hence it is said in Corinthians: 'touch not the unclean thing.'

Likewise, sin is likened to poison: for it is called 'venenum' since it goes 'per venas' (through the veins) to the heart. So too sin passes through the veins of thought and delight to the consent of the heart, or through the veins, that is, through the senses of the body, it steals into the secret places of the mind. Jeremiah: 'death has come up through our windows, it has entered into our houses.'

Likewise, poison does no harm except when it touches blood. Hence Lucan: 'the venom of serpents is harmful only when mixed with blood.' So too the venom of a wicked suggestion does no harm, unless the blood of delight is mixed in with it. Hosea: 'blood has touched blood' — since the delight of the deed follows the delight of the thought.
Likewise, all poison is cold by nature. So too every mortal sin chills, while it drives out the heat of charity.

Likewise, sin is likened to the 'burestis,' which (as Pliny says) is a small animal like a beetle, which hides among the herbs the ox loves; the ox takes it in, while cropping the herbs, and, once devoured, it inflames the ox's liver so much that it finally bursts it with the greatest torment. So too the malice of sin hides beneath the delights that a man loves; not noticing this, a man takes in the delight outwardly, and carries it in within himself, which both kindles his appetite disorderedly, and breaks the soundness of his mind, and finally brings on the torment of conscience, or of punishment. Isaiah: 'their worm shall not die.'

Likewise, it is likened to the ox-fly, which, as long as it remains fixed under the cow's tail, or on her body, does not let her rest, but, tail raised, maddened in a marvelous way, she runs everywhere through the fields. Likewise, as long as sin clings to the conscience, the soul cannot rest, and then wanders through various places, seeking and not finding rest, as long as the sin has not been removed through penance.

Likewise, man ought to hate and flee the stench of sin — an example of which is the ant. For Aristotle says that ants have a sense of smell, and hate everything foul-smelling; hence, if anyone smokes out their nests with something foul, they abandon them. So too man ought to abandon and flee everything in which there is the stench of sin. 'Flee from sins.'

Likewise, sin is likened to the basilisk serpent, that is, the regulus, which kills by its scent, and destroys by its gaze every living thing, at whose sight no bird passes unharmed; and even if it is far off, it is burned and devoured by its mouth; it is conquered by weasels. Hence men carry weasels to its lairs, for the Most High has left nothing without a remedy. And the basilisk, at the sight of the weasel, flees, but the weasel pursues it and kills it, especially if it has first eaten rue (as Aristotle and Avicenna say). Likewise, sin kills the soul, either through the scent of lingering delight in thought, or through the sight, that is, consent, of the deed. Hence birds, that is, the minds of men, are killed and devoured by sin through sight alone, that is, through consent, even if they are far from the deed. But the remedy against the basilisk, that is, against sins, is the weasel refreshed with rue, that is, penance full of bitterness, which the basilisk flees at the sight of it; for penance held only in contrition or in resolve sometimes purges sin. Psalm: 'I said' — namely, in the resolve of my heart — 'I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord,' and so on. But once the deed is complete, penance, enjoying it fully, extinguishes it. Acts: 'be converted, and do penance, that your sins may be blotted out.'

Likewise, sin is likened to the asp. For the asp stops up its ear, so as not to hear the voice of the man charming it, lest it obey him — and this pertains to the sin of pride, since the proud man does not hear the voice of God, and scorns to obey his commands. 'Like the deaf asp that stops her ears, which will not hear the voices of charmers.'

Likewise, the asp, once its mate — that is, its spouse — is killed, pursues the killer with a marvelous fury, and attacks him, whether alone or among a crowd, and seems to care nothing for danger, so as to avenge its mate; and this pertains to the vice of wrath, since the wrathful man, out of the desire for vengeance, exposes himself to every danger with headlong fury.
Likewise, there is a certain asp called the 'situla,' from the fact that it kills the one it strikes with thirst; and this pertains to avarice, whose thirst, that is, appetite, is unquenchable.

Likewise, there is a certain asp called the viper-asp, which kills by sleep; when Cleopatra applied it to herself, she was dissolved into sleep; and this pertains to the vice of sloth, which kills the soul with laziness and drowsiness.

Likewise, there is another, the hemorrhoid-asp; whoever is struck by it, his veins dissolved, ends his life in a flow of blood; this pertains to the lustful, since lust dissolves the body in a flow of seed, and leads the soul to eternal ruin.

Likewise, there is another serpent called the 'pester,' which always goes about with its mouth open, releasing venom; but, once struck, it swells up and is killed; this pertains to the vice of gluttony, since the gluttonous man always goes about with his mouth open, that is, ready for food, and openly displays the venom, that is, the vice, of gluttony.

Likewise, the asp has its eyes at its temples, not on its forehead; hence it does not look straight ahead, and so pursues its adversary more by hearing, or by scent, than by sight; for if it were not so, as Pliny says, a man could scarcely escape it — and this pertains to envy, since the envious man does not look straight, but with a grim and malicious eye, and pursues by detracting, only from hearsay, or from his own opinion, as though from something seen or certain. Hence: 'the venom of asps is under their lips.'
Likewise, it is likened to the crocodile, which, as long as it lives, always keeps growing: for sin, which is not washed away through penance, soon drags, by its own weight, toward another sin.

Likewise, sin grows stronger and more abundant in prosperity than in adversity, just as serpents are more abundant, and do more harm, in summer than in winter, and by day than by night: for all serpents, generally, are cold by nature, and strike only when they grow warm. Hence their venom does more harm by day than by night, since they are made cold by the night dew. In winter they coil themselves in their nests, and grow sluggish, but in summer they stretch themselves out, and come forth to do harm. Now what is understood by the coldness of a serpent's venom, but the malice of sin, which, when it reaches the heart through consent, at once extinguishes the warmth of charity? But by the heat of day and of summer is understood the lesser and greater fervor of worldly prosperity, just as, conversely, the cold of night, or of winter, signifies a shorter or lighter course of adversity; but in summer, or by day, the venom does more harm, since sin grows more perniciously from that very fervor of prosperity. Hence the Psalm: 'I will fear from the fullness of the day' — that is, of prosperity.

Likewise, carnal sins are more manifest and notorious than spiritual ones, but spiritual ones are nonetheless more harmful. Hence they are likened to serpents: for certain serpents are said to be so huge in body that they devour whole crows. Hence, in the Punic War, Titus Livy relates that a basilisk serpent, one hundred and twenty feet long, was killed by Regulus, the Roman general; its skin and jaws were hung before a certain temple at Rome. Under the emperor Claudius too, a serpent was killed in Italy, in whose belly a whole boy was found.

But there are other serpents so small in body that they can scarcely be seen, yet are the greatest in their power to harm, like the 'dipsas,' which kills before it can be felt. The 'tyrus,' too (as Aristotle says) is small, and yet there is no remedy against its venom. Great serpents, then, signify carnal sins, which are of great appearance and notoriety; but the serpents small in appearance and more harmful are spiritual sins, which, although less manifest, and of less notoriety, are nonetheless of greater guilt, as is clear with lust and pride. Hence Gregory says: sometimes it is less to fall into corruption, than to sin through a silent thought, a deliberate exaltation; but since pride, being thought less shameful, is less avoided, men blush at lust the more, the more they all know it to be shameful together. Hence it often happens that some, falling from pride into lust, blush at the evil of their hidden fault because of the open fall, and then correct greater faults too, since, prostrated in the smallest things, they are gravely confounded.

div.head: Cap. XCIIII. Satisfactorie penitentie modus ac partes, ipsiusque vis et fructus multiplex, per quamplurima leonis, panthere, sanguisuge, Leontophoni, nonnullarumque aliarum rerum naturalium exempla quam rectissime manifestatur.

cit.quote: Tearful penance makes God overlook sins. For the lion, which recognizes an adulterous coupling by scent alone, rises wholly to punish the adulteress; but if the lioness bathes in a river after the coupling, the lion then perceives nothing. Likewise, if the soul, the bride of Christ, is joined to the devil through sin, Christ himself, who is the lion of the tribe of Judah, is rightly provoked to vengeance against her. But if the soul bathes in the river of tearful penance, the sin is overlooked, and spared, by Christ himself. Ambrose: 'what cannot be defended, can be washed away; tears wash away the fault which shame forbids the voice to confess; tears beg for pardon, and deserve it.'

Likewise, penance is likened to the panther, which (as the Physiologus says) hates the dragon, and the dragon flees from it; the panther, having eaten, hides itself in a cave, and sometimes sleeps for three days; then, rising, it lets out a great cry, and from its mouth comes an aromatic scent, sweet beyond measure, on account of which all animals then follow it — the dragon alone flees, and, unable to bear its scent, fails within itself. But just as the panther hates the dragon, so penance hates sin, and sin flees from penance, which, shut up in the cave, that is, in the heart of the penitent, after it has persevered for three days, namely of contrition, confession, and satisfaction, rising up from the state of guilt, lets out a voice of praise, sensing itself freed from the sleep of sin. Hence, bursting into a voice of praise, it says that saying of the Psalm: 'you have broken my bonds; I will offer you a sacrifice of praise, and I will call upon the name of the Lord.' This verse, as Cassiodorus says, is said to be of such power that whoever says it in the confession of the threefold death, all his sins are forgiven him. Then too the penitent lets out from his mouth a sweet scent, namely of sweet and devout prayer, which all animals follow, that is, all the virtues, and all merits are restored to the penitent through this, and the dragon, that is, sin, fails and perishes.

Likewise, satisfactory penance requires the leech, which is applied to the body to draw out corrupted blood; but because it sometimes settles on venomous places, when someone applies it to himself, it must first be wrapped in salt and nettles, so that it vomits up any venom it may have absorbed. Likewise, penal penance is imposed, so that the soul may be purged of the corruption of sin, which is like corrupted blood, or so that the disposition to sin may be drawn from the soul; but, so that it bring nothing harmful, it must be applied to, or taken up by, the penitent with the salt of discretion, so that it is prudently considered what kind, how great, and on whom it is imposed.

Likewise, the nettle is necessary for the one who receives it, since it both burns and stings — and so it signifies the fervor of compunction, which makes every penance seem light to bear, and toward this same end it also serves that, if one pours hot water over the leech, it more quickly fastens itself to the limb. For the fervent compunction of tears is, as it were, hot water, which quickly applies the leech to the limb, since it makes one take up the imposed penance with a ready mind.

Likewise, penance extinguishes temptations. Hence it is likened to a certain small beast, feared and fled by lions, called the 'leontophonus.' For it carries a certain poison in its mouth that kills them at once. Hence this little beast is caught, and burned, and reduced to ash, and when meat is sprinkled with this ash, and placed at crossroads, lions passing by, once they eat it, die — as Isidore and Avicenna say. This little beast, then, represents humble penance, which lions, that is, demons, fear and flee. It carries poison in its mouth, when it says its sin in confession, and this poison kills lions, that is, the temptations of demons. This little beast is caught in the remembrance of sins, is burned in the sorrow of contrition, is reduced to ash in the meditation on death, recalling how, through death, the flesh is dissolved into ash; or it is reduced to ash in humble satisfaction: 'I do penance in ashes and dust.' And while the flesh is sprinkled with this ash, namely that it be afflicted by making satisfaction, and especially at the crossroads, that is, at the beginnings of temptations, or the senses of the body, which are the crossroads through which sins enter the soul — hence the ash is then sprinkled at the crossroads, when the very senses of the body are humbly guarded, or afflicted, so that the eyes weep, and the mouth abstains, the ears hear rebukes, and so of the rest. And so then the lions are killed by these means, since the temptations of demons do not prevail, but are quickly extinguished.

Likewise, the devil hates and abhors the bitterness of penance, just as a dog abhors eating a stag's intestines because of the bitterness in them. For (according to Aristotle and Avicenna) the stag has no gall except, perhaps, in its intestines. Hence its intestines are bitter and foul-smelling, so that the dog does not eat them, unless it is extremely hungry. So too, when the inward parts of the mind are foul-smelling, namely through the memory of the baseness of guilt, and sprinkled with bitterness through the sorrow of penance, the demons, who feed on the delight and sweetness of sinners, abhor touching them.

Likewise, penance frees from the heaviness of sin, and, after death, frees the soul from punishment. Hence it is likened to a certain stone found in stags (as Pliny says); when they feel themselves heavy, they swallow it, which helps them, and, after they die, it is found in their belly, and this stone marvelously helps pregnant women, and even makes them give birth without pain. So too the soul, when it feels the heaviness of sin, ought to take up the stone, that is, harsh and rough penance, which not only frees it in life from the weight of sins, but also, after death, its power is found in the soul, freeing it from the bitterness of punishment. This is also what helps pregnant women, namely souls carrying a good conception, that is, a good resolve, toward giving birth and bringing it to completion in deed: since harsh penance restrains the flesh, lest it hinder the effect of good works.

Likewise, bitter penance extinguishes the remorse of conscience, just as wormwood kills fleas: for wormwood is their poison, as Constantine says. For what are biting fleas, but the acts of sin troubling the conscience, which wormwood, that is, bitter penance, extinguishes by purging, and makes cease entirely? And likewise the leaves of the peach tree, which are bitter, kill fleas, and, for the same reason, colocynth is effective against them, if crushed and mixed with water and sprinkled where they are — and this signifies the bitter contrition for sins, mingled with tears.

div.head: Cap. XCV. Nonnulle ipsius Tygridis, stellionis, Cerui, ac Leonis proprietates naturales annotantur, quibus vere penitentes pluribus exemplis assimilantur.

cit.quote: ...the tiger, which is an animal swiftest in running, like an arrow, marked with various spots, as Isidore says; of which Pliny also says that, when its cubs are stolen, it pursues the thief by scent, who is carried off on the swiftest horse; and, hearing the noise of the beast pursuing, he throws down mirrors behind him on the way; and the tigress, seeing these, and gazing at her own reflection, and believing it to be her cub, stops, and wishes to take up her young, and meanwhile the hunter escapes. The tiger, then, running swiftly, is the sinner repenting fervently or quickly, who, marked with various spots, is pierced with compunction for various sins; who pursues his stolen cubs, when he strives to recover, through penance, the goods lost through sin, to whom the hunter throws down various mirrors, by which he may be delayed, since the devil sets various obstacles before him, by which he may be hindered.

Likewise, penitents are likened to the newt. First, since the newt is renewed in its skin, for it is said that the newt changes its skin like a serpent. So too the penitent ought to renew his conduct and life, casting off the old age of sin, and putting on the newness of righteousness. The Apostle: 'be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man,' and so on.

...since the newt walks on hands. For the newt is (as Pliny says) a kind of lizard, having four feet broad like hands, with which it creeps into the crevices of houses, where it makes its lair. Hence Proverbs: 'the newt supports itself upon its hands, and lives in kings' houses.' There are, then, four hands, or feet, of the newt, which are the four virtues of the penitent, by whose works he walks to royal, that is, heavenly, dwellings: namely justice, which he exercises in making satisfaction; temperance, which he exercises in abstaining; fortitude, which he exercises in continuing, or in resisting temptations; and prudence, which he exercises in guarding himself against what is harmful. These four virtues are like feet, when they are held in affection; but they are, as it were, hands, when they are held in use, that is, in action.

Third, since the newt is dulled in sight: for in winter it hides, and its sight grows dull. Now the time of winter is the harshness of temptation, in which penitents hide themselves in the secrecy of prayer, or in the hiding place of humility; yet it cannot be otherwise than that the sight of the mind is dulled by the darkness of temptation, since, at least while a man is being tempted, the gaze of contemplation is clouded over and slackened.

Fourth, since the newt's sight is made clear again: for, coming out in spring, and finding its sight dulled, it seeks a place where it can look at the rising sun; and, as it gazes at it, the moisture that was in its eyes dries up, and so it recovers its sight — as the Gloss suggests.
