So too the penitent, in spring, that is, in a time of tranquility, once the winter of temptation has passed, ought, through contemplation of mind and prayer, to look toward the Sun, Christ, who visited us, rising from on high, and, at the sight of him, the affection of the mind is inflamed, all the moisture, or undue affection, left by temptation is purged, and so the sight of the mind itself is marvelously made clear.

Likewise, penitents are likened to lions, which are born at first shapeless and small, like weasels, but afterward, as they grow, become very strong. So too penitents, beginning from servile fear, are small in virtue, and shapeless, since not yet grounded in charity, but afterward, growing through charity, are strengthened, and made very strong. Hence Gregory says that on the way of God one begins from fear, so as to arrive at fortitude.

Likewise, penitents are likened to stags, since (as Isidore says) stags are enemies of serpents, and, when they feel themselves burdened, draw them out of their caves with the breath of their nostrils; and, once the venom's harm is overcome, they are freed and restored by feeding on them. Serpents, then, are sins, which must be hated and fled as venomous serpents, according to that saying: 'flee sin as from the presence of a serpent.' When, then, through the remorse of conscience, some feel within themselves the burden of guilt, then, with the breath of their nostrils, that is, the fervor of penance (for by the breath is understood the fervor and sorrow of compunction, of which the Psalm speaks: 'a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit'; but by the nostrils is understood the discretion of satisfaction), they draw them out of their caves, that is, out of the hiding places of conscience, namely when they bring their sins to light, by confessing and accusing themselves; hence the venom of sin is driven out, and the memory of their sins becomes for them the nourishment of tears, by which they are freed and purged from the guilt of their sins.

Likewise, stags were the first to discover the herb dittany, by feeding on which they shake out the arrows by which they are wounded: for stags struck by arrows are men overcome by temptations. By dittany, however, which is an herb with the power to dissolve, draw out, and consume venom, penance is understood, which dissolves the venom of sin in contrition, draws it out in confession, and consumes it in satisfaction. Hence, when this is taken up by stags, that is, by sinners, the arrows of temptations are driven back, and the wounds of sins are marvelously healed.

div.head: Cap. XCVI. Miro siquidem Elephantis scorpionisque exemplo, peregrinos ac alienigenas dirigere, et tueri eque admonemur.

cit.quote: Elephants teach us to guide and protect pilgrims and travelers, for the elephant, if it finds a man astray on the road, first, so as not to frighten him, steps a little off the road and stands still, and then, gradually going before him, shows him the way, and, if a dragon should meet them, sets itself against the dragon to defend the man, and so defends him. So too great and powerful men especially ought not to despoil pilgrims and travelers, as many do, when they come into their territory, but rather guide them, themselves or through their men, and defend them from wicked men.

Likewise, those who harm pilgrims and guests, despoiling them, are worse than venomous scorpions. For Aristotle relates that, on a certain mountain, guests are not harmed by the scorpions there, but the native inhabitants are killed and harmed by them.

div.head: Cap. XCVII. Aurium hominum immobilitate naturali, nos firmiter in bona doctrina persistere, erudimur.

cit.quote: A man ought to persevere, and be firm, in the good teaching he has heard. For every animal that has ears moves them, except man. In which it is signified that those who do not persevere in the good teaching they hear, and are not steadfast, are like brute animals that move their ears, since they are quickly moved from what they have heard; but those who steadfastly persevere in the teaching they have heard are truly rational men. John: 'if you remain in my word, you shall be my true disciples, and shall know the truth.'

div.head: Cap. XCVIII. Canis naturalis usus varius et admirabilis, nec non Castoris, equi, atque ursi alique proprietates naturales patefiunt, quibus non absque ratione verbi Dei concionatores assimilantur.

cit.quote: The preacher is likened to the dog. First, since the dog loves its master; and likewise the preacher of the word ought to be a friend of God. Hence a preacher who does not love the Lord is not worthy to proclaim the words of God. Hence God said to the sinner: 'why do you declare my righteous acts, and take my covenant in your mouth?'

Likewise, since the dog guards and defends its master's house. This house of the Lord is the Church, which the Catholic preacher defends from heretics. Or this house is his own conscience, which the preacher ought diligently to guard, just as the strong man armed guards his own hall, so that all he possesses is at peace.

Likewise, since the dog exposes itself to death for its master, as we read of a hunter at Piacenza, Celoneus, attacked by armed men, whose dog defended him, and could not be wounded, until the dog itself was first killed. So too holy preachers expose themselves to martyrdom for the faith of God and the truth, as is clear in the Apostles and the Martyrs.

Likewise, since the dog willingly runs to the hunt with its master. For preaching is, as it were, a certain spiritual hunt, in which every soul won for God is like prey that has been caught; but the dog does not go to the hunt if it is not led or accompanied by its master, since the preacher would preach fruitlessly, unless God helped him and accompanied him. The Apostle: 'not I, but the grace of God with me,' and Corinthians: 'we are God's helpers.' The preacher, then, since he has God himself as his companion, ought not to shrink from, but rather willingly hasten to, the labor of preaching. Corinthians: 'so run, that you may obtain.'

Likewise, since the dog often does not abandon even its master's dead body, as we read of the dog of Titus Sabinus, which did not abandon its master when he was captured, even in prison at Rome; and when he was afterward killed, the dog, uttering sorrowful howls, did not desert him even dead; and, when someone threw it bread, it carried the bread to the dead man's mouth, and, since he did not eat, it did not eat either; and when the corpse was thrown into the Tiber, the dog, to support the body, threw itself into the Tiber too, with a crowd gathering to see the spectacle of the faithful animal. Likewise, preachers ought not to abandon the dead body of Christ, since they ought continually to keep the memory of Christ's death and passion, and preach of it frequently — following the example of the Apostles, in whose person blessed Paul said: 'but we preach Christ crucified,' and so on.

...since the dog does not eat the prey it catches for itself, but leaves it for its master; and the preacher is like this, who does not seek his own praise from a fruitful work, but leaves the glory and honor to God. John: 'I do not seek my own glory.'

Likewise, since the noble dog, even granted that it gets nothing of the prey it has caught, does not become unfaithful on that account, nor does it stop pursuing other prey because of it. So too, although the preacher receives nothing temporal from his preaching, he does not for that reason cease from preaching, nor preach any less faithfully.

Likewise, since the dog knows its own place: for our final and permanent place is not in the present life, as the Apostle acknowledged, saying: 'we have not here a lasting city, but we seek one that is to come.' And note that dogs remember journeys, however long, and are accustomed to return to their own homes over great stretches of land — which preachers do not only bodily, when they run about through various places preaching, and afterward return to their cloisters or dwellings, but also spiritually, since, although they are often compelled, for the salvation or care of their neighbors, to go out to outward business or duties, they nonetheless diligently and providently return to their own dwelling of the mind, according to that saying: 'the living creatures went, and returned, like the appearance of flashing lightning.'

Likewise, since the dog sometimes boldly attacks the strongest and largest beasts, as we read of the dogs of India. For the Indians (as Isidore says) are accustomed to leave female puppies tied up at night in the forests, so that they will be found by tigers; from these are born dogs so fierce that they can bring down lions. Hence a certain dog born this way, sent by the king of Albania to Alexander the Great, first killed a lion in his presence; then, when an elephant was brought forth, seeing its size, it first froze still, and let out a huge bark, yet nonetheless attacked it, and harried it so long that it brought it down to the ground. So too holy preachers, kindled with divine zeal and spirit, sometimes boldly attack great tyrants and sinners by rebuking them, as John did Herod. Hence Herod feared John, and, hearing him, did many things.

Likewise, the dog pursues fleeing beasts by wind and scent even through waters, and, finding their hiding places, betrays them with barking and muttering. So too holy preachers, driven by the wind, that is, the divine breath, and drawn by the scent, that is, the desire for heavenly salvation, pursue beasts even through the waters of tribulations, that is, sinners living like beasts, so as to draw them to penance, and expose their hiding places, that is, the vices in which they wish to lie hidden, by rebuking them.

Likewise, the dog loves human company. So too holy preachers do not at all flee human company, where they can bear fruit, following the example of him who says: 'my delight is to be with the children of men.'

Likewise, the preacher ought to be like the beaver, which (as Isidore says) lives on land with four-footed animals, and stays in the water with swimming creatures: for it is about the size of a small dog, having hind feet like a dog's, with which it chiefly walks, but front feet like a goose's, with which it swims in the water. So too preachers ought not only to run about on land through the active life, which suits four-footed animals, that is, those who are perfect in the four virtues, but also ought to move about in the waters of the Scriptures with swimming creatures, that is, the contemplative — and they ought to be like the dog in the barking of their preaching, but small in the humility of their mind; the hind feet, however, are bodily occupations pertaining to piety, and so are like a land animal's; but the front feet are spiritual meditations, and so are like a swimming creature's, by which it swims in the water of wisdom.

Likewise, the curious preacher is like the horse, which, if the water it drinks is clear, disturbs it with its hoof. Likewise, the curious preacher disturbs clear water, that is, plain and open Scripture and teaching, with his hoof, that is, with a desire to please, and to be thought learned, entangling it in philosophical reasonings — that is, he obscures it, so that it is scarcely understood. Or the clear water is tribulation patiently borne outwardly, which the patient man then disturbs with his hoof, when he does not love, in his inward affection, the one who injures him. Gregory: 'perfect patience is that which also loves the very one it bears with. For to endure and yet hate is not the virtue of gentleness, but a prop for fury.' Ezekiel: 'when you drank the clearest water, did you not trouble the rest with your feet?'

Likewise, the preacher is like the bear. For the bear ('ursus') is so interpreted and named because it shapes its young with its mouth (as Isidore and Avicenna say). Avicenna also says that a certain flesh is born which the mother, by licking it, forms into limbs. So too the preacher, by the teaching of his mouth, forms spiritual children for God. For, like a mother, in those he finds carnal, he forms, by the office of his tongue, the limbs of the spiritual virtues. Hence the Apostle: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'

div.head: Cap. XCIX. Veri Prelati precipuum munus, ipsiusque partes laude digne que sint, ut merito prosit, per quamplurima Arietis, Leonis, Camelipardalis, Cerue, aliorumque animantium cornua habentium clarissima exempla demonstratur.

cit.quote: ...the ram; since the ram is the leader of the flock, and the prince of the sheep. So too the prelate ought to be the leader of his subjects, both by presiding with authority and by going before them in the example of a good life. Likewise, since nature made the ram very strong, according to Isidore. Hence it is called 'veruex,' from 'vires' (strength), since it is, as it were, the man ('vir') of the sheep, more powerful than the other two-toothed animals. Or it is called 'veruex,' as he says, since it carries a worm in its head, whose itching often makes it shake its head most vigorously. It is called 'aries,' moreover, since this animal was sacrificed on the altars ('aris'), as is clear in the law of Moses — all of which fit the prelate, namely strength of work, and diligence of mind, which is like the worm in the head, of which the Apostle says: 'my daily concern, the care of all the churches.'
Likewise, the sacrifice of the flesh, of which the Apostle says: 'present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, to God,' and so on.

Likewise, the good preacher ought, with the cry of preaching and the groaning of prayer, to rouse his sleeping subjects, or those dead in their sins, following the example of the lion, whose cubs, when they are born, are said to sleep, or to be counted dead, for three days and three nights, and are then said to be roused by their father's roar and cry. Then the lion cries loudly over its dead cubs, when the prelate or preacher, by preaching or reprimanding, strongly rebukes his sinning subjects, and then lets out a roar, when he groans strongly, praying for them. Hence, just as the lion's cry and groan are said to rouse its dead cubs, so too the cry of preaching, and the roar of prayer, rouse subjects lying in sin: 'his roaring shall be as a lion's roar,' 'as the whelps of lions,' and so on. But when the prelate or preacher speaks to the good, he ought to speak sweetly. As a sign of this it is said in Judges: 'behold, a swarm of bees in the mouth of the lion, and a honeycomb' — for the bee stings, and yet makes honey, since the preacher ought to sting the lukewarm, and sweeten the devout.

...the camelopard, which, according to Isidore, is an Ethiopian animal, having the head of a camel, the neck of a horse, the legs and feet of a buffalo, and the spots of a leopard: for it is a beast sprinkled with white spots on a reddish coat, and so it takes its name from the camel's head and the leopard's spots (as Pliny says); but it is a beast more remarkable in appearance than in ferocity, so tame that it has almost taken the name of a sheep. Now all these features fit the prelate, taken in a moral sense: for the camel's head chews the cud with its mouth, and this chewing signifies meditation on sacred Scripture. The horse's neck is flexible, since it bends to the pull of the bridle, and this flexibility is referred to the mercy and piety of the prelate. The buffalo's feet have cloven hooves, and go about steadily, and this is referred to the prudence of discretion. The white spots shining forth are the pure works and examples that outwardly appear to others. The prelate, then, ought to have the camel's head through knowledge of sacred Scripture; the horse's neck, through the flexibility of mercy; the buffalo's legs or feet, through the prudence of discretion; the leopard's white spots, that is, purity of works; and he ought to have more of severity in appearance than in deed. Hence he ought to be fierce in appearance, but gentle in spirit or deed.

Likewise, prelates ought to relate to their subjects as stags relate to their fawns: for stags, after giving birth, feed on two herbs, called 'como' and 'sumole,' and, fed on them, return to their fawns, and, infused with the juice of these herbs, provide nourishment of milk to their young; they also train their fawns to run, and teach them to flee, and lead them to steep places, and show them how to leap. The two herbs, then, that make the doe abound in milk for nourishing her fawns are two virtues that make prelates nourish their subjects with the food due to them: namely wisdom, which makes them abound in the milk of spiritual teaching, and mercy, which makes them abundantly give the nourishment of bodily alms; they also ought to instruct their subjects to run along the path of the commandments, that is, to obey swiftly.
Likewise, to lead them to flee sins, to make known to them the precipices of temptations, and to show them the way of leaping, that is, of escaping.

Likewise, just as prelates are set over others in dignity, so they ought to be set over them in virtue too — an example of which is that every horned animal is four-footed, except a certain serpent in Egypt called the horned viper ('cerastes'); this is understood of horns that are of the nature of bone, on account of tortoises, or snails, which have soft horns. By the horned animal, then, understand the man raised to a position of dignity: for horns signify the eminence of dignity, on the head. Such men ought to have four feet, namely justice, temperance, fortitude, and prudence. But the horned viper, or horned serpent, that is, the hypocrite placed in a position of dignity, has horns without feet, since he holds the dignity, but lacks the virtues. Likewise the snail, having soft horns, signifies the carnal prelate, who does remiss works, and also lacks feet, since he has no inward virtues.

Likewise, the virtuous prelate is more easily lifted to the contemplation of divine things, when he withdraws himself from temporal cares — an example of which is that animals that lack teeth in their upper jaw are horned, since that matter passes into horns instead. Now by the animal fortified with horns, understand the prelate adorned with virtues; whose lower jaw is the provident management of earthly things, in which is the multitude of teeth, that is, the multiplicity of laborious and hard works; but his upper jaw, as it were, is the higher contemplation of divine things, which ought to be empty of teeth, that is, removed from temporal cares and labors. Yet he who wishes to preside virtuously must make use of both, each in its time.

Likewise, those who seek only their own interests are not worthy of the honor of prelacy. Hence no boar, having curved teeth (like the boar), has horns, since that matter passes instead into its tusks. That prelate indeed curves his teeth back, who turns and folds back on himself what he does; but he who, neglecting others, feeds only himself, is not worthy of the horns of dignity. Ezekiel: 'woe to the shepherds that feed themselves.'

div.head: Cap. C. Hominem quousque viuit commode proficere in virtutibus posse, cerui exemplo perspicacissime confirmatur.

cit.quote: A man can advance and grow in the virtues, like horns, for as long as the time of his penitent life lasts. For it is observed that stags' antlers grow until the seventh year, since, up to seven years, one new branch of antler sprouts every year; hence their age is determined by their antlers. Since, then, the number seven is the universal measure of time, that is, by which the whole span of our life is turned, as is clear in the seven days of the week, let us take, in the sevenfold count of years, the whole span of our days: for it is written, in Ezekiel, 'I have given you a day for a year,' and the Psalm says: 'the days of our years are threescore and ten' — for seven, multiplied by ten, that is, seventy, arises: so that it may be understood that we ought to dedicate the whole span of our years to the advancement of the virtues, which the growth of antlers signifies, and this comes about through the seven virtues, since there are four cardinal virtues and three theological ones, or through the seven works of mercy, together with the observance of the decalogue.

div.head: Cap. CI. Prudentie virtus quantum nobis expediat, ac quomodo ea homines uti debeant, Hericii formice, serpentis, muliorumque animalium naturali sagacitate, clarissimis similitudinibus exprimitur.

cit.quote: The hedgehog teaches us to have prudence in three ways. First, against the assault of temptations: for the hedgehog, by enclosing itself under a hard hide, hedged all around with rough spines, protects itself from attackers; for, as soon as it senses anything, it curls into a ball, and sets its spines against the striker. So too the hard, spiny hide is harsh penance and hard affliction of the flesh, into which, when a man hides himself through humility, and sets it against temptation, he escapes its temptations. Hence the Psalm: 'but as for me, when they troubled me, I was clothed with haircloth, I humbled my soul with fasting.'

Second, the hedgehog's prudence teaches us: for it climbs a vine or another tree, and knocks down grapes and fruit, and afterward rolls itself over them, and they stick to its spines, and so it carries food to its young, as Isidore says. He, then, climbs vines or trees, who lifts himself, through contemplation of mind, to consider the virtues, or the lives, of the saints. And then he knocks fruit from them, when, comparing himself to them, he recognizes his own failings: for it is as though fruit is knocked from the trees, when the deeds of the great are compared to those of the small; but then, like the hedgehog, he fixes them on his own spines, and takes them up to carry on his back, when he follows them as best he can, arranging them with keen affections; and then he likewise feeds his children, when he directs and nourishes his own works by imitating them.

Third, it teaches us to be prudent regarding the variety of the seasons. For Aristotle says that hedgehogs make one burrow facing the north winds, to which they take refuge in heat, and another facing the south, to which they take refuge when they feel cold. Hence it is said that there was a man in Constantinople who, by means of a hedgehog he kept, predicted all the winds to come, and no one knew how he had acquired this knowledge. So too the prudent man, in the heat of prosperity, ought to take refuge in the cold north wind, that is, in the memory of adversity, so that, through fear, he may be freed from pride and excess. But in the time of cold, that is, of adversity, he ought to take refuge in the warm south wind, that is, in the memory of prosperity, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sadness. Ecclesiasticus: 'in the day of good things, be not unmindful of evils, and in the day of evils, be not unmindful of good things.'

Likewise, we have an example of prudence in ants. First, in providing: for they provide for the times to come, gathering in summer what they will live on in winter. So too we ought, in this life, to provide for ourselves against the time of death. Proverbs: 'go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom, which, having no guide, nor master, nor captain, provides her food in the summer, and gathers in the harvest what she may eat.'

Likewise, in gathering: it gathers grains of wheat, taking no notice of barley. So too man ought to gather spiritual and eternal things, and take no notice of temporal, perishing things. Matthew: 'gather the wheat into my barn.'

For when rain falls on the wheat, it exposes it to the sun, so that it may dry out again. So too, when some temptation or corruption befalls us, which might corrupt and ruin our wheat, that is, our spiritual nourishment or merit, we ought to restore it by the heat of the sun, that is, the fervor of contrition, or the manifestation of confession, since what is exposed to the sun is brought into the light — or through the fervor of prayer.

Likewise, in guarding, first, its own food: for, as Pliny says, ants gather grains, form heaps, and hide them in the more secret part of their dwelling, so that they will not be seized by birds, or scattered by the wind. These grains are the words of God, by which the soul is fed and nourished; and, like the ant with its grains, of which we ought, in the more secret part of the soul, namely in memory, to build a heap — namely from the things we have heard, committing many of them to memory — and hide them there through humility, lest they be seized by birds, that is, by demons, like the seed that fell on the path, which the birds of the air ate. Or these grains are good works, like alms and the like, which we ought to build up by multiplying and hiding through humility, not boastfully displaying them, lest they be scattered by the wind of vainglory, or carried off by birds, that is, by the demons themselves.

Likewise, prudent men are found guarding gold. For in Ethiopia there are said to be ants shaped like dogs, which dig up golden sands with their feet, and guard them, lest they be taken away; the golden sands are, as it were, the spiritual virtues of the soul, which we ought to dig up with our feet, that is, with our affections, or with the steps of good works, and guard with all diligence, lest they be taken from us.

Likewise, the prudence of serpents is an example to us in many ways. First, since the serpent teaches us to love Christ. For the serpent guards its head above all things, since its life especially depends on it. Hence Pliny says that if the serpent's head escapes between two fingers, it still lives; on which account it sets its whole body against the striker, to save its head — so that we too should guard our head within ourselves, namely Christ, and, for his sake, from whom we have the life of grace and glory, neglect everything else, according to that saying: 'I have counted all things as loss, and I think them as dung, that I may gain Christ.'

Second, it teaches us to cast off sin, namely through the renewal of penance. For the serpent (as the Philosopher says), when it feels itself weighed down by old age, abstains from food for many days, so that its skin may be more easily loosened; then, having tasted a certain bitter herb, it is provoked to vomit, and vomits up a poisonous humor, since this was the cause of its sickness; finally, to soften its stiff skin, it bathes in water, and, seeking a narrow crack in a rock, enters through it, and, forcing its way through, strips off its old skin, that is, the covering that is called a slough ('exuvia') from stripping off ('exuendo'), since it strips it off and casts it away; and finally, exposing itself to the sun, dries out, and forms new skin, and so, its strength restored, sees more clearly, moves more strongly, and eats more eagerly. Avicenna and Pliny say the same about this renewal. We ought, then, following the example of the serpent, to renew our life through works of penance.

First by fasting, not so much from food as, still more, from vice. Likewise, by tasting the bitter herb of contrition of heart, vomiting up the poison of sin through confession, washing ourselves in the water of tears, or of teaching; casting off, in the narrow opening of penance, the slough of the old man, that is, of a wicked habit; drying out our softness and proneness to sin in the heat of the sun, that is, the love of Christ, and putting on the new skin, namely the man created according to God; taking up again the strength for doing good; contemplating spiritual things more clearly; loving God and neighbor more strongly; and taking up, more eagerly, the things that nourish the spirit.

Third, the serpent teaches us to resist the devil. For Isidore says that the asp, when it begins to hear the charmer, presses one ear to the ground, and stops the other with its tail, and so escapes the charmer's voice, and does not obey the charmer. So too we ought to resist the charmer, that is, the tempter, namely by repelling temptation with the tail, and the ground — that is, with the memory of our end, which is signified by the tail, and the frailty of earth, which is signified by the ground. 'Like the deaf asp that stops her ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers.'

Fourth, the serpent teaches us that it lies in wait for the woman's heel, and is her enemy. Genesis: 'I will put enmities between you and the woman; and you shall lie in wait for her heel.' So too we ought to lie in wait for the flesh, and attentively consider its heel, that is, its end. Augustine: 'nothing is so effective for taming the desires of the flesh as to think what it is going to become.'

Fifth, it teaches us to flee the world. For the serpent, because of the enmity it has with man, flees, and hides under thorns, and dwells in deserts. So too holy men, out of hatred of the world, and its snares, flee into the deserts of the cloister, and hide beneath the harshness of penance. For it is said that the serpent flees the naked man, and leaps upon the clothed one, since the devil fears the poor man, who strips himself of the desire for temporal things; but he prevails against the clothed man, that is, the one fortified with riches, and so those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil.

Sixth, the serpent teaches us that, while swimming in water, it holds its head raised, lest, if it were submerged, it would suffocate. So too holy men take care lest the head of reason be submerged by present delights.
Seventh, it teaches us to hold to humility. Isaiah: 'dust shall be the serpent's food.'
Likewise, the holy man also refreshes himself by thinking that he is dust and ashes, humbling himself as Abraham did: 'I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes.'

Likewise, certain earthly animals teach us to live and act prudently, as Augustine teaches us. For a marvelous prudence is found in brute animals, in which, though there is, properly speaking, no knowledge, a certain likeness of knowledge is nonetheless found: for they show clear skill in raising their young, in building lairs, in acquiring food, in tending wounds, in avoiding what is harmful, in foreknowing changes of the seasons, and in the love of their mates. They therefore teach men to be prudent, first, not only in the nourishment of their fleshly children, to whom, just as they have given the foundation of nature, they ought likewise to give the lessons of discipline and the sustenance of life; but also in the fostering of spiritual desires, which, once they have arisen in the heart, must be cherished as spiritual offspring.

Likewise, in the building of a dwelling — not only the outward one, in which the body rests, but still more the inward one, so that you build for God the house of your conscience, in which he may dwell.

Likewise, in the procuring of nourishment — not only that by which the flesh is refreshed, but still more that by which the spirit is nourished. For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word, and so on.

Likewise, in the tending of wounds — not only those of bodily weapons, but still more of vices, or temptations. They also teach you prudently to avoid what is harmful — not only what wounds the body, but still more what infects the spirit — and moreover they admonish you to foresee your dangers, and prepare fitting remedies for times to come. And what is sweeter than all these — they urge you to love not only a partner in the marriage bond, but also a companion in the fellowship of life.

div.head: Cap. CII. Quando ac que via filii sint a parentibus educandi, Aranearum exemplo, sacreque scripture testimoniis edocetur.

cit.quote: Boys and girls are to be accustomed, in childhood, to good and fitting works and pursuits — after the example of spiders, which, produced from eggs, as soon as they are born, begin to climb their webs, and work as though taught while still in the womb. So too was blessed Job regarding works of mercy. Hence he said: 'from my infancy compassion grew up with me, and came out with me from my mother's womb.' So too Tobit did with his son, whom he taught, from infancy, to fear God, and abstain from all sin. Hence Ecclesiasticus: 'bow down his neck while he is young.'

div.head: Cap. CIII. Quantum mentis puritas sit a fidelibus conseruanda ac diligenda, naturali animalium exemplo in fetu perspicitur.

cit.quote: Purity of mind is, of all things, to be loved the most: for every animal that bears many young loves the first one most, and reckons it most natural to itself. And so certain animals devour their young, except the firstborn. Now the first thing that ought to be in us, and go before all our works, is purity of mind; hence it is to be loved and preserved above all things. And so Gregory of Nazianzus says of it: 'the first wisdom is a praiseworthy life, and a mind pure before God, through which the pure are joined to the pure, and the holy are united to the Holy.'

div.head: Cap. CIIII. Quatuor Dromedarii naturalibus effectibus precipuis, quemadmodum Religiosi vitam agere debeant aperitur.

cit.quote: Religious are said to be like the dromedary, or 'dromas': for, properly speaking, the animal itself is called 'dromas,' while the keeper of such an animal is called a 'dromedarius.' The religious man, then, ought to be likened to the dromedary in four ways. First, on account of continence: for dromedaries are castrated from youth (as Avicenna says), so as to be fitter for running. Likewise, religious ought, from their youth, to keep themselves in cleanness of flesh through the vow of continence. Matthew: 'there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God.'
Second, on account of abstinence: for dromedaries are content with little food, and greatly love hay, and rinds, and date-pits. So too religious ought not to seek delicacies, but rather coarse food.

Third, on account of obedience, in which, like dromedaries, they ought to be swift and prompt: for dromedaries are the swiftest of animals; hence 'dromos' in Greek means, in Latin, a swift course. For they travel a hundred miles or more in a day. They also ought to be laborious and constant in obedience, just as dromedaries have long, sinewy legs, very strong for laboring, and firm for holding out.

Fourth, on account of the measure of their humility: for dromedaries are not large in body, being smaller in stature than camels; since religious ought not to be great in their own esteem, but humble and abject. The Apostle: 'if anyone thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself.'

div.head: Cap. CV. Potissime sanctorum virorum virtutes, animique dotes, per quamplurimas Agni, equi, elephantis, leonis, leporis, Taxique naturales, ac promiscuas proprietates, excellentes patefiunt.

cit.quote: Holy men are likened to lambs. First, on account of innocence: for the lamb, of all animals, is the most gentle and innocent. Hence it harms with no tooth, attacks with no horn, tears with no claw, strikes with no hoof. And so (as Isidore says) nature armed all other animals, but left the lamb alone unarmed. Now this innocence that is in the lamb was, above all, in Christ, who indeed never did harm to anyone — which even one of the thieves on the cross recognized, saying: 'we indeed receive what our deeds deserve, but this man has done no evil.'

Second, moreover, this same innocence suits also the other holy lambs, who were imitators of Christ, and so, like lambs, harmed no one, neither with the tooth of envious detraction, nor tyrannical domination, nor the claw of violent plunder, nor the hoof of unjust contempt or blows. The Apostle: 'we have harmed no one,' and so on. And so he also admonished others toward this, saying: 'giving no offense to anyone.'

Second, on account of justice: for it belongs to perfect justice not only to harm no one, but also to benefit everyone else, if possible. And the lamb shows this justice, since whatever it has in itself it usefully provides to men: for its hide is useful for various purposes, its wool for clothing, its dung for enriching the earth, its horn and hoof for medicine, and its flesh for food. Now all these things fit Christ above all, since he left us his hide, that is, his outward conduct, or his fleece, that is, his examples or works, as clothing, that is, as an example for imitation, in the way that the Apostle says: 'put on our Lord Jesus Christ.'

Likewise, he gave his dung, that is, his humility, as seasoning, namely for all the virtues and works. Hence he himself said: 'learn from me, since I am meek and humble of heart.' And this humility is the seasoning without which no work is pleasing to God. Hence Christ said to the Apostles: 'when you have done all things well, say, we are unprofitable servants.' In the horn, moreover, because of the anointings that were made with it, as is clear in Kings, is signified the power of Christ in the institution of the sacraments; but in the lamb's cloven hoof, the discretion of Christ's teaching. And he gave us all these things for our medicine, namely both his Scripture and his words; and moreover Christ, like a lamb, also left us his flesh as food, namely in the sacrament of the Eucharist, just as he himself said: 'my flesh is truly food,' and so on. These same benefits of lambs also fit holy men in a secondary way, since the saints themselves serve their neighbors in various uses and services. For they clothe the naked, feed and nourish the poor, and, out of compassion, frequently devote themselves to the comfort and care of the sick.

Third, on account of prudence: for the lamb ('agnus') is named from 'recognizing' ('agnoscendo'): for there are two things that the lamb naturally discerns and recognizes. First, its mother: for, among countless flocks, it recognizes its mother by her bleating alone. In the same way Christ is said to be a lamb from 'recognizing,' since, on the cross, he recognized his mother, taking special care of her, and commending her to John, when he said: 'behold your mother.' Following this example, holy men take care and diligence for their parents even unto death. We too, following John's example, ought to strive to have the Blessed Virgin herself as our mother: for the lamb seeks its mother by bleating, and, having found her, raises its head, seeks the teats, and, as it sucks them, bends its knees; and, so that its mother gives it more milk, it presses its head against her udder. So too the devout man, with bleating, that is, the voice of holy prayer, seeks the mother of mercy, and raises his head, that is, his mind, toward her through contemplation, seeks the teats of her pity and consolation, and also devoutly and often bends his knee to her in greeting, and, with his head, that is, his mind, fervently desiring, and importunately begging, in a certain way presses her, so that she may pour out the grace of her consolation more abundantly. Second, since the lamb naturally recognizes its enemy, namely the wolf: for even if it has never seen one, as soon as it first sees it, it recognizes it. Likewise Christ too recognized those who crucified him, not by hating them, but by praying for them. Luke: 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' In this prayer, note that, in praying for them, he called upon the Father, when he said 'Father.'
Likewise, he asked that they be forgiven: 'forgive them,' he said.

Likewise, he excused them, saying that they do not know what they do — and the saints too, following the lamb himself, do these three things toward their adversaries: namely, they pray for them, they pardon them, and not only do not accuse them, but even excuse them.

Fourth, on account of patience: since, bound by the butcher, it does not defend itself, even if it is stripped of its fleece without care; and, while it is carried to be slaughtered, it does not weep, does not cry out, does not murmur, does not kick back, but looks with a placid face upon the one killing it, as though he were carrying it to pasture. So too Christ, captured and bound in the garden, did not defend himself. Likewise, in the scourging, stripped of his garment, his flesh torn, and likewise stripped for the cross, he did not defend himself, nor, crucified, did he kick back, nor murmur. Hence Jeremiah: 'I was like a meek lamb, that is carried to be a victim.' And Isaiah: 'he shall be dumb as a lamb before his shearer, and shall not open his mouth.' Hence holy men too strive to imitate this example of patience and gentleness as far as they can. Apocalypse: 'these follow the lamb wherever he goes.'

Fifth, since the lamb, as a clean animal, was sacrificed and made a victim in the Law, to prefigure Christ, who, like a lamb, was sacrificed on the altar of the cross for our sins. Hence John the Baptist said of him: 'behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.' So too holy and spotless men make of themselves a victim to God, in the way the Apostle said: 'present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God.' And note that, in the Law, a yearling lamb was sacrificed, to signify that whoever wishes to make of himself a pleasing sacrifice to God ought to be a lamb through patience, sacrificed through purity, a yearling through continence: for it was said to be a yearling when it had completed one year, since it is then best, on the grounds that a lamb is better the further removed it is from milk. Hence he is like a yearling who is removed from milk, that is, from carnal delight, namely through continence.

Likewise, holy men are likened to horses. First, by reason of liveliness: since the horse is a lively animal, since it exults in the fields, scents battle from afar, is roused to combat by trumpets, is spurred to the race, and horses grieve when they are beaten, and rejoice when they win. So too holy men exult in the fields, that is, in the battles of adversities or temptations, according to that saying: 'count it all joy, brothers, when you fall into various temptations.'

Likewise, they scent from afar the battle of temptation, or the battle of death, namely in foreseeing and preparing themselves; they are roused to the battle against vices by trumpets, that is, the voices of preachers, or the trumpets of divine judgments. Roused by this trumpet, blessed Jerome said: 'whether I eat, or drink, or do anything else, that terrible trumpet always seems to sound in my ears: rise, you dead, come to judgment.'
Likewise, they are spurred to the race, that is, the swiftness of doing good, or of obeying, of which it is said: 'I have run the way of your commandments.'
Likewise, they are overcome by temptation, or negligence; they are purged by the sorrow of penance, and they rejoice in the victory over temptations and vices.

Second, by reason of the horse's sagacity, since certain horses shrewdly recognize their own masters, and do not let others mount them. So too holy men recognize the Lord, not only in benefits, but also in scourges, and do not let another lord, that is, the devil, or sin, mount the saddle of their mind, according to that saying: 'give no place to the devil.'

Third, by reason of piety, since certain horses shed tears at the death of their masters. So too holy men weep, considering, by reading or hearing, the Lord's passion, knowing that, just as they were companions in his sufferings, so they will also be companions in his consolations.

Likewise, although holy men avoid great vices, they are nonetheless frequently frightened by small ones. Hence they are like elephants, which, tamed for war, are excellent: for they lead the charge, bear armed men, and are not frightened by the ranks of armed enemies, nor do they flee the clamor of their own side.

Likewise, when wooden towers are placed upon them, fiery weapons are shot from them as from a wall; and though they are such as this, they are nonetheless afraid of a mouse. So too holy men, although they overcome great battles of temptation, and bear the arms of great virtues, and are frightened by neither tribulations nor persecutions, nor flee the tongues of slanderers or detractors, nonetheless sometimes some very small defect, or annoyance, is left to them, which always keeps them in fear and torment. So Paul, caught up to the third heaven, and having experienced the dangers of every tribulation, full of the graces and virtues common to all, was nonetheless pressed by a thorn in the flesh, and, though fearing and praying that it be removed, was not heard.
Likewise, holy men are likened to lions in many respects. First, in boldness, or magnanimity. For the lion's magnanimity appears in a threefold act.

For when hunters pursue it, it does not lurk or hide itself, but wishes to be seen, and, going into the middle of the field, prepares itself for battle, and counts it a great shame to hide or flee. So too holy and perfect men do not shrink from tribulations and persecutions when it is fitting, but sometimes even provoke their persecutors, or await them, and receive persecutions, when they come, with great joy. It is said in Acts that the Apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, since they had been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus.

The second sign of the lion's magnanimity is (according to Isidore) that it looks the hunters in the eye, so that, having seen them, it is less afraid, but rather more emboldened; whereas the opposite happens in timid animals, like the stag and the hare, since the more they look at the hunters, the more terrified they become. Hence Proverbs: 'the lion, strongest of beasts, will fear the approach of none.' So too holy and perfect men, placed among their persecutors, when they see them raging, look at and consider how brief and passing their power and anger are, and how their treachery is to receive eternal punishment, and how an everlasting crown is being forged for them by these very persecutors. And so, while they look at them in this way, virtue and patience grow all the more in them. They do the same regarding tribulations and infirmities, considering how brief and useful they are, and so become stronger from them. The Apostle: 'when I am weak, then I am strong.'

The third sign of its magnanimity is that, when it pursues, it uses leaping bounds; but when it flees, it does not use them, but rather walks at a slow pace. So too the saints pursue spiritual goods with the leaps of love and fervor. Philippians: 'I follow after, if by any means I may attain.' Song of Songs: 'behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains.' But placed in persecution and punishment, they do not proceed by leaping, out of impatience or the impulse of fury, but pass through it with the sweetness of patience and gentleness — on account of all which it is said in Proverbs: 'the just, like a lion, shall be without fear.' But note that, although the lion is so secure, there are nonetheless certain things it is said to fear, which holy men also fear.
The first is the public highway. And this highway is death, through which all must pass. Psalm: 'the fear of death has fallen upon me.'

The second is a certain small and venomous animal called the 'leonthosonus' ['lion-killer'], which signifies sin. Holy men flee its venom as the venom of a serpent. Ecclesiasticus: 'flee sin as from the face of a serpent.'

The third is the noise of wheels, that is, the threats of Scripture. And, as it were, the two wheels are the two Testaments, or the two fortunes, prosperity and adversity, whose rumbling is fearsome, since the state of both fortunes is perilous.

The fourth is a certain 'lazaimi,' from whose ferocity scarcely any beast can be safe, and it signifies the ferocity and severity of the supreme Judge. Psalm: 'I was afraid because of your judgments.'
[The fifth is] fire, namely of hell, or of purgatory.
The sixth is the snare, or trap, of the hunter: and this is the temptation, or fraud, of the demon, which the saints also fear.
The seventh is the whip: for the lion is afraid when it sees its cub whipped; and so the scourges of this present life are to be feared.

Second, holy men are likened to the lion in justice — first, distributive justice: for it is ashamed to eat alone the prey it has seized, and so often leaves some of its prey for other beasts following at a distance. This is that justice of which it is said in the Psalm: 'he has distributed, he has given to the poor; his justice remains for ever and ever.' Blessed Job had this justice, saying: 'if I have eaten my morsel alone, and the orphan has not eaten of it.'

Likewise, the lion exercises vindictive, or punitive, justice both toward itself and toward others: for it punishes itself when it flares up in anger, since, angered, it beats the ground with its tail, and with that same tail scourges itself so much that blood flows. In which it gives the example that a man ought to press down his anger upon himself, and not seek to pour it out onto another, since everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.

Likewise, the lion exercises vindictive justice toward others too. First, since it repels force with force, as it were, with the restraint of blameless self-defense: for if anyone throws a weapon at it, if it does not touch it, it certainly attacks him, but does not wound or harm him — which is contrary to those who, in their own defense, do not use the restraint of moderate vengeance.

Third, holy men are likened to the lion in prudence: first, since lions, when they walk, wipe out their tracks with their tail, so that they cannot be found by hunters. So too holy men, by later penance, blot out their earlier sins, so that it may be said of them: 'blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven,' and so on. It also seems a sign of caution and prudence in the lion, that it sleeps with its eyes open, so that its eyes seem to keep watch. Likewise, holy men keep watch, as it were, even while sleeping, according to that saying: 'I sleep, and my heart watches'; for the sleep of contemplation is, as it were, a rest, in which, free from outward acts, they keep inward watch over spiritual and heavenly things, opening the eyes of the mind.

Likewise, there is the sleep of death, in which the saints sleep, that is, receive the rest of eternal peace, where they open the eyes of the mind in the vision of God, so that they are never closed again. And although sinners too, because of the rest, or laying down, of the flesh, are said to sleep in the tomb at death — 'they have slept their sleep; and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands' — yet they sleep with their eyes closed, that is, they die, since they are especially blinded in death, and lose all sense.

Fourth, holy men are likened to the lion in temperance, or abstinence. For the lion, once it has eaten its fill, abstains for two or three days; but if it must flee, and is too full, it draws the flesh from its belly with its claw, and so becomes light. And again, the lion lives a very long time, which is understood from the wearing down of its teeth.

So too holy men abstain from bodily food, and, whatever carnal element they feel in themselves, weighing on the spirit, they labor to empty out with the claw, that is, with the violence of harsh penance, so as to become lighter. Now that the lion lives a very long time signifies what is said in Ecclesiasticus: 'he who is abstinent shall add to his life.'

Fifth, they are likened to lions in clemency, or piety. For it cannot be angry with a man who has not injured it, but is naturally kind to man: for, unless overcome by too great a hunger, it spares those prostrate before it, lets captives who meet it go free, and does not eat or kill a man unless driven by great hunger (as Isidore says). It also does not touch women, and rarely children, unless compelled by great hunger. Likewise, holy men are gentle to others, so as not to be angry with them disorderedly, or easily.
Likewise, they are kind especially to wretched men, such as captives, widowed women, boys, orphans, and the like.

Likewise, they spare those prostrate before them, that is, those who humble themselves, even from their own wrongs. The lion also shows piety toward itself, especially in death: for the lion, when it dies, eats and bites the earth, and weeps. And so a man too ought, at death, to be kind to his own soul, biting back in compunction for his earthly life, and weeping, or lamenting, his sins; hence Augustine, at the time of his death, had the penitential psalms written for himself against the wall facing his bed, and, reading them over many days, wept.

Likewise, holy men are likened to hares. First, by reason of swiftness: for the hare is an animal swift to run. Hence it is called 'lepus,' as it were 'levipes' (light-foot), since, running, it moves its feet lightly; for nature has given, against every harmful thing, a healthful remedy, as Avicenna says. Hence to the hare is given lightness of limb, agility of running, and hairiness beneath its feet, so that, when it must flee, it does not hurt its feet. So too holy men are swift in obedience, or attentiveness, to the commands of God, according to that saying: 'let every man be swift to hear.'

Likewise, they run to the observance of the commandments, according to that saying of the Psalm: 'I have run the way of your commandments,' and so on. For the grace of God, which grants remedies more powerful than nature, gives them lightness of limb through continence, agility of running through fervent charity, which makes all things nimble and light.
Likewise, hairiness of the feet, through harsh penance, which guards the feet of their affections unharmed.

Second, by reason of timidity: since the hare is a fearful animal. So too holy men are always fearful, whether of the divine judgments, according to that saying, 'I was afraid because of your judgments,' or of past sins — Ecclesiasticus: 'be not without fear about sin forgiven' — or of the precipice of temptation. 'Blessed is the man who is always fearful.'

Third, by reason of gentleness. For it is a gentle and unwarlike animal: hence it uses no defense but the refuge of flight. So too holy men are gentle in their conduct, unwarlike, that is, fleeing vices and temporal advantages, and quarrels or disputes, without offending their neighbors. And note that the hare, fleeing dogs, has the natural instinct to flee toward the mountains: for it has long hind legs, so as to lift its body more easily when it climbs a mountain. Hence a dog attacks it more easily when it comes down from the mountain, since then it does not run well, but moves along as though stumbling. Hence, when it can, it circles the mountain, until it turns itself toward the mountain, and so often escapes the dogs. So too holy men, fleeing temptations, flee to the mountain, that is, to Christ. 'The weak people, the hares, have set their bed in the rock' — that is, in Christ. For he is the mountain of which Isaiah says: 'the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the top of the mountains.' He is also the same rock of which the Apostle says: 'the rock was Christ.' Or they flee to the mountain, that is, to the contemplation of paradise: for the saints have long hind legs, that is, great desires for the life to come, that is, for the things that will follow after this life. And by such desires their mind is easily lifted up in the contemplation of that height. But when the soul comes down from the mountain of heavenly contemplation to deal with, or think about, earthly things, it then easily falls into sin, and the dog, that is, the devil, more easily catches it. And so the saints, in contemplating, circle around, until they rise up to some taste of that heavenly sweetness.

Fourth, by reason of usefulness. For it is an animal useful for food, for clothing, and for medicine, for its eyes are effective against poison. So too holy men feed others with their teachings, or their alms, and clothe them with their examples: for it is as though one is clothed with its skins, that is, with virtues, when one imitates its examples.
Likewise, they heal others with their counsels, or with the help of their prayers.

Likewise, the holy man is likened to the badger. First, by reason of penance: since the badger has a very shaggy, hairy hide, called 'melota.' Now what is a hairy, shaggy hide, but the humble and harsh penance of the body? Such a hide John had, whose food was locusts and wild honey, and whose garment was of camel's hair.

Second, by reason of foresight: for Pliny says that, when pursued by dogs, it holds its breath, and so puffs up its hide, and avoids the dogs' bites. Likewise, the holy man, when he suffers persecution and injury, restrains his spirit through patience, so that he does not burst out through impatience or wrath; and so he escapes the bites of the dogs, that is, the injuries of his persecutors, so that at least they do not harm his soul.

Third, by reason of foresight: for the badger foresees a coming storm, and so prepares for itself a burrow with several exits; and when the north wind blows, it stops the north-facing hole with its tail; when the south wind blows, it closes the south-facing one. So too the holy man, when the north wind blows, that is, when adversity presses, closes the opening with his tail, that is, sets against it the consideration of its brief end, and reckons light everything he suffers, since it will end in a brief passing: for all brief things are said to be bearable, even if they are great, as Cicero says. Likewise, when the south wind blows, that is, when prosperity smiles, the holy man sets against it the closing of the tail, that is, the memory of death: for he easily despises all things who always thinks himself about to die.

Likewise, the badger gathers food against winter in its lair, and, if food runs short, makes up for it with sleep — as happens with many animals, as is clear with the dormouse and the mouse. So too the holy man provides for himself against winter, that is, against the time of death, gathering the merits of good works through the active life. And if food runs short, that is, the exercise or the will to earn merit through the active life, he helps himself with sleep, that is, with the tranquility and quiet of the contemplative life. Hence holy men do not spend, idly, the times when they are free from the labors of the active life, since then they rest within themselves in holy meditations.

div.head: Cap. CVI. Sapiens quid agere debeat ut suam ostentet sapientiam: quadam araneam similitudine edocetur.

cit.quote: The wise man is like the spider, which, standing in the middle of its web, senses a fly; and, once it has caught it, wraps it round many times with its threads, and first cuts off its head, and so avoids all its moisture. So too the wise man consists, in the middle of his web, that is, in the contemplation of reason, whose middle is God, threatening in the acts of the moral virtues. And from there he seizes the flying flies, that is, the forms of sensible things, that come to his senses, or his imagination, and, drawing them inward to the scrutiny of reason itself, wraps them round with many considerations; and, the head cut off, that is, the judgment of the outward senses excluded, which was the beginning of their gathering, he draws out the inner truth, and turns it into his own food, that is, his own instruction, or advancement. Ezekiel: 'the eagle took the marrow of the cedar' — for the eagle is the wise and understanding man, who draws the marrow from the cedar, when he draws the intelligible truth from the sensible thing.

div.head: Cap. CVII. Homines aliqua scientia prediti, voluptatibusque vacantes, Onocentauris ac Hyppocentauris similes iure efficiuntur.

cit.quote: Knowledge combined with a bad life makes men like the monstrous animals called the ass-centaur and the horse-centaur. For the Physiologus says that the ass-centaur is an animal composed of ass and man: for from the navel upward it has a human form, so it is halfway between man and ass, just as the horse-centaur is between man and horse, as Isidore says. Such is the learned but pleasure-loving man: for on one side he is rational, and on the other bestial — spiritual in knowledge, carnal in deed.

div.head: Cap. CVIII. Hereticorum schismaticorumque peruersitas, qui lupis, leunculis, vipere filiis, ac Panthere catulis assimilantur, planis declaratur exemplis.

cit.quote: Schismatics and heretics are like young lion cubs, which tear their mother's womb, and so she often does not give birth again. Hence Aristotle says that the lioness first bears five cubs, then four, and so one fewer each year, until she becomes barren. In this, then, schismatics are like young lions, since they tear and rend the unity of the mother church and of the faith in which they were spiritually begotten.

Likewise, schismatics are like the offspring of the viper: for the viper ('vipera') is so named since it gives birth 'by force' ('vi pariat'); for, when the time comes for her to give birth, her young do not wait for the operation of nature, but gnaw through her sides, and come out at the cost of their mother's death. So too schismatics, begotten in the womb of mother church, not waiting for or enduring her correction, come out by rebelling, and, while they tear apart her unity, drag her, as far as it lies in them, toward ruin.

Likewise, schismatics and heretics are likened to the cubs of the panther, which, hating their mother, tear at her belly with their claws, as though it resisted their coming out. Hence the panther gives birth only once. So too schismatics and heretics tear apart the unity of holy mother church with their claws, that is, their malicious pursuits and teachings, since their treachery resists her.

Likewise, heretics are likened to wolves. First, by reason of infection: for the wolf, with its bite, infects the wool of the sheep it kills, and makes clothing made from such wool infested with lice, as Isidore says. So too the heretic, with the bite, or mouth, of his teaching, infects and corrupts the wool of the sheep, that is, the simplicity of a man's life, which false teaching spiritually kills, and makes it abound with lice, that is, corrupt deeds.

Likewise, a cord made from wolves' intestines destroys and ruins lute-strings made from sheep's intestines, once they are strung together. Cords from wolves' intestines are the wicked teachings of heretics, but cords from sheep's intestines are the thoughts and opinions of the simple. But if these two are joined together, that is, if the wicked teaching or false opinion of heretics is taken up by the simple, then the simplicity and sincerity of the faith is entirely destroyed.

div.head: Cap. CIX. Contemplativi pluribus exemplis capris siluestribus comparantur: Damonesque precipue solitarii insidiari declarantur.

cit.quote: Solitaries and contemplatives, that is, those perfect in the anchoritic life, are like wild goats. First, since such a goat is most rugged in its diet. Hence the goat ('capra') is named from 'cropping' ('carpendo'), since it crops rough places, and so hermits, dwelling in deserts or rough places, must crop a harsh diet, as is clear in John the Baptist.

Second, since it dwells in the highest places. Hence such goats are called 'ibex,' since, like those birds called 'ibices,' they climb steep places that scarcely lie open to human sight, as Isidore says. And such are perfect men, when they are lifted, through contemplation, to the highest and invisible things. The Apostle: 'we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.'

Third, since such a goat is keenest in sight: for such goats, dwelling on the highest mountains, spot hunters coming from afar, and, standing on broken crags, when they sense men or beasts approaching, throw themselves down from the highest points of the rocks, and are caught by their own horns as they fall. So too holy men, enlightened in the highest contemplations, foresee, from a long way off, temptations to come, and the malicious deceptions of demons; and when they sense these threatening from vice, they cast themselves down from the highest rocks, that is, from the contemplation of sublime things, into the depths, since they draw themselves back, through humility of mind, to the consideration of their own weakness, and, through the guarding of inward humility, escape the snares of the proud demons.

Fourth, since such a goat is swiftest in running. And likewise perfect men, in spiritual works, are not slow or lazy, but diligent and prompt, and run all the more, the more fervently they love: for he who loves more vehemently runs more swiftly, and arrives sooner, as Bernard says.

Fifth, since the wild goat is most shrewd in feeding: for it discerns its pasture by sight, taste, and smell. Likewise, holy men discern spiritual food by sight, that is, by reading, and choosing beforehand what is better and more useful.

Likewise, by taste, in contemplating: since they eagerly swallow heavenly things, but, despising them, are disgusted at temporal ones. By smell, in imitating: since they follow the scents of good food, that is, the examples of the virtues; but they flee and abhor the stenches, that is, the examples of vices.

Sixth, since the wild goat is healthiest in what it drinks: for Pliny says that if anyone drinks the milk of this goat, he avoids weakness. So too the milk, that is, the spiritual teaching, of such perfect men, once drunk, that is, taken devoutly and eagerly, makes the mind avoid the weaknesses of the vices.

Likewise, demons lie in wait especially for solitaries and spiritual men, and prevail most of all against the negligent and drowsy. Hence demons are likened to certain serpents that dwell in the woods, which eat birds and small creatures, sucking their moisture, as Aristotle says, and such serpents lie in wait for sleepers, and, if they find their mouths open, steal into their bodies, loving natural warmth and scent. But against these fights the lizard called the 'saura,' which, sensing the serpent's presence, leaps onto the sleeper's face, and scratches with its feet, so as to be able to wake him — as Avicenna says. By the birds, then, that dwell in the woods, are understood spiritual and contemplative men. And by the small creatures are understood coarser and simpler men leading the solitary life, whom serpents, that is, demons, devour, when they can draw and bend them to the consent of their own wickedness. And even if they cannot harm them otherwise, they at least try to draw out the moisture of their devotion and compunction. They lie in wait especially for sleepers, that is, the negligent and idle. And if, through carelessness or negligence, they find their senses open, and wandering around outward things, they enter into them more forcefully, to take from them the warmth of love and the scent of devotion, and so spiritually extinguish them. But the lizard mostly helps them, that is, angelic guardianship, rousing their negligence; or that lizard is the teaching of sacred Scripture, especially of the Savior, who urges us to watch and pray. Matthew: 'watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation.' And likewise Peter, rousing us, lest the serpent enter into us, says: 'be sober, and watch, because your adversary the devil,' and so on.

div.head: Cap. CX. In via Dei proficere volentes, malorum societatem debere omni tempore effugere: Cerue parturientis unico exemplo aperitur.

cit.quote: Whoever wishes to pursue and complete his resolve of salvation ought to flee the company of the wicked, as Aristotle notes — an example of which is the doe. For the doe, when about to give birth, moves away from the paths known to wild beasts, and draws near to the paths worn by men. Hence (as Aristotle says) she gives birth near the road, where, for fear of men, no wild beast approaches. So too, he who wishes to give birth, that is, to bring to completion, the good resolve he has conceived, ought to draw away from wild beasts, that is, from the wicked and unjust, and draw near, or cling, to men, that is, those living well and reasonably, by whose benefit he can be safer. But demons, whom they wish to corrupt, make them withdraw from men, that is, from the good, and live or dwell with wild beasts, that is, with the wicked, according to that saying: 'they shall cast you out from among men, and your dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals.'

div.head: Cap. CXI. Quo pacto sacre Scripture studiis, studiosi, quasque partes habere debent: animalium ruminantium pulcherrima, similitudine admonemur.

cit.quote: He who studies sacred Scripture ought first to seek the literal sense, and then investigate the spiritual sense. This is shown by the example of ruminant animals; for every ruminant animal has two stomachs, one large, and one small. The reason for this is multiple digestion: for such animals' food is dry, and not well chewed at first, out of eagerness to eat, so it must be chewed again; it is drawn from the larger stomach to the mouth, and, chewed there a second time, is sent on to the second stomach, so that it may be perfectly digested there. Now the rumination of food is the meditation on sacred Scripture, which must first be brought to the large stomach, that is, to the literal sense, which is the first and general sense of the whole of sacred Scripture. Then it must be led, through meditation, to the small stomach, that is, to the spiritual sense, which is indeed called small, since it must be sought humbly and soberly; for the mystical understanding of sacred Scripture is given only to the little ones. 'The Psalm gives light, and understanding to little ones.'

Likewise, it is called small, since, in this life, man grasps only a little of eternal, spiritual things. For 'we know in part, and we prophesy in part.' This food, however, is perfectly digested, when it is fulfilled in life and deed.

Likewise, the preacher deeply versed in sacred Scripture, whose task it is to fight the enemies of the faith, ought to scrutinize and learn it with discretion and sobriety: for those horses are fit to be led into battle which, while drinking, sink their nostrils deeper, since such horses (as it is said) are not burdened by their urine while running. By horses fit for battle, then, understand Catholic preachers, or doctors, who must dispute against heretics, since they ought to sink the nostrils of their discretion deep into the water of sacred Scripture, that is, study with discretion, so that they draw the sense of Scripture from its depths, and are understood, and so, in the course of their running, are scarcely harmed by the urine, that is, the conceiving of error, or its obstacle.

Likewise, the study of spiritual teaching consists in three things, namely learning, choosing, and retaining, as appears by the example of the teeth of animals: for there are certain animals that have teeth for seizing, like dogs and animals of prey, and so they have teeth that are separated and sharp, so that they can better seize their prey. Others have teeth for grazing, like the camel and the cow and the like, and so they have them even and continuous, so as to better crop the grasses. Others yet have teeth for holding their food, like fish: for fish, unlike other animals, have more than two rows of teeth, since, besides the teeth they have that are jagged and spaced apart, they also have, further within, teeth wondrously set, with which (as Aristotle says) they gather back their food, lest it be swept from their jaws by the slipperiness of the water. Now those have teeth for seizing spiritual food and teaching who are apt and diligent for learning. But because not all are equally apt for learning the same things, these teeth are therefore separated, and are the more fit for learning, the sharper they are found for understanding what they read or hear. But the animals that crop grass, cutting it with their teeth, seize what seems better to them, and pass over the rest, and so, in grazing, choose the better. Hence those have teeth for grazing who, of the things they hear or read, are diligent to choose the better and more useful, and to commit them to memory, or sometimes to writing; but those have teeth for retaining who are careful and diligent, not only in hearing or reading, but also in going over and thinking back over what they have learned, since frequent meditation preserves memory, according to the Philosopher. Hence, without frequent repetition, memory is found unstable and slippery.

div.head: Cap. CXII. Mali superborum mores, ferinaque vitia, ex pluribus Tauri, Draconis, Baracis, Bubalique naturalibus effectibus plane cognosscunturcognoscuntur.

cit.quote: The proud man is likened to the bull. First, by reason of ferocity: for bulls are most ferocious, although they are said to grow tame when tied under a fig tree (as Isidore says). So too the proud are ferocious, and prone to injure and harm others, unless they are tied under the fig tree, that is, restrained under the lordship of some upright man, who is gentler and sweeter. Judith: 'they bound Achior to the tree' — for Achior, whose name means 'mountain-dweller,' signifies one swollen with pride, since a mountain is the swelling of anger, which must be bound to the tree, that is, restrained to the will of a superior.

Second, by reason of solitariness: for Aristotle says that the bull grazes alone, except in the time of mating, and so the proud man wishes to be alone in the honors and dignities on which he feeds, unless perhaps he shares them with a few friends. 'The lone wild beast has devoured her.'

Third, by reason of inflation: for if anyone cuts a small piece from a bull's hide, and, blowing through a tube, lifts the skin a little from the flesh, it will swell up. It is also fattened with figs and raisins. So too the proud are fattened, or inflated, with the inflation of the tube, that is, with the words of flatterers and those who praise them, and with figs and raisins, that is, when sweet things that delight them are said to them, and offered them. But against their inflation it is said: 'do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull.'

Fourth, by reason of cruelty: for bulls have a hard, cruel heart. And Aristotle says that a hard bone is often found in the bull's heart, which signifies the hardness of the heart of the proud. Ecclesiasticus: 'a hard heart shall fare ill at the last.'

Likewise, the proud man is likened to the dragon. First, since the dragon is venomous: and so, when it is carried through the air, the air is stirred up, and, through its venom, the sea also swells. Such too is the venom of pride, which swells the heart within, and outwardly stirs up and brings on quarrels like storms of the air.

Second, since it is treacherous: for it lies in wait for the elephant, and thirsts for its blood. Hence, when the elephant sees a dragon on a tree, it strives to break the tree, so as to kill it. But the dragon leaps upon the elephant, and strives to bite it between the nostrils, and attacks its eyes, and sometimes blinds it, and sometimes leaps upon it from behind, and bites it, and sucks its blood; and, after a long struggle, from the loss of blood, the elephant grows so weak that it falls upon the dragon, and, dying, kills its own killer. Now the reason why the dragon so desires its blood is the coldness of the blood, by which it seeks to cool its own burning heat, as Isidore says. Just as the dragon lies in wait for the elephant, then, so too the proud and ambitious man lies in wait for one greater than himself and reigning, sometimes thirsting for his blood, so that he himself may reign. Hence he sometimes attacks him from the front, that is, openly and manifestly, sometimes from behind, that is, secretly and hidden, and sometimes casts him down and destroys him, and sometimes he himself, too, perishes from or because of him, as we frequently see happen among the princes of the world.

Third, the dragon is windy, since it follows and loves the wind: for Solinus says that the dragon is an animal so thirsty that it can scarcely be satisfied even by water; hence it opens its mouth against the wind, so as to soothe its own burning heat, and so its onslaught often overturns a ship's sail and mast. But sailors, when they sense a dragon coming — which they notice by the swelling of the sea — at once lower their sails, and so escape the dragon's danger. Likewise, the proud man is not satisfied by the waters of delights, but still thirsts for the winds of vanity and of good things, hence he follows the sails of ships, that is, glories, and the tracks of the great, whom he also sometimes overturns, while he thirsts for their wind and the glory of their honors. Hence it would be safer to lower the sail of honor, than to have such dragons against oneself. Job: 'I have become a brother to dragons, and a companion to ostriches.'

Likewise, the proud man is likened to the 'boracia,' that is, the toad, a venomous frog, which, as Pliny says, has a twofold liver: one most venomous, the other, however, is a remedy against poison, and is given as an antidote against something harmful. Hence, to know which is good and which is bad, they throw it into an ants' nest, and the ants at once flee the venomous part, and seek out the other. So too, in the proud man, there is sometimes an estimation or excellence of some grace, or uprightness; and this is venomous, since it contains the venom of pride. But on the other side there is in him some defect, or weakness of the flesh, and this is a humbling medicine, namely humbling the mind, and repelling the venom of pride. Hence the Apostle, lest he be killed by the venomous liver of pride, declared himself fortified with the antidote of the other, saying: 'lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a sting of my flesh,' and so on. Hence ants, that is, prudent men, turn away from esteeming their own greatness, lest they be infected with the venom of pride, and diligently look to their own weakness, so as to be saved through humility.

Likewise, the proud are likened to buffaloes, whose ferocity and strength cannot be tamed except by an iron ring fixed in their nostrils. So too the ferocity and presumptuous strength of the proud is not subdued, except by strong tribulation and oppression. Hence it is said to a certain proud man: 'I will put a ring in your nostrils.'

div.head: Cap. CXIII. Demonum in variis peccatis insidiantium, fraudulente tentationes, eorumque calliditates numerantur, quoue pacto tenteti seipsos tueri debent, ex Cerui, Apri, Cemeli, Hedi, Formice, Ursi, at diversorum serpentum naturalibus effectibus, multisque exemplis terminatur.

cit.quote: Holy men humbly fear, prudently flee, and effectively repel the deceitful temptations of demons: for the virtuous are, in a sense, like stags: for stags are said to fear the voice of the fox. Now what is the fox's voice, but the deceitful suggestion of the demon? But stags fortified with great antlers are men fortified with great virtues. Stags, then, fear the fox's voice, since holy men always fear the deceit and cunning of the demon. 'Stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.'
