Likewise, when the dog pursues the stag, if it finds a fork in the path, it does not run in a straight track, but changes its leaps crosswise, now this way, now that; for it then tries to cross by contrary paths, so that the dogs are deceived in following its tracks. Likewise too, holy men, when the devil pursues them by tempting them, do not run in a straight track, but crosswise; since, when they feel themselves assailed by pride, they at once turn back, not to the consideration of their own virtue, but of their own weakness, and, when, weakness having been raised against them, they are tempted to faintheartedness, they strive, as though by a crosswise leap, to recall to memory their own strong works. So blessed Job, lest the greatness of his virtues exalt him, ran to consider his own frailty, saying: 'spare me, Lord: for my days are nothing. What is man, that you should magnify him, or set your heart upon him?' And again, lest he should despair from the multitude of his calamities, he leapt to weighing his own innocence, saying: 'I have not sinned, and my eye continues in bitterness,' and again: 'oh, that my sins, whereby I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance! As the sand of the sea, this would appear heavier.' He gave, then, as it were, contrary and crosswise leaps, now begging that he be spared, now saying that he had not sinned, so that neither should his innocence lead him into the error of pride, nor should the calamity drag his soul into despair.

Likewise, when dogs pursue the stag, if it can, it flees to a river, where, its strength restored by the coldness of the water, swimming across, it escapes the hunter. Now dogs pursue the stag then, when importunate thoughts, or temptations, trouble and goad the mind, which then flees to the river, when, returning with fear to self-consideration, it pours out copious tears, saying to God in prayer: 'you are my God; depart not from me, for tribulation is near, and there is none to help; for many dogs have surrounded me, and the council of the malignant has besieged me.' For tearful prayer so strengthens and fortifies the mind that it not only escapes the dogs, that is, temptations, but even extinguishes them. Psalm: 'you have crushed the heads of the dragons' — that is, the temptations of demons — 'in the waters,' namely of tears.

Likewise, when the stag is caught, it bellows, and sheds tears. Hence a man too, caught by the tempter through consent, ought at once to let out the bellow of sorrowful confession, and pour out copious tears of compunction, before he is dragged into the depravity of the deed, or entangled in a wicked habit.

Likewise, the temptations of demons are likened to the movements of serpents. For certain serpents move, or crawl, always in winding curves, and such are demons that tempt insidiously, and under the appearance of good, beginning straight and bending toward the crooked. But some always move in a straight line, like the 'centris'; hence Lucan says: 'the centris always glides along a straight track'; and such are those who directly and openly suggest evils, like adultery, and murder, and the like. Others, however, always move bent over their breast; and these are demons tempting toward avarice, and bending man's heart toward earthly desires. But some serpents move erect from the breast upward, like a certain land-and-water serpent called the 'chelydrus,' and this serpent, when it runs, cracks if it twists itself. Such, then, are demons tempting toward pride, which lifts the heart on high through exaltation, and certain proud men would rather crack in dying than bend in humbling themselves.
Likewise, there are certain serpents that move slowly. And these are demons tempting toward negligence and laziness, which pertain to sloth.

Likewise, there are some of such speed that they seem to fly. Hence a certain serpent is called the 'javelin-snake' ('iaculus'), which is thought to fly like a javelin. This one leaps from trees, and if it meets anything in its way, it kills it at once. Such are demons tempting toward wrath, whose movement is swift, not waiting for the counsel of reason, and it strikes those it meets, that is, those who resist it. There are also, in Arabia, winged serpents called sirens, which run faster than horses, and so are said to fly, whose venom is so potent that a man dies before he feels any pain. Such are demons tempting toward lust, which is said to fly swiftly, since its delight passes away quickly; but it kills the soul with delight before its pain is felt.

Likewise, there are some that are treacherous and insidious, like the horned viper ('cerastes'), a horned serpent that hides beneath the sand, and shows only its horns, which it has in the shape of a ram's; and when an animal, or a bird, approaches it, thinking it a ram, it finds instead the worst of serpents. Such are demons tempting toward envy, since the envious man strives to catch and overthrow deceitfully and treacherously. There is also a serpent called the 'boa,' which follows herds of cattle and buffaloes, and hangs from their udders, and, while it drinks the milk, kills the animal. Hence it takes its name from cattle, or buffaloes ('boves' or 'bubali'), as Isidore says. Such are demons tempting toward gluttony. Hence they follow the herds of cattle, that is, of men living bestially, and, in the taste of milk, that is, in the delight of gluttony, strike and kill the soul. Proverbs: 'it enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent.'

Likewise, the temptations of demons are like the hunting of animals, of which the Psalm says: 'he has delivered me from the snare of the hunters.' For (according to Avicenna) certain animals hunt by night, like certain wolves; some by day, like dogs and bears and the like; but some by both day and night, like certain wolves too. So too certain demons tempt by night, that is, secretly, and under the appearance of good, and this is the terror of the night, of which the Psalm says: 'you shall not be afraid of the terror of the night, nor of the business that walks about in the dark.' For it sometimes suggests abstinence, so as to induce impatience, it suggests giving good example to others, so as to induce vainglory, and the like. But some tempt by day, that is, openly and manifestly suggesting evils, as when they tempt toward lust, murder, theft, and the like, and this is the arrow that flies by day. But some tempt by night and by day, since a demon sometimes tempts in both ways: for at first it tempts subtly, and enters, as it were, reasonably, but afterward makes one plunge into open evil. Hence, in this the devil is like a certain monstrous animal, said to have a man's face, a serpent's hiss, a scorpion's tail, the speed of a flying bird, and three rows of teeth, and it desires human flesh to eat. It has, then, the head of a man, and the hiss of a serpent, since it tempts first subtly, and, as it were, reasonably; it has three rows of teeth, since it tempts in three ways, namely through the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. It has the body of a lion, since it holds fast strongly; the tail of a scorpion, since it stings wickedly in the end; it runs as swiftly as a bird, and desires human flesh, that is, to violate and slaughter carnal men. This third temptation, then, is called the noonday demon, since it partakes, as a middle term, of the first two.

Likewise, holy men, watching for temptations, fortify themselves, like the boar against hunters: for the boar fortifies itself in three ways. First, by setting the harder part of its body against the attack: for on its right side it has a very hard spot, which it always sets against the huntsman's spear that pursues it, and, like a strong shield, it always offers that spot first. So too holy men, against the assault of temptations, offer up hardness, that is, the harshness of the body, according to that saying: 'but I, when they troubled me, put on sackcloth, I humbled my soul with fasting.'

Likewise, the boar fortifies itself by sharpening its tusks, that is, its long teeth, against trees: for, knowing danger threatens it, it sharpens its tusks, rubbing them against trees, and, rubbing, tests whether they cut well, and afterward, using them as swords, tears apart, by rending, whatever it strikes. These tusks, then, are the virtues of the penitent, which are sharpened when rubbed against trees; for to rub one's tusks against trees is, as it were, to compare one's own virtues to the virtues of the saints and strong men, by whose example they are rendered more fervent for the work, and sharper for the battle.

Likewise, the boar fortifies itself by chewing oregano: for if, rubbing its teeth against a tree, it finds them dull, it seeks out the herb oregano, by whose power, chewed, it sharpens its teeth, as Avicenna says. Oregano, then, is the word of God, by whose chewing, that is, consideration, the soul is fortified beforehand against temptations: for the word of God is living, and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword. Or oregano is divine protection, which we ought to seek through prayer, so that, by its power, our strength may be rendered safer and stronger against temptations.

...of the camel. For the camel, in the time of mating, loves solitude, and no one but its keeper dares approach it. And again, when it desires the female, it moves along bent upon its knees, and eats little at that time. So too a man, when overtaken by carnal love, or by temptation, ought to withdraw to the solitude of prayer, and commend himself fervently to Christ alone, his shepherd, and wear out his body with devout genuflections, and chastise his flesh with sparing food and drink, so that the sparingness of food and drink may root out the pride of the flesh.

Likewise, carnal temptations are also driven back and conquered by penance, and the fervor of meditations and prayers — an example of which appears in the kid, since its hide, which is shaggy (as Pliny says), heals venomous bites if bound on hot, and its burnt hairs, by their scent, put serpents to flight. Now what is the shaggy hide of the kid, but the austere penance of the tempted man? For the kid, which is a playful and wanton animal, signifies the man tempted carnally; its shaggy hide, then, that is, the harsh penance of the flesh, if applied hot, that is, made hot by charity, which is the vital heat of the soul — that is, set against the temptations themselves — heals their venomous, that is, deadly, bites. Hence the Psalm, using this remedy, said: 'but I, when they troubled me, put on sackcloth.' But, as it were, the hairs coming from the hide are the thoughts coming from the mind; or, since hairs, which are generated from the body's excess, signify alms, which ought at least to be given from one's excess, according to that saying, 'give alms of what remains,' these burnt hairs, that is, fervent thoughts, or alms done with the love of charity, put serpents to flight, that is, demons, or their temptations. Hence, of alms it is said: 'above a mighty shield and a spear it shall fight for you against your enemy.' And of the fervor of meditations it is said: 'the liver being set on fire' — that is, the mind, through fervent thoughts or prayers — 'it shall put the demon to flight.'

Likewise, note that temptations destroy some, and purge others. Hence they are like ants, which lay waste to plants, but purge bears. For ants, gnawing, damage flowers and buds, hollow out and eat fruit, and cause harm to man. Likewise, temptations sometimes corrupt and lay waste the flowers of thoughts, the buds of affections, and empty out the fruit of works of its merit, and so are, to the incautious and unwary man, the cause of many injuries; and yet ants help bears. Hence Pliny says that when bears fall sick, they seek out ants, and devour them, and so recover their health. Likewise, for holy men, temptations serve toward perfection, and toward the purging or freeing from vices. Hence James: 'blessed is the man who endures temptation.'

Likewise, note that the devil's temptation is at first weak, and easy to resist, but afterward, as it proceeds, becomes difficult and strong. For the devil is likened to the bear, which has a weak head, but very strong forelegs. The devil's suggestion, then, is like the bear's head, but his forelegs are, as it were, the very acts of sin, which, if they catch a man, are let go only with the greatest difficulty. Psalm: 'he shall crush their heads' — since the vices of temptation themselves must indeed be crushed.

div.head: Cap. CXIIII. Penitentiam incipere metuentes, Asino aquam intranti seu bibenti, rationabili profecto exemplo comparantur.

cit.quote: He who is afraid to begin penance is like the ass, which greatly fears to enter water, and dip its foot there, or cross through it — indeed, asses are not even willing to cross bridges, especially if they can see water below, since they easily suffer dizziness because of the weakness of their head, on account of which they fear falling from the bridge; nor do they drink readily, except at a place where they are used to drinking, which they can reach dry-footed: he fears to enter or cross water, who fears to begin penance, or to persevere in it. But he who, seeing water, fears to cross a bridge, is like him who, considering its harshness, fears to enter religious life — which happens because of a weakness of the head, that is, a defect of the senses; and so such a man does not wish to depart from the accustomed water, that is, his life, nor take up penance, except what he can bear easily. Judith: 'can I forsake my sweetness, and my most delicious fruits?'

div.head: Cap. CXV. Tyranni qui immaniter imperii viribus abutuntur, unicorni, Chameleonti, Simie, Gryphoni, ac Lupo assimilantur, ex quorum similitudinibus, eorum pariter vite ac exitus non inculta demonstratur.

cit.quote: The tyrant is like the unicorn, of which Pliny says that it is like the elephant in its head, and the horse in its body, but is like the boar in its tail; it lets out a heavy bellow, and has one great horn, two cubits long, on its forehead. This beast, they say, cannot be captured alive, but only by force. So too tyrants are, in their head, that is, their mind, like elephants, namely through the greatness of their pride; in their body like horses, namely through the flow of their lust; and in their tail like boars, on account of the brevity of their power — for the boar has an ugly and crooked tail. And likewise tyrannical power and dominion commonly has a swift and shameful end. The heavy bellow is their heavy rule, since they impose heavy and unbearable burdens on others; the great horn is the cruel persecution they inflict on the good, especially on those who do not consent to their wickedness.

Now living tyrants cannot be captured because of their impatience: for the unicorn (as Gregory says) is a beast entirely untamable, so that, if it is captured, it cannot be held, since, unable to bear it, it dies of impatience. So too tyrants and the proud sometimes consent to be killed, rather than be willing to be subjected to others, as is clear with Hannibal, who drank poison, and killed himself, so as not to fall under Roman rule. And Cato likewise killed himself, so as not to be subjected to Caesar.

Likewise, the ruling tyrant is like the chameleon, of which Aristotle says that it has a face like an animal composed of pig and ape; and its color changes when its hide is blown into, and Pliny says that no animal is more fearful than it, and so it changes, just as its color does, and says that, out of weakness, it feigns tameness, though it is in fact cruel. He also says that great power against hawks has been given to this animal: for it draws them flying toward itself, and offers them to other birds to be torn apart. Aristotle also says that in death it is of an ugly color, although in life it is of great beauty. So too tyrants have a likeness to the pig, because of the uncleanness of their life, and a likeness to the ape, because of their pretense of justice: for the ape's body begins with a man's face, but at the end shows its ugliness in the defect of its tail. So too the tyrant, at the beginning of his rule, or his deed, feigns gentleness and justice, and so begins with a man's face; but in the tail, that is, at the end of his deed, he uncovers and reveals the ugliness of his tyranny and malice; and when something is whispered against someone into his ears, his color changes and inflames very quickly, and this for the most part proceeds from fear, since all tyrants are fearful, knowing themselves to be hated by many; yet sometimes, out of fear or weakness, they feign gentleness, although they always carry in their heart the rage of cruelty. To these too, by divine judgment, power against hawks has been given, namely against plunderers, or usurers, and the like, since often those who have violently or unjustly despoiled many others are themselves despoiled by some rising tyrant who seizes them, and are, besides, sometimes inhumanly torn apart by him. Although the tyrant, while he lives and rules, appears magnificent and powerful, in death, nonetheless, he is ugly, since tyrants commonly die a shameful death.

Likewise, the tyrant is likened to the ant-lion, which is a small animal, harmful to ants, eating their grain, and, while it withholds their food from them, incidentally kills them; and so it is called 'ant-lion,' since it is, to the ants, as a lion; but since the ant cannot overpower it, yet it suffers a persecutor and conqueror of its own, and is itself devoured by other animals. And likewise, sometimes tyrants, who are oppressors and despoilers of the humble and the poor, are, by divine judgment, oppressed by others, and become their prey. Isaiah: 'woe to you who despoil; shall not you too be despoiled?'

Likewise, tyrants are like griffins: for the griffin is a feathered, four-footed animal, born in the hyperborean mountains, like a lion in every part of its body, but like an eagle in its wings, and has claws so large that cups are made from them, which are set before the tables of kings. Likewise, tyrants are like the lion in cruelty, and the eagle in rapacity; hence the great size of the claws is their great and manifold eagerness to plunder. Psalm: 'he lies in wait, that he may catch,' and so on.

Likewise, tyrants are like wolves. For there are certain wolves of the morning, certain of noon, and certain of evening. Morning wolves, who are not yet very hungry, eat part of a sheep, and leave part. Such are many tyrants, who seize the goods of the poor, but leave them a part. But noon wolves, who have not eaten until noon, since they are very hungry, and, on account of the heat, very thirsty, eat the whole sheep, and drink its blood. Such are many who take away all a man's goods, and, besides, plunder the possessions he acquired with much sweat. Isidore: 'petty judges, like wolves, seize everything, and scarcely leave a little for the poor.' But evening wolves, who have not eaten until evening, are so hungry that they eat the very flesh of the sheep, and drink its blood, and tear its hide, and break its bones. So too there are many tyrants who drain the poor of their money, plunder their possessions, take away their houses, strip off their clothes, and crush their persons. Zephaniah: 'her judges are evening wolves; they leave nothing for the morning.'

div.head: Cap. CXVI. Peccatoris cor quo pacto aperiatur, cyrogrylli, Heritiique similitudine declaratur, quantumque peccatoris mentem excitet, humilies, ac inflammet tribulatio, oritii exemplo planum agitur.

cit.quote: Strong tribulation, or fervent preaching, opens the sinner's heart: for the sinner is like the 'cyrogryllus,' or great hedgehog, which draws its hide together with such strength that its shell can scarcely be opened intact; but if hot water is sprinkled on it, it opens at once. So too the sinner's heart is sometimes so shut up in sin that it can scarcely be opened except by the breaking of death; but hot water, that is, fervent and strong tribulation, or hot water, that is, fervent and heartfelt preaching, opens the sinner's very heart, when it pours over it strongly and abundantly. Preachers desired this opening of hearts, saying: 'may the Lord open your heart.'

Likewise, vehement tribulations and persecutions drive sinners back to God through spontaneous penance, just as Pliny says that the stag, when too hard pressed by dogs, flees of its own accord to man. For threatening tribulations are, as it were, the pursuing dogs, which, while they press the sinner hard, drive him back to the Lord. Psalm: 'fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek your name, O Lord.'

Likewise, strong tribulation both stirs and humbles the mind of the 'oryx' — hence it is likened to the 'oryx,' which (according to Pliny) is a wild beast that, at the rising of the dog-star, stands facing the star, as though it wished to worship it, and this it does after having slept a long time. Now what is the burning dog-star, but vehement tribulation? At whose rising, or approach, the sleeping beast, that is, the sluggish mind of the sinner, is roused, and made ready, as it were, to worship, that is, is humbled toward penance and devotion. Psalm: 'they humbled his feet in fetters; the iron passed through his soul' — for by the feet and the iron are understood tribulations, by which, while the sinner is straitened and weighed down, his affection is humbled, and his soul is wounded toward penance.

div.head: Cap. CXVII. Unde inanis gloria ortum habeat, quantumque sit a fidelibus fugienda, tinee proprietatibus aperitur.

cit.quote: ...vainglory is likened to the moth. First, since the moth is born even from good cloth, when the garment is kept in thick air, unshaken, or is not aired by the wind. Ecclesiasticus: 'from a garment comes a moth.' Likewise, from good work is born the moth of vainglory. And this happens when the mind remains in thick air, that is, when it does not subtly notice or correct its own spiritual failings, nor is aired by the wind of inward inspiration.

...since the moth advances, as it were, imperceptibly: for it consumes the very surface almost imperceptibly, and, being an animal, hides itself within the very substance, so that it cannot be seen. So too vainglory is a vice so subtle and hidden that it holds the mind and destroys a man's merit before an unwary man notices it, and so scarcely anyone is free of it. For (as Valerius Maximus says) there is absolutely no humility so great that it is not touched by some sweetness of glory. Job: 'he has built his house like the moth.'

Third, since the moth is driven away by bitter and fragrant things. Hence, if the leaves of laurel, or cedar, or cypress, and the like, are placed with garments, and also with books, they cannot be harmed by the moth, as Constantine says. Likewise, vainglory is kept away either by the bitterness of tribulation, or by the fragrance of heavenly glory. Matthew: 'lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys': for the fragrance, that is, the intention, of heavenly glory keeps out the moth of vainglory.

div.head: Cap. CXVIII. Vera fides quid in nobis operetur, quibusque virtutibus sit copulanda ut opus bonum ad finem perducatur, cerue ac formice exemplis redditur manifestum.

cit.quote: The virtue of faith conceives a good resolve, humility guards it, but charity brings it to completion in deed. And so this virtue is likened to certain herbs which does help the stag after conception, by which it is helped both to retain the offspring in the womb, and also to give birth more easily. For he conceives offspring in the womb who, enlightened by faith, conceives a good resolve; which indeed does not perish in the womb of the mind, nor come out in vain, if discreet humility keeps it hidden for a time; which finally charity brings to completion, since, by a certain impulse of fervor, as though by a violent birth, it forces it out into deed. And so the Apostle says that faith works through love, since what faith conceives, love brings to completion in deed.

Likewise, virtue and prudence of mind make up, in some, for a defect of body. For ants (as Solinus says) often carry burdens larger than their own bodies, so making up for smallness of body through greatness of strength; they carry weights with their mouths, and what they cannot carry in their mouth because of its size, they strive to roll along with their feet. And so too the virtuous man contrives that what he cannot do one way, he does another. In this too the reality of virtue is greater than its outward appearance. And he bears his neighbor's burden with his mouth, when he leads him to patience by his exhortation. And if he is not able to do it with his mouth, at least with his feet, that is, he rolls it along with the compassion of his affections.

div.head: Cap. CXIX. Quemadmodum vita spiritualis alatur, at quibus virtutibus perficiatur, per nonnullorum animalium naturalia instrumenta, eorumque significationes diversas edocetur.

cit.quote: The spiritual life needs fewer things than the bodily life: and an example of this appears in the instruments by which an animal is moved: for (as Avicenna says) every animal having moving blood moves by four instruments, namely either four feet, like the brutes, or two feet and two hands, like men, or two feet and two wings, like birds. But there are certain animals that have more than four feet, as is clear in crabs, and certain worms, and some have more wings, as is clear in butterflies, and bees, and the like. But this happens from a lack, and a scarcity, of blood, for which reason four organs work more effectively in the first kind than many do in the second. He, then, has moving blood in himself, who has the moisture of grace. For the soul, that is, the life of all flesh, is in the blood, as is said in Leviticus. Hence, when blood fails, the life of the body fails. So too, when grace fails, the spiritual life fails. For (as the Philosopher says) to live is, for the living, to be; but spiritual being is through grace, according to that saying of the Apostle: 'by the grace of God I am what I am'; the soul, therefore, has spiritual life through grace.

The feet, then, by which anyone having grace walks in right living, are the four moral, or cardinal, virtues, namely prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. Likewise, the two feet of flying creatures, by which they tend toward good works, are the two loves, namely of God and of neighbor. But the twofold wing is, as it were, the twofold teaching of the two Testaments, which lifts one up in flying, that is, in contemplating, in the true contemplation of God. Or the two wings are prayer and fasting, by one of which the soul is lifted, by the other the body is lightened. Or, as the two spiritual feet of man, there are intellect and affection, of which one tends toward God by the way of faith, the other by the way of love. But there are two hands: to do well in prosperity, which pertains to the right, and to do well in adversity, which pertains to the left; or to do good to friend and to enemy. But the other, lowlier creatures, which, from a lack of strength, make use of many instruments, signify sinners destitute of grace and the virtues, who are entangled in many instruments, that is, many cares and occupations, which comes from the defect of a nature corrupted by vice, and not reined in by grace, or enlightened by virtues: for a whole nature, moderated by the virtues, is content with few and small things, according to Boethius. Hence it happens that carnal men seek out more supports for life than spiritual men, and spiritual men live more quietly with few goods than carnal men with many goods and riches.

div.head: Cap. CXX. Ex peccato uno capitali plura pariter vitia oriri, unumque vitium aliud crebro comprimere, veluti etiam venenum unius antidotum est alterius, scorpionis, aliorumque animalium venena fundentium, multis perspicuis similitudinibus affirmatur.

cit.quote: Vices are likened to scorpions. For, just as scorpions give birth to one another, so they kill one another: for it is said that the scorpion bears eleven offspring, all of which the mothers kill except one; but that one climbs upon its mother, and kills her, and is the avenger of its brothers' blood. And God did this, lest that pestilent brood grow too great. Now, just as many young are born from one scorpion, so too from one capital vice many daughters, that is, vices, are generated: for from avarice, as Gregory says, arise treachery, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardness against mercy. But that same mother, avarice, sometimes extinguishes these vices which she has brought forth; for the greedy merchant, since he sees that he profits all the more, the more he is held faithful by other men, guards himself most carefully, out of that very greed for profit, from treachery, fraud, deceit, perjury, and violence. He sometimes also shows himself merciful and kind through almsgiving, so as not to be believed a defrauder of others' goods, since he is more generous with his own. Sometimes, too, one of the aforesaid daughters extinguishes their very mother, avarice, namely restlessness of mind, since sometimes a man, wearied by the anxious solicitude and restlessness of temporal things, desires to cast off their burden, and, from the trouble of that restlessness, sometimes flees the world. And something similar to this could be shown in the other capital vices, if one wished to investigate it.

Likewise, the vices we ought to correct in ourselves are signified in those animals that could be sacrificed in the law of Moses: for, of four-footed animals, sacrifice could be offered from three kinds, namely oxen, sheep, and goats, as is clear in Leviticus. Hence a calf, a lamb, and a kid were especially offered. And as it is said in the Gloss on Leviticus 1: we offer a calf, when we conquer the pride of the flesh, a lamb, when we correct irrational impulses, and a kid, when we overcome wantonness. These animals are also referred to Christ, as is said in the same Gloss: for Christ is offered in the calf, on account of the power of the cross; in the lamb, on account of innocence; in the ram, on account of leadership; in the goat, on account of the likeness of the flesh of sin. For these animals were sacrificed in the Law. But note that these animals were offered to God not alive, but slain, so that, through the killing of these animals, the killing of sins should be signified, and that sinful men deserved death, as though these animals were killed in their place, to signify the expiation of sins. Through the killing of these animals too, the killing of Christ was figured.

Likewise, one vice is sometimes a check on another, just as happens with serpents, since sometimes one serpent is a remedy against another: for the fat of the grass-snake (as Pliny says) is effective against the bite of the crocodile. Now the crocodile is, as it were, the gluttonous man: for the crocodile fills itself so full that afterward it lies by the shore, belching from repletion. But the grass-snake, which licks the dust of the earth, signifies the avaricious man, who loves earthly things. Now the grass-snake is effective against the crocodile's bite, since avarice often restrains and checks gluttony: for the overly avaricious man frequently does not eat as much as he desires, according to that saying: 'there is a man to whom God has given riches, and substance, and honor, and nothing is wanting to his soul of all that he desires; yet God does not give him the power to eat of it.'

Likewise, one venom is the medicine for another: for Pliny says that, for one whom a dragon or an asp has wounded, the viper's head applied heals him, and conversely, when a viper stings someone, the flesh of the asp draws the venom to itself, and so helps the one struck. By the dragon, which is the greatest of venomous creatures, and the asp, which is a most pernicious serpent in bite and venom, is understood pride, which is the greatest and most pernicious vice; but by the viper's head is understood lust, since the viper is exceedingly lustful. For the male, putting his mouth into the female's mouth, transfers his seed to her, and she, turned to fury by the pleasure of lust, bites off the male's head. The viper, then, is the medicine for the dragon, or the asp, since sometimes the ruin of lust is the medicine for pride. Hence Gregory says: it often happens that some, falling from pride into lust, blush at the evil of their hidden fault because of the open fall, and then correct greater faults too, since, prostrated in the smallest things, they are confounded. And Augustine says that God casts down the hidden pride of the mind through the open fall of the flesh. But conversely, the asp, too, provides a remedy against the viper, since sometimes pride restrains lust: for while the proud man desires glory, fearing infamy, he shuns lust — but these are rather remedies of outward deed than of inward will.

div.head: Cap. CXXI. Voluptatis partes, que luxuria et gula existunt, voluptuosique defectus, per Amphibene serpentis, limacisque proprietates, atque eorum naturalia exempla quam latissime declarantur.

cit.quote: The pleasure of the flesh is likened to the amphisbaena serpent. For this creature has two heads, one at the front, and one at the tail, and it runs from either head. Hence Isidore says that the 'hydrus' is a serpent of several heads. This creature also, alone among serpents, exposes itself to cold. So too pleasure has two heads, that is, two capital vices, namely lust and gluttony. And in this the given-to-pleasure man seems to care least of all about the cold, that is, the harshness of punishment to come, of which it is said: 'they shall go from the waters of the snows,' and so on. Likewise, the given-to-pleasure man is likened to the snail, which is the worm of the mud, hence it is always filthy and unclean, and is of very slow movement. It also carries a certain shell on its back, within which it encloses itself, and seeks its way with certain horns, since its sight is weak, and if it senses anything in its path, it at once draws in its horns, and shuts itself into its little shell. So too pleasure is the worm of the mud, that is, the corruption of the flesh, or of carnal appetite, and so the given-to-pleasure man is filthy through gluttony, unclean through lust, and slow of movement toward penance; and the shell it carries, within which it shuts itself, is the bad habit it takes up, and does not know how to lay down. This also dulls the sight of the mind, namely toward spiritual things; and again the given-to-pleasure man, with certain horns, that is, certain pursuits, seeks his way toward the delights of the flesh, which pursuits pertain to the prudence of the flesh; hence whatever opposes the flesh, he flees, and draws himself back to his wicked habit.

Likewise, although the snail moves at a slow pace, it nonetheless climbs to the tops of trees, whose leaves it grazes on, and, wherever it crawls, leaves unclean tracks behind it. Likewise, the pleasure of the flesh grows gradually, and climbs to the tops of great trees, since it sometimes takes hold of, and conquers, great men, just as gluttony conquered Adam, and lust David, and Solomon, and lays waste, in them, the leaves, that is, the ornaments of the virtues; but wherever it crawls, it leaves behind it unclean tracks, that is, base and infamous examples.

div.head: Cap. CXXII. Usurarii vita, ipsiusque petunie breuitas, ex pigmei, aspidisque morsus exemplo, rite demonstratur.

cit.quote: Usurers, and others, who are rich from unjust gain, are likened to pygmies, who grow quickly, and fail quickly. For pygmies, who are of the height of a cubit, hence named in Greek from the cubit, dwelling in the mountains of India near the Ocean (as Augustine says), are of full age at three years, bear children at five, and grow old at seven. Just as pygmies, then, come quickly to their brief maturity, and quickly depart, so too the ill-gotten riches of usurers and others grow quickly, and fail quickly: for they quickly become rich, and quickly poor. 'Pride hastily gathered shall be diminished.'

Likewise, as Chrysostom says, usurious money is like the bite of the asp: for one struck by the asp goes, as it were delightedly, into sleep, and dies through the sweetness of that slumber, since the venom then secretly runs through all his limbs. So too he who takes money at interest feels, for a time, as it were a benefit; but the usury runs through all his resources, and consumes the whole.

div.head: Cap. CXXIII. Rhinoceroti, Vacce ruse aque expiationis, nonnullisque animantibus in veteri lege immolandis Dei iussu, Christus perspicuis figuris ac exemplis scite assimilatur.

cit.quote: Christ is likened to the rhinoceros, that is, the unicorn, of which it is said that it has one horn on its forehead, or in the place of its nostrils, with which it pierces everything, and is an untamable and most cruel animal, unless it is tamed and made gentle. But hunters, it is said, who wish to catch this animal, tie some naked virgin to a tree, near which the animal must pass; and, passing by, when it senses the fragrance of the virgin's scent, it is so changed that, all its ferocity laid aside, it lies down in her lap, and licks her breasts, and so, made tame like a lamb, is bound, caught, and held. So too God, who before his coming was most severe, drawn by the fragrance of the Blessed Virgin, of whom the Song of Songs says, 'while the king,' and so on — of the Virgin, I say, stripped of earthly delights, and bound by the vow of perpetual chastity — descending into the lap of her womb, was made so human, and so gentle, that he could be held, bound, and killed. Job: 'shall the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?'

The red heifer, from which the water of purification was made in the law of Moses: for the uncleanness of those who had touched any unclean animal was purged by the sprinkling of a certain water; for the Lord commanded that they take a red heifer, and kill it, and burn it outside the camp, and the priest dipped his finger in its blood, and sprinkled it seven times before the door of the sanctuary; that heifer was burned with fire, together with its hide, and its flesh, its blood and its dung given to the flame. To the burning, too, were added cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet thread twice dyed. The ash of the burning was gathered, entire, and put into water for purification. But the one who burned it, and the one who gathered the ashes, and the one who sprinkled the water in which the ash was placed, were reckoned unclean; yet they were purified from this uncleanness by the washing of their garments alone, and did not need to be sprinkled with the water. By this red heifer, Christ was figured, according to the weakness he assumed, which the female sex designates; but the color of the heifer designated the blood of his same passion. That heifer, moreover, had to be of unblemished age, since every work of Christ is perfect, in which too there was no blemish, nor had it borne a yoke: since Christ bore no yoke of sin. It was commanded to be led to Moses, since the transgression of the law of Moses, in the violation of the sabbath, was imputed to Christ. It was also commanded to be handed over to Eleazar the priest, since Christ, who was to be killed, was handed over into the hands of the priests. It was sacrificed outside the camp, since Christ suffered outside the gate. The priests dipped their finger in its blood, since the ministry of Christ's passion must be considered and imitated with the discretion that the finger signifies. It was sprinkled toward the tabernacle, by which the synagogue is signified, namely for the condemnation of the unbelieving Jews. And this seven times, either because of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, or because of the seven days by which the whole of time is understood. Now everything that pertains to Christ's incarnation is to be burned with fire, that is, understood spiritually: for by the hide and flesh, Christ's outward action is designated; by his blood, the subtle and inward power that gives life to outward things; by the dung, the weariness of thirst, and everything of this kind pertaining to weakness. Three things, moreover, were added: namely cedar, which signifies the height of hope, or contemplation; hyssop, which signifies humility, or faith; scarlet twice dyed, which signifies twofold charity. Through these we ought to cling to the suffering Christ. The ash was gathered by an unclean man, since the remains of the passion reached the Gentiles, who were guilty of Christ's death. It was placed in water for purification, since, from Christ's passion, baptism obtains the power to remedy sins. The priest who sacrificed, and burned, and gathered the ashes, and sprinkled, was unclean, since the Jews were made unclean by the killing of Christ, by whom our sins are expiated. And this until evening, that is, until the end of the world, when the remnant of Israel shall be converted. Or since those who handle sacred things, intending the correction of others, themselves contract certain uncleannesses in return, as Gregory says. And this until evening, that is, until the end of the present life.

Likewise, Christ was figured in those animals that were sacrificed for the sins of the priests in the law of Moses. For first the priest offered a calf for himself, and a ram for sin, as a holocaust. Then he offered, for the people, two goats, of which one was sacrificed to expiate the sin of the multitude, and the blood of this sacrificed goat was brought, together with the blood of the calf, into the holy of holies, and the whole sanctuary was sprinkled with it. But the bodies of the goats and the calf that had been sacrificed for sin were burned outside the camp: this happened when a sacrifice was offered for some grave sin, or for the multitude's sins. The other goat, however, was sent out into the desert. The priest laid his hand upon its head, confessing the sins of the children of Israel, as though that goat carried them into the desert to be eaten by wild beasts, as though bearing the punishment for the people's sins; or a certain scroll, on which the sins were written, was bound upon its head. Christ, then, is signified by the calf, on account of the power of the cross, and by the ram, since he is the leader of the faithful, and by the goat, on account of the likeness of the flesh of sin. And Christ himself was sacrificed for the sins of the priests and the people, since, through his passion, both the greater and the lesser are purged of sin. The blood of the calf and the goat is brought into the holy of holies by the priest, since, through Christ's blood, entrance to the kingdom of heaven lies open to us. They were burned outside the camp, since Christ suffered outside the gate. By the goat that was sent away was signified the divinity of Christ, which withdrew into solitude while the humanity of Christ suffered — not indeed changing place, but restraining its power; or it signifies the evil desire that we ought to cast away from ourselves, while offering virtuous impulses to the Lord.

div.head: Cap. CXXIIII. Coniugis zelotipiam semper fore a viris fugiendam, unica Onagri similitudine sacreque scriptura aucteritate ostenditur.

cit.quote:
A husband's carnal jealousy toward his wife drives him to rush into unstable suspicions and cruel deeds. Hence such men are like wild asses, whose males, led by jealousy, cut off the testicles of the females' male offspring, since they hold them suspect, even those born of their own mates; hence the mothers, knowing this, hide them, as Pliny says. So too many, out of jealousy, hold even their close relations suspect regarding their wives, from which suspicion wounds, and other cruel deeds, sometimes follow. Ecclesiasticus: 'do not be jealous over the wife of your bosom' — for between spouses there ought to be, not the jealousy of suspicion, but a devoted love, of which the Apostle says: 'husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the Church' — whom he betrothed, in the present life, through faith, and leads to the wedding-feast of eternal glory, where, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he lives and reigns, world without end.
HERE ENDS THE FIFTH BOOK.
